Assuming you are referring to the topic about retrieving analog values from the expansion module: Without knowing the physical measuring range of your sensor connected to AI1, it's not possible to interpret the displayed values definitively. Therefore, in your case, the AI1 value of 202 suggests the sensor’s measured value is near the minimum. You should scale the analog input to match the physical measurement range of your sensor using an analog amplifier.

Hello everyone, I've been using the new webserver on the latest [product_name] recently. It works perfectly on my home network, but I'm unsure how to monitor the [product_name] from the internet. Any advice?

To enable remote access to your [product_name], you first need to open the correct port on your firewall or router so incoming internet connections can reach your internal network. By default, routers and firewalls block these connections. If you are on a corporate network, your IT team should handle this. The following steps assume a home network setup: Web browsers usually use port 80, but you can configure your firewall or router to map any external port to the internal port that your [product_name] is set up to receive requests from. For multiple [product_name] devices, assign unique port numbers so the router can direct the requests correctly. In practice, connect using the router's IP address, not the [product_name]'s internal IP. The documentation claims port 8080 is the one [product_name] listens on, but in my experience, opening port 80 internally was required. Not sure why [company_name] specifies 8080; perhaps someone else can explain. You'll either need a fixed IP from your ISP, or use a dynamic DNS (DDNS) service because your router's external IP can change. DDNS gives you a constant domain name, like [url], which you use to access the network. Set fixed IP addresses for each [product_name] device so your router forwards requests properly. After these steps, remote monitoring should work; I'm able to monitor mine over the internet at remote locations. In some cases, I have connected devices wirelessly when Ethernet cabling is not practical. If you're not on a home network, your IT department is the appropriate contact for these changes. Hope this is useful.

Is it possible to use the same pushbutton (by pressing it again) to reset the contactor? I assume this would involve a latching relay or a similar mechanism, but I want to avoid issues in case the pushbutton is accidentally held down, causing the contactor to repeatedly turn on and off. Normally, a pulse logic relay needs two signals at its input to change state (on-off). Even a latch relay requires a reset input to return to the on state. I learned a few things about connecting to a controller via Ethernet: 1. Connect the controller directly to your PC's Ethernet port with a cable. 2. Disable other Ethernet connections like USB adapters and Wi-Fi, keeping only the one you use for the controller. 3. Assign a fixed IP address to the PC’s Ethernet port for initial setup. Run [product_name] programming software as Admin. If these steps are successful, you can then integrate the controller into your network to help pinpoint issues.

From my experience, the most reliable connection is to use an Ethernet cable to directly link your PC and the [product_name]. Avoid using networks with Wi-Fi or gateways, as unknown device IP addresses can cause conflicts. For example: 1. Device fresh from box. 2. Connected to a Wi-Fi router via Ethernet with default settings. 3. PC or laptop uses DHCP on Wi-Fi. Typically, issues arise because both the device and many routers default to IP 192.168.0.1. If you ping the device, the router may respond instead, making you think you’re connecting to the device when it’s actually the router. In this situation, the programming software cannot find the device. Also, always run the configuration software as Admin; Windows security may block it from adjusting network settings otherwise. Is there a way to overcome the issue where the Modbus address range for [company_name] [product_name] is VW 0-850, which corresponds to holding registers 1-425, while the key registers for ATV630 control are 8501 (command) and 8502 (frequency reference)? Is there a possible workaround, or is it not achievable? Kind regards, [user_name]

Hi, There might be some confusion here. In [product_name], VM memory is used for data exchange with other devices. Do you really need all of your device's registers in [product_name]? Typically, only a few registers are required, which you configure alongside the target VM memory in the Modbus data table. For example, you can transfer the value from a Modbus register (4024) to a designated VM memory address (VW10) in [product_name]. You only need to transfer necessary data. Note that [product_name] has only 850 bytes of memory available for this. Hope this helps.

Hello and thank you for your response. You're right, I don't need every register from my device in [product_name]. My focus is solely on registers 8501 (command) and 8502 (frequency reference). However, the attached image shows that the Modbus address space in [product_name] covers mapped addresses from 1 to 425 for address type VW, whereas I need only registers 8501 and 8502.

You're approaching this from the wrong perspective. If [product_name] acts as the server and, say, a Modbus PLC is the client, that PLC may not recognize operands like V, VB, VW, or VD from [product_name], making it unable to address the VM memory area directly. That's why VW0 matches HR1 from the Modbus PLC's viewpoint: VW2 = HR2, VW4 = HR3, and so forth. In your situation, the VFD should function as the server and [product_name] as the client. Accordingly, HR8501 from the VFD should be mapped to VW0 and HR8502 to VW2. Remember, [product_name] uses an offset of +1 for Modbus addresses.

Understood. However, I've configured things as shown in my attached image (similar to your suggestion), but the communication between [product_name] and the Altivar isn't working. According to the Altivar's communication map, data exchanges occur, but neither the command nor frequency reference registers have values. Also, with the offset +1 in [product_name] Modbus addresses, does that mean I should use 8502 for the 8501 register and 8503 for 8502? Am I misunderstanding?

I can't say for sure since I'm not sure whether the Altivar uses an offset of +0 or +1. If the Altivar offset is +0, then you're correct (HR8502 and HR8503). If it's +1, then use HR8501 and HR8502.

I'm also uncertain if using Unit-ID 255 is correct.

Found a solution! Two important points: 1) The unit ID should be set to 248 instead of the default 255. 2) An offset of +1 is required; for the 8501 command register, you must input 8502 in the Ethernet setup window. Everything works fine now.

VW0 includes bytes VB0 and VB1, while VW1 includes bytes VB1 and VB2—both registers use VB1, so they affect one another and produce different values. Also, you don't need a HIGH block for the message text—negating the input connector is enough to enable it. Now to your questions: If your engine is air-cooled, you may not need a PT100 sensor unless you plan to display temperature data. You could consider thermostats that fit into the cylinder head and provide a NO/NC contact, which can then be connected to [product_name] (similar to those used in small transformers or welding equipment). You can find such products online, e.g. [url]. For measuring battery voltage, you'll need a converter from 12 or 24 V DC to 0–10 V, such as those described at [url] (refer to 'interface technology', page 1–37). There are other solutions too, like battery chargers with auxiliary contacts: [url]. The AM PT100 module is typically around 100 Euros, but using a PT100 to 0–10 V converter is less expensive if you have an analog input available. Best of luck.

I have a question about configuring the external text display module. I'm setting up a system to show gas line pressure using an external display. In the message text block editor, I see two screens—green for the main module and blue for the text display. I place analog blocks in the blue section and leave the green empty. When I select the message destination for the text display, during program simulation, only the green screen appears (empty, since nothing’s set) and the blue section is missing. I checked the file and message text settings but couldn't find any options for the external text display. What am I missing?

This should help! When setting up the text display, the green and blue screens in the editor don't represent separate physical displays—they're just part of the same configuration. Both the onboard LCD and the external display can show messages up to 32 characters. In the message text properties (under FILE), you can select various character sets for different languages. For example, choose the Chinese character set to get 16 characters per line, versus the default 12. Adjust the ticker speed to 200ms as well. Make sure to enable your chosen character set at the top of the message text function block. Keep in mind that special characters (like degrees or umlauts) take up 2 spaces. For extra long messages, type up to 32 characters, spanning both green and blue sections. There are two ways to display long messages: set the ticker to 'line by line' or 'character by character' and tick the corresponding line number. To show the message on the LCD, set the destination to display, or pick the external text display, or both. When you activate the function block, the long message will be shown on either display, toggling or scrolling according to your settings. You can create multiple messages by enabling a second character set, which can be switched with a flag. All of this is using just one out of many message texts, so there's plenty of flexibility. Try experimenting with these features!

I tested your instructions and confirmed they work. I had assumed the blue screen was only for the external display, but it makes sense now. Thanks for clarifying!

A new question about adding special characters for larger text messages was split into a separate thread. Best regards, [user_name]

A quick question: How do I activate S7 protocol on my [company_name] PLC with [version_no]?

To enable access, navigate to tools menu, then Ethernet connections, and add an S7 server connection. This will allow you to access all inputs, outputs, and flags—refer to Snap7 documentation for operand details. For accessing internal analog signals from arithmetic, timers, or counters, map your required value in the VM mapping. You may also refer to operating instructions and online help. If your device is acting as the server, Snap7 should be used as the client. Regards, [user_name].

All devices with order number [article_no] and firmware version [version_no], as well as those with order number [article_no] and firmware version [version_no], support Modbus. However, devices with order number [article_no] and firmware version [version_no] do not support Modbus.

Yes, you can use Modbus TCP if you have a compatible Modbus client or server on your Raspberry Pi. If you programmed it as [product_name], Modbus TCP is available. If you used [product_name] Standard, you need to use the S7 protocol. If both protocols are available, [company_name] recommends using S7 protocol. Regards, [user_name].

Depending on the first address of your client for coils or registers, choose 0 or 1 in the provided excel sheet to set the starting address appropriately. Regards, [user_name].

Multiple major Linux distributions are supported as well. The same goes for the hours counter—even though you get a warning, there isn't an option to retain it, which seems like the most logical choice. Ideally, there should be a prompt during download asking whether to keep retentive values and block parameters. Currently, [product_name] Soft Comfort treats these volatile values as part of the nonvolatile project code. If separating them due to historic design or compatibility issues is difficult, perhaps Soft Comfort could simply read out these values before download and restore them afterwards—this would avoid a major redesign. One more inconvenience: you can’t do online simulation or monitoring if parameters are changed, as the project is flagged as "different". It would be more user-friendly if the current values could just be read and presented during simulation.

No, everything—including parameter values—is always transferred together as one package. If you want [company_name] to consider your change requests, you should open a Support Request so they are officially recorded and reviewed.

Thank you for your reply. I have submitted a request, although it seemed the form was aimed mainly at technical support rather than feature suggestions. It appears [company_name] may not prioritize feedback about new features. I doubt I’m the only person who has requested this kind of functionality. It seems [product_name] was designed for one-off programming, where updating projects and retaining previous values isn’t really expected. I’ll share any updates from support here.

With [product_name], only the full user program—including all data—can be downloaded. As a result, all data is lost after a program transfer. There is no option to transfer only selected elements. You can define a retentive feature during programming; if you simply stop, run, or reboot the controller, this data remains intact.

Hello, function block parameters are part of the overall program, so modifying them counts as a program change. The only way to capture the current parameters is by uploading the program from the controller and then editing the logic. Retentivity saves changes in situations like a power failure, but it is not intended for parameter protection. A suggested workaround is: if parameters change, first upload the program, then edit as needed before downloading.

This workflow becomes inefficient when you have a 'master' project duplicated across multiple controllers, as it forces you to maintain separate copies and update each individually—which is time-consuming. Plus, the hour counter is still reset with each download. While retentivity was designed to avoid data loss during power cycles, using RS retentivity for on/off settings is common because there aren't many better ways to store digital values. Regardless, these values do not survive a project download with the current [product_name] implementation, which is a significant limitation.

Which controller does not behave this way? Even for devices like an S7, if each CPU has unique parameter values, you must maintain a separate copy of the project for each one.

Regarding question 1: Any block or constant with an output port must be terminated, whether it's digital or analog, except for flags and output blocks. Digital connections can be terminated by linking the output connector to another digital block or constant, flag, output block, or an open terminal. Analog outputs connect similarly—either to another analog block, flag, or output block. For question 2: VB is a byte (8 bits) in the VM area, with VB0 containing bits V0.0 to V0.7. IB is a byte (8 bits) from the input range; IB0 covers I1 to I8. For question 3: The local address is the device being set up; the remote address is the device it's connecting to. For question 4: The VM area is a data memory section used for communication with other devices. For example, setting a bit in the VM area (like V0.0) with a button in the app lets you use that address as a network address in your [product_name] program. For question 5: I'm unclear on the question.

I'm still slightly confused, but things are clearer. For example: 1. If I link I1 to X4, how is it reflected in the VM area? Is it V0.1 or V0.4, and why? 2. Is VM a shared memory for all bits coming from X (open connector)? 3. By 'open terminal' do you mean 'open connector'? 4. Is it only when connecting a digital input to an X connector that the bit can be mapped to VM? 5. Does VB refer to a byte from digital inputs and VW from analog? Are these stored as V0.0 in VM? 6. If sending one digital input bit as VB1.0, does it become V1.0 in VM? 7. What happens in VM if I send a signal from I3 to X1? 8. VB is a byte in VM, usable for both digital and analog data. Typically, VW (a 16-bit word) transfers numerical values, but it can also send digital info. I did not claim IB0 or VB0 contain I1 to I7; there is only IB0, IB1, and IB2: IB0 = I1 to I8, IB1 = I9 to I16, IB2 = I17 to I24.

No, such a version does not exist for [product_name]. All relay variants only have one contact (normally open). Switching is possible only with relays that include a changeover contact, which provides both NC (normally closed) and NO (normally open) contacts.

For your scenario, you'll need to create a power circuit using contactors and similar hardware. It’s necessary to design your circuit with the awareness that your [product_name] only has NO outputs. I typically use external relays connected to [product_name] outputs, since external relays are more cost-effective to replace than the controller itself. The final result depends on the types of switching equipment, lighting, cabling, and other factors. In large facilities, switching is often sequenced using multiple contactors to distribute peak current and avoid overloads. Phase balancing is also taken into account by design. I am working on a home lighting control system—no motors involved, just lights as outputs. I do not need analog inputs but will use analog outputs to operate 0-10V dimmers. Or, for higher reliability, two 2.5A units can be connected in parallel.

You should calculate it as follows: the 20-75mA figures refer to dissipation current—20mA is when no inputs/outputs are active and 75mA is with all I/O active, excluding external loads. To be safe, use max current values: 75mA for each controller, 75mA for each digital expansion, and 50mA for each analog module. For three controllers with extensions: 75x3 + 75x6 + 50x3 = 825mA. Add the load current to this sum. The 2.5A [product_name] power supply should be sufficient for all components, as the auxiliary relays and signal lamps do not require much current. The 1.3A version may be inadequate. Please check these calculations yourself.

Hello, How does [product_name] execute its program? How can we determine the sequence in which instruction blocks are processed?

[product_name] starts with Block 001, then Block 002, and continues in order. Can you share why you are interested in this? Personally, I just need a reliably functioning [product_name].

No specific reason—I'm simply curious. The block numbers seem to get rearranged when you modify sections of the program, but apparently this doesn't impact execution.

There isn't an official description of how [product_name] handles block execution, but based on my observations and tests, here are some patterns: 1. Blocks are reviewed from lowest to highest repeatedly until all complete. 2. A block won't run if its input-linked blocks haven't yet run, and each block only executes once per cycle. 3. Parameters update instantly when a block executes, but this doesn't change execution order. When you use parameters, you might notice things don't execute in your expected sequence.

[product_name] operates similarly to larger PLCs. Step 1: Copies input states to the input register. Step 2: Runs the program using the input register values. Changes in input status during the cycle won't affect the program until the next cycle. While running the program, changing parameters update immediately (for instance, counter states, outputs, etc.). The program executes blocks from 001 onwards, but this isn’t documented and might not always be true. Step 3: Copies output statuses to the outputs. Step 4: Restarts from step 1. So, a change in physical input (or output) during the cycle only impacts the program in the following cycle. This explains the programming warning: 'Recursions of Input of xxxblock can only connect to output by a Marker or Output.'

[user_name], we seem to agree. When I mention block input from another block, I mean a link from one block’s output to another block’s input connection—not an input from the register. My rules fit well with your step 2. Here's an example using three blocks (numbered accordingly): - Block 001: Mathematical Instruction, V1 = 5 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Otherwise, it won’t function correctly. - Block 002: AND(EDGE) (Simulates one program cycle) - Block 003: Mathematical Instruction, V2 = 10 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Connections: - Input I1 links to Block 002's first input - EN input of Block 001 connects to Block 002's output - EN input of Block 003 connects to Block 002's output - Block 003's P1 parameter links to Block 001's Aq parameter - Block 001 output goes to AM1 - Block 003 output goes to AM2 Testing: 1. Reset all blocks to zero in the simulator. 2. Turn Input 1 on/off. AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 10. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 10. Execution explanation: - Block 001 is reviewed first but waits as 002 hasn't executed. - Block 002 executes (linked only to input registers); its output goes HIGH. - Block 003 executes since 002 already did; Aq on Block 001 is still zero, so Block 003 adds 0 + 10 for 10. - Now, all blocks are executed, the cycle ends. Test another setup: - Create Block 004 (AND(EDGE)), remove Block 002 - Link I1 to Block 004's input - EN of Blocks 001 and 003 connect to Block 004's output Run the same test: AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 15. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 15. Blocks 002 and 003 were skipped initially (since 004 hadn't executed). Block 004 ran after 003 was checked. On the second round, 002 and 003 executed because 004 was already done. This logic lets you predict block behavior. [product_name] might use a more advanced system internally, but this matches observable behavior.

Just to clarify: Mathematical Instruction Blocks need the setting 'OUTPUT When En="0", output is: Last Value.' Otherwise, the earlier example won't work. I've updated my previous post with these instructions. Apologies if you tried it and encountered issues.

Hello [user_name], I am aware that using an additional module allows for 0...20mA inputs, but I still can't explain why the 0...10V input can't handle a 4...20mA sensor with a 250-ohm resistor. Does anyone have more information?

First, make sure your [product_name] is powered by DC (12V or 24V). Second, use a 500-ohm resistor: 20mA x 500 ohm equals 10V, so 0-20mA x 500 ohm gives 0-10V, and 4-20mA x 500 ohm gives 2-10V. Third, connect the positive DC supply to your sensor, sensor output to both the resistor and the [product_name] analog input (I7 or I8), then connect the other side of the resistor to the negative DC supply. For programming, assign I7 as Ai1 or I8 as Ai2.

For the [product_name] Basis, only certain [article_no] versions are supported. For [product_name] Pure, there are other specific [article_no] versions. With the newer version ([article_no]), additional input options like I1 can be used as Ai3, and I2 as Ai4.

Hello everyone in this discussion. Here are some possible reasons: 1) If the sensor has 4 wires, 2 are for power and the other 2 are for the 0/4..20mA output. You should connect a 500-ohm resistor across these 2 output wires, with the negative lead going to the [product_name] common and the positive to the analog input (I7, I8 for some [version_no] modules, and possibly I1 & I2 for newer ones). 2) If it's a 2-wire sensor, it must be loop-powered—connect the 24V DC supply to the positive lead, the negative lead to the [product_name] analog input, and put the resistor between the common and negative signal line. 3) Many sensors don't work well with more than 250 ohm resistance in the loop. In that case, use a 250-ohm resistor and adjust scaling in the [product_name] program. 4) It's better to use precision resistors with low tolerance rather than standard ones because inaccurate resistance values can affect scaling and signal stability, especially due to temperature changes. I hope this clarifies things for everyone.

Hello! Is it acceptable to apply voltage directly to outputs in order to force certain devices to start? For example, if you install a manual switch in the control cabinet to turn on a machine independently from the controller’s permission, connecting the switch in parallel with the transistor output and then to the load. Alternatively, you can use the [product_name] system as intended: Send the 24V signal to a 24V input on the [product_name], and then configure the user program to set or reset the appropriate output.

However, this approach requires: - an available input, and - modifying the program.

Additionally, if the controller is non-functional as described by [user_name], another reliable solution involves using decoupling diodes, or if you have access to a changeover contact (1 normally open + 1 normally closed), wiring the break contact to the output, the make contact to +24V, and the common contact to the load. Regards, [user_name]

For most integrated circuits, it's common practice to connect unused inputs to either a high or low state to prevent unexpected behavior. You're correct; instruction blocks in [product_name] don't function like discrete electronic ICs, and unconnected pins are internally managed to be at an appropriate logic level. While I don't have specific documentation, I rely on many years working with [product_name]. Pay attention to 'retentive' memory settings, as blocks will retain their state but may behave differently after power interruptions. Also, consider how some memory markers (like M8) initialize regardless of previous state. May I ask what prompted your question?

Hello everyone, I'm having trouble with [product_name] and [product_name]. I'm confused why the marker AM15 and the output for B004 is 34, which is correct, but the output for NAQ1 (memory VW4) is only 3. Thank you for your help!

Your problem is related to overlapping in the VM memory area. VW4 contains VB4 and VB5. VW5 contains VB5 and VB6. To avoid overlap, use NAQ2 with VW6.

Can you elaborate more on this overlapping issue? Thanks!

VM memory addressing is organized by bytes. The smallest unit is a bit; 8 bits make up a byte. Two consecutive bytes (16 bits) make a word, and two consecutive words (4 bytes or 32 bits) form a double word. For example, V0.0 refers to bit 0 in byte 0. VB0 contains bits V0.0 to V0.7. VW0 includes VB0 and VB1 (bits V0.0 to V1.7), and VD0 includes VW0 and VW2 (VB0 to VB3 or V0.0 to V3.7). In bit addresses, the number before the dot is the byte address; the number after is the bit within that byte. For word and double word addresses, the number indicates where the sequence starts. To prevent overlap when working with words, always use even addresses (VW0, VW2, VW4, etc.), and for double words, use multiples of four (VW0, VW4, VW8, etc.).

The Unit ID corresponds to the address of a modbus slave device. Standard analog network inputs cannot be used to read 32-bit values, as those can only access integer values in the range -32,768 to 32,767. Can you clarify the register value formats? U32 means Unsigned Double Integer, S32 is Signed Double Integer. Your screenshot shows register 30772 with a value of 32,216, probably representing voltage as 322.16 V. In your program, use analog network input to read address VW2 rather than VW0. Add an analog amplifier after this input and select two decimal places for display.

Based on further testing, the register used for the actual value shifts depending on the reading format—it's either register 30771 or 30772. In binary, only the lower 16 bits (LSB) are utilized and the upper bits (MSB) are all 0. More advanced 'bit-sorting' options offer various representations. Apparently, the controller only supports Signed or Unsigned. If you select "Big-endian" format, the value appears in register 30771. However, I’m not sure which formats are supported by the controller.

[user_name], thanks! I will test that. Yes, it's DC voltage with two decimals.

Do you have a link to the manual or could you upload it?

Attached is the [company_name] Modbus manual. I configured the NI to read VW2. A few notes: The 16-bit range of +/-32767 (signed16) suggests that only up to 327.67 Volts can be read. Is it possible to use U16 for a 0-65535 range, allowing readings up to 655.35 Volts? I still get no data, even when trying to read from register 30777 which reports values always below 1,000 (Watts per phase), so no risk of exceeding the signed 16-bit value. Still, no data is returned. Is there any alternative method to check if variable memory is actually receiving data? It’s possible the Modbus connection isn’t bringing in data, and the challenge may be with the function blocks.

The analog values are known as S16 values.

You should be reading register 30778, not 30777.

No, the controller operates according to its programming. 32-bit registers consist of two 16-bit words. To read a double register using Modbus software, you must address the starting point of the double register—in this case, 30777. If you begin at 30778, you get one word from 30777 (the right word) and one word from 30779 (the left word).

If Modbus registers include floating point numbers, integrating them into the controller is easy with the F/I Converter, including scaling factors like 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, and 1000. If you only have UINT32 (unsigned 32-bit integer), use the provided converter. Note that if values exceed 32767, you will lose the last 1–3 digits depending on your maximum values. Creating a converter for SINT32 (signed 32-bit integer) may be possible, though usually not necessary.

Hello, I have a question about measuring current with the [product_name] AM2 module. My battery operates at 48V, typically ranging from 39V when discharged to 56V when fully charged. I plan to measure voltage indirectly using a resistor that limits current between 4-20mA. For instance, with a 3k Ohm resistor, 18mA flows at 56V, and 13mA at 39V. Is it unsafe to apply 56V directly to the AM2 module terminals?

Honestly, I don't think your approach is recommended. Using such high voltages, even with a resistor, isn't safe for the AM2 module. You likely need an amplifier or another device to bring the voltage down to a safer level. Just my opinion—maybe someone with more experience can weigh in.

Could you provide a drawing of your circuit and indicate where the load or charger connects? Also, consider searching online for '48V battery voltage indicator circuit' for reference.

It might be a better solution to measure the voltage directly using a divider. With just two resistors, you can easily stay within the 0–10V input range.

I've attached a drawing showing my setup, but this example uses 24V from the power supply instead of battery voltage.

Using just a resistor on a current loop input for the AM2 module is not advisable. Instead, use two resistors to lower the voltage (maximum 10V), then measure with the 0–10V input on the AM2 module. For example, connect a 5.6k Ohm and a 1k Ohm resistor in series and measure across the 1k resistor; you'll get roughly one-sixth of the input voltage—56V would result in about 8.5V at the input. If you have the correct [product_name] base module (the full DC variant), you might be able to use its analog inputs directly and skip the AM2 module.

You could consider a current transformer that's available in suitable ratios, then use a resistor for finer adjustment. Connect the output to an interface board that converts current to voltage. These boards are inexpensive online and allow you to tweak zero and span, so you could connect the analog input on the [product_name] base module without needing the AM2 module.

Are current transformer modules available for DC measurements?

Yes, DC current sensing modules are available. Some output 5V, and there may be 10V models too—contact the seller for confirmation. See example products on [url].

Here's another example of a DC current transducer module: [url]

Why convert voltage to current, then back using a current transducer, and let the [product_name] input module convert it again using its internal resistor? Just use two resistors as described, and connect directly to the analog input on the base module.

I agree—using only resistors is best, with 5.6k and 1k values recommended. At 56V, you'll reach about 10.1V, but if your charger supports equalizing it could go up to 60V. Keep it simple; with 1W resistors the current remains safe around 7mA.

Choose resistor values as needed, but remember the analog input's internal resistance introduces a load resistor in your voltage divider design. You can adjust scaling in the [product_name] to account for resistor tolerances and the internal resistance.

In a two-resistor setup, be sure to connect the battery's negative terminal to the correct point on the [product_name] power supply. Resistor calculations should also factor in tolerance and the internal resistance of the module. Calibration within the [product_name] software can help refine your measurement.

I've updated my original drawing to correct a small error regarding potential. The [product_name] pin M must connect to potential M—otherwise, the common ground has no purpose.

I prefer current measurement because it protects against overvoltage. If a resistor is bypassed by accident, it could put 24V straight onto the 0-10V ADC input.

Analog inputs on the base module can also serve as digital inputs with DC24V (max DC28.8V), so up to this voltage there’s no risk. Alternatively, you can use a Zener diode parallel to the resistor to limit voltage, for example, to DC12V.

Hello, this indicates that your PC cannot detect the [product_name]. For example, if your PC has an IP address of 192.168.0.10 and a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0, it can communicate with devices in the 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.0.255 range. To resolve this: (1) Change the IP address of your PC or the [product_name], or (2) respond "YES" to the message. This may allow your PC's network adapter to acquire a secondary IP address matching the range of the [product_name]. [user_name]

What is the purpose of the FE (functional earth) terminal? I notice many [product_name] modules work fine without it, but it must have some function.

These clamps are meant for connecting the shielding of shielded cables, but one of these terminals should be attached to the PE. However, this should not be confused with a potential equalization terminal.

If I have only one [product_name] module, does that mean there's just a single FE terminal and I simply wire it to ground? From what I understand, it's standard to connect the shield of a shielded cable to PE, so what is the specific purpose of FE?

The idea is to keep the signal-carrying wire and its shield together for as long as possible before connection. If you separate them a meter before the connection point, the wire is exposed for that distance, which increases its susceptibility to interference.

I agree with your approach: carry the signal right to its endpoint and then connect it (say, after 60 meters) to PE instead of FE. Is there a difference between connecting to PE versus FE? There must be, but it's not clear to me.

The FE terminal on the [product_name] PLC module is primarily used for the network connection side. Under normal circumstances, the [product_name] PLC doesn't require it. It's generally intended for cases when non-shielded cables are used or the RJ45 connector lacks a shield. As [user_name] mentioned, the network relies on ground as a reference. I've also seen many installations without the FE terminal, using basic cables, which sometimes resulted in communication glitches. Adding a ground wire to the FE terminal resolved these issues. In my home setup, seven [product_name] PLC modules are on the same network as computers and other devices. I haven't yet connected the FE terminal to ground and have had no issues, but I use high-quality Cat6 cables with all shields grounded at the switches, except for short patch cables which are unshielded.

Thank you both for your explanations.

The values stay as long as they remain unchanged from the initial program. If modified from the [product_name] web editor, those changes seem fine. However, after a power outage and restoring power, the original values from the factory program are reestablished, not the latest values set via the web editor. For example, if a timer is set to 10 seconds in [product_name] software and later changed to 20 seconds using the web editor, everything works until a power loss occurs; once powered again, the timer reverts to 10 seconds. Is there a way to retain the last modified values even after losing power? Can the [product_name] be set to keep these settings after a power cut? Thank you for your assistance.

Which operands in the [product_name] store the values set by the web editor? Are these saved in analog inputs? If possible, please upload the web editor project and the [product_name] program zipped together. If privacy is a concern, you can send me the zip file via private message.

I've included an example for reference. Thank you.

Check the attachment. Instead of writing web editor values to the timer via standard parameter mapping, store them in the parameter V1 of a math instruction. This way, the value is saved in flash (voltage-fail-safe) memory. Pass the result of the math instruction to the timer by reference. Be sure to select the correct timebase and use the appropriate data format in the web editor—for simple timers, select unsigned instead of HEX.

Thank you for sharing this information. I will test it and update you with my results.

Flash memory retention seems to work after a power cut followed by reboot. However, there’s another issue: when updating a value on the web, and triggering a start from entry V0.0, the system adds 256 to my set value. I've attached screenshots and strategy files for reference. Thank you.

There’s only a single VM memory, byte-addressed. User addressable range is V0.0 to V850.7, a total of 6808 bits or 851 bytes. VM memory bytes are VB0 to VB850. For instance, Word 0 in VM memory (VW0) contains 2 bytes: VB0 and VB1, with VB0 holding bits V0.0 to V0.7 and VB1 holding V1.0 to V1.7. If you’re using VW0 for a timer, you can’t use V0.0 to V1.7 for other functions such as starting the timer.

Hello everyone, I created a project where I connected an encoder to the I4 input to measure speed in meters per minute. I set the target value with AI1 (I7), which determines the distance for each meter. I compare this target with the actual speed, and use two digital outputs to control a valve to adjust a turbine motor, ensuring it reaches the desired speed per meter. The encoder roller radius is 40 mm, and it generates 2000 pulses per revolution. I uploaded the program and would appreciate feedback or discussion, as I suspect there might be a calculation mistake or other issue I’m missing. Thank you for your assistance.

Hello [user_name], here’s a link with examples for [product_name] that could be helpful for your project: [url]

I’m concerned about how to calculate speed in meters per minute, as I’m a bit confused. Since [product_name] only works with integer values, maybe there’s a mistake in this area.

If anyone with more experience could check my calculations, I’d like to know if they’re correct in my program.

What’s the maximum value you need for meters per minute? For instance, if 32,767 m/min is sufficient, it’s best to calculate directly in mm/min and use three decimal places for accuracy. Regards, [user_name]

Hello, the speed is much lower than 32,768—maximum is around 10 m/min. So, is my speed calculation correct?

Your calculation seems fine, but 2 * Pi * 40 / 2000 * 1000 is about 125.66. To improve accuracy, you can change your formula: instead of multiplying by 60, multiply by 6; instead of dividing by 1000, divide by 10,000. Then, multiply by 12,566. So: mm/min = frequency * 6 * 12,566 / 10,000. Alternatively, adjust the gate time setting of the digital threshold trigger. One rotation equals 2 * Pi * 40 = 251.33 mm, or 2000 pulses, so each pulse is 0.1257 mm. For 10,000 mm/min, that’s 79,577 pulses/min, or about 1.33 pulses/s. For 1000 pulses, the cycle time is roughly 0.75s. If you set the gate time to 0.75s, calculations complete in one step. You just need arithmetic for decimal places, as the threshold trigger doesn’t allow decimal place settings. Your current method is valid, but this is another option. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks a lot for your suggestion about the alternative approach. I have another question: In B002 (the counter for actual distance), once it reaches 32,768 pulses, B007 can’t calculate further. If the total distance is 350 meters, how can I calculate and show this on the [product_name] display? Best regards, [user_name]

Split your counting into two stages: one counter for mm and a second for meters. For every 1000 mm, you get about 7,958 pulses. When the first counter hits 7,958, reset it and increment the meter counter by one. Display them as: mm = first counter * 1000 / 7958 and m = second counter directly. If cascading the counters is tricky or you need more details, feel free to ask. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks again. I got it working with two counters—one for mm and another for meters. Best regards, [user_name]

The results in the attached test file are accurate. The issue occurs when trying to retrieve 'delivered power' at address 14 and 'returned power' at address 15 (refer to the document from my first post). Because values are provided in kW, [product_name] returns zero for anything less than 1 kW.

Your first screenshot shows voltage transmitted as an unsigned integer (U32). If VD0 is set to unsigned in the data table, a value like 233200 displays, which corresponds to a voltage of 233.200 V with three decimal places.

Using a file I found in a previous discussion, I achieved the results you described and was pleased—though I was missing millivolt resolution. My core issue: How can I read all 32-bit unsigned data from the [company_name] P1 module? I still cannot read the returned power value, which is in kW, so anything below 1 kW (999 W or less) shows as zero in the software. Perhaps it's best to set aside my previous attempts—can you assist with a routine that reads all 32-bit uint registers from the P1 dongle, as outlined on the manufacturer's website [url]? The actual challenge is that [product_name] is only designed for 16-bit signed integer data, making conversion of 32-bit values impractical. What specific values are you targeting? Are they less than 32,768 W (32.768 kW)?

If the power value is below 32,768 W, that's ideal for my setup. If the same routine can be used for voltages less than 260 V, all the better.

It seems you're not very familiar with data formats, which may make providing assistance difficult. For example, a voltage value like 233,200 cannot fit in an integer (0-32,767) range.

Hello everyone, I have a standard load cell providing a 0-10V signal via an amplifier into AI3. With the correct span and offset, I see values from 0-1000 for a 100kg load cell, giving a resolution of 100g. The cell is overrated for safety, despite its overload tolerance. My question is: can I configure [product_name] so the ADC's 1000 values cover just the 0-5V portion of the analog input, effectively doubling the resolution for my working range to 50g? What's the best approach to achieve this? Kind regards, [user_name]

No, that's not possible. The resolution cannot be changed. An input change of 0.01 V always remains one unit after the A/D conversion.

Thank you for responding. I'm not clear on what you mean by 0.01V. My goal isn't to change the resolution of [product_name] but to clamp the input range to 0-5V and apply the 10-bit measurement to this truncated voltage. Are you saying that 0-1000 always maps to the full input range? How does offset and multiplier affect this? A flowchart would help.

For [product_name]'s analog input, the A/D converter maps any input (current, voltage, or PT100/1000 sensor) to 0-1000 units. For a 0-10V signal, each 0.01V equals one unit (10V divided by 1000). If you only process 0-5V, you get 0-500 units, so the resolution stays the same—0.01V per unit. It's not possible to change this via software.

Check the online help in [product_name] engineering software for guidance; there's information about handling analog signals. To improve overall resolution, you'd need to choose a more suitable sensor or install a signal converter between the sensor and input. For example, selecting a sensor with a narrower range increases your measurement resolution. Alternatively, a signal amplifier with adjustable gain and offset could help. Regards, [user_name]

Hi, [user_name]'s advice is correct: you cannot change the input resolution in [product_name] itself. The only real solution is to use a load cell scaled for your range (for instance, 0-10V for 0-50kg). Make sure to check accuracy as well. According to the [product_name] manual, expect a typical error limit of around ±1.5%. Hope this helps.

Thanks all. I have a load cell amplifier, and I've set analog zero to the lowest point, with payload at 62/1000. I'm used to programming software where you can truncate the scale and multiply analog input before feeding the ADC, which is why I thought about configuring [product_name]'s input to 0-5V to pump up resolution. Setting for 0-50kg could be risky in an industrial setting. I reviewed the documentation and vaguely recall a 0-5V input option—it might have been a different brand manual though. In any case, seems it's not feasible, so thanks again.

Configurable analog inputs would be great. Some PLC systems like [version_no] controllers offer this, but at a much higher cost. There are requests for [product_name] analog modules with better accuracy, but no one knows when—or if—they'll become available. If you're using [product_name] with network features, you can investigate remote analog modules that work with Modbus TCP/IP. Regards, [user_name]

We used an analog sensor with a 0-10V output over a range of -20°C to 100°C (accuracy 0.12°C when sampled by [product_name] as 0-1000 units). We fed this signal through a 2x gain amplifier (DIN rail, includes ESD protection, runs on +12V from [product_name]). This adjusted the range to -20°C to 40°C, improving accuracy to 0.06°C. Since our sensor mainly operated between 16°C and 30°C, the extra resolution was helpful. Remember that in [product_name], scaling involves offset and multiplier adjustments.

Great approach. It would be simple if [product_name] offered a software setting for a 0-5V input to accomplish this!

I've used [product_name] for many years. Sometimes you want finer analog resolution, and I believe it’s technically feasible in firmware. But consider: higher resolution usually means higher cost. Also, many users lack experience dealing with the challenges of accurate analog measurements (EMC/EMV interference). The default 1000-step resolution in [product_name] meets my needs; if I need higher, I switch to larger systems. But everyone’s requirements differ.

Agreed. My point is that 10-bit resolution is sufficient, but having user control over input range (clamping/truncation) would improve flexibility. This function doesn't require hardware changes—just code updates managing input parameters. For current/voltage conversion, you can use a resistor, but my suggestion is even simpler. All the best, [user_name]

Your request makes sense, but [product_name] does not have this feature. Physical analog signals are digitized using a 10-bit ADC, which is limited to 1000 steps, and this determines your resolution. Software can't remap the range so that 0.01V equals only part of the load cell's full range.

It's not possible to increase A/D converter resolution through software. You can truncate results to get a 0-500 range, but the step size remains the same. If higher analog resolution is needed, you must use hardware like a different sensor or a signal amplifier, or choose a controller with a more suitable input range. For current signals (0/4-20mA), proper resistor selection is crucial, as many sensors have maximum load limits. Sometimes, it's most efficient to buy a new sensor with the required range. Regards, [user_name]

The translation may be off: The bit resolution isn't changed, but narrowing the measured range increases precision within that window. In audio terms, it's like oversampling—reducing the bandwidth increases quantization detail. For [product_name], a 0-5V input measured with 10-bit ADC would use the full set of digital values over a smaller voltage window. This would require a software switch mapping the ADC to a narrower range. Am I misunderstanding something?

These are not equivalent—audio sampling and analog input measurement in PLCs work differently. If you're unsure despite the feedback here, consider submitting a support request to [company_name] directly. Marking this topic as 'Support Relevant'.

I fully admit I may be missing something, given my background is audio engineering. I appreciate everyone's explanations—even if the analog-to-digital conversion processes for audio and weight sensors differ, I'd love clarification for everyone's benefit. Thank you all for your patience and insights.

All relevant points have been covered. The analog input range (0-10V) in [product_name] is always mapped to 0-1000 units, and there is no option to set the measuring range to 0-5V. Measuring 5V simply equates to 500 units on the input scale.

Audio signals are handled differently; they have fixed peak-to-peak values and resolution is managed by filtering and sampling frequency. In automation, analog signals are measured for their magnitude, not for time-domain analysis. Regards, [user_name]

You are correct—it's confusing to compare time and amplitude domains. Expressed as amplitude: halving the input voltage increases quantization accuracy. However, anything above the threshold is effectively clipped. My suggestion was to allow [product_name] to ignore voltages above a set limit, so the ADC only focuses on the desired range. I understand this isn't available at present, and thanks everyone for the explanations and patience.

Ideally, an ADC with configurable maximum measurement value would help in these cases, but in practice it’s handled by additional hardware, like a pre-amplifier. This adds cost—alternatively, select a sensor with the needed range to save expense. For more advanced needs, use a PLC with higher resolution analog inputs, such as [version_no] modules. Regards, [user_name]

Thank you; for most of my tasks, [product_name] works well—it's easy to program and cost-effective for small tasks and web interfaces. Moving up to a more capable PLC is expensive for just a bit more analog resolution. For example, some AC drives have 12-bit analog inputs, but lack simplicity and built-in web servers. One last question: If a voltage over the input range (e.g. 0-12V) is supplied, and there's no input filter, what happens? Is this handled by hardware? Maybe a sensor with Modbus output could do external processing, but then using a more advanced PLC may be easier overall.

Note: The base module's analog input can also function as a digital input for 24VDC (maximum 26.8VDC). Just a thought—any other questions?

Here's an example of displaying weight with a single decimal place for simulation: Value of analog input: 200 = 0.0 kg (4 mA), 600 = 50.0 kg (12 mA), 1000 = 100.0 kg (20 mA).

This setup allows a single word sent by the Modbus master to control outputs Q1 and Q1 on both controllers, with each bit in the word indicating which output should activate on which controller.

There’s an example in the attachment.

The issue appears to relate to the SD card. [product_name] devices cannot save parameter changes directly to the SD card. As previously mentioned, [product_name] devices can't write changes of block parameters to the SD card; only FLASH memory can retain such changes. Upon restart, if the program on the SD card doesn’t match the one in FLASH, the SD card program is loaded. I’ve used the [product_name] for 2 years without saving the program to the SD card, and after many power failures, it’s worked flawlessly.

Alternatively, the SD card can be used to transfer the program between [product_name] devices without needing a PC.

Split from another thread about hours counter issues.

I don't want to debate this. For me, it's only an issue if something is broken or only partially working.

I've tested both older and newer versions of the web editor. The newest is much slower on both hardware types, transferring data at only 20-50 KB/s, even for small amounts. Loading takes about ten minutes. It appears that reading and writing to the microSD card is slower with new editor versions, while CPU calculation speed seems unchanged. A German-speaking forum noted that encryption is required due to new regulations, possibly EU export restrictions. But there hasn't been an official statement demanding encrypted connections between all devices. On other company platforms, users can select communication security modes; it would be good to have similar choices in the web editor. Currently, warnings appear when activating unsecured ports, leaving it to user responsibility. The explanation for forced encryption feels more like a justification for not changing the current setup.

I've tested the same hardware version 8.3 with different web editor versions: 1.0 loads pages very quickly in non-secure mode, while 1.1 is 50-200% slower, even without secure mode. The speed is extremely slow in secure mode despite browser certificates. Even in non-secure mode, the newer editor version is always slower.

Web editor version 1.0.1 can't upload projects to the 8.3 hardware due to a firmware error.

I tested on 8.2 hardware (article_no hidden). The newer web editor version 1.1 uploads to 8.2 hardware but still causes slow loading. The problem seems to be with the software-created web pages, not the hardware itself. Using version 1.0 on both hardware types results in faster loading.

Project loading speed from a different editor (like [product_name]) is much faster, but with 8.3 hardware it's noticeably slower. Web editor projects are especially slow with latest hardware.

Also, the [product_name] project loading speed is different too (those projects were always very fast), but on 8.3 hardware they're noticeably slower. Web editor projects are extremely slow on 8.3. You need web editor 1.1 for 8.3, but it can also be used with 8.2. Web editor 1.1 makes all hardware slow and upload/download speeds poor, whereas using version 1.0 on both types solves the problem, though with fewer text and trend features.

Is there any workaround besides using 8.2 hardware? The slow speed and response times make it impossible to build projects for clients without complaints. The speed is unacceptable, and changing security settings or memory card doesn't help.

Switching back to web editor 1.0 brings much better speed than 1.1. However, version 1.0 lacks decimal points, trend graphs, and text formatting options.

Unfortunately, don't expect a quick solution. Since development moved abroad, everything slowed down—bug fixes and service packs are rare. I reported a web editor 1.1 bug in March 2021 and was told it would be forwarded. Nine months later, still no action; when development was in Germany, things were different.

Don't expect a quick solution. Since development moved to another country, bug fixes and updates have slowed. I reported an issue months ago and haven't seen changes. Strange how identical hardware performs so differently with web editor versions. I hope a firmware update or new editor version improves SD card read/write speeds soon.

I suspect the SD card read/write is too slow because the web pages are stored there. If that's not the cause, maybe the web editor itself limits transfer speed. I hope performance can be improved soon.

You may have to wait a long time. There won't be a solution for 8.3 hardware. If anything, maybe a fix will come with future product versions.

This appears to be a case of inadequate firmware programming and a lack of interest in addressing bugs. The hardware shouldn't be so much slower than older versions. Moving development to China seems to have worsened things. Older product lines are already end-of-life, so customers are stuck with flawed 8.3 versions, and [company_name] doesn't seem to mind.

I am using a [product_name] module with [article_no]. I have 16 inputs wired to the EN, configured to record the state of inputs 1-16, outputs Q1-16, and some timer values. From what I understand, when any input changes from 0 to 1, it triggers a log of all selected signals and timer values at that moment. Recently, I received a data log from a customer and noticed cases where an input was activated, but the log doesn't show any activity. The info screen for the data log only specifies that logging begins with a 0 to 1 transition on the EN input of the block. Is there any additional documentation about this process? For example: Does a normally-on (1) signal need to be inverted for triggering? Once logging begins, how long does it last? Does a further EN input stop it? How long does it take to record a log? Also, I see lines of data separated by minutes with no change—how is that possible? Is there a way to identify the triggering input for each log entry? Additional information to help with diagnostics would be greatly appreciated.

Please refer to the attached file.

When the EN input on the Data Log module detects a rising edge from 0 to 1, a new row is added. If EN stays high, further changes are not logged until the next qualifying edge. There must be a minimum gap of 500 ms between edge changes for subsequent data to be recorded.

Thanks for your reply! I have attached the file in question, highlighting the 'on' states and the columns representing persistent inputs (such as limit switches). I am uncertain why, if the EN signal remains ON and blocks further data log writes, there are multiple rows at different times. I will upload the relevant code for clarity—it's part of a larger program, but only this section is relevant.

Here is the code that produced the data log.

How are you controlling the EN input in your code? It's possible that logging is not occurring properly. If events intended to trigger logging are switched in parallel, the required 500 ms interval between triggers may not be maintained.

The inputs shown occur at different times unless a specific input is already active. This is for a gate system with inputs for up/down commands, limit switches, and safety signals. Some inputs might happen within 500ms, but not consistently. There should be multiple rows with I2 or I8 being high, but those entries are missing.

Therefore, it's uncertain whether: (a) the 500 ms pause between events is maintained, and (b) fewer than two inputs are active at the same time. If one input is already on and others arrive at overlapping times, those events are not logged.

Thank you. I resolved this by assigning each input its own edge-triggered timer and triggering the data log block using a 0.2s timer output. This approach seems to work more reliably. Is it possible to increase the time resolution in the log? I would like the time field to include seconds, as many operations happen within a minute.

No, increasing the time resolution in the Data Log is not possible. You can only select the operands to be logged; further adjustments are unavailable.

Hello! I have two [product_name] PLCs set up with one acting as master and the other as slave. The slave reads multiple values from the master and outputs them. Are you using a true Master/Slave configuration? Have you configured one [product_name] as a slave? Or are you referring to a Client/Server setup instead?

In a Master/Slave arrangement, the slave device does not have its own program and isn't able to write or read data independently. You just assign the device as the slave and that’s all; the master accesses the slave's hardware inputs and outputs. Alternatively, both [product_name] devices can be set as masters with individual programs, in which case you would configure one as a client and the other as a server. The client can then read and write data from the server according to its programming.

I have two PLCs, one configured to act as a master and the other as a slave.

Sorry, I'm not sure I understood your advice. Both PLCs have their own programs. The slave PLC—which is actually set as master in the system—reads values from the other PLC. If the master PLC disconnects, the slave should display zeros, but it continues showing the last values received. If I try to set the slave as a true slave, the system only lets me download if it is configured as master, so both units are set as master.

Actually, this suggests you have a Client/Server connection, not a Master/Slave one, because both [product_name] devices have programs running. In a Master/Slave configuration, the slave does not have its own program and only serves hardware resources to the master.

The [product_name] detects communication errors in different ways, and sometimes does not recognize them at all. 1) If the client is switched to STOP mode, the server detects it and all memory bits (VB0 to VB850) are set low. 2) If the client loses power, the server does not notice and the bits keep their current state. 3) If the Ethernet cable is unplugged: 3.1) With direct connection, the server is aware but memory bits retain their state. You can detect this with a network input using the 'Ethernet error' diagnostic. 3.2) If connected via router, the server won’t recognize the disconnection and bits will not reset. Use a life bit query programmed in both units for better error handling.

That matches my situation. Could you please explain how to add a life bit query and which blocks to use in the client and server to set all memory bits low? Also, how do I implement an Ethernet error diagnostic function? If possible, provide a screenshot or example. Thank you so much!

To clarify: I am not aware of any method to reset all user memory bits (VB0 to VB850) to low in response to a communication error—this can only be done per bit or word. Attached is a small network project illustrating how to query for an 'Ethernet link error.' It also includes the setup of a life bit and how to evaluate it. The client generates a signal that changes state every second, sends it to the server, which checks if it's been HIGH or LOW for more than 1.5 seconds to detect communication loss. The server also echoes the life bit back to the client for evaluation.

It looks like you've removed your previous post. The network project actually uses two [product_name] devices, each with a separate program. To view the programs, double-click on each device in the project and open their respective code. See the attached screenshot.

Is there a way to build a 32-bit shift register using multiple blocks without output duplication? In my example, I created a 32-bit shift register setup where Block 005's output connects to Block 006's input, and so on. However, after S1.7, when S1.8 is activated, its output also turns on S2.1, causing overlap. Because of this, I end up with three 7-bit and one 8-bit register, totaling 29 bits. Does anyone have suggestions for achieving a full 32-bit register?

Could you clarify what you want this solution to achieve or simplify for the PLC? There may be easier approaches, such as using a counter. If you can provide more details about the requirements, we might suggest alternative solutions.

Thank you for your response, [user_name]. I didn't see your reply for a few days. My question is for learning and experimenting. Most PLC systems typically provide an extra output bit, so an 8-bit shift register's output would become a ninth bit, enabling you to link multiple registers in a cascade. 's configuration seems unusual in this aspect. I'll think about possible workarounds.

I've found a neat solution to this problem. Please refer to the attached animated GIF. In this setup, the memory and output blocks update only at the end of each program scan, not instantly as the diagram might suggest. Therefore, changes are visible in the subsequent scan, effectively adding a one-scan delay for both activation and deactivation. By inserting a memory block between the output of the first shift register and the input of the next, bit 2.1 will activate just as bit 1.8 deactivates. Using this approach, it's possible to cascade all four shift register blocks (maximum allowed on [product_name] V8.3) to successfully create a 32-bit shift register.

I'm seeking advice on how to properly calibrate a pressure transducer. Everything is set up and working as expected so far. I connected my calibrated Druck DPI705 to the same source and noticed a 30 unit difference between the readings. Should I adjust the gain or the offset on the analog amplifier? Any help would be appreciated since this is my first time working with pressure transducers. I'd like to do it correctly before making any changes. Try using two analog amplifiers in series for your setup.

Thanks for your suggestion, but I'm unsure how the settings on the pre-amplifier will account for the 30 unit difference, or any adjustment at all. Could you provide more details on how it works?

The analog input's A/D converter in a [product_name] module normally converts signals (such as 0-10V, 0/4-20mA, or PT100/1000) into a range of 0-1000 units. These units are then scaled with an analog amplifier to match the encoder's measuring range. For a 4-20mA sensor, the first 200 units represent the 4mA baseline, leaving 800 units for scaling. For example: from -1,000 to 1,500 bar is a span of 2,500 bar. So 2,500 / 800 = 3.125 for the gain factor. However, only two decimal places are supported for the gain, so rounding occurs (3.125 becomes 3.13), which introduces minor deviations in minimum, maximum, and offset. To address this, using two analog amplifiers in series helps. The first converts 800 units to 1000, and the second uses a gain factor (e.g., 2.5). The offset is then corrected so that the values align to the desired range, such as shifting 0.000 to 2.500 bar to -1.000 to 1.500 bar.

This thread was split from a discussion on connecting an input analog sensor (4-20mA) to a [product_name].

Which analog input are you referring to? AI1, AI2, AI3 or AI4?

I want to connect sensors to all available analog inputs. My sensors output 4-20mA, and I plan to connect them to the base module using a 500 ohm resistor. However, I’m unsure about proper wiring setup.

Does your sensor have its own power supply, or is it just a 2-wire sensor?

No, the sensor lacks a dedicated power supply. It’s a 2-wire vibration sensor.

In this case, connect +24V from the [product_name]'s power supply to the sensor’s positive terminal. Connect the sensor’s negative terminal to one end of the resistor and to the analog input terminal of the [product_name]. Attach the other end of the resistor to the negative terminal (M) of the power supply.

Alternatively, you could use a 4-20mA to 0-10V signal converter. These are cost-effective and let you fine-tune zero and span settings for optimal input adaptation.

A 500 ohm resistor works well too. Any tolerance issues can be offset by using an analog amplifier.

Using a resistor results in a 20% loss in possible resolution, which can lead to missing values—so it's not always 'just as well.' This might be fine for some users. For example: - A dedicated 4-20mA to 0-10V converter gives you 1000 distinct values as output. - With a 500 ohm resistor (which I personally use and can confirm works), remember that: • Your sensor’s zero point is at 2V (200 units) • The max sensor value is at 10V (1000 units)

If someone is highly focused on achieving 100% resolution, they usually aren’t using a [product_name].

You're right about loss of resolution—optimal results require a suitable signal converter with offset and gain adjustment. However, most users connect analog signals directly to the base module to save money, avoiding an analog expansion module or converter. Consider both the accuracy of the analog inputs and the converter itself. Users often search for very precise resistors, but a 499 ohm resistor with 1% tolerance serves the same purpose and is inexpensive. You can calculate resolution as follows: - For 0..10V or 0..20mA, it's range/1000 - For 2..10V or 4..20mA, it's range/800 Then, determine what works best for your setup. Sometimes issues arise from using the wrong sensor, such as choosing one meant for 4000mm when you only need 2000mm, or opting for a sensor output of 4..20mA when other outputs might be more appropriate. Regards, [user_name]

I am wondering if it is possible to have active voltage on the input side when the device loses power, or if this could cause hardware damage. I need this information for both 12/24 Vdc and 230 Vac systems.

Could you provide more details?

If the power fails, there will be no active voltage present.

That's not always correct. There can be a power failure only for the [product_name] and/or the expansion modules, while the peripherals remain powered. The wiring and protection setup are unclear here—the original poster should clarify.

If you're referring to just the [product_name] or its expansion modules losing power, but the connected peripherals still being powered, then there should be no issue.

Yes, that's the case for my setup. I have a [product_name] powered by a 230V supply with its own switch, referred to as 'SERVICES'. There are inputs coming from a separate 230V supply dedicated to lighting, called 'LIGHTS', each with their own protection. Both originate from the main supply, so they're only connected when both switches are on. If SERVICES is off but LIGHTS is on, some inputs to the [product_name] remain active while the device itself is off. Is this safe? The same scenario could happen with a 24Vdc system, if the input and device power lines are switched separately. You might get active inputs while the device power is off. Hello, Be cautious with 230V lines—SERVICE and LIGHT may be supplied by different phases. As long as inputs within a group use the same phase, it's fine. If different phases are mixed within one input group, you must separate them; otherwise, hardware damage may occur. A [product_name] has two input groups: I1–I4 and I5–I8. Don't connect different phases to inputs within the same group. For a third phase, you'd need a suitable expansion module ([product_name]). Refer to the wiring diagram in the [document] for correct setup. Hope this helps.

On your referenced site, you’ll see HR130 mapped to VW12, which means two registers (HR130 and HR131) are mapped to VW12 and VW14 (or VB12, VB13, VB14 and VB15—equivalent). For the F/I converter, the parameter VM12 is used. Selecting Float means two registers = two words = four bytes (next free address is VM16). Selecting Double uses four registers = four words = eight bytes (next free is VM20), but you need to handle four registers. If you have more sequential registers, you can transfer them in bulk—just select the correct number. Watch out for numbering: registers HR1, HR2, HR13 may be mapped to VW10, VW12, VW14, since the [product_name] variables are byte-oriented. I can read a holding register without issues. My challenge is using the same connection to read holding registers, digital inputs, and write coil data. Generally, it’s possible to select coils, input registers, or holding registers in both directions—you just need the respective addresses and can choose the connection direction. Read a coil with Network Input, write with Network Output, read a holding register with Analog Network Input, write with Analog Network Output. Use Vx.y for coils, VWx for holding registers, VMx for floats. Regards, [user_name] P.S. If your problem isn’t clear, consider making a sample program with comments and upload as a ZIP.

Use local mapping to VM memory instead; then you can organize the memory into areas for digital and analog signals. For sequences of eight digital signals with DI or coil, a compact design (see attachment) is better. For analog signals (holding registers in sequence), use another compact arrangement even if some values aren’t needed. Registers are 16 bit (one word, two bytes), so start VWx at an even number to avoid future issues. For floats (two registers, four bytes), begin VWx at a number divisible by four. For double (four registers, eight bytes), likewise. First, list all needed signals, then plan the VM memory to prevent overlaps and problems. Regards, [user_name]

You can later expand with additional [product_name] units, starting at V200.0 or V400.0. Partition sizes depend on your requirements and preferences. Don't use hundreds of signals if you only need a few; excessive signals will increase latency. Regards, [user_name]

Regarding your second question: I'm measuring four temperatures for a heating application, using four build-it-yourself transducers connected to affordable PT100 sensors through operational amplifiers, resulting in an output voltage ranging from 1V to nearly 10V. These simple circuits aren't very accurate at zero, nor can I precisely calibrate the slope. That's why the calibration settings in the analog amplifier appear unusual. With a gain factor close to 10, any change in the input signal of 0.01 V becomes ±10 units after amplification. I'm not sure how steady your power supply and self-constructed converter outputs are.

That matches my understanding. I wanted to confirm because in other home automation modules I've used, similar specifications came with warnings against mixing low safety voltages (12V) with higher standard ones (230V) due to the components being close together, which could cause arcing in case of failure. I wanted to check if [product_name] has a similar safety restriction, or if its construction avoids these issues.

Hello everyone, I'm creating a control program for the shutters in my home. Everything generally works as intended (timed closing, alarm integration, etc.), but I need assistance displaying the shutter position. For example, in my test setup (see attachment), the values on outputs may eventually exceed 28 or drop below 0. Could someone guide me on how to address this issue? This issue is expected since you're using two timers without physical limit switches, and operate outputs for preset durations. For instance: if your system restarts, both timers are at zero. When you command the shutter to move up, then stop by briefly activating the opposite direction, the timer for the movement direction might stop at 15 seconds. If you next activate the down direction and let it run uninterrupted, the timer counts 28 seconds. When calculating position, you subtract the 'up' value from the 'down' value: 15s - 28s = -13s. Without a sensor counting actual movement, these offsets will always occur.

Thank you for your reply. I understand this issue. My question is whether it's possible to determine the shutter's position, using only open/close timings, without encoders. Perhaps another function block might help, or maybe restricting the counter range to between 0 and 28 could solve it? It's a basic shutter—the total movement time is 28 seconds up or down. If you apply longer running time, limit switches will stop the motor. Open to any suggestions :-) Best regards, [user_name]

Is that even feasible? Without an encoder, you cannot reliably know the shutter's position—there's no way to account for all partial movements. If you change direction mid-way, the full movement time isn't always used. Without synchronization, these offsets remain.

Try checking the program attached. In that example, the movement is monitored with a pulse counter. Upward movement is capped when the counter reaches 28 (seconds) and downward movement can never go below zero, preventing negative values entirely.

Thank you, [user_name]! That's exactly what I needed. Since this isn't for industrial automation, precise positioning isn't required—it's only for visual feedback. Your approach works well, and I've incorporated it into my application. I'll observe over a few days to verify consistent position display, but it seems to be working fine. I hadn't thought about calculating position using one-second pulses. Thank you again. Best regards and have a great day, [user_name]

Hello everyone, I'm facing a seemingly simple issue but don't know how to solve it. I can show the frequency of a high-speed input in a message text, but I'm unsure how to convert that value to gallons per minute. For example: 0 Hz = gpm, 1 kHz = 20 gpm, 2 kHz = 40 gpm. Any suggestions?
