Hello [user_name], This type of problem is often encountered: counting pulses over a time interval and converting the result to a physical value. I previously shared solutions on the German forum. Here's a summary: One way is to use the "threshold trigger" function connected to an input pin. If you set the time interval (gate time) parameter, you get the input signal's frequency. You can adjust the gate time to convert pulses into desired units, for example, by applying a translation factor. However, the manual specifies limitations on the minimum gate time, and you can only display the value, not use it further within other [product_name] functions. Another option is to add a frequency divider before the threshold trigger. Using blocks like counter and digital flag, you can set parameters so the trigger function receives the input frequency divided by a factor. This allows you to adjust the gate time and scaling accordingly, but again, you can only display the value. To overcome these restrictions, I programmed a modified threshold trigger. Check the attached example (comments are in German). In summary: replace certain simulation blocks with an input signal, set an impulse generator to define the gate time, and use a counter to count pulses within each measurement interval. The result is held in a memory block and then amplified to convert to the correct units, adjusting for decimals as needed. Advantages of this approach: 1) You can reference the scaled result in other logical blocks, 2) You can adjust display precision, and 3) You can synchronize multiple triggers. Hope this explanation helps you solve your issue. Best regards [user_name]

That's great, thank you! I considered sampling the rate using a time gate but wasn't sure how to capture the updated value—using the multiplexer was the missing piece. I appreciate your guidance. Also, thanks to everyone in the forum—I’ve learned a lot from reading the posts and hope to contribute myself in the future.

Hello [user_name], Thanks for your encouraging feedback! Many new members don’t look for existing answers, even though many questions are already addressed in forum posts. Perhaps you didn’t check the German area. Without knowing your exact application details and gate times, I’ll mention that my design has a limitation similar to the original block: with long gate times, the display doesn't update during measurement. That's why I shared a modified circuit in the German forum under "Average over 8 hours" — you can download the attachment named "Demo_gleitender_Mittelwertzähler.zip". In this approach, the measurement period is divided into eight sub-periods using counters, with a ninth counter for display memory. For example, if the gate time counts pulses over 8×n seconds (n is set by the impulse generator), each counter updates and stores results cyclically for improved periodic updates. The comments are in German, so if you have any questions, feel free to ask here. Best regards [user_name]

The Stopwatch’s measured value is 32 bits wide (DWord), but the analog comparator handles only 16-bit inputs. Therefore, you need to enter 5, not 50, into the comparator; the circuit works only if the measured time doesn’t exceed 5 minutes, 27 seconds, and 67 hundredths. Screen attachment

Now you have a foundation for your next step with CR6. I can't provide detailed help for that device, but can assist with Modbus in general. If you encounter Unit ID issues, adjust the relevant settings in your Modbus client software for [product_name]; default value is 255. Make sure the same Unit ID parameter is set on both CR6 and [product_name] to ensure proper communication (for example, use 1). The holding register numbers 1 and 5 in my test program are just examples—you can use any number, as long as those registers exist in CR6. If registers are consecutive, you can simplify client settings by just using the starting register and increasing the block length as needed (2, 3, 4...). Remember, Modbus registers are 16-bit, while [product_name] variables may be 8-bit. Reading 4 registers starting from VW10 leads to the next ones at VW12, VW14, and VW16. The word VW10 covers bytes VB10 and VB11, so the following available number would be 12. With 4 registers in VW10 to VW16, you shouldn't use bytes VB10 to VB17 or bits V10.0 to V17.7 to avoid overlapping memory values. Good luck with your project, [user_name]

Hello, Is it possible to expand a [product_name] [article_no] with a 230V AC power supply by adding a [product_name] [article_no] digital expansion module designed for 24V? I understand each module needs a different power supply, but will they be able to communicate together safely without causing any damage? Thanks for your response.

You cannot directly connect a 24VDC digital expansion module to a 230VAC base module or a 230VAC digital expansion module. The internal bus for communication is not electrically isolated. The S0 interface transmits measured data using impulses. These impulses can have a frequency lower than 1Hz and a width of 30ms. According to the [product_name] specifications, the maximum input frequency for standard digital inputs is 4Hz. Based on this, it appears that normal digital inputs can handle S0 interface pulses, but can they consistently count 30ms impulses at frequencies below 4Hz?

For full assurance, it's better to use a [product_name] model equipped with fast counter inputs.

Hello, my understanding is as follows: For frequency measurements, a 50% duty cycle is usually required. If the pulse duration is less than 50%, it changes the requirements. A 30ms pulse requires the input's ability to detect that short period. If the device is limited to 4Hz, it likely cannot detect a 30ms pulse reliably. Which [product_name] and [article_no] are you using? The DC versions offer built-in high-speed counters, with some supporting up to 5kHz depending on the model. Testing it may help clarify. The input frequency for DC versions depends on the device's cycle time, so review the manual (be sure to reference your specific [product_name] version and use the correct manual). For example, in [product_name] V8, the function block cycle is typically under 0.1ms. If you use around 400 function blocks, the total cycle time is about 40ms. So with programs under 300 function blocks, handling these pulses may work. The manual also describes how to measure cycle time. Hope this helps.

[user_name]: Unfortunately, [product_name] only provides 4 fast inputs, and its expansion modules do not provide additional fast inputs. [user_name]: My preferred model is the 12/24RCE(o). Regarding frequency definitions, if the specification lists 'frequency,' it likely refers to a 50% duty cycle signal. If a signal isn't 50/50, perhaps it doesn't technically have a 'frequency.' Possibly, [company_name] means the frequency for signals with a balanced duty cycle. For your point about 4Hz and a 30ms pulse: It depends on the internal implementation. If each input has an interrupt latch, in theory it should detect impulses down to 1 microsecond, provided they don't repeat more than once every 0.25 seconds. If inputs operate just as I/O leads, then impulses shorter than 0.25 seconds may not be detected. This specific behavior is not documented.

Hello, the minimum pulse length that a [product_name] can detect is critical for your application. This depends on input/output delays and device scan time. The manual provides examples for calculating scan time. For instance, if the scan time is 100ms, the shortest pulse detectable is approximately 101ms. That corresponds to 10Hz. If you have 10ms pulses with a period of 100ms (10Hz), the device will not capture these pulses. The scan process for a [product_name] is roughly: read inputs, run the user program, and write outputs. Note that unlike a PLC, [product_name] does not have input interrupts or pulse capture features. There may be alternative solutions, though. Can you provide more details about your application, such as frequency, minimum pulse length, and any other constraints regarding S0 pulse counting?

In summary, handling S0 pulses requires fast inputs. However, this leads to a new concern: can a fast input reliably detect every 30ms pulse, even if the scan cycle exceeds 100ms? If not, then the fast input of [product_name] may still be unable to process S0 interface signals accurately.

If you remove I2 and leave only Q1 in your program, its state becomes controllable via Modbus.

The current value within the range (150mm - 2494mm) is multiplied by the gain factor, then the offset is subtracted. V2 divided by V3 gives you the gain: 4266 / 10000 = 0.4266 V4 represents the offset, which is -150, marking the starting point of the calculation range. The latest version of [product_name] Web Editor ([version_no]) supports decimal places.

For calculating the gain: Maximum output = 1000 (100.0%) Minimum output = 0 (0.0%) Maximum input = 2494 (2494mm) Minimum input = 150 (150mm) Subtracting minimum from maximum output gives 1000 - 0 = 1000. Then divide by the difference between maximum and minimum input: 2494 - 150 = 2344. So the gain is 1000 / 2344 = 0.4266.

Hi [user_name], interesting question! One advantage of our PT100 module is that it supports 3-wire measurements. This setup lets the module estimate the resistance of the lead wires, which is useful for calculating the true temperature at the sensor tip. Unlike signal measurement with 0/4..20 mA, temperature is measured using the resistance of a platinum filament—100 ohms at 0.01 °C. Lead length, wire thickness, and local temperatures can affect resistance. Using 3 wires, the module corrects for lead resistance before relaying results to the [product_name] system. For 2-wire sensors, accuracy depends on wire quality and environment. The manual recommends 10 meters of shielded wire for best accuracy (as noted on page 263). With 15 meters, accuracy may decline by about 50%, e.g. from ±1.0% to ±1.5% for positive temperature ranges and even more in the negative range. A 3-wire setup greatly reduces this loss of accuracy. I hope this helps. You can find more information about temperature measurement principles online. (Background: experience in temperature and humidity calibration, standards, and measurement applications — always interesting to see these principles in use with [product_name].)

Based on my experience, even 100 meters should be possible without significant problems. The accuracy has been confirmed in many installed systems, including one with a wood-fired home heating system boiling water at 99.75–100.00°C from 30 meters away. The most important part is ensuring the shielded braid is continuous and properly connected to the PE [product_name] connector. Hope this helps.

In the Parameter-VM-Mapping table, use the parameters in DWord format. The addressing in [product_name] is byte-oriented. A DWord consists of 32 bits, or 4 Bytes, or 2 words. Input I8 is a standard digital input, suitable for frequencies up to 10 Hz. For faster signals, you should use one of the fast counter inputs (I3 to I6) of your [product_name]. Refer to the attached wiring instructions. Note that the signal is inverted when using NPN type sensors.

The value <30 mA is the consumption, while the output can handle a maximum of 10 mA. It's advisable to use a resistor higher than 2.4 kOhm, such as 2.7 kOhm, 4.7 kOhm, or even 10 kOhm. Start testing with a 10 kOhm resistor and decrease as necessary.

The 30 mA is the consumption of the flow sensor, which has three wires: two for power connected to the PSU and one to the input. Is it still necessary to increase the resistance in this scenario?

Could you clarify what you mean by 'online simulation mode'? In [product_name] programming software, there is a simulation mode and an online mode. The online mode shows current states and values from a connected [product_name]. Without seeing your program, it's difficult to determine why M1 flashes intermittently.

Having a 3-wire sensor does not guarantee direct compatibility with every input. Your sensor uses an NPN open collector output, which functions like a relay contact bridging the output to 0V. [product_name] inputs are PNP type and require a positive voltage to detect a high signal. Think of the open collector output as a relay contact connecting the input to 0V, essentially acting like an unconnected input. Combining the external resistor with the internal resistor (~72 kOhm) of the [product_name] input forms a voltage divider. For example, using a 10 kOhm resistor, when the output is open, 24V is split across both resistors, resulting in around 21V at the input—sufficient for a high signal. Reducing the resistor increases the voltage further, but isn't necessary for a high level. When the output is closed, the input drops to 0V and current through the open collector is 24V / 10kOhm = 2.4 mA; ensure it doesn't exceed 10 mA. For exact voltage levels, consult the operating instructions for your [product_name] and sensor documentation.

Hello! Apologies if there are any language mistakes, as English isn't my native language. I'm new to programming with [product_name] and have some questions. I am sending temperature data from Arduino to [product_name] using MODBUS and need to read these values as floats, but to use them in [product_name] I need to convert them to integers. I'm not very familiar with memory mapping yet, so maybe there's an error there. I believe the number received from Modbus is stored at VW2 (since a long value = 2, it occupies VW0 and VW2). Could someone explain how to handle this value at VW2? The manual outlines these common steps for converting float/integer: 1) Transfer float data via Modbus to VM. 2) Convert float data in VM to integer using a converter. 3) Work with the converted integer. 4) Convert back to float if needed. Are these the correct steps I should follow? If possible, could you provide a simple example? I would appreciate it very much. Thanks.

The addressing in [product_name]'s VM memory is byte-oriented. To input a 32-bit float, you need to use 4 bytes—transfer VB0 to VB3 (VW0 + VW2). For conversion, use the F/I converter at VM0. To reverse it (integer to float), use an I/F converter—enter VM4 so it covers VB4 to VB7 (VW4 + VW6). These 4 bytes must then be sent to two Modbus registers.

Hi [user_name], thank you for your reply! I am already using VM=0 with the float/integer converter, as shown in my code, but it's not working. I’m unsure about your point on 'inputting a 32-bit float via VB0 to VB3 (VW0 + VW2)'. If I send data from HR=11 to VW0 (long=2), shouldn’t the data be available at VB3? In the data table, I see bits marked V3.0 to VB3.7, but only receive float values up to 255. I've attached my [product_name] code.

To clarify: VM memory is addressed by byte, while Modbus holding registers are addressed by word. A 32-bit Modbus value consists of 4 bytes (2 words), using two consecutive registers, e.g. HR11 and HR12. Similarly, in [product_name]'s VM memory, it uses 4 bytes or 2 words. For transfer, only the start address for the VM region in [product_name] is set; a 32-bit value from HR11 gets written to VW0, and HR12 to VW2. The converted integer is shown on the output (Aq) of the F/I converter, not at the VM locations themselves. Additional notes: In [product_name], holding registers start at address 1; if Arduino starts at 0, add an offset of 1 to the connection table. That means Arduino's register 11 is HR12 on [product_name] if Arduino starts at 0, and HR11 otherwise. I do not know if the Arduino Unit ID is 255, and you must make sure the F/I converter uses the correct resolution for your integer values.

You can experiment in simulation mode. Make a program using F/I (VD0), followed by an analog amplifier. Add a message display tied to the analog amplifier parameter. During simulation, add VD0 to the data table as a float format. Enter a test value like 1.2 in the 'new value' column. The resulting value will show in the message text. Adjust the F/I properties or the amplifier as needed. Note that [product_name] does not support floating-point calculations directly, so further processing must be done using integers. Hope this is helpful.

Check the example attached for float and double handling with a message showing the result. This sample uses a diagram rather than forming a network project; if I have a single Modbus partner, I prefer diagrams. Change your program as you like. In your code, remove the direction from [product_name] to Modbus unless you are sure the holding register can be written safely. In my example, play with HR numbers (+/-1) to get the needed value, and adjust IP addresses as necessary. Regards, [user_name]

I don't understand why you opened a new thread for the same Modbus communication problem discussed in your previous topic.

When [company_name] provides a Modbus driver, it tries to adhere to Modbus specifications (originally designed for Modicon PLCs) on its hardware. Modbus registers are 16-bit and mainly transmit word-sized values, typically integers in specific ranges. Floating-point (REAL) numbers require two sequential registers because they use 32 bits, formatted per IEEE 754. If volts start at address 2 in the mapping, read both address 2 and 3, and move them into a 32-bit REAL register in your [product_name] program to interpret the value. Typically, it's more important to select the correct offset than the function code (3 or 4), unless your mapping differs significantly. Here’s an IEEE 754 conversion example: If the value is 240.0 Volts, you’ll send the corresponding binary and hexadecimal 32-bit values through two Modbus registers. Hope this clarifies things. Edit: I saw your discussions with [user_name] and noticed [product_name] is involved in your setup. However, [product_name] CPUs can't process floating point numbers internally. To clarify, let me outline an example: I want to read the counter parameter of the up/down counter, which is of DWord type and mapped to the VM address 0. According to the Modbus address mapping, VW (variable word) 0 aligns with HR (holding register) 1. Since DWord occupies two registers, I need to read HR 1 and 2. Similarly, to write to the Off Threshold parameter, also DWord type at VM address 4, the mapping according to Modbus tables means it uses HR 3 and 4. It seems that VM addresses reflect bytes, and DWord covers 4 bytes. The Modbus address table shows that the VW range is nearly double the HR range. If this is correct, I'd recommend updating the table for clarity. Thanks for reading.

No, the range shown is correct.

Thanks for the response. For clarification, when I mentioned byte in brackets, I meant the range is counted by bytes. Are you indicating that the unit is a word? So, VW0 is the zeroth word, VW1 is the first word, VW2 is the second word, etc.?

No, your reply makes it clear you haven't understood my previous answer in your other topic. The VM area is organized by bytes. There are 851 bytes, ranging from VB0 to VB850. If you write into VW0 and also VW1, they overlap. VW0 covers VB0 and VB1, VW1 covers VB1 and VB2, so both VW0 and VW1 affect VB1. Please see the attached explanation for further details.

Is there any way to send an email from my [product_name] controller over LAN? I want an email to be sent when specific variables in my program go high. I found that sending emails is possible using a [product_name] communication module, but, as far as I can tell, this only works over a wireless mobile network. This requires a SIM card and a data contract, which I would prefer to avoid due to poor cell reception at the installation site and additional monthly costs.

No, sending emails directly with just a [product_name] controller is not possible. The Eaton easyE4 controller can handle up to 3 system emails and 32 user-defined emails. It triggers an email server to send messages, but compatibility is limited to certain email servers.

I've implemented this using a [product_name] and a Mikrotik Routerboard. The latest RouterOS beta adds modbus support, and with scripting plus scheduling on RouterOS, you can poll modbus registers and act accordingly. RouterOS can send emails and SMS messages natively. The setup involves RouterOS continuously reading modbus holding registers from the [product_name] every second. If a value exceeds a set limit, the [product_name] sets an 'alarm bit.' RouterOS detects this 'alarm bit,' reads the current value via modbus, composes an email, and sends it over LAN/WAN/LTE/3G. To avoid repeated alerts while the alarm condition exists, RouterOS sends an 'ack bit' to the [product_name] or maintains acknowledgment states itself. While RouterOS can calculate threshold exceedances, it's easier to do this within the [product_name]. Boolean operations like setting or resetting bits are more challenging in RouterOS scripts but achievable with persistence using bit-shifting and masking.

You should use a mathematical instruction. Map the value from the HMI into parameter V1 of the mathematical block using VM mapping.

Thanks for your suggestion. I'm curious if anything needs to be configured in parameters V3 or V4, since my current setup always outputs zero from the mathematical block.

If you're following my example, the value assigned to parameter V1 (from HMI) is multiplied by parameter V2 (which should be set to 2 or 20 based on your needs). V3 and V4 are not necessary and stay at zero—these are simply added in the calculation. The formula executed by the block is (((V1 + V2) + V3) + V4). Make sure the mathematical instruction is activated. You can enable it by linking the EN input to a HIGH block or by negating the input, for example by inverting the connector in your setup.

Thank you, I hadn't activated the block before. I followed your advice and negated the EN input, and it works perfectly now. Apologies, as I'm new to programming and sometimes overlook basic setup steps. Thanks again for the help.

You are making the same mistake—you haven’t activated the mathematical instruction block. There are two ways to do this: 1) Connect the EN input of the block to a HIGH signal, or 2) Invert the EN input connector (right-click on the EN-Input and choose 'Invert connector'). Also note: The analog output requires 1000 units as its input. If the HMI value is 500 (for 50.0 Hz), the multiplier should be 2. If the HMI value is 50 (for 50 Hz), the multiplier should be 20.

The steps below are a bit lengthy but solve the issue. I've translated them here—feel free to print them out for reference! 1) Open your affected program 2) Zoom out until you see the entire program 3) Go to TOOL --> OPTIONS --> COLOURS, select BLACK for simulation colors and APPLY/OK 4) Make a small change in the program (add and delete a block or move one slightly) 5) Start SIMULATION mode and check all lines are black 6) While simulation is running, close the software 7) When asked to save because of changes, select YES and save (either same or new file) 8) Reopen the software—make sure it's the only open instance! 9) Open your newly saved program 10) Return to TOOLS --> OPTIONS --> COLOURS and set the standard colors for everything, then APPLY/OK 11) Repeat this for every affected program, since the error is saved in each one—not just a global setting Hope this helps! A key lesson: Always stop simulation and return to editing mode (ensuring lines turn black) before saving or making any changes. Also, only run one simulation at a time. This is good programming practice. Good luck managing the color changes!

If the [product_name] controller and SCADA system are not in the same subnet, you will need a gateway such as a router.

Hi, I would like to suggest a solution if possible. Is any recommendation welcome here? Please let me know which method would be the best.

If your SCADA system can communicate with the [product_name] controller over a LAN, then using a VPN is the simplest way. For more targeted responses, please provide specific questions. Regards, [user_name]

There is currently no setup in place. The project involves connecting between 4 and 25 [product_name] controllers in separate locations to a central monitoring station elsewhere. A SCADA system is one suggestion, but alternative solutions are also welcome.

As [user_name] mentioned, more details would help. Your question is too general. When you mention Ethernet, do you mean a company network, or are these locations far apart, requiring public internet? Also, specifying 4 to 25 [product_name] controllers isn't precise. What do you expect from SCADA—would an HMI suffice, or is something more complex needed? Also keep in mind: this is a user forum, not an official hotline or support center. The platform is provided and monitored by [company_name]. For direct support, please raise a support request or contact your local [company_name] office.

Currently, there is neither hardware, software, nor a defined plan, but you seek guidance on connecting everything. Start by mapping out the existing locations, including internet access details like fixed IP or dynamic DNS. Explain what you want to monitor via SCADA or PC. Using VPNs lets you treat each controller as a local device. You could also use the internal web server or an enhanced server created by [product_name] web editor software, which simplifies monitoring multiple signals. Note that real-time connectivity over the internet is not possible, and sequence data might sometimes be lost. For further guidance, consult manuals for the controller and web editor software. There are no generic solutions suitable for every situation. Regards, [user_name]

Thank you all for your valuable advice. I've attached a project layout to clarify: 1) Four [product_name] controllers are in different locations without LAN connectivity between them. 2) The goal is to monitor both analog and digital signals nearly live (some minor data loss is fine), mostly related to water salinity, and no rapid actions are expected. 3) As outlined, we want to centralize monitoring of these signals from all four controllers at one location, aiming for a cost-effective solution. Do you think the [product_name] web editor software is suitable for this? Also, to avoid using routers with static IPs, can dynamic DNS be used?

You now have an initial project design, but still lack essential details. Since there's no direct connection between the [product_name] controllers and the monitoring station, every site needs an internet connection, usually via a router for each location. If those routers are part of a company network, the network administrator should determine whether VPN connections are permitted. Download the controller and web editor manuals to review the internal and extended web server features. The internal web server can display values and messages, and allows monitoring up to eight variables on a separate page. The extended web server offers more features and custom layouts, needing at least [product_name] V[version_no] and SDCards for each controller. Depending on your needs, you can implement more advanced solutions such as creating your own interface, with clients and servers available online for various programming languages. Start by testing the internal web server locally, then add VPN connectivity for remote access if suitable. Regards, [user_name]

Your technical support is extremely useful—thank you! I have one final question: Is it possible to use public internet connectivity without VPN, if security is not a concern? Referring to the attached image, if that's feasible, which communication processor would you recommend? VPN is available, but I am exploring a more cost-effective alternative.

Direct communication between two LAN networks is not possible—see the 'private networks' section in this [url]. LAN packets need to be encapsulated for WAN transmission, typically using VPN or IP tunneling. Since I'm not a WAN/VPN/IP Tunnel expert, I suggest searching online for further details, beginning with the provided [url]. Regards, [user_name]

Hello everyone, I have a question about the data log feature. I need to save the date and time whenever an input turns on or off. Is this possible through the data log function? Thank you in advance, [user_name]

Yes, this is possible. Every entry created by the data log feature includes a time and date stamp. However, you should wait at least 500 ms between each log entry to ensure proper logging.

Thank you for your quick response. My next question: how can I keep these values accessible later using the access tool? The device is installed in a location where the SD card cannot be easily reached.

The [product_name] Access Tool cannot read or process a data log file directly. You either create a data log on an SD card, or you use the Access Tool separately.

So, is it not possible to read the information stored by the data log function remotely? Can we instead store the data as variables? From what I’ve seen, it appears possible to read variables through the access tool. [url]

Refer to section 2.4 (Getting [product_name] Variable Value) in the help document. There are two different concepts: - Data log ([product_name]) - A log file produced by the access tool The data log is a file generated and saved automatically to the SD card by the device. The access tool produces its own log file. Instructions for creating a log file using the access tool are found in section 2.4 (page 15) of the help document.

Hello, we typically use the "Softkey" block with retentive enable as a software selector, adjusting the "Status" parameter via the BM display (see [document]). Now, we want to change this "Status" block parameter through ModBus, but "Softkey" blocks can't be included in the VM configuration. Is there any way to implement such functionality? No, this isn't possible.

However, I can't modify this "Network input" bit from the BM display. Is there a way to change the "Network input" from the BM display? Thanks.

No, that's not possible either.

However, I might have a solution for your problem. Try converting the softkey into a button and generate a dynamic signal from the network input. You can use a cycle pulse, created from the static network input signal, by continuously resetting a network output with the same address using a LOW block. Then, connect the softkey output and network input to an OR block, and link the OR block's output to the trigger input of a pulse relay. [document]

I'll try your suggestion tomorrow and provide feedback!

Your solution works well. The only drawback is that on the BM display, I need to set up two fields: one that lets the operator change the switch state (which immediately reverts after being set) and another that shows the retentive state of the selector (whether changed by switch or ModBus). Thanks again!

Hello everyone, I have two questions about the special flag M8 (power reset): 1) What is the relationship between the power reset and the retentive flag for special functions? For instance, if I set the R parameter for a latching relay and connect the R (reset) pin to M8 (power reset), what will happen? Does the power reset clear the latching relay and then restore its state from before the power failure, or does it overwrite the retained state? 2) Is it possible to access M8 (power reset) from within a user-defined function (UDF)? Sometimes it's necessary to reset a pulse relay at startup, but if the relay is inside a UDF, direct access to M8 seems unavailable. I appreciate any advice.

The special flag M8 serves as a startup indicator. After a device restarts, M8 goes high only during the initial cycle, which is useful for triggering specific actions right after startup.

However, the core question remains: Is this executed before or after the retention process? If it's after, will it overwrite the retained state?

Please refer to the attached document for further details.

If you use an RS relay with retention enabled, and the relay is ON when the device loses power, after power is restored, the RS relay will also be ON. But if you connect the R input to the M8 flag, the RS relay will be OFF during the first cycle after power-up and will stay OFF until you set it again. When powering up any programmable logic device, the initial step sets all retentive values (timers, counters, relays, etc.) to those stored before power loss. The program then proceeds with the first cycle: 1. Read all input statuses and store in registers 2. Execute the program, writing outputs to registers 3. Update outputs with the values in the registers 4. Repeat from step 1 Throughout one cycle, the input status remains consistent. Any input change during step 2 will be processed in the following cycle. If you want M8 used in both the main program and in a UDF, you need to first utilize M8 in the main program and connect it as an input to your UDF.

Thanks everyone! 1) If I understand correctly, the retentive function executes before any part of the program. This means the elements' states are first restored, and then the circuit behavior, such as power reset via M8, begins. 2) Unfortunately, my user-defined function doesn't have enough I/O pins to accommodate M8 as an input.

I'm having trouble retrieving Modbus data from an Intesis module that acts as a gateway between my heat pump and Modbus RTU. The Intesis is connected to the [product_name] CIM, which indicates that an S7 connection is active between the [product_name] and CIM module. With Modbus Poll and a direct RS485 laptop connection, logical data appears from Intesis. However, attempting to connect from my laptop to the CIM using Modbus Poll (Modbus TCP, slave ID 1) results in repeated read and write errors. The laptop's IP is already allowed in the CIM settings, and CIM claims a valid Modbus link. Using "Network Analog Input" with the provided settings only returns a value of 0, where a value near 200 (room temperature in decidegrees) is expected. I could only upload one attachment initially, but will try to add more attachments in a follow-up. How can I successfully retrieve data from my Intesis module?

If you need further information, just ask. Is it possible to upload my actual program here?

Did you check if the Intesis RTU data is appearing in the CIM? If you access CIM through a web browser, use the RestFulAPI to verify if the RTU values (such as 200) are present in CIM VW0&2. You may need to offset the register number by 1. Access example: [url] This browser command shows VW0 as unsigned. If the value (like 200) is present, configure data exchange from CIM memory to [product_name] using the S7-data configuration table within CIM. That places the RTU data in [product_name] at your configured VM address. Hope this helps.

It only displays zero for the value.

Here are the Modbus Poll settings (read values near 200 shown on lines 4 and 5). After attempting this, I reconnected the CIM to Intesis, added a new line to request HR6, and tested several links for data: [url] Using variants like vu1/vu2 at the end, I finally received results. For vu1, the outcome was 195, likely representing my real-time room temperature or setpoint times 10. However, vu1 sometimes shows 195, sometimes 50115 or 49920 upon refresh. These changing numbers don't appear when querying Intesis directly by RTU. Cable between CIM and Intesis is 20cm STP, between laptop and Intesis is the same cable at 1m. Shielding isn't connected on Intesis (no option), but is grounded at laptop and CIM. What could explain these three different values showing up while refreshing?

If you read vu0 via Restful API, that's bytes 0 and 1. If vu1 returns the desired result, it's likely a question of data format or missing offset. I suggest applying a +1 offset to HR/IR as needed. The unstable value could mean multiple RTU devices are being polled, sharing the same memory area. To transfer the value to [product_name], configure an S7-data transfer from CIM (VW1) to [product_name] VM memory. The simplest method to display the result is to use a network analog input leading into an analog amplifier, then show it on the [product_name] display as a text message. Alternatively, use the online test and datatable VWx. Hope that helps!

Applying an offset is typical—and easily done. I don't see how the CIM would be polling multiple devices if its configuration is set only for device 1, as shown in your screenshot. Polling at 1 second seems reasonable for Intesis. Experimenting with terminating resistors and power cycling didn't improve things—values change but are still sometimes illogical. Converting results to HEX doesn't reveal any Modbus error codes. The P1 LED blinks rapidly even though CIM is polling once per second—could CIM actually be polling more quickly, or is Intesis sending data at high frequency? Testing data requests with both CIM-Intesis and laptop-Intesis (using identical cables) results in: laptop—zero errors and good data; CIM—mostly incorrect results. Two data table rows in CIM, requesting the same parameter: - VU0 yields 49920 consistently - VU1 yields 195 consistently - VU2/3/4/5... all yield zero CIM Modbus settings are in the attachment. Does this point to a CIM malfunction? I'll try to read the 195 value on [product_name] tomorrow.

My suggestion: first, make sure only CIM, your laptop (with browser) and the ModbusRTU device are connected. This guarantees no other hardware or software interfere. Next, only link one RTU device register to one memory address in CIM. Third, determine if an address offset is needed. Test HR register variation (-1/0/+1): e.g., for HR3, also try HR2 and HR4. See the provided RTU photo. Then, use RestfulAPI to verify the value's validity and stability. If it's good in CIM, then use the S7 connection to [product_name], and confirm if the HR parameter is accurate and visible on the [product_name] display or online data table. Check your RTU if the desired parameter is truly in HR—it could be IR. Polling at a 1s rate shouldn't affect data transfer consistency. Good luck!

The plan seemed simple but turned out otherwise... After following the steps, RestFul API shows VU0 (Modbus register 4) stable at 195—good start. However, changing the thermostat setpoint to 20 (should show 200), the value stays at 195. Changing the register to 5 (expecting 196) returns 0. Power-cycling CIM results in a slow, unresponsive web interface. A full reset restores responsiveness, but the value switches from 195 to 0 despite carefully checking the wiring and settings. Connecting RTU cable to laptop yields flawless, logical values. Reconnecting to CIM only gives zero from RestFul API. Tweaking RTU register between 3 and 6 (expecting 195 for setpoint and ~195 for measured value) only yields zero. Swapping RTU cable does not help—values remain zero. Testing new cable with laptop again yields correct results. Just to confirm: is the CIM wiring correct? The ground at the top ties to the casing (not RTU shield), and casing is grounded with other 230V equipment. The RTU cable is 2-pair STP.

Modbus register 4's value is now fixed at 195, no matter how I change the setpoint. The measured temperature is 19.6, so expect 196 if that is the register being read. Reading as HR or IR yields no difference. Is there a way to further debug what's preventing CIM from correctly reading data from Intesis? If I were using Modbus Poll, I'd get explicit error messages—read/write timeouts, etc. Can CIM reveal such feedback?

Good news—I finally have the setpoint and measured temperature readings working! The main issue seemed to be wiring. I sometimes saw values and sometimes got nonsense. Eventually, I stripped a longer section of insulation so there was more copper exposed at the bottom of the CIM. With the wire pushed in as deep as possible, connection became reliable. It seems CIM's wire connector is deeper than my USB-RTU dongle, and only a small amount of copper was making contact in CIM before. This caused unreliable readings. Troubleshooting was made more difficult by some unclear points in the CIM and Sinamics tutorial, along with limited feedback from the CIM. Currently, everything is stable after one day. Is [company_name] interested in detailed feedback to improve the tutorial or to clarify the CIM interface further?

I assume the process begins from the home position. Is it possible to position the sensors so that the one triggered first indicates the direction of rotation?

Yes, the sensors are offset so that after leaving home, rotating left triggers sensor A before sensor B, and rotating right triggers B before A. Actually, it's only one sensor made by Kubler called an Encoder prox, which when triggered by the sprocket produces an output similar to a typical encoder.

You can use whichever input is triggered first after the home position to set a flag for left or right rotation, and use this to determine whether to count up or down. Make sure only one flag can be set at a time—the first one disables the other. Then use the home input to reset both flags and your counter every revolution.

That alone isn't sufficient. This setup is for a fire truck ladder where the operator controls the direction from the ladder end. Once the rotation moves from home (say, 150 pulses clockwise), the operator doesn't necessarily complete a full turn back to home—they might rotate 150 pulses clockwise and then return 20 pulses. So, direction monitoring needs to be continuous, not only after leaving home.

When moving clockwise, the sensor A positive edge will occur with sensor B OFF; moving counterclockwise, sensor A's positive edge will occur with sensor B ON. You can set up a counter using sensor A as the count input and sensor B as the direction input, or use two counters to keep track of your position and rotation direction. Hope this helps!

Hi [user_name], thanks for the [product_name] example. What calculations are needed to modify the output ranges?

This setup uses a simple linear equation for each segment. The general formula is: Input value * Gain + Offset Example: Input range: 3.01V to 5.00V Output range: 2.50V to 4.50V Given Input value: 4.00V Gain calculation: (Output Max - Output Min) / (Input Max - Input Min) Gain = (450 - 250) / (500 - 301) = 1.005 Offset calculation: Output Min - Input Min * Gain Offset = 250 - 301 * 1.005 = -53 Output value: Input value * Gain + Offset = 400 * 1.005 - 53 = 349 (which is 3.49V)

My reasoning was to have one master with the main configuration/diagram, and two slaves simply following the master, so only the master needed updates. One more thing: Based on what you said, are the two slaves not working because the master reports a S7 Client Disconnected error? Initially, I checked the built-in average function, but it requires a fixed monitoring period to be set ahead of time, which I don’t know. My goal is to monitor the average temperature only during operational cycles of a heating system (excluding pauses), but these periods vary each time. Sometimes the cycle is 20 minutes, sometimes 50, and pauses also change. The calculated average should cover all periods until a reset is triggered, not just one cycle. I think a program that uses a clock to calculate the average every minute could be a solution, but I’m unsure how to implement it on [product_name] hardware. Any suggestions would be appreciated.

It’s not possible to directly transfer all functions of an S7 function block into [product_name] programming. Also, I’m not clear why the average shouldn’t be calculated continuously. The logic behind this isn’t obvious to me.

Perhaps this is similar to what you’re looking for.

Continuous calculation makes sense, but since the sample time isn’t known beforehand, I chose 1 minute as an interval. However, I need a cumulative average covering entire periods (e.g., 20 min, 45 min, or any variable length) and across multiple periods until reset. Regarding your program: I’m having trouble understanding it enough to test effectively. I’ve modified it slightly to better fit my needs (please see version 2). Could you clarify a few things: - Where can I check the average output? Is it B005 Aq? - Is sampling every minute? How can I change it, if needed? - Is there a way to reset the calculated average and start over? Testing as follows, I received unexpected results: - First minute: Set A1 to -10°C (output B005Aq displays -10° as expected) - Second minute: Quickly set A1 to +10°C (after one more minute, expected average for both minutes is 0, but display shows 10°) It seems to only calculate the last minute’s value, not cumulative average. It behaves like the regular average block. I added B007 for comparison. For I1 (simulating active period): If set to zero (pause), the average should freeze until a new active period starts. It doesn’t seem to work this way; the output keeps updating, which is problematic. Maybe I just don’t fully understand how to use the program.

Maybe this chart showing the temperature over various ON periods will clarify: I want the average to include all ON cycles, not just the last minute.

I misunderstood your requirements. You may need to use another PLC for this task. The reference to S7 and the FB works in other PLCs, but not in [product_name], since [product_name] lacks data block memory. Based on this, I won’t provide a full explanation. In my view, some users expect too much from [product_name]. [company_name] even categorizes the device as a programmable relay, not a full PLC like the S7.

[user_name], calculating an average from a limited number of values isn't difficult. Even S7 FB average can’t handle infinite samples because you must sum all values (X1, X2, X3…Xn) and divide by n, which requires storage space for each value. Depending on available resources, handling 50 values may be possible (using 50 Min/Max blocks plus arithmetic blocks). Check the attachment for a sample using 9 blocks and arithmetic operations. The computation is split—groups of three need one arithmetic block, then a final block combines these. Supporting more samples means a larger, more complex program. The provided example uses a pulse generator for simulation; adjust its timing to change sample intervals (e.g., to 1 minute). You can expand the Min/Max chain depending on available resources. Best regards, [user_name]

Thanks, I didn’t expect this to be so complex or demanding in terms of resources. Ideally, I'd like to average at least one ON cycle, even if it lasts anywhere between 20 to 180 minutes. This only seems possible by changing the average sampling interval to 20 minutes instead of 1 minute in your example. I asked a friend (an S7 programmer) for advice; he proposed an S7 block-based solution, but I wasn’t able to adapt it to [product_name], hence my question here. Please let me know if the concept is correct and if it can be implemented with [product_name]. (Assumed network I/O would behave similarly to data blocks in S7) P.S. He suggested triggering samples based on value changes rather than using a clock—unsure which approach would be best for processing.

There are two general methods for calculating the arithmetic average. The first is to store all values, sum them, and divide by the count. There’s also a second method, usable in S7: accumulate values directly and track a counter. This method doesn’t work in [product_name] due to 16-bit integer limits (-32768 to +32767). Some tricks might enable higher values (like 32-bit), reducing block usage, but that gets complex. For that, I’d need details about your value range: e.g., -100 to +100, -1000 to +1000, etc. If you’re not committed to [product_name], it’s better to use a logic controller supporting 32-bit integers instead. You can add larger values many times before overflow, unlike in [product_name]. Also, check if arithmetic average is the correct calculation type for your needs—Wikipedia lists arithmetic, geometric, harmonic averages... Best regards, [user_name]

Yes, I understand the difference. Regarding values: after 0-10V conversion, max readings are -20°C to 60°C, but realistically the heating system operates between 20°C and 55°C. Monitoring and analysis are important because output temperature affects heat pump efficiency. I’ll review the explanation of averaging. Correction: 20.0 to 55.0 is just a display format (one decimal point); actual calculated values range from 200 to 550.

My questions relate to possible solution options. I once assisted someone in another forum to build an energy meter by accumulating power in an arithmetic block every second. When the block exceeded 3600, I increased a counter and subtracted 3600, allowing precise kWh counting. A similar method could work for you, summing values every minute. The challenge is dividing the sum by n (number of samples/minutes), since it’s split across counters and arithmetic blocks. See attachment for a possible solution and try to follow the basic principle; comments are included throughout. There may be some errors in the program. Hello, I'm new to [product_name] and have a challenge in calculating meters on a plastic film line. My setup uses a roller with a 60mm diameter and one proximity sensor, which generates one pulse for every 188.5mm of roller movement. The speed of the line is about 20m/min. How can I set things up so that the measurement results in exactly 1000mm? Any advice would be appreciated. Regards,

1000mm can't be measured exactly, because 1000mm isn't a precise multiple of 188.5mm. You can scale your measurement in millimeters, but it will only round to increments of 188.5mm, with possible adjustments for full millimeters. Check the attached example with comments for more information. Regards, [user_name]

The display may show exactly 1000mm, but this isn't the true measured length. With 1834mm divided by 11, you get 166.73mm per pulse—but your setup actually gives 60mm x Pi = 188.5mm per pulse. You can't freely choose these values if you want displayed and actual lengths to match. Regards, [user_name]

You're correct again; that's the difference between running a simulation and actual operation. I'm learning more every day. Thanks again,

Using Windows 10 and a [product_name] device ([article_no]). The connection attempt starts, but the system says PC and [product_name] are not on the same subnet.

Ethernet cable to [product_name] device. Device IP: 192.168.0.123, Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0, Gateway: 233.0.0.0. PC IP: 169.254.142.102, Subnet mask: 255.255.0.0, Gateway: 0.0.0.0.

Your PC and [product_name] device are on different subnets with different subnet masks and gateways. The device is on subnet 192.168.0.x, while the PC is on 169.254.142.x, so they can't communicate. The first three numbers in the IP should match on both, but the fourth should differ. Both subnet masks must also match, e.g., 255.255.255.0. If a gateway is used and devices connect via a router, it must be the same for both devices.

Assign your PC an IP address manually, such as 192.168.0.120, ensuring the same subnet and gateway as [product_name]. The 169.x IP address appears because you're not connected to a DHCP server to assign an IP. According to RFC5735, the 169.254.0.0/16 range is allocated for link-local communication, auto-assigned when DHCP is unavailable.

70% OFF-TOPIC Hi, Reading your post, my first thought was: "Here is someone hoping for a ready-made solution." But seeing [user_name] as your name, I know that's not the case. I propose you create a sample program and let us know where you encounter issues. This way, you learn the most. We can then help you move forward—does that sound okay? If you're under time pressure, feel free to disagree or skip my suggestion. [user_name], what do you think?

You can set up a counter yourself. Use an asynchronous pulse generator to create pulses every second. Count the seconds while the motor is ON, and use another counter for the OFF state. By dividing total seconds by 3600, you get the hours. You can reset at any time—this is a flexible way to obtain an hour counter.

Hello, Thank you for responding. My other posts are for personal learning, as I purchased [product_name] hardware to improve my skills with [company_name]'s products. I appreciate everyone’s assistance. Back to the topic: I’ll put together a sample and share it here.

Please check if I'm heading in the right direction. I just need guidance on how to obtain the final result.

Are there any files available to review, besides empty folders?

Hello [user_name], There is a specific function for your requirement: Hour Counter. With it, you can set: - OT: Operating time—duration machine runs. - MI: Maintenance interval—the next maintenance time. - MN: Time until next maintenance. MN = OT - MI (hh:mm) These times can be displayed and reset partially or completely. If you want maintenance scheduling by weekdays, change input I1 to connect a Weekly Timer enabling the Hour Counter function. See attached draft for reference.

Hi, thanks for the example. I tested it in the simulation and now understand how the output works. Thank you.

I am trying to read parameters from a photovoltaic device to improve energy management. After some testing, I can communicate and accurately read single-word registers, but registers with more words (2 or 4) return zero values. I suspect that Float32 or Float64 types require additional handling with the [product_name] Integer/Float block, but I also cannot read unsigned Int32 or UInt64 types. Currently, I'm reading only the final word from the multi-word register sets, but this approach fails once it reaches the limit for a single word value (65,000). What am I missing? Maybe [product_name] is too limited to read multi-word registers via Modbus TCP?

The [product_name] only supports Int16 data types. It does not handle Int32 or any unsigned integer types.

To display UInt32 or Int32 values in [product_name], you would need to use an up/down counter. Write values (from 0 to 999,999) into the VM area of [product_name] using a 4-byte start address. Then, link the VM Mapping parameter to the counter's value. Note, this method only allows for display purposes, not for mathematical processing.

Is it possible to resolve this issue using F/I converters? In one example, a device provides double-word values as floating point numbers. These values are assigned to the [product_name]'s variable memory at a designated start address. However, [product_name] operates only with integers and cannot process floating point values directly. For further handling, you need to use the [product_name] block called the F/I converter (floating point/integer converter). [url]

The F/I converter cannot read UInt32 or Int32 values. It can only handle Float32 or Float64 types.

When running online, certain network inputs unexpectedly switch states without any indication on the screen, appearing to respond to analog input values in the code. Because I am not familiar with your [product_name] programs or HMI configuration, I can only make an educated guess. I suspect there is overlap in the VM storage region. Addressing within VM memory is based on bytes. For bits: address format is byte address, bit address, e.g., V0.0 means Byte0.Bit0. For bytes: a byte consists of 8 bits, for example, VB0 encompasses bits V0.0 - V0.7. For words: a word is made of two bytes, the starting address is the left byte, VW0 covers VB0 and VB1, or V0.0 - V1.7. For dwords: a dword has four bytes, with the left byte as the start address, VD0 covers VW0 and VW2, or VB0 - VB3, or V0.0 - V3.7.

Hello [user_name], thank you for your response! I found your addressing scheme on the forum—it clarified things and I've already tried it. Can I use V0.0 on [product_name] 1 (with IP 192.168.1.10) and reuse V0.0 on [product_name] 2 (IP 192.168.1.20)? Is there any conflict in the HMI, or does each IP keep things separate? To prevent issues, I've reorganized all VM and network input parameters, and will test tomorrow to see if the spontaneous switching is resolved.

Each [product_name] maintains its own memory space. You can transmit V0.0 from one [product_name] to the HMI without issue, so long as each [product_name] has a separate connection. The HMI uses the connection details to distinguish which V0.0 belongs to which [product_name].

Understood! I think I've identified my mistake. I started allocating addresses to network inputs before setting up VM mapping. [product_name] software automatically begins with VW0, and this overlapped with some of my NI addresses. I’ll be able to test and confirm this tomorrow. Thank you for your assistance!

That's the issue. If you assign V0.0 - V1.7 for digital bits, you cannot use VW0 elsewhere—doing so causes address overlap.

Use VW2 instead of IW2.

Your gain formula has an error. Gain = (500-5)/(5-1) = 123.75 [L/min]/V. But in your [product_name] program, 5V corresponds to 500 units, and 1V to 100 units. So the actual Gain is (500-5)/(500-100) = 1.2375.

If you use an analog amplifier with appropriate settings, minimum and maximum values are calculated automatically. At 1V input, you get 5 L/min; at 5V input, about 500 L/min after amplification.

Why use Modbus to communicate between two [company_name] devices ([product_name] and [product_name])? Communication is simpler over Ethernet TCP/IP using their native protocol. Who requests such a configuration? Two [company_name] devices, both capable of using the native protocol, communicating unnecessarily over Modbus TCP/IP seems questionable. People choose based on their requirements, but I have no explanation for all data resetting to zero every 30 seconds.

Modbus allows you to set the interval for data gathering; native protocol connections do not. If you need to collect data from remote locations via NB-IOT or GPRS, perhaps once an hour, Modbus can be more efficient as the native protocol is quite 'chatty' (with traffic between 3 and 30 kbit/sec depending on the number of data points, and traffic remains constant). Please consider this before dismissing the choice.

For my needs, it's not ideal.

Depending on your application, it can make sense to favor Modbus due to the continuous traffic of the native protocol. [user_name], have you verified that your server device was fully set up as a Modbus server and is continuously providing data?

The main concern isn't protocol 'chattiness,' but the issue where, after a certain period, all data resets to zero.

Try customizing the polling interval for Modbus queries from your client device. By default, [product_name] polls Modbus registers every 80 milliseconds—which is more frequent than necessary. Setting it to around 500 milliseconds or even longer may be sufficient for most tasks. Frequent polling may occasionally cause unexpected issues.

By default, there is no active polling interval set—the time values are inaccessible and greyed out in the settings.

The default polling rate is at its maximum, with approximately 10 to 12 queries each second.

Let me clarify some basics: The analog converter of [product_name] converts input signals into units ranging from 0-1000, regardless of whether it is 0-10V or 0/4-20mA. For a 4-20 mA signal, the initial 0-4 mA is outside the usable range, leaving you with 800 units (since 20 mA - 4 mA = 16mA). Here's the breakdown: 0 mA = 0 units, 4 mA = 200 units, 6 mA = 300 units, ... up to 20 mA = 1000 units. To set up the analog amplifier, you would use: Gain: 1.25 for a total of 1250 units. Offset: -250 so 1250 -250 = 1000 units. Min: 0 (offset correction), Max: 1000 (offset correction included). For example, at 6 mA the number after A/D conversion is 300. 300 * 1.25 (Gain) = 375, then 375 - 250 (Offset) = 125. The final, processed value is 125, which at one decimal is 12.5.

I'm still not clear… Is it possible to use both NPN and PNP sensors with the same [product_name] 24RCE/24RCEo unit (for example, connecting 2 NPN sensors and 3 PNP sensors to one [product_name])? Is it possible to mix [product_name] modules/units that have NPN capabilities with ones that do not (for example, main [product_name] 24RCE linked to a DM8, with NPN sensors to the base and PNP sensors to the expansion)? How should NPN sensors be wired?

Hi, It seems there is some confusion. Generally, you can connect anything to [product_name] as long as the connector fits! You mentioned NTC, PTC (for temperature measurement?). For [product_name], no NTC/PTC modules or functions are available. Since NTC/PTC are resistors whose value changes with temperature, you can technically use them by driving a current through the NTC/PTC and measuring voltage via an analog input on [product_name] BM or an AM2 analog module. However, keep in mind [product_name] only has a resolution of 1000 steps, so the measurement range may be limited. Using a sensor with a 0-10V or 0/4-20mA output, or a PT100/1000 with an AM2 RTD module, is recommended for better accuracy in temperature measurements. Hope this helps.

I would like to connect NPN-type inductive proximity sensors similar to those found here: [url]

However, by placing a resistor (about 1000 Ohm) between the positive supply and digital input of [product_name], then connecting the NPN sensor between the digital input and negative supply, it will function. The exact resistor value depends on the characteristics of your sensor. Remember to invert this input in the programming software ([product_name] software), which is straightforward. If possible, consider using PNP sensors, as they generally connect directly to [product_name].

I was able to rent a sample [product_name] 24R v4 from [company_name]. We tested it with our sensors successfully. The wiring was: - 24VDC from power supply, M to P1 and L+ to P2 on [product_name] - 3-wire proximity inductive sensor: blue to M/P1, brown to L+/P2, and I1..I8 to black on [product_name]. This allowed us to use all our NPN 24VDC sensors with [product_name] 24R without issues. Finally: 1. Is it possible to connect [version_no] extension modules to [product_name] v4? 2. Can any extension module with transistor outputs be used on [product_name] 24R with inverted polarity? Hello all! Yes, the [product_name] 12/24RC(o), 24RC(o) and 230RC(o) models include potential-free relay outputs. The internal program only closes the relay contacts. For example, you can connect an AC voltage like 220V to one side of the Q1 relay, and when the relay is activated, that voltage becomes available to the connected circuit. Similarly, Q2 can have 12V DC on one side, which gets delivered to the circuit when the relay is switched by the program. This applies to all relay outputs, including those on [product_name] expansion modules, though the current is limited to 5A on expansions. The main module relays support up to 10A AC current, whereas for DC current, it's best to stay below 8A for longer relay lifespan. text:
Hello everyone, I recently started working with PLC programming and am currently using this PLC device. Programming is going well, but now I need to share some data from my analog inputs with our company's SCADA system. For example, I have a PT1000 sensor on AI1 linked to an analog threshold trigger [article_no], and its output is mapped in my software as a Word at address VW4. The SCADA communicates using S7 drivers, and I've already configured the server connection on the [product_name] device including the correct TSAP, which works for reading digital input bits. However, I'm unable to read the value from VW4, which I've mapped. What physical address should I use in the SCADA tag to access VM mapped values like in my setup? Sorry if anything is unclear—I'm still new to this and appreciate any guidance. Thanks in advance for any help!

There aren't special SCADA addresses within the VM memory area. Any unused address in the VM memory space can be used. It's important to understand how the memory area is structured to prevent overlapping accesses. The user-accessible memory area is 851 bytes, from byte 0 to byte 850, and is addressed by byte. For bits: Vx.y, where x is the byte address and y the bit inside the byte (e.g., V0.0). For bytes: VBx, representing each byte (e.g., VB0 = V0.0 to V0.7). Word is VWx, composed of 2 bytes (e.g., VW0 = VB0 + VB1 = V0.0 to V0.7 plus V1.0 to V1.7). DWord is VDx, made of 2 words; VD0 = VW0 + VW2 = VB0 + VB1 + VB2 + VB3, covering bits V0.0 to V3.7.

Hello [user_name], I appreciate your answer. I had already read your helpful PDF attached to another forum topic! That's why I'm unsure why I can't see output on my SCADA. I'm attaching a section of my software with Q1, which I used to check the SCADA and [product_name] connection linked to SCADA via I/O physical address Q0.0. Based on your PDF and these tests, I expected the physical address for my [article_no] to be VW4, but it's not showing any value.

Everything in your program looks correct, and there's no overlapping. Are you aware that the value in VW4 is an integer value? What type of SCADA system are you using?

Just to clarify: Should I be able to view any Word value I've mapped by inspecting it bit by bit? Specifically, if I look at bits V4.0 to V4.7 and V5.0 to V5.7, should I see boolean values that match my mapped Word?

In Parameter-VM-Mapping, 'Word' refers to the data width (16 bits), not the data type. Byte is 8 bits, Word is 16 bits, and DWord is 32 bits.

Yes, that's how it works. I was also expecting to browse the mapped word by checking its bits from V5.0 to V4.7. Anyway, I've resolved the issue! The correct way to link the tag in my SCADA is to use the address DB1.DBW4. Thanks for your support!

I had asked which SCADA system you are using but didn't get a reply.

You're right, sorry about that. During our discussion, I managed to figure out the correct way to access the memory. For reference, I'm using Movicon Next 3.4. Thanks again for your assistance!

feature_keywords: VM mapping || Word address || S7 driver || SCADA integration

Advice explaining VM memory layout, tag addressing, and differences in memory data width and format supported user understanding, leading to successful configuration.

text: Hello everyone, The [product_name]-[article_no] introduces several new function blocks. In this review, I'd like to discuss the "analog filter" block from an application-oriented perspective: The "analog filter" block computes a sliding average based on n previous values over time. Achieving this in hardware typically requires significant effort, so my previously published circuits were limited to n = 4, 8, or 10. The block's capability to handle up to 256 values, as noted in the documentation, is impressive. However, the permitted n values are restricted to a few predefined options (it would be far more useful if users could freely select any value between 1 and 256, with referencing and external triggering also supported). I have concerns about how the time interval between sampled values is specified—it is strictly linked to the (variable) cycle frequency of [product_name], which is essentially the program frequency. As per documentation: “[product_name] processes analog values every cycle. The number of cycles matches the configured sampling count.” Since the cycle frequency changes, this implementation only ensures the filter is suitable for analog values from blocks updated each cycle, not directly from analog inputs. Sampling intervals for analog input values should be defined by their own sampling rates, with user-adjustable update frequencies (typically every 50 ms or 300 ms, or a multiple thereof). Otherwise, incorrect results may occur depending on real signal characteristics. Summary: The "analog filter" block unfortunately cannot reliably filter analog input signals, because its operation is based on [product_name]’s cycle frequency, which diverges from the actual input sampling rates (e.g., 300 ms for basic modules, 50 ms for expansion modules). This can cause significant differences between the filtered outputs and true signal values. Since external triggering for sampling times isn’t available, the block generally falls short for accurate moving average calculations in most use cases. Best regards [user_name]

Hello, I'm new here and would appreciate feedback on MODBUS connectivity between [product_name] modules (currently considering [product_name] 24CEo). The system consists of one PC, a central controller, and 11 remote controllers over 2.2 km. Given the distance, I was considering using several RS485 extenders (about every kilometer or less) and connecting everything using MODBUS. Is this feasible, and what challenges might arise? Thanks in advance.

Unless [product_name] is notably different from the standard, it utilizes Modbus TCP/IP (ethernet) instead of RTU. Using fiber optics might be your best choice; it would simplify the setup compared to employing extenders.

The [product_name] variant has Ethernet functionality equivalent to the standard version. However, to use Modbus TCP/IP, it must be an FS4 model ([version_no], second generation or newer). Previous generations, like the first [version_no], can only use Ethernet TCP/IP and not Modbus TCP/IP.

Sharing my experience: for devices requiring MODBUS RTU, I use affordable MODBUS TCP-to-RTU converters (e.g., Protoss PE11). It's essential to have a separate converter for each device, as polling multiple devices through one converter may cause communication issues—if a device does not respond, the subsequent addresses might not be polled. For instance, with devices at addresses 2, 3, 4, and 5 in the network, if address 3 fails to reply, devices 4 and 5 won't be polled since they appear as a single device with one IP address. So, using one converter per device solves this problem, and fortunately, these converters are not costly.

Hello, I am seeking a method to trigger an action based on entropy. I want to delay an analog signal for a specific period and then use a comparator. Is it possible to apply two average value calculations with different intervals, use a mathematical function on the results, then run it through an analog threshold trigger to determine high or low outcomes? The challenge is that averaging tends to reduce deviations, so the first average interval should be short, while the second must be long enough to detect changes, which impacts both averages over time. This approach quickly becomes complicated and resource-intensive, leading to experimental solutions. Is there a way to time-delay either an analog signal or its digital value, and set the comparator to trigger at intervals longer than the delay?

Hello [user_name], what you're describing isn't easily achievable given limited resources. Analog signals can't be directly time-delayed in terms of their shape, though it's possible to delay sampled values. Irregular timing is possible to some extent, but both approaches consume significant resources in [product_name]. What exactly do you have in mind?

Perhaps it's feasible, but I'm unsure what to search for. I've tried using multiplexers and counters to store values, but they lose information when an input arrives. Could you suggest search terms or methods? Alternatively, if it's easier, please help with this: I want [product_name] to display "up" when temperature rises and "down" when it falls, using a deviation of 1°C with a calculation every 15 seconds, and repeat 15 seconds later. Please skip setting up the message text and assume the starting point is immediately after the analog amplifier.

Try exploring the help sections for relevant blocks and focus on understanding how each works.

Hello [user_name], how does this relate to the original topic? From your earlier post, you seem to want to sample the temperature at fixed intervals, compare the new measurement to the previous one, and then evaluate whether the value has increased or decreased. Is that correct?

I realized my earlier observation was mistaken. After reviewing the watchdog solution, it only works near a specific temperature. In such cases, a threshold trigger serves the same role, and if you need two positive outputs you can invert the signal. [user_name], you are correct. While we can't directly measure entropy, we can indicate if it's positive or negative, for example through a closed surface.

I've found some progress. Is it possible to keep the value of a "data storage after 5 seconds" counter stable through a reset? Can a digital value be converted into an analog one? If so, I could add an average and complete this approach.

You can use an analog multiplexer or a mathematical function to convert a counter's digital value to analog. For storing analog values, set "When EN=0, Keep last value" in the block parameters; a short pulse at EN will save the value. The best method to check "Is the value increasing or decreasing over the last 15 seconds?" is to compare two averages—one over 15 seconds and another over 1 second—using the "Average value" blocks. Shift registers and mathematical blocks could enable storage of up to 32 values for comparison, but the program would become quite large (roughly 200 blocks), likely offering little benefit over the simpler average and comparator setup.

Using two averages has issues with repeatability, as mentioned. After the second round, the program loses accuracy because counter updates outpace the averages, leading to invalid comparator values. I doubt a more complex program would offer any improvement. Could you share the initial structure of your proposal? Also, I tried looping the same signal to create a perpetual cycle, but that didn't work.

Thank you, [user_name]. Here's how to store two temperatures and calculate their difference: If result is positive, use output X1; if negative, X2. In the example, the general sampling time is 11 seconds, interlude is 10 seconds, first sample at about 5.01s, and second sample at about 10.01s.

Keep in mind that any new message activation cancels navigation and displays the highest priority message. It's best to use lower priorities (under 100) for regular settings, and set higher priorities (above 100) for alarms or notifications. Welcome! FS is the German abbreviation for production status (Fertigungsstand). Regarding program downloads to your new [product_name], usually a new series starts with production status FS01. For instance, the first generation of [product_name] basis modules had the identifier FS01-FS03, with firmware versions between V1.08.01 and V1.08.03 (updates weren’t possible). The programming software version used was V8.0. Later, in October 2016, the second generation appeared – same order numbers, but hardware identified as FS4, with software version V8.1, and production statuses FS04-FS06. This was a break from previous numbering logic. Firmware updates became possible from then on. The most recent release changed order numbers and reset production status numbers (FS01, FS02) for versions 1.82.01 and 1.82.02, and software version V8.2 (and V8.2.1). Security firmware updates are now available for recent generations due to vulnerabilities. The next major version is scheduled for release in October 2020.

Hello again, Using the [product_name] RTD module works much better for temperature measurement—thanks for pointing that out! Next, I want to use a fan to maintain my wood stove temperature at 120°C. When the stove heats to 120°C, the fan activates; as the temperature increases, the fan runs stronger, and as the temperature falls, the fan reduces its speed. I found a related discussion at [url], but currently, no current output comes from the [product_name] AQ module. Could someone assist me further?

Be aware that the [product_name] RTD module only supports a fixed temperature range of -50°C to 200°C. This means it cannot measure temperatures above 200°C.

The 300°C measurement was taken without the fan running. If the fan keeps the stove around 120°C, high readings shouldn't be a concern.

If you need to maintain a set temperature, a PI controller is advisable. Set the target at 120°C and let the PI controller adjust its output depending on how far off the temperature is from the target. However, there's some confusion about running the fan down to 80°C, which seems inconsistent with keeping the stove at 120°C.

When the temperature drops to 80°C, the air isn't warm enough to heat the room, so the fan isn't needed—thus the idea to switch the fan on above 120°C and off below 80°C. You could also implement stepped operation, for example: 120–140°C = 25% fan speed, 141–160°C = 50%, 161–180°C = 75%, and 181–200°C = 100%.

If I understand correctly, you're aiming for at least 25% fan power as the minimum. What should the output be while cooling down (from 120°C down to 80°C)? Also, according to the datasheet, the Niko dimmer module ([article_no]) isn't suitable for use with inductive loads (like fans). [url]

That's accurate. You could set the On/Off point at 120°C and exclude the Off control at 80°C. Regarding hardware choice, I relied on my supplier, who was trained on [company_name] products. Does this mean my project won't work with this equipment?

From what I know, the Niko dimmer module isn't appropriate for use with inductive loads such as fans.

Hello everyone, I'm trying to connect an analog signal (4-20 mA or 0-10 V) to both a [product_name] controller and a Microcom DataLogger. Is parallel connection possible, or do I need an additional module? Thank you

Hi [user_name]! For 0-10 V or 0/4-20 mA analog signals, you generally cannot measure them with two different devices (analog inputs) connected in parallel. The internal resistor networks within the devices convert current signals to voltage signals before analog-to-digital conversion, which can cause interference when connected in parallel. Instead, with your [product_name] controller, it makes sense to use the signal as an input, and then, via the program, branch that input directly to an output (or possibly through an analog amplifier with a gain of 1). By adding an analog output module, you can send the untouched signal to the second measuring device or analog input. This is my best suggestion — since you already have the [product_name] controller, it's more straightforward to add an analog output module than to seek a special signal splitter. This gives you a secondary output for other purposes, and you can handle all signal manipulation inside the [product_name] programming software, which is quite user-friendly.

Details: Pressure sensor 1 SP (0-20 Bar, 0.5-4.5Vdc): measured at 1.80Vdc = 6.50 Bar, system enters override and won’t run. Threshold to start: 2.20Vdc = 8.50 Bar. Boosted value must not exceed 2.50Vdc or 10.0 Bar. Pressure sensor 2 DP (0-50 Bar, 0.5-4.5Vdc): measured at 1.00Vdc = 6.25 Bar, system enters override and won’t run. Threshold to start: 1.30Vdc = 10.0 Bar. Boosted value must not exceed 1.50Vdc or 12.5 Bar. For automatic control: use an analog threshold trigger. If the temperature is too low, use an OR condition to start the chiller until the pressure reaches an appropriate level, then switch to normal operation. 3. If you use a PI loop: implement an analog threshold trigger to swap the PI loop to a fixed manual output. Once pressure and temperature are stable, you can revert to automatic mode. Hope this is helpful.

In this scenario, I would split the logic into two modes: one for startup and another for steady state after stabilization. The shift from mode 1 to mode 2 would be based on the system achieving specific pressure levels within a set time frame. Once the pressure is adequate, the system would switch to permanent operation.
