This is normal behavior. You're measuring current output but have your meter set to voltage. There’s a difference between measuring voltage versus current (for example, a 230V outlet—what if you set your meter to amperes?). With a current output, you only get accurate current readings if the total resistance is within a reasonable range (for example, 500 to 1000 Ohms). The measurement should be in current (mA), not voltage. If the [product_name] module is outputting 15 mA, what would the voltage be? Use Ohm’s Law: U = I x R. You know I; now consider R.

Thank you for your response. When I connect a current meter in series with a 220 Ohm resistor between M1 and I1, I correctly measure the 4-20 mA range. At 20 mA, the voltage drop across M1/I1 is 4.4V. There must be a potential difference for current to flow. I’ve attached a clearer description of my question for this discussion. Best regards, [user_name]

If the smartbox uses a standard signal input of 0/4-20 mA, there will be a low resistance (around 500 Ohms) between input + and input -. There’s no cycle or cross voltage or current. Higher voltages only occur with larger resistances, such as the 10 MOhm found in voltmeters. Regards, [user_name]. P.S. Share a link to your smartbox if you want us to check whether the input supports your requirements.

Just to note, the [product_name] AM2 module has an active 4-20 mA output. Do you have more details about your smartbox device?

The controller performs internal calculations using floating-point arithmetic, but externally it only provides values as fixed-point numbers. The result always shows at least one decimal place, rounded accordingly: values below 0.5 are rounded down, and values of 0.5 or above are rounded up.

Here, 0 corresponds to 0 Volt or 0 mA (or 4 mA depending on configuration), and 1000 represents 10 Volts or 20 mA. Adjust the mathematical block settings so your output falls within 0 to 1000. How can I apply a mathematical formula like X/100 × (Y-Z) + Z, where X is the analog input (0-100%)? Is there a way to do this directly?

You should first multiply, then divide, and finally add Z. In other words: X/100 × (Y-Z) + Z is equivalent to calculating X × (Y-Z), then dividing by 100, and finally adding Z. What are your actual input signal (analog input), and what do you use for X, Y, and Z?

To perform such formula calculations, use the "Arithmetic Instructions" function block. As mentioned before: internally, the controller uses floating-point numbers, but results and parameter entries must be fixed-point values only.

Hello, I have a [article_no] [product_name] and I would like to control an analog clock that requires pulse inputs (one pulse per minute). Is it possible to create a pulse every minute, synchronized with the internal clock? I know I can use the asynchronous pulse function, but then the pulse isn't aligned with the device's clock (NTP). Is there a way to trigger a pulse when the seconds hit "00"? Thank you,

No, direct access to the internal time isn't available. You can only re-synchronize the asynchronous pulse generator with weekly timers at intervals you set.

As [user_name] pointed out, the time isn't accessible from within the [product_name]. Personally, I haven't tested whether the asynchronous pulse generator syncs with the clock—it's unlikely. You could try a workaround similar to how railway clocks work in Switzerland: use a slightly faster pulse than real time, then at the end of a defined period, wait for a precise trigger to start the next cycle. For example, you might use two weekly timers to send a pulse every 4 hours. During those 4 hours, an asynchronous pulse generator would emit a pulse every 59.99 seconds. After 3 hours, 59 minutes, and 57.6 seconds, the system sends its 240th pulse. It then waits for the weekly timer (synchronized via NTP to millisecond accuracy) to provide the next pulse and begins the next cycle in sync. Keep in mind, if the asynchronous pulse generator slows down unexpectedly, the system could become inaccurate—so you'll need to carefully test for consistency! Kind regards, [user_name]

Please check the screenshot attached. You can use a pulse relay in the program. For HMI operations, use a bit in the VM area (Vx.x) and configure the action as "Set bit on click." The bit is automatically reset in the program, as the network output with the same address as the network input is written to zero via a LOW block.

Referring to the picture below, my goal is to use the HMI to log the counter value when triggered (e.g. using M1). An event happens every hour, and the rising edge sets the bit to 1 (it should be retentive), allowing the HMI to log the counter value by event trigger. After logging, the bit should be set back to 0.

How large can the counter value get within one hour? Does it stay below 32,768, or does it exceed this value?

If the counter value doesn't go above 32,767, the approach shown in the attachment will work. The value in the mathematical operation will remain until the counter is reset.

I have considered that, but the requirement is to set a bit (from the program) to notify the HMI that logging should occur. The HMI then completes the logging routine, resets the bit (from the HMI), and the falling edge resets the counter. Overflow is not a concern because the counter will not reach 32,767 in one hour.

How do you propose this should work? You don't want to use a storage block like a latch relay. There isn't a retentive bit that's set by the program and reset by the HMI with this controller. You also declined the previous suggestion. Unfortunately, I'm unsure how to assist further.

1. In your example, you use M1 and need it to be retentive. With a rising edge, M1 stays on for only one cycle. There's no need to reset the bit unless you're using latching or pulse relays, which are retentive. 2. If you want to log data every hour via HMI, consider using a timer event in the HMI instead of handling this in the controller. This would be simpler. Regards, [user_name]

Hello everyone, I have a thermal controller project using [product_name] controllers. Specifically, we're using a base module ([product_name] with display, [article_no]) plus an RTD module and a power supply rated at 0.6A. The temperature sensor initially reports zero, then corrects itself to the actual value after a few seconds. I swapped the base module for another [product_name] version and it worked flawlessly, so the sensor and wiring are functioning. Any advice would be appreciated.

I understand the issue you're describing. Could you clarify the problem in more detail? Would you be able to upload your program file? Also, where is the sensor positioned and which module is it connected to: the base module or the RTD extension?

My concern is that the temperature display briefly drops to zero before returning to the actual reading. Is the power supply sufficient for the setup? This behavior doesn't occur with one [product_name] configuration but does with another. I'll share the program soon.

From a functional standpoint, it shouldn't matter whether you're using either [product_name] variant. There might be another reason for the problem. Have you fully inserted the contact slides and checked that the contact points are clean without resistance? Did this issue always exist, or did it start after a recent change?

Are you able to measure how much current the power supply is delivering? The [product_name] module typically requires between 0.025A and 0.1A (0.6W to 2.4W). A 24VDC 0.6A power supply might be too weak. Could you try using one with higher current?

The module shown in your video appears to be a different [product_name] variant than the one you mentioned. Your base unit has either 2 or 4 analog inputs by default. The first analog input from the extension module is typically numbered as AI3 in the software. You may need to update the analog input number in your program. Note that on the base module, you can select either 2 or 4 analog inputs; this may affect how the extension module’s analog inputs are mapped (e.g., the first could be AI5).

I can't measure the current usage. However, I did test with a different power supply rated at 1.6A and saw no improvement. Please review the attached connection diagram; everything is connected properly. Contacts are clean, no resistance. The issue started only after switching from one module variant to another.

How do you change the analog input assignment? Is it through the settings menu (on-board AI settings)?

It appears there’s been some confusion regarding your module type. You stated it was a 24RCE, but it’s actually the 12/24RCE version, which is significant. The 24RCE has no onboard analog inputs, while the 12/24RCE has four. By default, two are enabled (AI1 and AI2), and their addresses are reserved for the base module, regardless of usage. This means that the first analog channel on your RTD extension will be AI3. You should update the program address from AI1 to AI3 or disable the onboard analog inputs in your configuration. To deactivate onboard analog inputs, go to: File > Properties > Offline Settings > I/O Settings (reference attachment).

In addition to potential address issues, an incompatible extension module might be the cause. For your [product_name] controller, you will need a compatible extension module with [article_no]. I couldn't read the module order code in the video. The correct part number should be [article_no].

You can also update the I/O settings via the controller’s menu options.

Additionally, I want to set a pressure threshold (e.g., 5 bar) on the screen. If the inverter signal drops below this value, a digital output activates, and when exceeded, it deactivates. Yes, converting a 4-20mA signal into 2-10V with a 500 ohm resistor is possible. For temperature, you can choose a converter with a measurement range suited to your needs—there are models that let you select the range.

Thanks for the quick response. I have another question regarding programming: When using a pressure sensor (4-20mA, converted with a 500 ohm resistor to 2-10V), how should I calculate the settings for analog input modules (like minimum/maximum range, gain, offset) if I change the pressure transducer's range to 0-50 bar?

Every analog input on the [product_name] converts signals (0-10V, 0-20mA, 4-20mA, PT100) to 0-1000 units. For a 4-20mA sensor (or 2-10V), you can only use units 200-1000, since 0-200 units correspond to 0-4mA. To scale 800 usable units up to 1000, amplify the signal by 1.25 and apply an offset of -250. This means: 1000 units * 1.25 = 1250 units, offset -250 = range from -250 to 1000 units. 0 mA = -250 units, 4 mA = 0 units, 20 mA = 1000 units. On the [product_name] display, 0-1000 units (with two decimal places) map to 0.00-10.00 bar. So, for a 5 bar switching threshold, use input value 500—this equals 5.00 bar.

From experience: Reading PT100 sensors directly with a basic 0-10V analog input involves a lot of effort, especially if your power supply isn't stable and resistor tolerances vary. Using a [product_name] RTD expansion unit for PT100 temperature measurement is much more reliable—just install, wire, and select PT100 in the function block. If you're installing a standalone PT100 sensor (for pipes or similar), this is easiest. Alternatively, a third-party temp/humidity unit with 0-10V output can work, especially for room air monitoring. Most pressure transducers allow you to select output as 0-10V or 4-20mA, so you may not need a 4-20mA expansion module. In general, avoid using external resistors where possible, as it complicates the setup and increases troubleshooting time. I do sometimes use resistors for monitoring supply voltage, which isn't natively supported by [product_name].

Hello everyone, I have some questions about Modbus and the data transfer table. How many transfers can be done in practice? In one project, I managed 26, but in another the table only allowed adding 32 transfers. I need to do more than 32— is this possible? Also, how many holding registers (HR) and VW (variables/words) can be used? I’d like to use up to HR=151. Hoping for advice. Thanks for your help.

You can reduce the number of entries by grouping them. For example: update the line with HR11 to cover 4 words, then remove the HR13 line—this will combine HR11 and HR13 being transferred to VW0 and VW4. Similarly, set the HR15 line to 8 words and remove the HR17, HR19, and HR21 lines—this way, HR15, HR17, HR19, and HR21 are transferred to VW32, VW36, VW40, and VW44. Repeat the process accordingly, making sure the VW numbers are properly sequenced (step 2 for single registers, step 4 for double registers, etc.). You can reduce even more lines if the register and VW numbers are in ascending order on both sides, though you’ll need to organize the VW numbers in your program. Around 125 registers can be transferred at once, though I’m not certain of the exact value. Regards, [user_name]

VW2 (2 words) to HR1 means VW2 transfers to HR1, and VW4 to HR2. You can only enter 32 lines in a connection table, but it’s possible to use more than one connection.

The pattern is consistent in both directions: register steps of 1 correspond to VW steps of 2, and steps of 2 registers use VW steps of 4, etc. Use distinct areas for each direction and for digital or analog signals; this gives you four areas and helps with logical organization. Consider creating an Excel sheet listing all signals both ways to summarize everything clearly. Be careful not to overlap areas with different signals, as that could cause confusing results. I expected 228->92, 230->93, 232->94, 234->95, but after testing I found HR=94 was correct. Not sure why. Three images are provided for reference—'VWSendValue' shows ResolucioT2=VW238 and ResolucioT3=VW242. Thanks for your help, this forum is very supportive for beginners. Regards.

The limitation is due to TCP/IP packet sizes. Modbus TCP/IP requires a header plus data values, so each register may use slightly more than two bytes. For details on packet size and protocol specifics, please review the relevant online resources ([url]). Also, clients and servers may start register counting at either 0 or 1; please check how your system does it. For example, [product_name] starts at register 1, while Arduino might start at 0—confirm this in your Arduino documentation. Make sure to align register mappings accordingly. Regards, [user_name]

For similar applications, it's common to use a local pushbutton for each blind (up/down). If you want central control for all blinds across the floors, you can wire central pushbuttons in parallel to all 4 [product_name] units. You’ll find examples like 'Control for 8 shutters with central control for UP/DOWN.' Use the same program for each [product_name] on each floor and connect the central control buttons to I17, I18.

Connecting 4 or 5 devices is possible—but you need to determine exactly what signals each device should accept or send. For communication, use inputs and outputs. You’ll need: a KNX/EIB communication module for every [product_name] (with 24V AC/DC power supply), KNX network cable, KNX-compatible power supply, KNX/USB gateway, and software like ETS3 and [product_name] programming tool. Hi all, I've programmed a [product_name] and everything works fine locally. However, I'm running into issues integrating the [product_name] logic with Modbus TCP/IP in my SCADA system. Just to clarify, if I connect a memory bit (M1) directly to its coil, all works as expected—setting M1 via Modbus updates its state online. The problem starts when I add more contacts in series with coil M1; then the program fails to set M1 from 0 to 1. Photos 1 and 2 illustrate this: the first setup allows M1 to be set to 1 or back to 0, while in the second, adding an RS contact prevents M1 from being set. Interestingly, coil M1 works even unconnected, and if I cross-connect memory bits (e.g., M1 to M2 and vice versa), changing state results in both blinking. Any advice on using these memory bits correctly? I'm using a ladder-to-FBD converter to import into my network project.

That's a downside of ladder diagrams in [product_name]; they're prone to errors. The operation M1 = M1 in ladder isn't allowed in FBD. My strong recommendation is to use only FBD for programming. In FBD, a flag can only be set HIGH or LOW if it isn't linked to logic elements at the input side.

Thanks. Is there a way to reset an M flag in the program if nothing can be connected to its left (since it's set externally via Modbus)? If not, should I switch to network I/O or another block type? Also, about retentivity—is it only possible with certain blocks like pulse relay or latch in [product_name]? For example, I set M4 to 1, so Q4 turns on, then power off and back on, but Q4 isn't set again, so retentivity doesn't work as I expected. Is there any way to make an M flag or other element directly retentive?

No, that's not possible. Why do you want to do this?

In your circuit, you reset the RS block with M4 low. On startup, M4 is low since it doesn't retain its value.

Can you explain why you want to reset the flag? Without context, it's difficult to provide help.

I enable the remote fault output Q1 using M1 when remote control is active (input I5)—that's shown in photo line 1. I want Q1 reset when I acknowledge a fault locally (photo line 2). After that, I need to reset M1; otherwise, line 1 will always be active when remote is enabled.

This approach isn’t feasible in FBD. If M1 is set by the remote source, only the remote source can reset it. What type of signal is your remote source—dynamic or static?

I control M1 via Modbus TCP/IP, writing the bit to a coil, so it's a static signal.

If you write to a VM memory bit, this can work as shown in the attachment. Use a network input with a free address, like V0.0. Network order matters—the last action should be setting V0.0 low, which creates a pulse cycle for V0.0.

That's promising, but when I tested in FBD it didn't work. I need this to function in FBD for my network project using Modbus.

It does work, otherwise I wouldn’t have recommended it. You mentioned converting from LAD to FBD. Even in FBD, the important rule is: the final action must be writing LOW to the network output!

Perfect, it works now. Regarding retentivity: I want V0.1 to turn Q4 on and off and maintain the state through power cycles. I tried as before, but after resetting, V0.1 defaults to 0 and Q4 resets in my code.

The screenshot you shared doesn’t make sense. I’m not clear about your issue.

I'm setting V0.1 remotely; its contact should simply turn Q4 on/off and be retentive—that is, Q4 remembers its state after power loss. For that, I need to use a latch or pulse relay because V0.1 can’t retain state itself. Now, I’d like to read Q4’s current state via Modbus after a power cycle to know how to respond. I managed to make retentive control as shown in the image, but I don’t know how to check Q4’s state—writing Q4’s state to V0.2 (address 3) is unclear, and Modbus keeps showing 0 at address 8196, which corresponds to Q4.

The Modbus address for Q4 in [product_name] is coil 8196, that’s correct. V0.2 uses coil 3. I can't give more details. What Modbus device are you using?

Hi, Retentivity is available in FBs such as RS or latching relays. If you use [product_name] version [version_no], you can also try the new VRx-Memory. Hope that helps.

Hello, in my program I calculate flow from pulses over a duration of 9 seconds. The value updates every 9 seconds, but I want more frequent updates by running three 9-second periods staggered by 3 seconds each. That way, the display could refresh every 3 seconds. I tried two approaches: the first didn't work because I couldn't delay the blocks without an enable mode, so their periods overlapped. In the second, I created my own version of a threshold trigger block, which did work, but the display update was affected by the analog MUX block because inputs S1 and S2 change state at different times (try varying I3's frequency to see this). Eventually, I plan to use a 30-second period so the refresh would be every 10 seconds. Do you have any suggestions for a simpler solution? Thank you!

I'm sorry, but I don't understand your programming approach or the reasoning behind it.

Let me clarify: You want to count pulses in 9 seconds using three counters, each offset by 3 seconds? For that, I'd use a clocked counter that resets at the ninth second. You can implement 9-second delays triggered by three analog differential threshold switches at 0, 3, and 6 seconds to activate the counters. Timing is critical and some delay between periods introduces minor inaccuracies in counting. Best regards, [user_name]

Here's an example for reference: Flowrate with pulses LOGO 8. My water flowmeter gives pulses between 0.33 and 5.55 pulses per second, and I want the momentary flow every 10 seconds, but a 10-second sample isn't very accurate, so 30 seconds is better. Is it possible to run three samples delayed by 10 seconds each? Every 10 seconds, calculate and display the flow rate from the results of these samples. I'm struggling to understand how.

A program can demonstrate much more than descriptions. Here's an example. I used reset pulses for individual counters, so the first run may count the same value and might need adjusting to suit your requirements. Kind regards, [user_name]

Thanks [user_name], I've made two versions including your sample. I used a MUX timer to avoid display glitches. For testing, I set a refresh every second, so with three counters the total period is three seconds. The results differ between versions, especially at a test frequency like 100Hz. Thanks!

How did you perform your test? Was it on real hardware or with the [product_name] simulator? The simulator runs slower and suffers from timing variations due to the operating system, which can be problematic for time-sensitive logic. Also, there's a 'dead' interval from clock generator delays or internal block processing, noticeable at high pulse rates. Why not use a simple threshold switch for fast inputs, capturing for three seconds and extrapolating to nine seconds? [user_name]

Yes, I've realized the added 0.01s introduces dead time as well. I replaced the asynchronous pulse generator with a timer-on-delay, which improved results but I'm still only simulating because I don't have the hardware. Thank you for the reassurance! Check the attachment from my first post: There's a simple example with a threshold switch, but I don't see how to have three equally long periods offset in time since only the gate time parameter exists, and no enable connector. If that were possible, it'd be much easier. In reality, the sampling period will be 30 seconds or possibly one minute. If using 30 seconds, the user would wait that long for an update, which is too slow. By staggering three 30-second periods by 10 seconds each, the user only waits 10 seconds for updated flow data.

Hello [user_name], I'm unclear on your intent: If the user only sees the first 10 seconds out of a 30-second measurement before it's replaced, the remaining 20 seconds seem irrelevant. It would be simpler to record pulses for 10 seconds then multiply by six to estimate the per-minute flow, since the user is interested in the current value. This method is less complex, more stable, and you could even shorten the sample interval to one second (multiply by 60) if the pulse rate is high enough. Why the need for three offset measures if two-thirds aren't used? [user_name]

The 30-second window is needed because the pulse rate is quite low. Longer measurement periods improve accuracy but make updates slower. With three staggered periods, you count pulses for 30 seconds and get updated results every 10 seconds. This method allows three measuring periods with results more frequently. I hope this explanation is clearer now.

Now I understand your approach! Best regards, [user_name]

Do you think a solution is possible using threshold triggers? It seems simpler than using many blocks.

I don't think that's feasible since the module sets its own interval duration. You might be able to simplify your program by optimizing the block use, but only slightly. With your structure, measurement outliers persist until all measurement cycles are complete, which lowers result accuracy. For example, if you continuously count 100 pulses in 10 seconds, the result is 100. An irregular count (e.g., 102) in the first cycle would affect all counters and skew the next two results. Capturing impulses in just one period (as I suggested) would let such irregularities disappear by the next cycle's output, which is more accurate. If the pulse count is still too low, consider increasing the sample time or using a transmitter with a higher pulse output.

@ [user_name], check the attached program—maybe it'll suit you. The logic measures the time between two pulses and converts it into quantity. The pulse value is set in parameter V2 of block B005 (e.g., 10 ml in the demo).

Thank you [user_name]. I considered your solution: measuring the interval between two pulses (Solution 2), instead of counting for a fixed period (Solution 1). I'm unsure about the limits and accuracy of this with the [product_name] module. In practice, the flow ranges from 1 to 20 m³/h. The pulse factor K is either 1L or 10L per pulse, depending on the transmitter, which I can choose. Which solution is more appropriate? For K=1L: - @ 1m³/h = 0.278 pulses/sec: Solution 1: 8 pulses/30sec, 16/60sec. Solution 2: 3.60s between pulses. - @ 20m³/h = 5.56 pulses/sec: Solution 1: 167 pulses/30sec, 333/60sec. Solution 2: 0.18s between pulses. For K=10L: - @ 1m³/h = 0.028 pulses/sec: Solution 1: 0 pulses/30sec (too short), 1/60sec. Solution 2: 36s between pulses. - @ 20m³/h = 0.56 pulses/sec: Solution 1: 17 pulses/30sec, 33/60sec. Solution 2: 1.8s between pulses. I prefer K=1L/pulse and Solution 1, with a 60-second sample period, either a single 60-sec threshold trigger or my variant with three staggered periods and value refresh every 20 seconds. For Solution 2, can the module handle intervals as short as 0.18 seconds? Also, how do I reset to zero when no pulses are received? A 5% error margin is acceptable; more than that is not. Thank you both for your help. (translated from French)

For example, if I have a pressure sensor measuring 1–100 PSI, and the [product_name] handles 0–1000 units, I assume that 500 units should represent 50 PSI. How can I get the sensors to correctly display actual values, such as temperature, humidity, or pressure? What am I missing? Thank you!

The analog inputs of the [product_name] and the analog extension module convert any signal, whether 0–10V, 0/4–20mA, or PT, into a range of 0–1000 units. You need to scale these 1000 units to the physical value of your sensor. Depending on your sensor's measuring range, usually an analog amplifier is sufficient, but if the range is like yours (1–100 PSI), you may need to use two amplifiers or a mathematical function to accomplish the scaling. There's also a limitation: [product_name] only supports integer values, no floating point, affecting calculation accuracy. For a 4–20mA sensor, consider the following correspondence: 0mA = 0 units 4mA = 200 units 8mA = 400 units 12mA = 600 units 16mA = 800 units 20mA = 1000 units This means that instead of 1000 usable units, you actually have 800 units, since 0–200 units are reserved for the initial 4mA current. So your usable range is 200–1000 units. There's no universal solution; it depends on the sensor's specific characteristics.

Looking at manual examples, it's clear the power supply usually shares its phase with I1–I4. Perhaps that's because it's unnecessary to have a phase without inputs? Hello, I'm new to [product_name]. I've written a program to convert encoder input to millimeters. However, the math instruction I have needs to switch several outputs, and I'm unsure how to achieve that. Is it possible to count the millimeters (from the output of the math instruction) using a counter or similar? Please see the attachment for clarification. I hope my explanation is clear! I need a pulse or something for each millimeter so I can create a setpoint and disable an output when the target is reached.

If I understand correctly, you'd like to compare the calculated millimeter value to one or more setpoints and perform actions accordingly. Is that right?

Yes, that's exactly what I want. When it reaches a specific millimeter value, it should slow down, and when it matches the setpoint, it should stop.

You can achieve this using various function blocks, such as the analog comparator, analog threshold trigger, or analog differential trigger.

I think you're referring to this (see attached image). In this setup, it counts down to zero, and the output changes accordingly.

Yes, that's one possible solution. Another example is shown in the attachment.

Thanks! I'll try these methods to see which one works best.

The code works well, but the maximum millimeter output I get is 16161 mm. Please see the attachment with the calculation. I know the max output is 32767, but I'm unsure what I'm missing.

It's challenging to assist without knowing your exact parameters. For example, how fast do the pulses arrive? What's the value of one pulse? How many pulses in total over the measured distance? According to your formula, each pulse represents approximately 0.4932 mm, similar to a multiplication factor of 0.5. The math instruction can only process values up to 32,767 at the inputs. If the counter provides values exceeding 32,767, the system limits it to 32,767. Thus, 32,767 * 0.4932 = 16160.6844, rounded to 16161.

That's correct! Your calculation matches mine. I need to find a solution since I require a range up to roughly 25,000 mm for cutting. Perhaps using a second counter for each meter and then resetting the millimeter count. Thank you.

Alternatively, you can use the threshold-switch function of the counter. For 25,000 mm: 25,000 / 0.4932 = 50,689 pulses. Use two counters in parallel; set the ON parameter of the first counter for switchover to slow and the ON parameter of the second counter for shut-off.

The operator wants to enter the value in millimeters directly. I need to simplify the interface so only millimeter values are input on the display. While [product_name] is easy to use, it's somewhat limited. Next time, I may opt for a standard PLC.

In that case, you'll need an HMI. If you add a second counter to convert millimeters to meters, be aware there could be lost pulses. Only fast input processing with counters is fast, while standard logic runs per cycle. If the fast input isn't directly linked to the counter input, counting speed depends on [product_name]'s cycle time.

I think I need to switch back to PLC. Is there truly no way to use a variable higher than 32,000? Are all [product_name] modules the same in this regard? Otherwise, I may return to [product_name]. Thank you for the help!

With all [product_name] modules, mathematical functions are limited to -32,768 to 32,767, using 16-bit integers.

Assuming your pulse source is a wheel or roller: If you increase the wheel circumference by a factor of 2.027575, each turn will correspond to one millimeter, depending on your distance resolution. If you can't get a wheel exactly 2.027575 times larger, you can apply a correction factor in the formula.

I'm having trouble getting data from a MODBUS device connected to a [product_name] via a MODBUS RTU/TCP converter (Waveshare RS485 to Ethernet) set in RTU to TCP mode. Accessing MODBUS data from my PC using Windows tools like ModbusPoll works perfectly, indicating the communication and converter setup are correct. When reading with PC software, the Link LED stays solid blue (TCP connection established), but with [product_name] attempts, the blue LED just flashes briefly then goes green, and diagnostic info shows no MODBUS connection. I experimented with different register addresses, starting at MODBUS 0x0000 (should be 1 in [product_name]), tried 30001, 40001, and other variants, but the connection consistently breaks. I've tested both client Ethernet MODBUS connections and analog network inputs, including adjusting poll time, but nothing worked. Notably, if I use the wrong MODBUS device ID, the blue light remains ON and diagnostics show a MODBUS connection - suggesting TCP link is established, but the following request (reading MODBUS data) terminates the connection. Debugging became difficult, as my switches don't let Wireshark see the traffic.

Which [product_name] device do you have specifically? Sorry, I missed your information about version [version_no] (8.4). What is the unit ID (slave address) of your Modbus RS485 device?

I've tried several unit IDs; currently using 1. I also tested with another controller and had no issues there. It seems [product_name] doesn't accept the MODBUS TCP response and closes the connection. When testing with PC software, data transfer works fine. Whenever the MODBUS TCP-RTU gateway responds to [product_name], the TCP link is dropped for an unknown reason. Additional testing showed the MODBUS connection to the converter is established, but sending a response causes the TCP connection to end. If the RS485/RTU part is purposely incorrect (so no answer goes back to [product_name]), the TCP connection remains open, as shown by the Link LED status.

What type of Modbus RTU device are you using?

I captured new Wireshark traces today and learned more: The MODBUS TCP request and response appear fine in the logs, but instead of a single keep-alive TCP request, [product_name] sends multiple TCP packets, which eventually causes the TCP connection to shut down. As a result, [product_name] doesn't process the returned MODBUS data. I attached the Wireshark logfile. Use filter for ip.addr == 192.168.1.224 (the MODBUS gateway). [product_name] is at 222.

Hello, did you manage to find a solution?

PT100 sensors are not simply temperature-dependent resistors.

You can find a resistance table at [url]. Most PT100 sensors are very similar (within 4% variance), generally measuring from -200 to 850 degrees Celsius and having a resistance of 100 ohms at 20 degrees.

For your setup, you should use an AM2-PT100 Module ([article_no]). However, it only works within a -50 to +200 degrees Celsius range.

Hello everyone, I've previously calibrated Pt100 sensors at a calibration facility, so these details are helpful for industrial work: 1) A Pt100 uses fine platinum wire, measuring 100 ohms at 0°C, or at the triple point of water, which is a standard calibration reference. 2) Other kinds of platinum temperature sensors have different resistances at this reference point (e.g., Pt25 is 25 ohms, Pt1000 is 1000 ohms at 0°C). 3) The [product_name] AM2 PT100 and the newer RTD expansion modules contain intelligent resistance bridges similar to a Wheatstone bridge. 4) When connecting a Pt100, the AM2 module applies a known voltage and current to the sensor. 5) Measuring values of resistance, voltage, and current creates bridge imbalance, reflecting the temperature. 6) The module then produces a 0-1000 output value to the [product_name] program, proportional to the signal. 7) The RTD module can detect whether a Pt100 or Pt1000 is connected. 8) The PT100 expansion module only supports Pt100 sensors; using other types yields highly inaccurate results. 9) The RTD module provides correct readings only for Pt100 or Pt1000 sensors. 10) Signal scaling is only intended for Pt100 and Pt1000 in the -50 to +200°C range; the internal 0-1000 value matches only this temperature range. 11) Using other sensor types or ranges will cause incorrect scaling. 12) It is recommended to use Pt100 or Pt1000 sensors for the -50 to +200°C range, as they are standard and widely available (from various suppliers). 13) If you must use different types or ranges, add a signal converter (to 0-10V, 0-20mA, or 4-20mA) and adjust scaling yourself in the [product_name] configuration. Hope this clarifies things!

Hello, try setting the virtual COM port for your USB cable to a lower number. While I'm not certain this will resolve the problem, it's my best suggestion.

Hi everyone with slow [product_name] communications! The USB-to-COM port driver often struggles when many virtual COM ports have already been created by Windows, especially if Bluetooth is active on your PC—these drivers typically add several virtual COM ports. If you install the [product_name] USB cable after that, it may get assigned a high COM port number (such as 17), causing [product_name] [version_no] to take a long time to detect and communicate with the device. The best approach is to uninstall your Bluetooth devices and drivers (sometimes you need to disable Bluetooth in BIOS or use a hardware switch), remove the [product_name] USB cable driver, restart your PC, and install the [product_name] USB cable driver first to ensure it gets a lower COM port number (preferably below COM 5). Afterwards, you can reinstall your Bluetooth devices, so those virtual COM ports are assigned higher numbers, keeping the [product_name] USB port assignment low and making communications faster. Hope this helps!

Afterward, reinstall the USB adapter driver and verify the port number is below 10 before connecting to [product_name]. Once confirmed, you can reconnect your other USB devices. Always use the same USB port for the adapter; otherwise, you might encounter the same issue again if the port number changes. Hope this helps.

Hello everyone, I recently encountered an unusual issue with a 24V 1.3A [product_name] power supply. It operated normally only when there was no load; once I closed the circuit by adding a fuse on the +24 line, the power supply output stopped and the status LED no longer showed green. After a few attempts, it started working again. Can anyone suggest what might have caused this? Currently, I have intentionally grounded my circuit to the negative terminal of the power supply. The maximum current draw is 0.5A, and this problem appears randomly during machine operation. I haven't observed any current spikes. I read that this model has electronic protection—how does this work and when does it trigger? Thank you.

If you're confident there is no overload and safety diodes on your external relays are functioning properly, I can think of two possibilities: 1. Electromagnetic interference could be entering your 24V circuit through the protective conductor connection. 2. The power supply's smoothing capacitors might be faulty, which is often visible when they become deformed.

Thank you for your response. I would rule out the second possibility, since this issue occurs sporadically across multiple machines with identical electrical setups. I have considered the interference option as well. Do you think I could measure this with a standard tester? Thank you.

Using an oscilloscope or frequency analyzer may help diagnose the issue. Alternatively, try using a higher capacity power supply.

If inserting the fuse acted like closing a switch, your description suggests the presence of inrush current—a brief spike in power draw when a device is switched on, which isn't always well documented. Certain electronics may request more current than typical after being off for an extended period. Repeated power cycling charges internal capacitors enough for stable operation. [url] As mentioned earlier, consider upgrading to a power supply that can accommodate the greater inrush demand at startup.

I have a digital oscilloscope and attempted some measurements but didn't detect anything unusual. What specific readings should I focus on?

You should look at the sine wave of the AC voltage, residual ripple in the DC voltage, and the startup current curve. There should be no significant harmonics or signal spikes, especially when switching occurs.

I'll try your suggestions. I don't think sudden surges are the issue, as I've only connected a [product_name] logic module with its expansion, plus a 4G 24V modem. As mentioned, the highest current measured is 0.5A. Thank you for your support.

You may find current measurement more revealing. If your oscilloscope supports it, use a 0.1 Ohm shunt resistor in series between the power supply and load. If the oscilloscope input isn't isolated, place the resistor on the negative side. Be careful if your oscilloscope's ground is earthed. Regards, [user_name]

Just a thought: 4G/LTE modems draw more current when transmitting. Have you checked whether transmission pushes the power supply past its 1.3A rating? Have you tried using a higher-capacity power supply? What other devices are connected to the [product_name] module and power supply? I also suspect the issue may be overloading—consider measuring the current with the oscilloscope and shunt.

After recalculating the load, accounting for possible peak currents on the +24 line, I see a maximum possible current of 1.685A. According to the datasheet, the internal limiter on this power supply is set at 1.6A. These occasional current peaks likely cause the random shutdowns, even though the normal idle current is just 0.5A. This outcome is unlikely but not impossible, as I've verified.

Hi, ultimately you should use a more powerful supply to prevent overload issues.

Avoid the MODEM CABLE — it just alters pinout for connecting a [product_name] serial cable to an industrial telephone modem (used for remote engineering via analog phone lines). Instead, use the SERIAL [product_name] cable. The USB type requires a PC and an OS to assign a virtual COM port. Welcome to the forum. The analog-to-digital converter of [product_name] converts any analog signal (current, voltage, or PT100) into values from 0 to 1000 units. The [product_name] module is calibrated for a measuring range from -50°C to 200°C, which is a total span of 250°C. This means the resolution per unit is 250°C / 1000 = 0.25°C. Each increment represents a change of 0.25°C. You can display the converted value in three formats: without decimals (-50°C to 200°C), with one decimal (-50.0°C to 200.0°C), or with two decimals (-50.00°C to 200.00°C).

Could someone explain the steps for connecting these devices? I'm having trouble understanding it. Thanks, [user_name].

The [product_name] and your PC each need unique IP addresses. By default, the [product_name] has 192.168.0.2, which you can view in its menu. For the PC, choose an IP in the format 192.168.10.xxx, with xxx less than 125. Set the PC IP manually. Make sure to also configure the subnet address—both the [product_name] and the PC need to use 255.255.255.0. More information can be found here: [url]

My Mac's IP address is 192.168.1.108 and the [product_name]'s IP is 192.168.0.2. What should I do next?

Change the [product_name] IP to match the same subnet as your Mac, such as 192.168.1.xxx.

Your Mac is at 192.168.1.108 and the [product_name] is at 192.168.0.2. Both devices must be on the same subnet. Update the device's IP address to 192.168.1.2 or change your Mac's to 192.168.0.108 (it's easier to change the [product_name] IP). With a netmask of 255.255.255.0, there are 254 possible addresses; the first three numbers should match, and the last should be unique for each device (e.g., 192.168.1.XXX). For the /24 subnet, IPs range 1-254.

For networking, each address must be unique, similar to how no two houses share the same address. Ethernet addresses should have the same network portion but different host numbers. Set each device's address in the same range, like 192.168.1.xxx or 192.168.0.xxx, but not across ranges. The host part (xxx) must be less than 125 for the [product_name]. The subnet mask for all devices should be 255.255.255.0.

text: Hello everyone, During my tests with the block "stop watchwatch" of the [product_name] ([article_no]), I observed the following: - The block's output can range from 0 to 65636 for each permitted time unit. The documentation and online help do not mention this. - The "time base" parameter can be set using a text message, but its usefulness is limited since the entry only allows seven characters, making it hard to clearly represent value and unit. Also, when "10 msec" is selected, the unit shown as "msec" does not match the actual output value (which isn't true milliseconds). - For presenting output values, having an optional date format such as hh:mm:ss.xx0 would greatly help. - The block's internal time base for "s", "m", and "h" units is not 0.01s but somewhat less, which means that activating blocks with input pin "En" in parallel, especially with frequent ON/OFF switching, produces inconsistent end-time values. Please refer to the attached circuits: - Test_Stopuhr_01 ([article_no]).lsc: Demonstrates how, using a trick with the "switching delay" block, a value display can be achieved through two units. Particularly, with the 10 ms setting, only durations up to 32 seconds can be shown. This is because the "Ta" parameter in the "switching delay" block requires value input in ms, but the allowed solution is only 10 ms, and the referred value's unit is simply cut off without rounding. A required multiplier for the output value of "Stop watchwatch" prevents its value range from being exhausted. - Test_Stopuhr_02 ([article_no]).lsc: Shows that using an "analog comparator" block, you can achieve at least a 65-second display duration with a resolution of 0.01 s, using a time format of ss:xx0 seconds and another trick. - Test_Stopuhr_03 ([article_no]).lsc: Demonstrates a demo, where, according to my own findings, a time indication with a maximum duration of 99 hours and 59 minutes at a resolution of 0.01s can be achieved. (Hint: In PC simulation, switch to "font 2" in the text message area for a suitable date display...) My conclusion: If you need times at a 1/100 s resolution (which is not fully supported by [product_name]), the "Stop watchwatch" block provides a useful alternative to complex circuit solutions required for [version_no]. For other time units, it's worth considering whether a circuit-based solution using impulse generator and counter blocks might be more effective, depending on your needs. Enjoy experimenting!

The 'switch' functionality can only be defined for simulation and is only saved within the program file. Apologies for any confusion. If you connect a switch to terminal I1, then I1 behaves as a switch in the program. If you connect a button, I1 functions as a button. Is it possible to configure the [product_name] [article_no] to generate an alarm condition if the controller fails, stops, or loses power, through an output contact that changes state in case of any malfunction?

Hello, You can use a latching relay triggered by an initialization flag to control an output. When the controller is stopped or loses power, the output will be off. When the system resumes operation, the output will be set again. Regards,

It's simpler to keep a digital output always set high; if the program stops, the output drops to zero. Is the intention here to build a watchdog circuit?

Yes, the goal is to implement a watchdog. The controller's role is to monitor a critical electronic filter circuit and provide feedback in case it becomes nonfunctional. I'm looking for a normally closed contact that opens while the controller runs, and closes to signal an alarm if it stops or loses power. Hello, When the [product_name] is powered off, all digital outputs are also off. Additionally, if you set the device to STOP mode, the digital outputs are off as well. Best regards

There are two situations to consider: 1. The [product_name] fails to run 2. The [product_name] is stuck in a running program (although this is rare) You can make an output relay that is always ON when the device operates normally; it will open if the [product_name] fails (e.g., on power loss), but this won't help when the device is stuck in a program. Possible solution: Set an output to turn ON for 1 second every minute. Connect this output to a time delay relay (OFF-Delay) with a delay greater than 1 minute. Also connect it to an ON-Delay relay with a delay less than 1 minute. If the OFF-Delay relay is ON and the ON-Delay is OFF, the device is operating correctly. I'm new to the [product_name] environment and would appreciate advice on configuring an analog threshold trigger. I'm currently using a [article_no] module. My setup includes a pressure transducer with a range of 0-5 PSI and 4-20mA output. I'm converting this to a 2-10V signal via a 500 ohm resistor, but I'm uncertain about what measurement range, gain, and offset values to use. I need the output to activate (1) when the PSI reading is at or above 0.22 PSI, and deactivate (0) for any value below 0.22 PSI.

Switching exactly at 0.22 PSI without hysteresis will cause instability, as the output could toggle frequently. Also, with your 0-5 PSI sensor, setting the switch point so low (0.22 PSI) puts you within the lowest portion of the measuring range, where tolerances can be significant. A sensor with a range better suited to your switching point, such as 0-0.5 PSI, would be more accurate.

Here's a sample method for scaling your signal.

I'll describe my scenario in detail: It's a tank filling process with low level indicated by 6 inches of water (0.22 PSI), where the output will control a pilot light signaling low tank level. The high level is at 4 feet of water (1.73 PSI), with the output controlling the fill pump. When the tank is below 6 inches, the low level output remains off (0), turning on the low level pilot light. When the tank reaches 6 inches, the low output activates (1), turning off the pilot light. If the tank is below 4 feet, the high level output is off (0), letting the pump operate. Once 4 feet is reached, the output turns on (1), stopping the pump.

The same issue applies to the pump control. Below 1.73 PSI, the pump turns on; above that, it switches off. Without hysteresis, the pump may repeatedly toggle.

I'm receiving an error message when attempting to open your example.

If you don't have [product_name] [version_no], programming a [product_name] [version_no] device requires the matching software version.

Pump control is handled manually—the operator must first press the fill button. As long as the tank level remains below 4 feet (1.73 PSI), the pump can be turned on and the operator can leave. The pump continues running until 4 feet is reached; it won't turn back on unless the fill button is pressed again.

I've faced this connectivity issue twice today—trouble linking the PLC to my PC via ethernet cable. I read that this could be due to not having the latest software version. I couldn't download the newest release since I wasn't registered. Is there a quicker way to access the latest version without waiting for registration approval?

Alternatively, buying a new DVD with the software is an option, though it's uncertain if this would be any faster. I'm using version 8.2.1.

Here’s an example compatible with [product_name] version 8.2.1.

Thanks! Could you also explain how you determined the required settings?

The A/D converter translates any analog input signal to a scale of 0-1000 units. For a 4-20 mA (or 2-10 V) input, only the 200-1000 units are valid for measurements, the units below 200 correspond to 0-4 mA (or 0-2 V). Select the sensor type as '4-20 mA.' In your situation, set the minimum to '0' and the maximum to '5000' (for three decimal places on the display). The software automatically calculates gain and offset.

I'm unclear on the threshold setting you used—220. This would mean the high level setting would be 1730, which exceeds the measurement range. Should my low threshold be 22? This would make the high value 173.

It seems you're having trouble with the settings. The minimum is 0 mpsi and the maximum is 5000 mpsi, representing 0.000 to 5.000 PSI (three decimal places). 0.22 PSI equals 220 mpsi, and 1.73 PSI equals 1730 mpsi.

Hello, We use an analog input expansion module to connect a 4-20 mA level transmitter. The end user performs input scaling directly using the integrated [product_name] display, since measurement ranges such as 0-5 meters or 0-10 meters could be applied. Two decimal places are shown on the display, giving centimeter-level precision. To scale the analog input, we utilize the 'Analog amplifier' function block with corresponding configuration. We have two questions after reading the [document]: 1) We observed that scaling depends on parameters such as 'Min', 'Max', 'Gain', and 'Offset', but only 'Gain' and 'Offset' are editable via the 'Message text' block. Is it correct that adjustment is only possible for 'Gain' and 'Offset'? Is there any way to change 'Min' and 'Max' differently? 2) For a 0-10 meter transmitter, we set: - Sensor 4..20 mA - Min 0 - Max 1000 - Gain 1.25 (autocalculated) - Offset -250 (autocalculated) - Decimal 2 For a 0-5 meter transmitter, we set: - Sensor 4..20 mA - Min 1 - Max 505 - Gain 0.63 (autocalculated) - Offset -125 (autocalculated) - Decimal 2 In theory, setting Min 0 and Max 500 would be correct, but the logic software returns an error. Is this expected? For a 0-5 meter level transmitter, should we configure as if it were a 1 to 5.05 meter device?

The issue is that the analog amplifier block only allows two decimal places for the gain factor setting. With a 4-20 mA sensor and a 0.00 to 5.00 m range, the ideal gain is 0.625, but the amplifier rounds it to 0.63. This rounding leads to unexpected min and max value requirements. Min, Max, Gain, and Offset are linked and can't be altered separately. See the attachment for details. In such situations, I usually use two analog amplifiers in sequence: the first converts 4-20 mA to 0-1000 units, and the second remaps that to 0.00 to 5.00 m.

The logic in this branch seems correct, but the logic in the upper branch fails on the actual PLC, even though it works in simulation. During the 15+10 seconds, the Ta parameter stays at zero in real hardware, although it increments in simulation.

In this case, it's more than just a display problem—the program itself behaves differently in the PLC versus simulation. After reviewing the process, I've identified the cause. The trigger drops out in the actual PLC during the transition from TL to TH in Block B063 due to a low signal in Block B071 for a single cycle. From what I understand, adding a WISE-4010/LAN to the [product_name] controller could allow for higher resolution on the analog input. My goal is to connect a 10 kg load cell and read 10,000 units (representing 10,000 grams). Will the [product_name] controller be able to read 10,000 units from the load cell via the WISE-4010/LAN? Also, do I need a separate load cell amplifier or can the load cell be connected directly to the WISE-4010/LAN? Thank you.

The analog inputs of the WISE-4010/LAN offer 12-bit resolution, meaning 4096 units. When measuring 10,000g, each unit will represent approximately 2.44g (10,000g / 4096 units). The analog inputs work with 0/4-20 mA signals, but load cells typically output only millivolts. You’ll need a load cell amplifier that outputs 0-20 mA or 4-20 mA.

If you’re using just a load cell, consider amplifiers with Modbus TCP capability. This often increases the resolution to 16 bits and enables two-way communication, so you can do more than just read the weight.

You mentioned the ADAM-6717 I/O Module. I found a similar module, ADAM-6017, with a good price. It supports Modbus/TCP, provides 16-bit resolution, and includes 8 analog inputs. [url] Is this module compatible for transferring load cell data to the [product_name] controller at higher resolution? I’ve already obtained an amplifier. Kind regards, [user_name]

The ADAM-6717 module can handle small voltage signals and should be suitable for your application. However, you’ll still require a special load cell amplifier since load cells cannot be connected directly to standard analog inputs.

Regarding your note about having the amplifier: Do you now have load cells equipped with the appropriate amplifier? Please specify what kind of signal you’re getting depending on the weight. The ADAM-6017 can communicate with [product_name] controllers, but pay attention to the range of integer values supported. These controllers typically handle integer values from -32,768 to 32,767 (15 bits plus sign) for arithmetic or comparison blocks. Floating point (32 or 64 bit) is available for display, but conversion to 15-bit integer can lose accuracy. If the ADAM-6017 outputs 16 bits without sign (0 to 65,535), values above 32,767 are recognized as negative numbers by the controller. This can be addressed via software blocks, or you can ensure your values remain below 32,767, depending on your application. Regards, [user_name]

I chose the PEPPERL+FUCHS KFD2-WAC2-1.D amplifier based on forum recommendations. I need 10,000 values, aiming for a 1 gram resolution on a 10 kg load cell. From what I’ve learned, the ADAM-6017 should be up to the task. Thanks for the detailed information. Kind regards, [user_name]

The setup should work: connect the load cell to the input of the KFD amplifier, then the amplifier’s analog output to the analog input of the ADAM-6017, and finally, use a patch cable to link the ADAM-6017 to the [product_name] controller. For best results, configure the KFD for 4–20 mA analog output and the ADAM-6017 for 4–20 mA input. The ADAM-6017 can output data as either 16-bit integer or 4-byte float, both readable by the [product_name] controller. With proper scaling, you can achieve a range of 0 to 10,000 for 0 to 10 kg. One point of consideration: investing over 400 euros in components to connect to a controller costing about 100 euros may not be cost-effective if you only need basic weight display; ready-made weight systems might be more economical. Regards, [user_name]

The Modbus holding register (50514) is a double register (50514 + 50515). You need to transfer two words starting at address 50514. There is an issue though: this value is a 32-bit unsigned integer, while the [product_name] can only read 32-bit or 64-bit float values using its F/I converter, not 32 or 64-bit unsigned integer values.

Example: Transfer two words from start address HR50514 to your [product_name], start address VW0, two words. If the value is less than 32,768, you can read the value in the right two bytes, which is VW2, with a standard analog network input. Are you certain the Modbus port is 505? And is the Unit-ID set to 255?

Thank you very much for taking the time to help. Here is a screenshot of the communication table. Regarding port and ID: The port is configurable on the [company_name] E24, and typically port 502 is set. The default ID is 255, but I will try 1. Concerning the tables, dealing with 32 bit is a problem as the sign can be misplaced on the BIT. I will read it using a specific software like Modbus Doctor to see if these correspond to the expected value.

You may need to use 50515 (+50516) as the start address if there is an offset of +1. Modbus servers commonly use port 502 by default, so it is surprising you set port 505 in the transfer table. I am not sure what unit ID your Modbus device uses as the documentation does not specify. What voltage are you measuring – is it 230VAC? If so, a simple analog network input should work. For 230 VAC, you would read 230.00, and analog inputs may go up to 327.67 VAC.

I'm looking for a way to store an analog input as a setpoint in non-volatile memory during setup (teaching). When running, I want to compare the same analog input with the stored value to control an output based on defined limits. The output should be true as long as the value stays within allowed limits (around the stored setpoint). Saving the value to non-volatile memory is essential. I've read about doing this using timer/counter functions, analog multiplexers, and by writing to variables, but I'm searching for the simplest approach. Thanks to everyone for sharing their knowledge on this forum.

You can try the following method: Set the properties of the MAX/MIN function block as follows: - Enable Retentivity - Set MODE to 3.

Another option is to use the Analog Watchdog block, which is designed for this type of function. When the EN input receives a positive edge, it stores the analog value. As long as the EN input remains on, the block compares the stored value with the current input. If the difference goes beyond the parameter limits, the output activates. More details about this block can be found in the online help.

Hello everyone, Is it possible to perform mathematical equations in [product_name]? I have a temperature sensor connected using a 4-20 mA signal. For reference: 0.1 mA corresponds to 0.78°C. I want to display a value X on the screen calculated as: X = 28 * (1 + 0.00336 * Temperature value). Appreciate any guidance.

Do you mean: X = 28 * (1 + 0.00336 * Temperature value)?

Yes, that's correct.

Could you share the sensor range? Specifically: What temperature does 4 mA represent? And what temperature does 20 mA represent?

The issue with [product_name] is that it handles only fixed numbers. Floating point calculations are restricted to mathematical instructions. For example, a value like 0.00336 can't be directly used because only values between -32768 and 32767 are supported. Which type of sensor are you using and what range does your 4 to 20 mA represent? As an example: You could enter 336 divided by 10,000, resulting in 0.0336. If you need 0.0036, you'd have to use 100,000, but since the upper limit is 32,767, that's not possible.

Thanks for your response. For this sensor, 4 mA equals -25°C and 20 mA equals 100°C, following a linear relationship. The actual formula is: X = 28.084 * e^(0.0336 * T) = 249.44 when T is 65°C. Alternatively, you can write it as: X = 28.084 * [1 + 0.0336*T + (0.0336*T*0.0336*T)/2 + (0.0336*T*0.0336*T*0.0336*T)/6 + ... (Taylor series expansion) ...] = 249.41 for T = 65°C. There are many terms to compute for accuracy. I don't think it's possible to achieve this level of calculation directly in [product_name].

If the relationship is linear, you only need to use the analog amplification and you don't have to perform complex calculations. I'll provide an example for you later.

There is a linear relationship between the analog input and temperature conversion, but the connection between X and temperature is non-linear. As shown by the formula, it involves an exponential function. It's specifically the X value that I need displayed on the [product_name] screen.

If the relationship is non-linear, you won't be able to achieve this in [product_name]. It only supports fixed-point numbers and does not handle exponential functions. For such requirements, you should consider using [version_no] instead.

To transfer this value to the web server, use VM memory on [product_name] and the 'Parameter VM Mapping' function found under Tools. In [product_name] Web Editor, use an 'Analog Value' component and configure it with these parameters: Block type: VD, Block number: 0, Block format: Unsigned.

Yes, you can, but only in the other direction. Use Parameter VM Mapping to write the value to a parameter in the mathematical instruction. Note that mathematical instructions only accept integer values (VW), not double integers (VD).

Remember: VM area addresses are byte-based. User addresses range from 0 to 850. For bits, V0.0 means byte 0, bit 0. For bytes, VB0 contains bits V0.0 to V0.7. For words, VW0 includes VB0 and VB1, corresponding to bits V0.0 to V1.7.

Is it possible to change the digital input of a [product_name] [version_no] using [product_name] [version_no] and an SMS command, or is it only possible to modify the digital transistor input/output of the [product_name] [version_no]? You can control both digital outputs of the [product_name] [version_no] via SMS and then connect up to two digital inputs of the [product_name]. Alternatively, sending an SMS can toggle a bit in the VM area, which can be used as a network input in the [product_name], allowing for more flexibility beyond just two inputs.

Currently, we use the first method, but we want the output of the [product_name] to automatically switch to 0 after two seconds. So, we intend to use the [product_name] instead of a relay as we currently do. What kind of SMS commands can set the network inputs of the [product_name] to 0 or 1? We now monitor the outputs of the [product_name] via SMS. Is the process similar for network inputs, only reversed?

If you want to switch a network input in the [product_name] via SMS, note that the [product_name] will set the input statically. This generally requires sending two SMS messages: one to turn on, and another to turn off. For example, 'Password; [product_name]=VM100,1,BYTE' to switch on, and 'Password; [product_name]=VM100,0,BYTE' to switch off. These commands toggle the VM bit V100.0. You can select other VM addresses depending on your setup. Dynamically switching network inputs (for a timed action) in the [product_name] requires an additional step in your program. I've attached a small example program to demonstrate both approaches.

Understood. Thank you very much; your explanation was much clearer than anything I found in the manual. This will help us move forward.

We programmed the [product_name], but each time we try to set the network input to 1, we get the message: '[product_name]=VM50,1,BYTE:No Success'. Any idea what might be causing this issue?

Have you declared the variable in the [product_name] [version_no]?

Please check [url]. It describes how to set up everything needed to perform an action with an SMS in the [product_name], including communication between two [product_name] Controllers via [product_name] [version_no] and SMS.

I need to power my [product_name] base module and two [product_name] expansion modules, along with several buttons and other devices. I use 1.5 mm² wiring, but because of the wire end sleeves, I can only fit one wire in each contact. How is this usually managed? Also, my analog output module features two L+ and two M terminals that appear to be internally connected. Why are there two connections for each? Sorry if these are basic questions—I'm just starting out. Thanks in advance!

Welcome to the forum. In practice, bridged terminal blocks are typically used to distribute +24V and M (or L and N) from the power supply to each module. For analog modules, the power terminals are duplicated, meaning connections with the same name (like M) are internally bridged.

All [product_name] wiring supports max 2x 1.5 mm² or 1x 2.5 mm² cables. It is recommended to use ferrules. Make sure to review the manual.

For beginners, note that 'twin' ferrules are available for two 1.5mm² wires, which are easier to fit than using single ferrules on each wire.

If you see a message saying the program on your PC and the [product_name] device are different, there are usually two explanations: either the program codes genuinely differ (although you say you've checked), or parameters on the device have been changed without updating the PC version. Another test — disconnect the Ethernet cable from the [product_name] and try to ping its IP address; if you get a response, another device may be using that IP. I have two [product_name] controllers on my network: one directly cabled to the router, the other connected via WiFi repeater. I can run online tests on both, but only if no parameter changes have been made. In such cases, I need to do an upload. Hope this helps.

The quoted duration for memory backup during power loss is 80 hours at 25°C. We need this to last at least 90 days to keep the hour counter intact. Is there a way to achieve this, apart from modifying the device's memory circuit with an extra lithium cell? Any advice is appreciated!

There is no battery module available for [product_name]. The program itself is saved in internal non-volatile memory, but data retention lasts only several hours when power is lost. The only workaround is to prevent extended power outages. For larger systems like [product_name], data retentive during power-off periods longer than several hours requires a battery module, which can last about 200 days. If you require 90 days of power-off time, you'd need to replace the battery after two cycles of 90 days. Additional details and order numbers are listed in the relevant manual chapters.

Could you please clarify: If I have a program stored in [product_name] and lose power, what gets lost? Is it just the program and parameters? If I use a colored memory chip, does that ensure safety beyond 80 hours, or is the program still deleted after a few hours? I appreciate suggestions to prevent losing my program, which operates a large aquarium system.

Dear customer, your program in [product_name] is stored safely in the internal non-volatile memory, so it survives a power interruption. Block parameters are also saved if marked as retentive; otherwise, they are lost during power loss. External memory modules serve for copying, transferring, or backing up your program. The internal clock is only buffered after power failure for about 80 hours under standard conditions. Your technical support team.

Replies explain that while program storage is non-volatile and unaffected by outages, runtime values such as clocks and counters are only kept for around 80 hours. Since the device lacks an official battery backup module, upgrading to a higher-end product with battery support is suggested.

First, on the PLC side, you need to create a server connection as shown in the first screenshot. You’ll see Local Properties set to TSAP 21.00 and Remote to 21.11. On the second page, you mirror this connection in NetPro for OPC—Local TSAP 21.11 and Remote TSAP 21.00. In the Variable Memory definition, specify which PLC variables you want to access from OPC. In OPC, you can use an address format like [Logo]DB1,W4,1. In my NetPro example, the connection is called “Logo”, and it always maps DB1 as the area. Hope this helps.

If you select “Logo_TCP1” on the left, you’ll see various items listed on the right, one of which is “&statepath”. Drag this to the watch list to read its value—it should show 'UP', 'DOWN', or 'RECOVERY'. If it's 'UP', your PLC connection is active. Note that the connection won't be established until you poll a value, so you need to specify an address. For example, you can also drag “IB0” to the watch list. I’m unsure if [product_name] supports browsing of datablocks as standard S7 CPUs do, which may explain why DB1 isn't visible.

You have a couple of options: drag “&statepath” to see the syntax and copy it to another line. When you click in the 'ID' column, a button lets you open a dialog to change the 'Item ID/name.' Depending on which PLC address you wish to access, you can enter: S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,INT2,1 or S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,INT4,1. The PLC always uses DB1 for addressing. 'INT2' maps to DBW2 as an integer, and ',1' means only one element is read (an integer). Another example would be: S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,X0.0,1. If you prefer, you can set up symbolic addressing by entering these addresses into the OPC Symbol Editor. Then, within 'Communication Settings -> [product_name] NET configuration -> OPC Settings -> Symbols,' load the symbol file and see your symbolic names in a '\SYM:' folder.

text:
Hello. I am having some trouble understanding the VM memory area and how to communicate with a [product_name] data block in a [product_name] controller. How can I send temperature values stored as real numbers in my DB to the LOGO VM area? Currently, I receive this value in a NAI block in the LOGO program from a remote device. When the block type is DB, I can only access .DBW. If I try sending the integer value from the [product_name] DB using the PIW, the scaling in LOGO doesn't match, even if I use the same scaling range (-50 to 150 degrees) as in the PLC. Has anyone else experienced similar issues with communication between LOGO and [product_name]? Regards

The key point is that LOGO only supports analog values as integers, specifically whole numbers from -32,768 to 32,767. It doesn't recognize double integers or real numbers. For example, if you measure temperature with a PT100 and an AM2 RTD, you'll get values from 0 to 1000 units at first. You can then scale this with an analog amplifier for a display in the range -50 to 200°C without decimal points (-50 to 200), or -50.0 to 200.0°C with one decimal place (-500 to 2000). Decimal placement is only shown on the LOGO or TDE display. If you want to transfer the temperature to [product_name], you send the value as INT from -500 to 2000. In [product_name], convert this INT to a REAL value and divide by 10.0 to get the decimal temperature. For LOGO, you can use VW0 in the VM area, corresponding in [product_name] to DB1.DBW0.

To illustrate: LOGO sends a temperature such as 157.5°C (represented as 1575 INT) to the [product_name] controller. You first convert the INT to DINT, then DINT to REAL, and lastly divide the REAL value by 10.0.

Here’s one way to interpret your situation: If the temperature is a real value in your [product_name] controller and you want to use it in a LOGO controller, there are two main approaches: 1) Convert the real value to an integer in [product_name] first (for example, multiply by 10 for one decimal precision and change to signed 16-bit integer). Then use NAIx in LOGO to read the integer, with an analog amplifier set to gain=1 and decimals=1. 2) If you want to read a real value (single float is 4 bytes, double float is 8 bytes) in LOGO, use the FI block (float to integer). This block lets you select Float or Double and specify the VM area start address, e.g., VM0. Single float at VM0 uses 4 bytes (VB0-VB3 = 2 words = 1 double word); double float at VM0 uses 8 bytes (VB0-VB7 = 4 words = 2 double words. Check how many bytes your DB uses in [product_name] for the real value. The first method is usually easier for sending temperature readings from [product_name] to LOGO. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks! That was really helpful!

feature_keywords: real to integer conversion || VM area mapping || analog input scaling || float to integer block

You should keep in mind: Addressing in [product_name] devices is byte-based, while holding registers use word-based addressing. For example, transferring register 40001 to VW1 writes to bytes 1 and 2; transferring register 40033 to VW2 writes to bytes 2 and 3, causing some overlap. Therefore, always assign word addresses at intervals of two, starting from zero in [product_name]. Recommended setup: VW0 <- HR40001, VW2 <- HR40033. I'm still dealing with the red question mark error, but I'll try to resolve it.

It's because 1 refers to the first holding register. According to Wikipedia: Coil (Read-write): 1 bit, addresses 00001-09999; Discrete input (Read-only): 1 bit, addresses 10001-19999; Input register (Read-only): 16 bits, addresses 30001-39999; Holding register (Read-write): 16 bits, addresses 40001-49999.

Hello, I need to record temperature samples twice per day and want to store data for the last month, resulting in a total of 62 data points. My question is: Can I configure the data log to have exactly 62 entries, so when new data is added, it overwrites the oldest entry and always keeps just 62 records? Best regards, [user_name]

It is not possible to set the number of Data Log entries to 62. The [product_name] keeps writing data until the data log is full. If you use an mSD card for storage, each Data Log file can hold up to 20,000 lines.

Hello, There are two ways to handle datalogging with [product_name]: 1. With an inserted mSD card, as previously described. Data will be saved in records on the card, and once 20,000 lines are reached a new record is created (up to 50 records). Only the current record can be uploaded via [product_name] configuration software, while older records require removing the card to read them on a PC. 2. Without an mSD card, the data log uses internal memory, which can hold up to 200 lines. Once this limit is reached, the oldest entries are overwritten automatically (FIFO). These records can be uploaded using the [product_name] configuration software. Note: Neither method allows you to set a custom number of lines like 62. Based on your requirements, the second option may be more suitable, as you could record up to 200 values per day if needed. Hope this helps.

What happens to your logged data in option 2 if there is a power outage?

Data in option 2 is stored in internal EEPROM memory, so data is retained even in the event of a power failure.

Hello, I have a straightforward project using a [product_name] 24V unit with relay outputs. The setup includes a latching relay activated by two physical push buttons wired to the inputs, controlling a single coil output. Everything works initially, but at times the outputs turn off unexpectedly, as if someone pressed the stop button, though no such action occurs. I’ve also tried a conventional start-stop latching circuit with the same outcome—the outputs shut off. Even when simplifying the program to just a couple of lines, the issue persists. Could this be caused by electrical noise in the control cabinet? There are three inverters in the system, all controlled by the PLC outputs, but otherwise it’s a simple arrangement. Any advice or insights are greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!

If electromagnetic interference is the cause, add on-delays of around 0.1 seconds between the button and the latch. You might also want to troubleshoot the issue using diagnostic tools. For example, connect counters to all relevant inputs and monitor their values—if any counter increases without a button being pressed, electromagnetic issues may be present. Regards, [user_name]

Make sure the switch doesn’t suffer from voltage leakage. Also, ensure the [product_name]'s power supply is capable of properly powering the switch with adequate current. Check that the power line connection at the [product_name]'s terminal is secure and provides good contact.

Every terminal connection should be properly secured and have solid contact.

Check if supply issues are causing the PLC to restart at irregular intervals due to voltage disturbances. Inspect the supply voltage and consider enabling remanence on the latch to see if that resolves the problem.

Thank you all for your assistance. The issue was traced to an input drop from my 3SK2, which was just enough for the PLC to register, possibly related to the dark test feature of the 3SK2. Adding a counter as suggested resolved the problem. Much appreciated!
