Hello [user_name], Yes, you can use this configuration, but there are some important considerations: 1) Check if all 220 V AC inputs are from the same phase (L1, L2, or L3). If not, only 4 inputs from the same phase can be connected to each 'group' of digital inputs. On the 230RC, the first 4 inputs (I1 to I4) are physically separated from the next 4 (I5 to I8) to ensure isolation between different phases. 2) When using a DM 8 module for additional digital inputs, all inputs should be from the same phase. For a DM 16 module, you’ll notice inputs are split into 2 groups, allowing for different phases. If all inputs are from the same source, you don't need to group them by phase. 3) The base module (CPU) supports 4 outputs (10A relays) directly. Additional outputs (5A each) on the DM 8 module can be used as needed for other functions. 4) The 10A and 5A relay ratings apply to resistive loads like heating elements or regular light bulbs. For inductive loads (like motors), the current capacity is reduced. 5) The [product_name] Contact 230 provides excellent performance for loads up to 20A (resistive) and 4kW (inductive), offering reliability and good value compared to alternative brands. Hope this helps with your power project! [user_name]

Could you provide the exact sensor manufacturer and model? Is it a 2-wire sensor? What output signal does it provide: 0-10V, or 0/4-20mA? The analog inputs on this base module accept only 0-10V. If your sensor outputs a current signal, you'll need a 500 Ohm resistor to convert the current to a voltage signal.

Make sure your [product_name] is powered by a DC power source (12 or 24VDC). Your sensor should ideally be a 3-wire sensor with a DC output, maximum 10V. Insert a 500 Ohm resistor between I7 (or I8) and the negative terminal of the power supply. In your program, you can treat a 4-20mA sensor as a 2-10V sensor after conversion.

Yes, your [product_name] supports two independent analog inputs by default, so you can connect two different sensors for analog data. Note that if you configure I7 as an analog input (AI1), it cannot be used simultaneously as a digital input. Hello, I'm experiencing a problem when trying to use the average value from two analog sensors. Calculating the mean using a math function works correctly, but when this value is sent to an analog threshold trigger, the output appears to be incorrect. For example, with manual inputs of 500 and 300, I receive 400 as the average, but the threshold trigger seems to output 500 instead. I appreciate any advice on what might be causing this issue.

Welcome to the forum. You've set the analog amplifier values to the correct measuring range. After adding the two values and dividing by two, the mean calculation is accurate. With 500 and 300, you get 400. However, when you use the threshold trigger with additional amplification, the 400 is converted back to 500. The calculation is: input value (400) * gain (2.5) + offset (-500) = output for the threshold trigger. 400 * 2.5 = 1000, 1000 + (-500) = 500. For correct operation of the threshold trigger, set the gain to 1 and the offset to 0, which are the default settings.

I realized the solution myself: I needed to adjust the gain and offset values, since they were already handled earlier in the process. Thank you.

Initially, an older SIM card from the carrier was working fine, but after being unused for a while, the phone number was deactivated. We tried new SIM cards from the same provider, but none were recognized by the module. Switching to another carrier worked briefly in my office—confirmed by the module connecting to the network on the status screen. However, when tested elsewhere, I received a diagnostic message indicating the module couldn't connect to the mobile wireless network. Upon checking, I found it had automatically connected to the previous carrier instead of the intended one. Testing the SIM card in a mobile phone confirmed it works, and restarting the module did not help. Is there a way to manually select which network it connects to? Regards.

Hello [user_name], If your provider's mobile network becomes unreachable and you have enabled the "Allow roaming" option, the module will connect to any available mobile network.

Hi [user_name], I've tried enabling and disabling roaming, but it hasn't helped—the device still connects to the wrong network and won't allow mobile data. Should I restart the module after making changes?

Hello, Please try restarting the module as suggested. If it still doesn't resolve the issue, consider performing a factory reset and reconfiguring everything from the beginning.

Still no solution. The device continues to connect to a network but won't allow for a mobile connection. I also updated the firmware and performed a factory reset before reconfiguring, but no luck. Should I reach out to the carrier?

Try these steps first, if you haven't done so yet: 1. Remove the SIM card. 2. In the web management tool, go to the 'WAN' > 'Mobile wireless settings' tab and uncheck the 'Activate mobile wireless interface' option to turn it off. 3. Power down the module by holding the SET button for 5 to 10 seconds until all LEDs are off. 4. Disconnect the module from its power supply. 5. Remove and then reinsert the SIM card. 6. Restore power to the module. 7. Go back to the same settings tab and check 'Activate mobile wireless interface'. 8. Enter the SIM card's PIN in the settings. If this doesn't help, it's recommended to contact support.

At the moment, it's working in the original location where I tested it, but I'll try the suggested solution again in an area with connectivity problems. Thanks for your support—I'll keep you posted.

You're welcome.

Hi [user_name], Could you share what steps you took to get it working? Any specific action that made the difference? I'm facing a similar issue and would appreciate any advice or details about what you did differently. Thank you.

Hello, I haven't been able to resolve the issue completely. Occasionally, SMS messages are received even when it's connected to the wrong network, but sending them is unreliable. Try repositioning the antenna, as signal location seems to be a major factor. In some areas, the correct network connects, but in others, it doesn't. Best of luck.

Hi [user_name], Thanks for your response. I was able to resolve the connectivity problem—previous attempts may have failed due to missing steps. Make sure that the 'Enable mobile wireless interface' box is unchecked when swapping SIM cards. With the module powered off, insert the new SIM card, power it up, and check the 'Enable mobile wireless interface' option followed by 'Apply'. Confirm 'Mobile Wireless Interface Connection Established: Yes' is shown, then you can send and receive SMS. To change SIM cards again, uncheck 'Enable mobile wireless interface', hit 'Apply', go to maintenance and set the module to safe status, power off, swap SIMs, power back on, login, and enable the mobile wireless interface followed by 'Apply'. Once 'Connection Established: Yes' is shown, SMS functionality should work.

Hello, I have a driver with a 0-10V input. When [product_name] sends 0 Vdc or 3.2Vdc, the voltage increases to 4.2Vdc once connected. How can this be resolved? The driver requires a minimum current input of 0.15 mA. This driver accepts a dimming signal of 0-10V, variable resistance from 0-100kOhms, or a PWM signal with 0-100% duty cycle.

The issue is with the input interface because it is not a standard type. [product_name] can only control typical 0-10V interfaces reliably. This topic has been discussed often in the German section of the forum. Potential solutions include: using a resistor in parallel with the analog output, where you need to determine the correct resistance value; or using an isolating amplifier for 0-10V conversion, which I consider the best choice.

I experienced a similar issue when connecting to an LED driver and was able to fix it by placing a 10k resistor in parallel across the output. More details can be found at: [url]. That said, [user_name]'s suggestion to use an isolating amplifier is the most effective method, though it is more costly. My setup has been working for over 8 months without any problems.

How can I measure the time between an input being activated and an event occurring? The goal is to record the duration after every 20 activations of input I1.

Hello, could you share what you've attempted so far? Also, what specific timing results are you aiming for?

In this application, after every 20 activations of input I1, we need to measure the time interval. This interval typically ranges between 15.0 and 25.0 seconds, and it should include a decimal point for precision. I’ve attached my current approach for review.

Understood, the initial requirement is to count up to 20 and then reset the counter. At each count of 20, you could use a RS block to indicate the measurement phase and reset it after taking the measurement. For timing, I recommend utilizing an asynchronous pulse generator set to 0.05 seconds for both on and off times, yielding 10 pulses per second. You would then use a secondary counter to track these pulses, configuring one decimal point in the counter settings. This provides the precise decimal output needed in the message block. Before repeating the process, ensure the second counter is reset. This is how I would set up this solution in [product_name] software.

Hello, this is the completed program. Please review and let me know your recommendations. Thank you.

Hardware: [product_name] [article_no] Software: [product_name] [version_no] I'm trying to understand if changes to program parameters are saved automatically by the device. When I edit a parameter but don't use the 'Save prg>sd' command, and then reboot, the changes still seem to be there. I checked the .bin file on the SD card using the software, and it reflects the updated program. Is this expected behavior, or am I missing something? Thank you!

When you change parameters on the actual [product_name], those changes also get stored in the bin file on the SD card, even without using the save command from the device menu. Here's some background: On startup, the device first checks if there’s a program on the SD card. If it exists, it compares the SD card program to what’s in flash memory. If there’s a difference, it loads the SD card program into flash memory. If parameter changes weren’t automatically saved to the SD card, each restart would revert to old parameters.

I did a series of tests: - At each startup, if the SD card is present, the program loads from it. - Changing a parameter while the program is running results in the modification being automatically saved to the SD card's bin file. - If I change a parameter while the program is stopped, the change is not saved automatically to the SD card unless I manually use the 'Save to card' command. Is my understanding correct, or am I missing something? Thank you.

You're correct—when editing parameters in Stop mode, saving to the SD card has to be done manually. Whether this is a bug is unclear.

Thanks for clarifying. I wasn't expecting this behavior because the manual suggests that unsaved changes would be lost after reboot, regardless of the program's status. Anyway, now that I know, it makes sense for me. Thank you again,

I don’t consider this a bug. In fact, I use it as a useful safety feature. I have about 84 [product_name] devices installed as extra control/monitor units on multiple ships. Engineers often like to tweak settings to avoid alarms and other issues. Previously, without the memory card, this led to improper system operation and required sending a new device or going onboard to reinstall the original program. Now, I either install or send a pre-programmed SD card. By stopping the device, inserting the card, and powering up, the correct program loads automatically. If changes are made and issues arise later, I simply advise a power cycle. If this resolves the issue, I know someone altered the settings. This setup provides a reliable safety backup for situations where users modify system settings. So far, no one has figured out how to save their adjustments permanently to the SD card, so I haven’t had to explain its real purpose.
pain_keywords: unexpected save behavior || manual intervention || parameter loss risk
feature_keywords: automatic save || manual save || SD card backup || parameter change
gain_keywords: automatic saving || data persistence || process safety
insight_summary: Users shared their experiences with how parameter changes are saved on [product_name] devices. Automatic saving occurs if changes are made while the program is running; otherwise, a manual save is needed if the program is stopped. Initially, users found this distinction unclear but later saw it as a helpful safety measure to prevent unintended permanent updates to system settings.
user_expectations: Users expect every parameter change to be saved to the SD card automatically, regardless of whether the program is running or stopped, as implied by the documentation. They want modifications to remain after a reboot, without needing to manually save changes.

My concern is that the [product_name] module might send voltage into the DCS, which I'd like to avoid. Please refer to this as part one of the scenario: Analog in to analog out, then freeze the signal. Thanks!

Could you clarify further what you're trying to achieve?

Before installing the [product_name], I had two pressure sensors connected to the DCS via two wires each (+ and -); the DCS provided the power, and the sensors returned a 4–20 mA signal. Now, with the [product_name] in place, I have a module that both sensors connect to, and the output is sent to the DCS. The program is simple: signals entering the input module are relayed to the output module and into the DCS. The reason for this setup is to freeze the output signal to the DCS during cleaning, as water can cause erroneous readings. Now, my problem is that the output module supplies loop current on both channels, while the DCS already provides power to the sensors as they are 2-wire devices. I’m concerned about damaging any equipment. Is there a way to connect the output module so it works exactly like a 2-wire 4–20 mA pressure sensor?

What voltage does the DCS system use? Is it 24 VDC similar to the supply for the [product_name] module? In that case, you would just connect the ground (M or 0V) of both sources together.

From what I have seen, the DCS provides roughly 24 volts. The 2-wire sensor is usually powered from the DCS side, which is why I’m concerned—how will the [product_name] module behave in this scenario? I don't think I should mix the voltages from my 24V supply next to the controller with the DCS voltage. Maybe I should try powering the module using the DCS voltage on both L+ and M terminals?

I still need more details to fully understand your goal. If you want to pass the current output from the transmitter through the controller, you'll need an analog input module. For a 2-wire transmitter, it must be supplied with the same voltage as the module's input. So: +24VDC from the input module's power supply to the transmitter's (+) terminal. Connect the (-) terminal of the transmitter to the appropriate I-terminal. For the output module: connect the I-terminal to the (+) input on the DCS analog input. Do NOT connect the DCS's +24VDC to the output module's I-terminal. Connect the module's M terminal to the (-) input of the DCS analog input.

I am using an input module for the analog signals. That’s the setup I’ve come up with. See the attachment—the 24V power supply is on a DIN rail next to the controller. It works on a test bench, but the DCS input provides voltage for powering the sensor (when the PLC isn't present). What happens when the output module sends a 4–20 mA signal to the DCS?

If the DCS analog input is configured for voltage signals (0–10V), you cannot use the current output of the module. In that case, you should use the voltage output of the module.

The DCS is definitely set for 4–20mA. The sensor configuration is 4–20mA—I’ve confirmed this many times. The DCS supplies 24V over two wires to power the sensor and read the 4–20mA output. My question is: what would happen to the output module if 24V from the DCS came back into its output channel, which provides the 4–20mA signal? I admit I’m a bit confused.

The current output from the module works like a 4-wire sensor, as the output module is active and needs 24VDC supply. Your drawing was a bit confusing because it showed the wrong output terminals. To clarify: connect I1 to the (+) terminal of the DCS analog input, and M1 to the (-) terminal.

If you connect the two wires from the output module directly to the same DCS pins previously used for the sensor, it will not work. Look for a ground or GND pin on the DCS, or provide a wiring diagram. For example, which DCS pin was the sensor’s red wire connected to? You should avoid using this pin with the output module. Regards, [user_name]

It appears you’re not considering my advice, so proceed as you prefer. 2-wire sensor inputs are typically designed so that one connection is internally connected to +24V, and the other to ground through a shunt resistor for the 4–20mA signal. That means one side is +24V, and the other side is the 4–20mA input, which could be from a sensor or from an output module. The M terminal of the output module should be connected to the DCS’s internal ground (M, 0V, or GND). For certainty, obtain a wiring diagram for your hardware. Good luck.

Hello again, I found a solution and wanted to share. I used a 4–20mA signal isolator—simply plug it in and out. It’s a straightforward approach that avoids modifying the wiring since this is just a test setup for a sensor cleaning system. PHOENIX CONTACT | Repeater power supply - MINI MCR-SL-RPS-I-I - 2864422

I’m stepping away from this topic, as it seems you either haven’t understood the advice or are unwilling to. Without precise information regarding your DCS signal setup, this problem can't be resolved—signal isolators alone won't help. Goodbye, [user_name] P.S. See the attachment for an example of how a 2-wire sensor input may be designed. In that design, pin 1 is suitable only for passive sensors, pin 3 only for active sensors, and pin 2 is used for measuring.

You saved the day. Thank you!

I'm struggling to calculate the necessary gain and offset for converting this signal to engineering units. I can display the value in the message text, but the scaling isn't accurate. Any advice would be appreciated.

To translate your input to output using an amplifier, use the equation: output = input * GAIN + Offset. For your conversion: 1 V (100 internal units) maps to 0°F, and 5 V (500 internal units) maps to 135°F. Calculations yield GAIN = 0.3375 and Offset = -33.75. Set GAIN to 0.34 and Offset to -34 for practical implementation. This means 1 V displays as 0°F, and 5 V as 136°F. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you for the explanation, [user_name]!

Hi! Another approach: since any analog function lets you choose a 0-10V input, if 5V equals 135°F, 10V matches 270°F. Just select an input range from 0 to 270°F for direct scaling. Hope that helps!

Note that this method requires 0V to represent 0°F. However, the original question is about translating 1V to 0°F. For anyone needing to scale analog inputs, here's a concept: The relationship between input voltage and output using gain and offset is explained in section 4.3.6 of the manual. The general equation is output = input * GAIN + OFFSET, valid for inputs within 0 to 1000 units (0-10V). If the minimum input isn't zero, use the derived equations in the manual for OFFSET and GAIN. Example calculation for your specs results in OFFSET = -33.75 (~-34) and GAIN = 0.3375 (~0.34). Carefully select the range and decimal display options, since analog functions only handle integers and round as per the handbook. If you want to show decimals in messages, define the number of decimal places and adjust your calculation sequence accordingly. Only certain input terminals and module types support particular input ranges; see the manual for details. Best regards, [user_name]

Wow! I overlooked the 1-5V input, sorry. Normally, I divide the range by 4 (135 / 4 = 33.75) and create a conversion table: -33.75° at 0V, 0° at 1V, and so on, up to 303.75° at 10V. My question is: Since the base module already provides multiple analog inputs (I1, I2, I7, I8), does the expansion module assign I1 as AI5 and I2 as AI6?

This depends on the current configuration. The numbering of analog inputs in the expansion module starts after those used in the base module. For example, if you use four in the base module, the expansion module inputs begin at AI5.

The addresses assigned to the analog inputs of the first analog expansion module are determined by the I/O settings for the base module. In the configuration software, under File > Offline Settings > I/O settings, you can see how many addresses are reserved for the base module. Reserved addresses for the base module aren't available for expansion modules, regardless of whether you use the base module's analog inputs. By default, AI1 and AI2 are reserved for the base module. If zero addresses are reserved for the base, the first analog expansion module uses AI1 and AI2; if two addresses are reserved, it uses AI3 and AI4; if four addresses are reserved, it uses AI5 and AI6.

I am using a [product_name] and a [product_name] communication module, which are assigned IP addresses in the 192.168.20.x range. My regular network uses 192.168.1.x. The [product_name] uses a Class C network, meaning the IP range is 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255, and the subnet mask is typically 255.255.255.0. The IP address has four parts: XXX.YYY.ZZZ.NNN. For successful communication, all devices must share the same first three IP segments; only the last segment should differ per device. For example, my PC was using 192.168.178.NNN and the [product_name] was 192.168.178.030. I tried changing the IP to 192.168.0.030 to test. The programming software indicated that the [product_name] and PC were on different subnets and suggested a temporary IP for the PC, allowing communication and program transfer. This demonstrates that the [product_name] cannot communicate directly with devices on different subnets.

If you change your PC's subnet mask to 255.255.0.0 from 255.255.255.0, it will be able to access other subnets in addition to its current subnet.

Hello, What happens when there is no current at the analog 4-20 mA input? For example, if the sensor wire is cut or not connected. What value does the analog input show in such cases? I'm working on a project where we're currently monitoring the offset value. Why isn't zero displayed?

Approximately -32767 will be displayed if the analog input is active, but you disconnect the transmitter or there is a wire break. This value indicates an open loop, disconnected state, or wire break in the input.

Hi [user_name], Before electrical current signals became standard in control systems, pneumatic networks were widely used for input signals. Pneumatic signals typically operated in the 3-15 psi range for analog measurements. The 3-15 psi range meant that a tube break causing the system to drop to atmospheric pressure (0 psi) would trigger an alarm, rather than producing a zero signal. This idea carried over to 4-20 mA electrical loops: a wire break creates a 0 mA signal, which can be used for alarms. More information is available in online resources like this article: [url] Hope this helps, [user_name]

Hello [user_name], Welcome to the forum. You've posted in the [product_name] hardware section. Are you sure that's correct? If so, here’s what you should know: The A/D converter for an analog input translates the signal (regardless if 0-10V, 0/4-20mA, or PT100) into a range of 0–1000 units. With a sensor using 4-20 mA output, only units 200–1000 are valid. The first 200 units correspond to 0–4 mA. For a scale like 0 (min) to 1000 (max) in an analog amplifier, gain is set to 1.25 and offset to -250.

The offset referenced by [user_name] reflects this behavior. If gain = 1 and offset = 0, a reading of 200–1000 is shown with a sensor connected, and 0 appears for an open input. Generally, the physical value starts at zero, so you need to subtract an amount based on gain. For example, with gain = 2, set offset to -400 to make zero the physical start value; if the input is open, you’ll read -400. Regards, [user_name]

The PI controller operates in only one direction, which you define: Upward regulation means if the pressure drops below the setpoint, the controller will increase the value until the setpoint is reached. You need to treat the outputs of [product_name] as switches and also take into account the contact’s maximum current rating. Don’t connect loads that exceed this; otherwise, the contact will get damaged. It’s best to connect a relay to the output contact and use it to drive the load.

[product_name] is not ideal for precise RPM measurement—this applies even to the latest versions. It's useful to review the HELP documentation in the [product_name] software for UP/DOWN COUNTER instructions. This function counts on 0 to 1 transitions but ignores 1 to 0 transitions. Use inputs I3-I6 for high-frequency counting (up to 5 kHz if connected directly to the Up/Down counter block) and other inputs for low-frequency counts (typically about 4 Hz).

Your [product_name] device counts rotations accurately—if inputs and signals are correct and within frequency limits (up to 32767 whole numbers, sometimes more). If the precision seems off, it could be a programming issue. Please clarify your exact requirements.

The issue isn't with pulse counting but with the measurement time basis. A shorter time period increases error due to extrapolation. If you want RPM (x/min), you need to count over a full minute for updates every minute—otherwise, error increases. For better detection and evaluation, consider using a threshold trigger (e.g., based on frequency).

Thanks everyone. My application is to read the actual rotation of a generator and compare against a setpoint. For example, if RPM reaches 1530, an output is switched ON; if it’s below 1505, it's switched OFF. The system refreshes every 5 to 10 seconds. I'm trying to determine the time interval between pulses.

Hi, does your [product_name] have fast input channels?

Yes, it does—specifically I3. I’ve checked all available options.

Mistakes occur in these kinds of programs, regardless of using a budget [product_name] or an expensive alternative from another brand. To measure RPM, set your time base (for example, 1 second), count pulses in that window, and multiply by 60 to get revolutions per minute. There will always be a margin of one pulse in each timebase, common to all PLC systems. After multiplication, the results will fluctuate by 60. To reduce fluctuations, increase the time base (e.g., 60 seconds), which narrows error to ±1 but slows the calculation cycle to once per minute. If you use revolutions per second (RPS) instead, you won't need to multiply by 60, and fluctuations are smaller. Increasing pulses per revolution (e.g., 10 pulses per revolution, multiply by 6) can also help reduce fluctuations. Just ensure you don’t exceed the input’s max frequency. These principles apply to all PLCs, not just [product_name].

My understanding is that the [product_name] slave does not necessarily need its own program, although it can have one. Is there any additional information about this? The key distinction is that a [product_name] slave operates without a user program, whereas a [product_name] master utilizes the I/O of the slave. Masters can exchange data using S7 communication, allowing you to configure one [product_name] (master) as clients and the others as servers. In your setup, you could create three S7 client connections on one device, and assign the other three devices as S7 servers. In this arrangement, all four [product_name] devices are considered 'masters.'

There are two types of communication for [product_name] S7 connections: 1) Master/slave communication, where one device is set as master and the other as slave, with the slave not running its own program and providing hardware resources to the master; and 2) Client/server connections, where one device is the client and the other the server—here, both devices have their own programs. The client determines what data is sent or received, and device roles are defined during connection setup. There are several methods available to create such connections.

After setup and uploading via Ethernet, is a display necessary or can all monitoring and adjustments be handled through the web interface using Windows 10? I intend to have it on a LAN with a fixed public IP address. Would be unfortunate if a display was mandatory. Thanks in advance. [user_name]

The web server cannot fully replace a [product_name] display or a text display module. The web server is limited to showing programmed message texts. Accessing the system menu is not possible through a web browser.

Since this version lacks a display, initial IP address configuration must be done using [product_name] programming software. You need to set it up once on the CD, then updates can be performed anytime as long as the software is supported. The default IP is 192.168.0.1, meaning you should directly connect your laptop or PC to the device with another fixed IP in the same subnet (192.168.0.xxx, subnet 255.255.255.0). After configuring the device's IP/subnet, you can access it from a normal network after resetting your laptop's IP (possibly to DHCP).

I'm somewhat disappointed. As someone experienced in remote admin and using network storage devices with full remote access, I expected more. The manual (refer to the attached details) suggests the web server offers more control and functionality than just displaying message texts.

Just to clarify, the question was whether a display is required. I stated that the web server can only show programmed texts, and cannot be used to access the system menu or change system settings. For example, you can enter setpoints within message texts and use cursor buttons in the web interface, but full access to the system menu is only available via a display or text display. Additionally, the web server's main benefit is that it can emulate the display and keyboard of the text display module even when such hardware is not present. I may provide an example and screen video later.

Sorry if my question was unclear—I'm new to the [product_name] series. If I purchase the SPS starter kit with article number [article_no], which supports both 12V DC and 24V DC, does the combination of base unit and web access provide all necessary functionality for setup and use?

Here is the promised example screen video.

Remote switching isn't possible for digital inputs; those require direct interaction with hardware.

Is it possible to create a 'software input' that can be activated via the web server to achieve similar functionality if programmed appropriately?

Yes, you can use function and cursor buttons programmed in the [product_name] tool to run switching operations or other tasks.

Perfect, that's what I needed to know. The [product_name] will do what I require; I only need to switch between four modes remotely, and my demo program handles the rest. Thanks for the quick response—this has been very helpful. I'm sure I'll have more questions as I go, but I'm ready to place my order.

You can also assign the same function and cursor keys to multiple tasks, as long as appropriate locking mechanisms are implemented.

These numbers apply when 5 [product_name] modules are networked together with their compatible extension modules. One module acts as the master, and the other four are networked as slaves, making their hardware available to the master. 88 DI represents 88 digital inputs (from the German term 'digitale Eingänge'), with 24 coming from the master and 64 from networked inputs. 84 DO stands for 80 digital outputs ('digitale Ausgänge'), with 20 from the master and 64 from network outputs. 40 AE means 40 analog inputs, 8 via the master and 32 via the network. 24 AA refers to 24 analog outputs, 8 via the master and 16 via networked modules.

For the master [product_name]: 4 outputs are available on the base module, combined with either two modules offering 8 outputs each, or four modules offering 4 outputs each, reaching a total of 20 outputs. For each slave [product_name]: similarly, 4 outputs are on the base module and then additional outputs (either two 8-output modules or four 4-output modules) can be configured via network outputs, totaling 20 outputs per slave for the first three slaves. The fourth slave provides only its 4 base outputs via the network.

Here's a description of the physical setup and my goals for the finished system: This is for an automotive workshop with three main ventilation components: 1) Roof ventilator: The main exhaust fan, controlled by the PLC using four relay outputs which set four different fan speeds. The outputs connect to a frequency controller with digital inputs, allowing each speed to be adjusted through the frequency interface. In the event of PLC failure, the frequency controller can be operated locally or remotely by switching modes. 2) Exhaust gas extraction fan: This independent fan removes car exhaust from the shop and works separately from general ventilation. 3) Air delivery unit: This unit features a door with two positions—slightly open for lower fan speeds, and fully open (via damper motor) when high airflow is needed. It also includes two sets of heating elements for warming incoming air, which the PLC activates based on temperature. There is a two-speed fan to cool these heating elements when required. This custom solution was used since residential controls lack needed features and commercial options are too extensive for a smaller workshop. High pricing and feature overkill influenced the decision. For [product_name]: Manual control is provided via pushbuttons. Input 1 toggles the exhaust fan; inputs 2 to 5 select the four roof ventilator speeds, each timed weekly with a pulse output. The 'button push' times for each fan speed are configurable, and the setup reverts to automatic mode after scheduled events, even if manual changes occur. When the exhaust fan is activated, it draws more air than the roof ventilator on low settings. Thus, if the exhaust fan is on, the roof fan is shut off—unless running at full speed, in which case it downgrades to speed 3. When ventilation demand is high, the damper motor opens the door wider to increase airflow. Heating and cooling in the air delivery unit are managed by yearly/weekly timers and two thermostats. If temperature drops enough to trigger thermostat 1, 50% heating is enabled and the fan starts at speed 1, stopping with a delay to cool the element. Further drops trigger thermostat 2, activate second heating, and increase fan speed to 2, followed by a timed cooldown period. A dual-sensor setup would be more advanced but isn't implemented currently—potentially for a future update. Feedback and suggestions are encouraged!

I suspect the relay could be damaged inside the [product_name]. If the contacts were stuck due to overload, I'd expect the problem to be permanent, but here, Q1 works again the next day and the issue recurs intermittently. The output controls a 20W LED lamp. Any suggestions? Thanks

Consider checking out this [url]. It may offer some helpful information about how capacitive loads can be demanding for relay contacts.

I'd recommend using a Solid State Relay (SSR) that switches at zero crossing to control the LED. The SSR could then be switched via the [product_name].

Can you clarify what is powering the LED? Is it AC or a constant current DC supply? Zero crossing detectors aren't effective if it's DC powered, as is often the case with LEDs. Could you provide more details?

I suspect the issue lies elsewhere. Each [product_name] output is protected by a 6A fuse in series with the load, and all fuses are intact.

Could you specify the type and voltage of the LED? Is it 230VAC, 24VDC, or something else?

I've attached a picture of the LED light and its driver. The output from the [product_name] switches 230V AC for two LED drivers (two lights) connected in parallel.

LED lamps are particularly challenging for relay outputs because their inrush current can be dramatically high—a capacitive load. This can quickly deteriorate ordinary relay contacts. Search for "Power-on surge limiter" devices and consider adding one to your circuit. A relay output on a [product_name] has, according to its manual, a maximum surge current of 30A. Considering LED lamps can have inrush current many times higher, this poses a significant risk for relay outputs. I hope this helps.

Are you certain the issue is the output relay failing due to overload? What are your options—should you replace the relay, or is there an alternative way to fix it? Thanks

You then enter the value 155. To input minutes and seconds separately on the HMI, you have to set up two distinct input fields for minutes and seconds. These values are then transferred to [product_name], where the total is calculated. See the referenced screenshot for clarification.

Hello [user_name], You should be able to use a single analog input for this setup. Here's a straightforward approach you can use:

A single analog input should suffice for your requirements. Here's a simple method: Hi [user_name], Thanks for your suggestion, but I'm not certain this solution will behave as intended. If I understand correctly: - When the temperature goes above 27.9°C, the refrigerator turns on, but the heating also activates since the same signal triggers the 'high' condition. Is that accurate? If you run a simulation, you'll notice the 'high' signal will only reach output Q2 when the analog threshold output is 'low'. Once the analog input value is above 279, the threshold trigger's output is 'high', and this activates the refrigerator. At this point, the heating switches off because the 'high' signal is linked to the negative input of the 'AND' condition. I'm seeking advice about a [product_name] controller (firmware [version_no]). Initially, I configured an IP address (192.168.1.xx) for the device. Later, our network shifted to 192.168.2.xx, so I updated the IP in my program using [product_name] programming software and downloaded the changes. At first, it seemed fine, but recently the customer reported that the device was unreachable. Upon inspection, I discovered that after a reboot, the IP and gateway were reset to their original values (192.168.1.xx). Despite several attempts to change the configuration, including restoring defaults, the IP reverts to the initial setting whenever the device restarts. Am I missing a step, or is this a firmware issue? Hoping for some guidance.

Could it be that an SD card containing a program with the old IP address is inserted into the [product_name] controller? If so, this would explain the issue. Each time the device restarts, the program (and its network settings) are loaded from the SD card into memory.

Try manually setting the IP address in the [product_name] controller setup on the device's display, configure it to a static IP, and observe what happens after a reboot. Check if the address still changes.

The issue might occur because SD card program copying is enabled and the loaded program contains an embedded IP configuration. You can test this by loading the program, running it, and then removing the SD card. If, after reinserting it, the address changes, it likely means the SD card program defines a different address. Alternatively, you can ensure consistent IP assignment by configuring your router to reserve an IP address for the controller’s MAC address.

I connected both a [product_name] and a [product_name] separately, tried direct connection and through a modem/router, but the outcome didn’t change. Where can I find my PC’s IP and subnet mask in Windows XP? The network settings show the IP is set to automatic. Screenshot shows [product_name] connected via a router.

At the DOS prompt, type: ipconfig /all

The issue is your PC and the [product_name] are on different subnets. PC’s IP is 192.168.1.101, subnet mask 255.255.255.0, and gateway 192.168.1.1. The [product_name] is set to 192.168.0.5 with the same subnet mask. Change the [product_name]'s IP to 192.168.1.5 and try again.

Thanks. I changed the IP on the [product_name] and clicked the test button; it was successful. However, when attempting to upload the program to the PC, it failed. After that, even the test button no longer worked. This solution only worked once.

Update: Connecting the [product_name] via router succeeded and I can now transfer programs. How do I connect to the [product_name] using a web browser? Is the IP address 192.168.0.3 correct?

You have the same IP address issue. Assign the [product_name] an IP in the 192.168.1.x range, for example 192.168.1.3.

Can you ping the [product_name]? At the DOS prompt, type: ping 192.168.0.3

The issue with the [product_name] persists. [product_name] software cannot locate the device, and trying several IPs in the browser hasn't worked; I get 503 Service Unavailable every time.

Your PC can reach the [product_name], so another problem must exist. If you enter the IP directly in the browser (IE11) address bar and press Enter, it prepends 'http://', as seen in your screenshot. In this situation, you should submit a support request.

Not sure if this has been resolved elsewhere, but I found a workaround myself. Using the install DVD, copy the folder "Application_winXX" (XX for 32/64-bit architecture) from your optical drive to your computer. Then run the executable from your new folder. You can open or create projects, and ensure file extensions are set to open with the proper program. This workaround allows successful operation until an updated installer becomes available. Hi, A bit of a late reply, but to clarify: There’s no limitation in [product_name] that stops the use of other VBA code. Your code should function properly as long as the connection to the PLC via [product_name] is established and the cell contains either 0 or 1, rather than a non-numeric error like #VALUE!. Hello, I'm trying to set up communication via Modbus using a software suggested in this forum, but I can't read a specific variable memory address. I've attached two screenshots showing what I've managed so far. My goal is to access VM address 60 through holding register 2, but currently I can only read/write mapped VM positions as shown. Using a Float/Integer converter with VM address 60 and using 60 as the starting register doesn't write the value as expected. What could I be missing? Thank you, [user_name]

From the screenshot, I'm trying to read register 21, assuming it corresponds to VW21, but instead it's reading the variable with ID 21, which is the ON time for the weekly timer found at VW40. How can I access a variable at VW60 that's not listed in this table?

A user called [user_name] posted a discussion about [product_name] and Modbus in the German-speaking section and shared an Excel spreadsheet as a PDF file.

Be aware of the difference in address numbering: Modbus registers use word-based addresses starting at 1, while V-memory is byte-based and starts at zero. Reference #1: [IMAGE], Reference #2: [IMAGE]. The PDF provided by [user_name] is useful for understanding how [product_name] software handles address mapping.

Thank you for the PDF; it's been helpful. I see that the Float/Integer block uses VM instead of VW. With this info I've managed to change VW values but still don't understand how VM relates to Modbus register addresses. If I set the block to VM.60, which Modbus register address do I change to send a float to the controller? Thanks, [user_name]

There isn't a VM60 in [product_name]; only VW60 exists. VM covers the entire variable memory area. Open [product_name] software and use the help function to search for "VM" (see screenshot).

[IMAGE] It's recommended to avoid using float data types. Floats are 32 bits (occupying two Modbus addresses and four VB segments), and [product_name] has limitations handling floats. It's better to use integer values.

Variables can react differently, sometimes causing excessive update messages (hundreds or even a thousand just to transition from 0 to 999), which is what you want to avoid. Fixed frequency updates are safer, but can lead to unnecessary messages when values are stable. For now, I don't plan to use additional hardware after [product_name], even though it might be more efficient long-term, as it adds maintenance. Another issue: Only part of the [product_name] program has been uploaded. There is no parameter VM mapping, and you have memory overlap problems in the VM region. [product_name] models are available for 230V (not 220V) with relay outputs compatible with that voltage. The digital inputs handle 230V, and relay outputs can support various voltages. However, for safety, you might consider designing your setup around 24V, but that's your decision. The standard [product_name] offers 8 digital inputs and 4 relay outputs, but you can expand up to 24 inputs and 16 outputs using extension modules, which should be sufficient for your needs. You can also use level sensors providing a 4-20 mA output—ideal for managing level (0-100%). [product_name] allows up to 4 analog inputs for 4-20 mA, which is suitable for this situation. Please note, analog expansion units for [product_name] require 24V (or 12V) DC. For your components, consider [product_name] 230 RC or [product_name] 24 RC (selecting voltage per your requirements), preferably in the [article_no] series. Here's an example for achieving the maximum speed.

No, the stopwatch can only measure time, not generate timing signals. Plus, it reads in 10 millisecond intervals, not single milliseconds. The smallest adjustable time unit remains 1/100s.

I've discovered PWM through trial and error. I'll experiment with it.

For higher frequencies, the value changes with the cycle time of your controller, which limits resolution. Check the attached sample program for different pulse generators and test directly on the hardware (PC simulation won't reflect actual frequencies). The fastest generator can use a counter to set frequencies, but more details on your required signals are needed. Connect your transistor output in the program to a generator and check output with an oscilloscope if possible.

Thanks, I'll try tomorrow. How do you establish the relationship between output frequency and the 4-20 mA sensor signal, ignoring units for now? For example, 0 mA equals 0 Hz, 20 mA equals 20 Hz. This is a new task for me and quite confusing.

I found a solution in another forum but will verify the results tomorrow by measuring the actual output frequency.

The input pulse for Counter2 should come from your external device, such as BCD thumb wheels or a potentiometer. 3. Counter2 resets when it reaches its maximum value (e.g., 9,999). 4. The [product_name] program allows use of AM parameters. However, I can't figure out in [product_name] portal how to add AM tags in the HMI tag table. I’ve managed the M flags but I’m stuck with AM. Programming logic between [product_name] and [product_name] portal is fundamentally different. The AM data type in [product_name] is unique and can't be split into digital flag bits. Likewise, flag bits aren't accessible as analog flag words. They are distinct and don't correlate within portal tag architecture.

Your explanation is very insightful. To summarize, the interface designed using [product_name] isn't directly transferable. I’ll need to replace AM flags with network analog inputs in order to move setpoints and parameters into the [product_name] program.

It's preferable to move setpoints or parameters using VM mapping. For example, saving setpoints in a parameter of a mathematical instruction ensures protection during power loss due to storage in the EEPROM of [product_name].

Analog markers are best used solely for analog values intended for display on the web server, like actual temperature or pressure readings.

Thanks. I kept thinking I was missing something. The help documentation for [product_name] mentions VM mapping and identifies AM1 as VM address 952. How does this connect to [product_name] portal and HMIs like KTP700? Essentially, it doesn't. So, use VM mapping for parameters and, when that's not possible, use network blocks. (statement and question)

When programming with [product_name], you can only directly access VM addresses ranging from 0 to 850. It's not possible to read or write VW952 in a [product_name] program. Note: AM1 refers to VW952 in [version_no], and to VW1118 in [version_no] (see attachment).

Thank you for sharing the table. It turns out the HMI can access the VW address and transfer values into [product_name].

That’s right—remote devices can reach VM areas beyond VB850. The [product_name] program, using parameter VM mapping or analog network IO, cannot.

Thanks, that helped.

text:
Hello, I'm new to [product_name]. I'm working with analog temperature and humidity sensors that require scaling: Temperature uses a 2-10V signal mapped from -40 to 140F: T = 0.225x -85F Humidity uses a 2-10V signal mapped from 0 to 100%RH: RH = 0.125x -25% Since the analog amplifier only allows gains with 2 decimal places, I've added two amplifiers in sequence for each sensor: the first uses a gain of 0.1, followed by gains of 2.25 for temperature and 1.25 for humidity. Monitoring the process via the software, I notice the temperature resolution is quite coarse—around 2 degrees—even though the underlying analog input value (ranging from 0 to 1000) updates smoothly. Is there a more effective way to achieve better resolution? Am I missing something? Thanks!

The issue arises because [product_name] only operates with integers in the range of -32,768 to 32,767; any decimal points are purely for display. Gains can be set with two decimal places, but this is just for visual presentation. Internally, the values are handled as integers multiplied by 100 (e.g., a gain of 1.00 equals 100). If you set a gain of 0.1 followed by 2.25, the intended output is 0.225, but in [product_name], the calculation is 10/100 * 225/100 = 0.225. Due to integer rounding, this becomes 0.23, meaning the actual total gain is 0.23. Such rounding introduces noticeable value jumps with small gains. As an alternative, consider using a single gain of 2.25 and displaying one decimal place. You can compare the results using the example provided.

Thank you for your clear explanation. Looking through the program, I'm still unsure about the specifics of the second calculation, although it seems closer to what I'm aiming for. Could you further clarify what's happening with how the range and scaling are being handled? Is the output value in the calculation (when it shows a decimal) suitable for use as an input to other calculations, such as subtracting from a reference temperature, or is it only meant for display? My goal is to use reference temperature values for heating/cooling control, preferably using floating-point values similar to what your second calculation shows. Thank you!

In the second example, the amplification factor is multiplied by ten. With the first method, after analog amplification, you get output values between -40 and 140, which are shown as such. With the second method, you receive values from -400 to 1400, corresponding to a displayed range of -40.0 to 140.0 if you display a decimal place in the analog amplifier. If you use the second approach and, for instance, set up an analog threshold trigger, remember to account for the decimal place in your calculations. For example: ON = 100 (which is 1000 when considering 100.0); OFF = 75 (which equates to 750 for 75.0).

Hello, I'm looking to select the correct [product_name] PLC with suitable outputs for managing heating devices, such as 3-point mixing valves. From what I can tell, choosing a version with relay outputs may not be ideal since controlling a 3-point mixing valve involves many on-off cycles, which could cause the relays to fail relatively quickly (unless this period is actually longer). Should I opt for the transistor output version and connect coupling relays for better durability? Also, can I safely detect 220VAC inputs using the right protection for the PLC? Is it possible to use coupling relays with 220VAC coils, connect 24VDC to the output terminals, and feed that to the PLC input? --- Split from discussion on Transistor outputs vs. Relay outputs.

It's generally not advisable to connect a mixing valve directly to a [product_name] with relay outputs. The relay contacts in the PLC aren't designed for this type of usage. Swapping out a downstream relay is much easier and safer than replacing the whole PLC. Whether you use a downstream relay with a PLC with transistor outputs or with relay outputs doesn't make a significant difference in practice.

Thank you [user_name] for your response. I realize that using proportional valves controlled by analog outputs would be a better solution, but some setups already have 3-point mixing valves. I don't have much experience with relay selection, so I searched online and found these example relays: [url] and [url] Are these relays appropriate for connecting to [product_name]?

I believe the first relay type is suitable. It uses a 24VDC coil, so it can be connected to either the transistor output version or the relay output version of [product_name]. It also has a built-in flyback diode, which protects both transistor and relay outputs. This type comes recommended.

The second relay has a 220VAC coil. I have some 220VAC signals or sensors, and I need to provide input to the PLC. My idea is to connect the relay coil to 220VAC, then wire one of the relay contacts to +24VDC power and the other contact to a PLC input. Is this wiring approach correct? Or could voltage spikes from the 220VAC supply damage the PLC inputs?

Your method of bringing 220VAC signals through coupling relays to the PLC is correct. However, the 24VDC PLC inputs cannot tolerate 220VAC directly; applying high voltage may destroy them.

Hello, I want to manage the temperature of an aquarium using a PT100 sensor and a [product_name] controller. Is there an example available? Thanks in advance.

It's not possible to connect a PT100/PT1000 sensor directly to a [product_name] controller for evaluation. You need either the [product_name] expansion module [article_no] or an external transmitter that converts the PT100/PT1000 signal to a 0-10V or 0/4-20mA signal. The choice of analog input depends on the hardware setup, such as using an expansion module or a base module's analog input.

I've implemented this before—the hardest part was finding an affordable waterproof PT100 probe, around £80 in my case. There are many waterproof PT100 sensors on the market, and I attached mine to a filter inlet pipe. Connect it to the [product_name] expansion module and set the control so that if the temperature is below the setpoint, the heater turns on, and if above, it turns off. I included a 0.5°C hysteresis based on a sample from [company_name] to prevent rapid switching. The temperature setpoint can be adjusted via front panel buttons, though in my setup (26°C), I didn't need frequent changes. I also added a switch that, if held for 3 seconds, disabled the heater during maintenance and flashed the display as a warning. Temperature was logged to an SD card every 30 minutes, though the actual variation was small—between 25°C (while heating) and up to 28°C during hot days. The heater thermostat was set to 28°C as a backup in case of code errors. In retrospect, except for temperature logging, the built-in heater thermostat worked as effectively as my [product_name] program, but with much simpler configuration. Attached is a picture of the early prototype before the module was installed.

I already have the [product_name] expansion module. I am looking for an example for temperature control at +25°C with a -0.5°C ON-OFF setting. Thank you!

Here is one possible approach.

Connect the corresponding RTD input block to an analog threshold trigger. Within the block, set the inputs for PT100/PT1000 with a resolution of 0.1. Configure the ON level to 255 (25.5°C) and OFF to 245 (24.5°C). Note the inversion: when the output is high, the heater is off. The actual inversion was done with an external relay so that if the PLC stopped or someone missed the run mode, the heater would stay on, relying on its own thermostat for safety. This setup switches the heater on below 25.5°C and off above 24.5°C. We also encountered various interference issues due to weak RTD signal levels, so the system must be carefully designed and programmed with safeguards against false signals.

The 3-wire PT100 probe is wired into its dedicated module. Thanks everyone for your support. Wishing you all a great day, [user_name].

The tuning was successful and the control loop is stable overall. However, even minor fluctuations in pressure (from wind or minor air flow adjustments) are causing small, unnecessary changes in the manipulated output. If deadband were available, these minor changes wouldn't cause constant fan speed adjustments. This isn't a process issue since pressure variation of +/- 10Pa is fine, but nearly continuous small fan adjustments may cause excessive wear over time. I've added filtering with two analog filter blocks in series, set to high sample counts, and it helps a bit. Filtering the PI output is another option, but it's surprising that deadband isn't available as a standard feature. I tested a possible solution that might help you. By using a MAX/MIN block as a memory, controlled via a pulse generator, I can save the latest value when the block is switched off.

Thank you! I also tried to create a deadband by switching the PI controller to manual mode within the deadband, and using the previous output as the manual value. Implementing this was tricky due to circular references, and the behavior wasn't as expected. Using the max/min block as a memory may simplify manual control. Thanks again—I'll update with results.

The solution with the max/min block functioning as a memory works well now. In my attached setup, Input I1 starts the PI controller. The block B003 provides the setpoint, which is sent to both the PI controller and the comparators. If the process variable is within the deadband (+/-5), the max/min block stores the value and sends it to the PI controller’s manual input. After a short delay, the PI controller goes to manual mode until the process variable leaves the deadband.

VW0 is set by the HMI panel. The B002 math instruction uses reference data from the B009 Up/Down Counter (for example, start value 70 or another value in the 60-90 range). During simulation, the VM mapping table is empty, but this was also the case in [product_name] [version_no] simulation. Previously, the analog threshold trigger referenced the Up/Down counter's output data.

The counter's maximum value is 999,999. To handle this, you need a double integer word (DINT), which is VD0 and consists of VW0 and VW2. Values between 0 and 32,767 are stored in VW2. If the counter value exceeds 32,767, you can't read it using this method.

A PI regulator is meant for adjusting values (inputs/outputs). The integral part will continue changing the output, even when the input remains constant. If you simply need a fixed value at the analog output, you can use a mathematical instruction block.

I have a sensor that provides a reading every second and it's connected to Analog Input 1, which I then connect to the PV of the PI controller. My setpoint is 50 degrees. If the temperature rises or falls suddenly, I want it to return quickly to the setpoint (50 degrees).

With this PI controller, it can be configured to regulate in only one direction. Depending on the control direction: either the output increases when the setpoint is exceeded, or the output increases when the setpoint is lower—each depending on the control deviation level. The controller cannot handle both deviations (higher and lower) at the same time; it only manages either up-regulation or down-regulation.

Hello! I am considering a 2-channel encoder with a high resolution of 250 pulses per revolution, but the counter seems limited in how high it can count. Also, I'm not clear on how to interpret the counter signal. The frequency inverter only needs digital inputs, which is not my issue—the counter setup is my main concern. I might use a proximity switch and a 10 pulses per revolution single channel, but I still don't understand how to use the counter output for positioning purposes. Any suggestions?

Hello [user_name], Unfortunately, the [product_name] does not include a function that can independently evaluate two-channel incremental encoders in a cycle-time independent manner. For example, evaluating signals "A" and "B" for rotational direction presents limitations. I've shared concepts and circuits for this on the German forum ("Wie ist eine Auswertung der Signale 'A' und 'B' von Drehgebern möglich?" [url]), focusing on direction impulse counting and maximizing information recovery (such as flank evaluation). All circuit-based solutions face restrictions on the maximum allowable signal input frequency due to direction analysis. This is based on the smallest possible system cycle time of [product_name]. With simple evaluations (like using counters), the highest signal frequency is halved, while achieving full directional information restricts it further, to an eighth of the cycle rate. I have posted circuit diagrams for various approaches (search for "Forum_Inkrementalgeber_V03.zip") and simulation setups. Based on your information, it sounds like you are more interested in measuring speed instead of counting impulses for position. There's a block called "threshold trigger" which can help measure speed, but it's generally difficult to scale results into physical units. I published a more flexible circuit for this in the forum, which you can adapt (for example: "Display of scaled High Speed Input Values" [url]). I prepared a modified circuit for your application with a two-channel incremental sensor. Here’s a brief overview: - B110 sets the measuring time, - B003 and B007 store previous measurement values, - B005 and B008 amplify and scale these values, - B001 handles direction by multiplying by -1, - The final direction value is processed by B012. Channel A impulses are counted during the measuring time, with a typical maximum of 2 kHz. Analog amplifiers convert the counter value to physical units. Direction can only be determined up to half the system frequency (by analyzing A and B), with a threshold of 50 Hz. Above this threshold, the last known direction is stored until speed drops below the limit. This procedure works well for motor control, as reversing direction usually involves slowing down first. There are references to dividing the signal frequency using external circuits ([document] and [document]). Sensor signals A and B can also be externally processed by ICs (see datasheet [document]) for pulse and direction output, which can then be used with [product_name]. In [product_name], you can use a simple counter, digital threshold trigger, or adapt the "threshold trigger" circuit for rotation sense display. Best regards [user_name]

The analog comparator can only compare counter values up to 32,767; if the operating hours minute value exceeds this, using the analogue comparator is no longer feasible. To work around this, I've created a user-defined function (UDF). There's a sample program and the UDF attached. The counter values are transferred to VM memory and then read back into the program.

Hi, I would like to learn how to program a [product_name] so that an output switches only when the input is 100 ohms or less, but if the resistance is higher than 100 ohms, the output should remain off. The ohm value is just for illustration—the main idea is to trigger the output when a person touches two separate metal bars, using human resistance. Thanks.

[product_name] devices cannot directly measure resistance; they only recognize voltage (0-10V), current (0/4-20mA), or specific sensor signals like PT100/1000. Modules such as [product_name] analog or RTD expansion options are designed for these inputs. Some basic modules do support 0-10V analog inputs, but only with 24 VDC power. For your scenario, placing a 100 ohm resistor in parallel with an analog input means input impedance won't affect readings significantly. You could use a voltage divider: connect +24 VDC to a 240 ohm resistor in series, then to the analog input. Attach one end of the 100 ohm resistor to the analog input and the other to ground. This creates a voltage drop between roughly 0 V and 7 V for resistance values in the 0-100 ohm range. At zero ohms, all 24 VDC goes through the 240 ohm resistor, resulting in a 0.1 A current and a 2.4 W load—so use a resistor rated at 240 ohms, 5 watts.

If not, the program won't be activated and your computer will receive a message. Possible reasons include a poor connection or faulty connector. Try reinserting the connectors on both the computer and device. If the issue persists, slightly change your program (such as adding a marker) and attempt the transfer again. Good luck.

Which version of [product_name] software are you using? There was a BIOS update between [version_no] and [version_no] that affects checksum verification during transfers. Hello, I'm unsure how to wire a 2-wire sensor to the AM2 analogue module. The documentation in the [product_name] manual and this forum suggest connecting the sensor ground to the M1 terminal, but the schematic shows the M wire connected to the M terminal and leaves out the ground. The page [url] even suggests linking PE and M, which works in practice but isn't clearly recommended. The schematic connects the shield to PE, but it's unclear where the sensor ground should go. Following the current instructions, the ground and M end up linked, and the sensor itself isn't grounded. Appreciate any feedback on this.

You should connect the PE conductor from your electrical installation to the PE terminal of the AM2. If you’re using shielded cable to connect the sensor, connect the cable shield to the PE terminal as well.

On the link you provided, I see a schematic indicating PE joined to the cable shield, and a sensor outputting current to the current input. M terminals are at 0V DC or GND and need to share the same potential, so they are interconnected. It’s true that sensor connection diagrams often create confusion.

The link describes a 2-wire 0/4..20 mA sensor – a loop-powered sensor that must form a power loop: the sensor’s positive wire goes to the positive supply, and the negative wire to the current input of the expansion module, completing the circuit. For 4-wire sensors, two wires would connect to power supply and two to current input and ground on the module. Connecting PE and shielding as described is correct; PE protects the system and should connect to the metal enclosure and any touchable metal parts. Shielding the cable reduces electrical noise entering the sensor input – connecting it to PE makes a 'Faraday Cage' to minimize interference. Mixing PE and signal/sensor grounds is discouraged; it may result in unwanted signals or spikes on your sensor inputs, especially if there are faults elsewhere. Keep PE together for protection and signal/sensor grounds together for signal integrity.

Your explanation is clear, though I'm unsure about the ground connected to the Min terminal. Is it best to connect the sensor ground to the M input of the AM module alongside the M from the power supply, instead of connecting it directly to the system's ground or PE? Is connecting the ground to the negative safe, considering it's often linked to the sensor's case? Could that affect signal quality or safety?

Thank you for your follow-up. Good engineering practice keeps electrical protection (PE and shields) separate from supply and signal wires (power supply minus, and sensor grounds/negatives). Schematics often use different symbols to indicate these grounds. Linking PE and signal/sensor grounds can create ground loops, causing devices using the same PE (like large drives) to leak current that can interfere with sensor readouts due to potential differences between PE and M. Keeping them separate helps avoid these issues.

Thanks again for your response. Still wondering: why not connect the sensor ground directly to the system ground/PE instead of M?

You can connect the sensor ground to the system’s PE – it will function, but it's not considered best engineering practice. Doing so tries to route the sensor loop via the power supply. [company_name] [product_name] power supplies are isolated, enclosed in plastic, and don't need a PE; just L1 & N bring you 24V DC L+ and M. If using such a supply and connecting a sensor to the AM2 module, with the sensor signal to I1 or V1 and the negative/ground to PE, the PE has to link to M somewhere for the sensor signal to register. Connecting PE, M on the AM2, and M on the power supply creates one ground potential and works, but risks more ground loops. Keeping PE and M separate ensures all devices operate at the same reference potential, so input values remain consistent. Mixing PE and M references across the installation can lead to unreliable sensor readings. I’ll try to clarify further with a diagram.

Refer to the manual’s relevant sections for further clarification.

Thanks [user_name]! I feel silly for making a detailed diagram that was basically already in the manual. Reviewing the manual diagrams, you’ll notice the small stripes beside the sensor wires indicate shielding connected to PE (similar to my dotted green lines). Also, the final notes about shielding for Pt100 sensors and the guidance on using/not using isolated power supplies seem a bit contradictory – I’d like to look into that more. The confusion brought up earlier is clearly justified. If anyone can clarify sensor, signal, ground, earth, and PE connections further, please share!

Thank you all – this diagram makes things much clearer. Before posting here, I checked the manual and support page but still found the topic confusing, which prompted my question. Basically, there are 2-wire and 4-wire sensors, and some 2-wire sensors with an extra ground wire (effectively 3-wire). My E&H sensor is a 2-wire type but includes a third ground connection. If you connect this ground to the cable shield, it makes sense, or use a third wire in a 3-core cable, which is what I did. To summarize: DC 24V to sensor input, sensor output to AM2 analog input, sensor ground (or shield) to PE, and M connected to M input of the AM module. M and PE should remain unconnected (though possible), given the discussed issues.

Internally, the inputs likely trigger a hardware interrupt to the processor, making their operation independent of the user program cycle time. I have a level transmitter with a fixed 4-20mA output connected to my [product_name] controller and displaying the level on the [product_name] display. When the tank is full, the transmitter only provides a 16mA signal. Since adjusting the transmitter isn't possible, how can I scale the 16mA signal so the display reads 100%?

You can use an analog amplifier function block. This block allows you to set measurement range, gain, and offset for your analog variable.

I'm currently using an analog threshold trigger block with a measurement range of 0 - 104, a gain of 0.13, and an offset of -26. When I adjust the measurement range, both gain and offset change, which causes my display to start at a negative percentage.

You'll need to adjust both gain and offset values to achieve the correct scaling. Set the gain for the empty-to-full range, and the offset so that zero corresponds to empty. Using the formula y=mx+c (where m is gain, c is offset, y is % full, and x is the input value): 16mA (100%) is read as 800, and 4mA (0%) as 200 (approximate values). Therefore, m=100/(800-200)=0.1666, c=100-(0.1666*800)=-33.28. Double-check these calculations and logic before applying.

There is an Excel file available, created by [user_name], which helps calculate gain and offset values by entering your measurements. See [url] to download the zip file. Hope this helps.

This can be done with four relay outputs, or with two if using a 48V three-wire power supply. However, the most reliable method is to use an external relay to control the motor direction.

Thanks for sharing the splitting program—it was very useful. Could you clarify the formula used? For example, I don't understand the use of 29 as a threshold in SF004, or the reasoning behind the analog comparator. If you have a mathematical formula for converting minutes to hours and minutes, I'd appreciate a detailed explanation.

Here's how SF002 works: The HMI's hours setpoint is in parameter V1; it's multiplied by 60 (V2) to convert hours to minutes. The minutes setpoint (V3) from the HMI is added, determining the total minutes. This value references the off-delay timer setting. The remaining time of the off-delay timer is transferred to memory (VW8) using Parameter VM Mapping, then read back via analog input and managed through SF009 and SF003 instructions. The analog threshold trigger (SF004) checks if total minutes exceed 29—if so, the analog MUX (SF005) outputs 30, otherwise 0. The total minutes from SF003 go to SF006; here, hours are calculated by first subtracting SF005's output (either 0 or 30), which ensures integer math and prevents rounding problems when dividing by 60. For example, dividing 54 by 60 rounds up to 1, but (54-30)/60 rounds down correctly to 0. SF006 produces the hour value, which is multiplied by 60 in SF007 to get the minute portion of the hours. SF008 then determines the remaining minutes by subtracting the total hours in minutes from the total minutes. This gives the minutes portion.

We have used modules with article numbers ranging from [article_no] to [article_no]. Recently, we encountered a significant issue when upgrading from [version_no] to [version_no]: inputs 1 and 2 on the newer hardware are much more sensitive. For instance, on [article_no], an input required about 6800 ohms or less to activate, but on [article_no], inputs 1 and 2 activate at 47000 ohms. This has caused problems at one of our installation sites. I recall reading that inputs 1 and 2 are high speed inputs—could this sensitivity be a settings issue? As a temporary fix, we're avoiding the use of inputs 1 and 2, but sometimes all 8 inputs are needed. Using shielded wire isn't feasible for us, as we don’t control the wire type used. Wire runs are typically 12 feet, occasionally up to 100 feet. Thanks for any advice. [user_name]

On [article_no], an input required about 6800 ohms or less, but on [article_no], inputs 1 and 2 activate at 47000 ohms. Hello! I imagine you’re using a variable resistor or voltage divider to detect a digital stage—could you explain your setup a bit more or clarify how the resistance change is affecting your system?

We're just using a push button switch at the end of 12-100 feet of wire. The newer module is giving us false input signals when the switch isn't pressed. When the site tech disconnected and reconnected the wires, the system assumed the input was triggered and executed the program. I suspected the input impedance changed between versions, so I checked the resistance threshold at which the inputs activate. Not every installation uses a mechanical switch; sometimes we use a solid-state relay, which could also trigger problems if the off-state resistance is 47000 ohms. 47000 ohms wasn’t the highest tested; it’s just where I stopped for now—more testing will be done Friday/Saturday. The issue is only present with inputs 1 and 2 so far. I've noticed that inputs 1 and 2 are also AI3 and AI4 on this version, which is new. Regarding our application: the system sequences unlocking/opening a pedestrian doorway, operated by a push button inside and card reader outside. Thanks. [user_name]

I’ve identified the issue—the hardware model has changed. We're using the 12/24RC version. In [article_no], I1-I6 require 1.5mA for high status, while I7 and I8 require 0.1mA. In [article_no], I3-I6 need 2mA for high status; I1, I2, I7, and I8 need 0.15mA. Previously, using I1-I6 avoided this issue, but that's no longer possible. Because we don't use shielded wire, the cable is likely picking up stray voltage or current, triggering the now more-sensitive inputs. Thanks for reviewing. [user_name]

Hello all. The inputs in the [version_no] models have been updated for 12/24 RC & RCo as well as for [product_name] 24 & 24o devices. I1 & I2 can now optionally accept 0..10V analog signals (AI3 & AI4), so input current sensitivity was likely altered for analog-to-digital conversion. Inputs I3-I6 also changed—these are now high-speed counters up to 5kHz instead of just I5 and I6 as before, so their sensitivity may differ as well. The detection threshold for HI or LO status is more driven by voltage than current. This situation demonstrates why high-quality shielded cable is essential in industrial environments with longer wiring or nearby switching devices—unwanted signals are easily picked up! Good to see progress and practical solutions.

Hello! One workaround is to add a relay at the input—electrical noise typically won't trigger a relay, but a legitimate ON signal will. That's one option for solving this issue. Does anyone have additional suggestions?

Another possible solution is to add a pull-down resistor to keep the signal reliably low.

Update: Shielded wire is now required based on test results. I laid out 100 feet of 18 AWG lamp wire on the shop floor, which stored enough charge to trigger inputs 1 and 2, but not 3 through 6. As another user suggested, adding a pull-down resistor (we’re using 4700 ohms) aligns the input impedance with other channels. I currently have 50 units in the shop and was worried for a couple days, but this fix is inexpensive—looks like it will be a good weekend.

Using a relay would be much more reliable. Hope this solution works for you.

I had a client who used Honeywell HOA0892-T55 transmissive sensors (slotted photointerrupters) with all 8 inputs of the controller. The output phototransistors could sink about 1.4mA. Using 8.2K ohm pull-ups on I1, I2, I7, and I8 was effective, giving logic levels of 0.26V (low) and 10.8V (high). But with the high-speed inputs (I3-I6), the sensor output couldn’t reach above about 5.5V, behaving as if [article_no] has a 5860 ohm input resistance to common. Since our sensor signals are inherently low-speed, a simple quad op-amp (LM324) with RF/noise filter and 100 ohm series resistors to I3-I6 solved the problem. The manual describes different input current requirements by pin, but elsewhere input impedance is shown as 80K ohms per input (72K ohms when enabled as analog), and it would be helpful if input loading values were clarified. This would give users a clearer path for reconciling resistor values needed for consistent logic levels.
