Hello, I want to confirm my understanding of the Data Log feature. I've attached a timing diagram illustrating which signals trigger logs and when. There are two buttons for starting and stopping a cooling machine, as well as a temperature sensor monitoring the container's temperature. The Data Log in the program is set to record I1 to I8, M1 to M8, and the analog amplifier (which converts the analog signal to an actual temperature reading). My interpretation is: For digital signals, the rising and falling edges of I1, I2, and M1 are captured; for analog signals, their actual values are logged only when a rising or falling edge on I1, I2, or M1 occurs. Additionally, when the Data Log Enable input is on, a value from the analog amplifier is recorded. Is this correct? I'm working with [product_name] [version_no]. For this setup, the interval between I1 and I2 pulses should not be shorter than ten minutes. Thank you.

Since the enable input (EN) is consistently held high, only one log entry is created. A new record is generated when an edge changes from low to high. There must be a minimum pause of 500 ms between edges; otherwise, any edge transition within 500 ms is disregarded and not recorded.

Thanks for your response. So, does this mean one data record is logged for each positive edge in the Data Log function? I defined my logging data as: I1 to I8 (1 byte), Q1 to Q8 (1 byte), and Analog parameter (1 byte). Suppose I switch the Data Log Enable input with 500 ms on and 500 ms off. Without an SD card, approximately 30 records are stored in 30 seconds, and new records will not be captured until an upload is performed. Is this correct?

Yes. The analog parameter uses either 2 or 4 bytes. A high signal is sufficient for one logging cycle, followed by a 500 ms low signal. The internal memory for Data Log allows 1024 bytes, with up to 512 bytes for logging. Once this 512-byte threshold is reached, the data tries to write to an SD card. If an SD card is not present, further logging cannot continue.

Thank you again.

As a tip: there is a 'To thank' button below each post if you'd like to show appreciation.

Hello, Is it possible for a [product_name] with [article_no] and another with [article_no] to share their variable memory? Is it just about making two connections in [product_name] and assigning a variable mapping to each direction (client to server & server to client)? Both are set up as master devices.

Can you clarify what you mean by sharing the variable memory? The VM area refers to variable storage. If you wish to exchange data between two [product_name] devices ([article_no]), use each device's VM area. Set up a connection for master-to-master communication, designating one as server (slave) and the other as client (master). Specify read or write direction in the connection. If you need more details, I could provide an example.

I would like both devices to have identical memory areas, so writing a bit or byte to either doesn't matter. Here's more context: Three years ago, I began with one [product_name] ([article_no]) and two I/O expansions for my first floor. I used negative edge detection on digital inputs to control outputs. Later, after discovering an app to control the device, I added a network input to each input. When I renovated the ground floor, I purchased a new [product_name] ([article_no]), more I/O expansions, a communication module to interact with my automation system and dimmers. On the new floor, I added network inputs to digital inputs, starting variable indexing from where the first module ended. I changed my programming logic so each digital input sets a variable, which links to an output, making it easier for a home server to communicate, since it only reads/writes variables and not outputs directly. With shared variable memory, I wouldn't need to specify which device to update, and common actions (like panic or day/night) are universal across both devices.

Sorry, I still don't quite understand. Each [product_name] has its own variable memory area, with its own addresses like V0.0 or VB1. That's why I'm confused about what you mean by sharing.

Thanks for the response. I'll try to clarify further. I'm open to taking a completely different approach if that suits my situation better—I don't consider myself an expert in automation systems. I realize every device has its own VM area, but I want both to have identical VM data, so any change made in device #1 is automatically transferred to device #2 and vice versa. Perhaps I'm looking for some sort of variable mapping where addresses VB0 to VB100 on device #1 correspond to VB0 to VB100 on device #2 in both directions. For example, VB0.0 might represent a light in the living room controlled by device #1, while VB0.6 is the master bedroom light controlled by device #2. No overlap exists in their usage, so variables always represent the same function no matter which device is accessed.

It's possible to copy values from one device to another. Synchronizing values, however, is complex since you need to track which values are most recent. It's recommended to maintain "remote" and "local" sets and use logic to determine which is newest. Alternatively, assign one device as the master keeper of values, and have all networked devices use its data. When a value changes on the slave, the master should distribute it to all. Consider these options to see which may best fit your needs.

That solution won't work. You can't write to the same variable memory address from multiple sources (devices and apps) simultaneously.

Thank you for your input. Based on the advice given, it might be best to use a master-slave setup—one device handles input and output, and the other (connected to the communication module) is the master, storing all logic and variable data. Is this correct? I have no experience with master-slave configurations, but I'll investigate further. As a side note, I've already ordered a new [product_name] ([article_no]) to replace the older module, which will be relocated to the garage for exterior and garage light controls.

Be aware that master-slave communication has limitations. The slave device simply acts as a hardware extension with no autonomous program. If the master fails, everything stops. In contrast, master-to-master communication allows each device to operate independently.

Just to clarify, what I mentioned about "master-slave" concerns central value keeping and value usage, not actual master-slave protocol. A single device can act as both keeper and user. For now, focus on how you want information to flow between devices (and other interfaces, like phones), create a diagram, and then identify what information is available. A flow diagram may help clarify your approach, as relying solely on text can lead to misunderstandings.

Dear [user_name], Based on my understanding, [user_name] is trying to create a network of collaborating devices. For best results, identical requests and configurations should be available to all network units. I've outlined general approaches, but you have the expertise for implementation. I welcome your strategies for building such a cooperative device network.

For example, if a bit is set in the newer module, the same bit should also be set in the older one by parallel writing—and vice versa. This would require sending all variables from one device to another in matching addresses, in both directions, but that's not possible.

[user_name]: Please check the attached proposal.

[user_name]: Attempting to synchronize two numerical values is unnecessarily complicated—a demonstration is attached.

This isn't simple to describe, but I believe it works (see attachment).• If one device fails, the other continues to operate independently.• One device is the communication hub, handling automation system integration; to transfer data to the other device, I use extra network outputs.

In your initial post, you stated you're using two different modules ([article_no]). In your new example, you describe two units of the newer type. In that case, your approach works as programmed. What is the shortest input duration needed for an edge-triggered wiping relay to activate its output? I understand it reacts to the rising edge, but is there a minimum pulse width requirement?

The typical maximum input frequency is 4 Hz (refer to the handbook), so the minimum time should be around 0.25 seconds.

Yes, that's what I thought, since the timer responds to the rising edge. Thanks for your response.

There are often unreliable electrical signals due to noise and spikes on the network. It's important that the controller reacts only to valid signals at the input and not to noise. Each input is equipped with a filter to ignore brief signals. For this input module, signals shorter than 0.25 seconds are disregarded, based on the 4 Hz specification. However, certain versions include a high-speed input for counters, functioning up to 4 kHz; this is specific for counter operations. To detect signals shorter than 0.25 seconds, you can connect the fast input to a counter, set the counter to a max of 1, and reset it after each detection. The reset pulse can be used for the edge-triggered function. Quick inputs depend on your controller model—consult the manual. Fast inputs are available only on DC versions; the 230V version does not have this feature.

Hello, I have [product_name] with two [product_name] modules ([article_no]). Today I discovered that one of the modules (nearest to the main unit) stopped measuring, and both inputs returned zero. After switching the device off and on, functionality was restored, but for several hours it continued heating at full power. How can I easily identify this type of hardware failure and implement self-recovery without turning off the device? I appreciate any advice.

Hello [user_name], If an analog input module freezes, it may be due to interference from the sensor or the power supply. For programming, you can monitor input values with a threshold switch for zero readings, which activates an alarm after a set period and switches the heating to safety mode. A hardware reset cannot be performed via software, but you could configure an output to control an external relay with a delay, temporarily disconnecting the unit from power. Kind regards, [user_name]

Hello [user_name], thanks for your response. This month, we've encountered two issues with [product_name], both following extended power outages. Prior to this, the system ran for months without failures, even with occasional power drops. The first issue involved changing a WM parameter right after power was restored, which happened during the next data logging cycle. The second issue began three hours after power recovery. I've now added a threshold under 50 for all four sensors (two controlling, two for additional monitoring), and will rewire the sensors so each control sensor connects to its own module. Thanks and best regards, [user_name]

Sudden restoration of the power grid is risky for electronic devices due to voltage surges, which can cause damage. I once lost an audio amplifier to a similar event. If your [product_name] operates on 230V and the issue persists, the device may be damaged.

Good afternoon. Can someone clarify the measurement accuracy of the current input 0-10V on the [product_name]? I am trying to connect a custom pH electrode without a standard converter. The input signal will range from 80 to 750 mV—can the [product_name] accurately measure this? Also, is there a method to enable or disable the input so current only flows during measurement, or can this only be done with an external relay?

First of all, voltage should not be confused with current. The [product_name] analog input can measure a voltage from 80 to 750 mV, but it's not ideal. The analog input converts this to 8 to 75 out of 1000 units, meaning you'll be working at the lowest range where error is highest. Using an amplifier to match your sensor's output to the 0-10V range of the input or a sensor that directly provides a 0-10V signal would be a better approach.

The analog input error margin on the base module is +/-1.5% Full Scale, which means a difference of 15 increments throughout the range—even at low values. With your sensor's 80 to 750 mV range, that's 8 to 75 increments—a span of 67 increments. If your sensor spans 0 to 14 pH, each pH step equals about 5 increments, while the error is 15 increments. This will affect sensor accuracy when using a [product_name] analog input. You could try calibrating ranges for specific pH values with a precise pH meter, but usability won't surpass the error limit. Best results require a sensor with a 0-10V output. Also, why do you need to disable the sensor? The analog input has an impedance around 80kOhm, resulting in a maximum of 10 µA current. What is the reason for wanting the sensor disabled?

For low-level signals, using the [product_name] without an amplifier doesn't yield good results. An isolation amplifier with input at 0-1V and output at 0-10V could help. The analog input of the [product_name] cannot be turned off or deactivated.

A valve actuator controls the valve opening between 0 and 100%. However, the feedback sensor provides 5.2 mA at fully closed (0%) and 20 mA at 80% open. How can the feedback sensor be scaled to accurately represent the full 0 to 100% valve position?

To subtract 200 units from the signal, you don't necessarily need a complex mathematical function; a basic analog amplifier with an offset of -200 should suffice.

Can this method solve the following issue? A valve actuator opens from 0 to 100%, but the feedback sensor sends 5.2 mA at fully closed and 20 mA at 80% open. How can the feedback sensor be scaled so that it matches a true 0 to 100% valve position?

You asked: Can this method solve the following issue? A valve actuator opens from 0 to 100%, but the feedback sensor sends 5.2 mA at 0% and 20 mA at 80%. How can the feedback sensor be scaled to match a full 0–100% valve position? The way the question is written makes it difficult to understand. If 0% = 5.2 mA and 80% = 20 mA, then 100% would be about 23.7 mA, which [product_name] cannot handle. So [product_name] won't show 100%. It's not clear what type of signal your sensor actually produces, but guessing from your mention of subtracting 200 units, perhaps it's a 4–20 mA signal. Would you instead like to scale the 0–80% range as 0–100% for display purposes? If so, it could be approached differently.

Thank you for your assistance. Assume the sensor is faulty; I would like to use a software method to ensure the valve opens fully.

The simulation is usually slower due to emulation overhead and depends on operating system performance and background processes. Even block timing within a program can be affected, and online queries always involve some latency. On real [product_name], execution will always be faster than simulation on a PC. The same instructions on hardware could theoretically execute faster in PC-based simulation, depending on implementation. I suspect Java performance might factor in. A similar process in Python takes less than 1ms to execute, so the performance gap seems significant. I believe [company_name] could improve this, and that's why I'm sharing these findings—Java-based simulators may have limitations.

For time-sensitive tasks, cycle-oriented programming is generally used. Regards [user_name]

I understand there is a difference between a simulator and emulator. Perhaps [product_name_software] is meant to simulate execution and logic without matching hardware performance exactly, and this is often sufficient. However, it doesn't explain why resetting a timer and increasing a counter can take 50ms. Performance is always key in software development, and improvements should be sought where possible. I'm using VW0 to initiate actions in my project, with values coming from a remote system. The issue is that in the example I followed, VW0 gets reset from a MUX linked to NAQ1 every cycle, which is too frequent. Ideally, VW0 should only be set to 0 after the process in the project completes. Is there an analog function to move a 0 into VW0 only after a specific bit turns true? Thanks.

Could you clarify which block provides the value during normal operation in each cycle?

No other block writes to VW0 apart from a remote device and the analog MUX shown. The remote system only writes a value once. I need VW0 to be reset to zero after the task triggered by the nonzero value is completed. All actions are based on boolean logic. Example: when the remote system writes 50 to VW0, it starts a pump. After the pump starts, I need to write 0 to VW0 within the controller.

Here's a possible solution. If you want VW0 to be set to 0 for just one cycle or until a new start occurs, try using an AND (Edge) block, labeled as B002. If you want VW0 to remain at 0 as long as the cycle end is pending, then you can remove B002.

I think I understand. The first rung takes the value from the remote system, and if I1 turns true, it resets VW0 to 0. In my scenario, I1 only pulses, but that's sufficient since the subsequent actions will be executed, which weren't happening with the previous method that reset every cycle. I just need the reset to happen after a boolean trigger, not every cycle.

In the initial network, VW0 is read and linked via the analog amplifier to the analog MUX's first parameter. The MUX writes the value to VW0. If I1 shifts from 0 to 1, the MUX writes 0 into VW0.

I'll test it in the morning. It looks like you've answered how to write a value after a task completes via a boolean trigger. Now I can process the task and reset the value to zero afterward, instead of clearing it before the task starts. I'm using a communication interface module to send values, so there is some SMS latency and shifting of values in the user data memory. Thank you for your assistance!

Hello everyone, I need some assistance. I'm working with a [product_name] with [article_no] and require one analog input. In the hardware settings, I've configured for two analog inputs using channels I7 and I8. My analog device is connected to I7. The issue is that I'm running out of digital inputs (I need seven in total) and would rather not buy an expansion module if possible. Is it feasible to use I8 as a digital input while I7 stays analog? Will the [product_name] automatically detect a high/low signal on I8 and handle it appropriately, or are both inputs reserved only for analog once configured? I hope this is clear. Any advice would be appreciated. Thank you.

Yes, you can use one of the two analog inputs as a digital input. There's no extra setup required for this, everything works as expected. You just need to choose whether to use I7 or I8 as the analog input. It's technically possible to use an input as both analog and digital in your program. In most cases, the program won't operate reliably, but if you're experienced with [product_name], you could multiplex the signal: for one second use I7 as digital input and store its state, then the next second use I7 as analog input, alternating accordingly. You can save the analog measurement in a math function at the intervals when it's used as a digital input.

Additionally, I plan to use a PT100 sensor for temperature input to determine the 0-10V DC signal. My main question is whether it's possible to map a variable like this to the output of the PI controller.

Thank you for the guidance. Is there a way to achieve higher resolution with a multiplexer rather than just four points, or do people usually chain several multiplexers together for greater precision?

Can anyone clarify the following? In the PI Controller function block, there's a SP (setpoint) value and a button labeled 'reference' beside it. What is the purpose of this? Is it possible to have the same SP variable (changed manually via text input) in two different PI controllers? Also, is the analog marker a flag or an actual value stored in memory?

Hello! The 'reference' feature allows you to use the value from an existing analog block as a parameter for the current block. You can indeed use the same value in multiple blocks by utilizing 'reference.' Just assign the desired value as SP in the output of an analog block, then set this block as the reference in the PI Controller. Hope this clarifies things!

[product_name] Soft Comfort typically uses port 8080 to connect to the [product_name] Basis Module. When the [product_name] Basis Module is behind a router, additional challenges arise. First, the remote site's 8080 port may be used by other applications, preventing access. Second, if multiple [product_name] modules are behind a router, port 8080 will only refer to one [product_name] Basis Module, so others cannot be accessed using the same port. Third, port 8080 is commonly targeted by attackers. Is it possible to redirect [product_name] Soft Comfort communication to a different port, similar to changing ports in a browser (for example a.b.c.d:3456 instead of a.b.c.d:8080)? Thanks for any advice.

[product_name] [article_no] uses ports 102 or 8080 for communication: 8080 for its web server, and 102 for HMI and compatible controllers. With the newer [product_name] [version_no], port 8080 is also used for communication with Modbus devices. These port assignments are fixed and cannot be changed by users. Changing port numbers generally does not improve security. If you connect a [product_name] over the internet, using a VPN tunnel is the safest option.

Hackers tend to target common ports, such as 80 or 8080. Running a web server service on a non-standard port can lower the risk of attack and significantly improve security. However, sometimes a VPN-capable router is not available where online [product_name] program updates are needed. In those cases, you can open a port for the soft comfort connection to download new programs, but this port cannot be 8080 if it is used by another application.

If attackers get access to your network, the port number makes little difference. Hackers use port scanners to detect all open ports, including newly selected ones. In the [product_name] software or through the [product_name] menu, the port number cannot be changed. If you have concerns, consider submitting a support request.

Each port is typically assigned to a specific service. Using a standard web port like 80 or 8080 makes the protocol easy to identify, as they are defaults. If you change to a non-standard port, attackers must scan a larger range and match the protocol, which takes more time and resources. As a workaround, if you run Soft Comfort under Linux, you can translate ports using an SSH client and server, allowing remote [product_name] connections over a non-standard port. This enables program loading and full functionality of Soft Comfort. On Windows, this option is not available.

On the HMI, you need to use a Word tag (for example, VW10) as the trigger. Each individual bit in this Word can then be used to trigger a different alarm message. There isn't separate memory dedicated to bits, bytes, words, or double words in VM Memory. Addressing works by bytes, with the word address always corresponding to the first byte. Hi, The high-speed inputs are actually I5 and I6. If your input signal's pulse width is longer than the device scan time, you can use I3 and I4. How are you connecting the wires from your flow sensor? Avoid connecting both wires to I3 and I4. Supply voltage should go to the common input (either +24V or 230V depending on your [product_name] version), and the signal wire goes to I3 or I4. Usually, one input is for counting up/down and the other could be for reset, or one handles counting up and the other counts down. Can you specify your [product_name] version? What's the max pulse rate of your flow sensor, and how many pulses does it emit per unit volume?

Which flow meter model are you using? Are your flow meter's output pulses distinguishing high and low voltage levels sufficiently? Check your device manual for these specifics. You might need to use a pull-up or pull-down resistor.

It seems the low signal isn't dropping enough voltage for the digital input to read as zero. The flow meter operates at 260 Hz, and 3500 pulses correspond to 1 liter of fluid. According to the flow meter manual, it uses a 10K pull-up resistor on an open collector output, which explains the measured 8.86V. To reduce this voltage, insert a resistor in series between the flow switch wire and digital input I5/I6. To select an appropriate resistor, consider both the flow switch's current consumption and the input module's current requirements. Alternatively, you can use a 10K potentiometer in series, gradually adjust it until the voltage nearly reaches zero, then measure its value and replace it with a fixed resistor matching this measurement.

Hello, I'm using [product_name] with an HMI over Ethernet. I need to implement an hourly schedule set by the user via the HMI, letting them select a start and stop hour to control a memory function. In the image, this is labeled NAI1 and NAI2. How can I achieve this logic?

Which HMI are you using?

Sorry, I meant NAI1 and NAI2, because the HMI is sending an analog signal (from 1 to 24). I'm using a Kinco HMI.

The issue is that there's no direct access to the real-time clock on the [product_name]. Typically, you'd use the Weekly Timer block, but switching times use BCD format. Alternatively, you could create a custom counter that increments every hour.

I'm interested in the counter logic. Can you help me set it up? I'm still getting used to this PLC.

Here's an example, but note: The logic works correctly only the day after the [product_name] restarts.

1-24? In my opinion, that's not correct; it should be 0-23.

I understood up to NAI3, but then I got lost. Can you explain NAI3 and what it's doing? Sorry for the confusion, I'm eager to learn! Yes, 0-23 works too.

The counter value uses a double integer format. If you check Parameter-VM-Mapping (under Tools), the counter value is mapped to VM memory at VD4, where VD4 equals VW4 plus VW6. Counter values below 32,768 are in VW6. So it's possible to read the counter value back into the logic.

So if I understood correctly, you can select any type of block in the software and change its output format? That's good to know!

I forgot to ask, is there a way to force the PLC to run the program without waiting for the next day?

No, the block formats are all fixed.

No, the design relies on the weekly timer resetting the counter at midnight and starting a 1-hour timer. The timer increments the count every hour. That's why it doesn't work on restart day—the program can't detect when it started.

Thanks for all your help! I'll test it tomorrow when the timer starts to check if it's working. I hope I can reach out again if I need more assistance.

If your panel supports hexadecimal input format, I know an easier method.

It seems not, but thank you anyway!

But does your panel support BCD format? Is that correct?

Yes, it's possible to switch to BCD—does that matter?

In that case, you can use a weekly timer and change the On-Time and Off-Time using the HMI. Both parameters are BCD-coded words, with one byte for hours and the other for minutes. Use Parameter-VM-Mapping to transfer these values into VM memory.

I think I'm doing something wrong. Can you tell me what it is? It's just an On-Time activator.

[IMAGE] You will find Parameter-VM-Mapping under: Tools > Parameter-VM-Mapping.

Alternatively, in LAD: [IMAGE]

Addressing in the [product_name]'s VM memory is byte-oriented. VW0 = VB0 + VB1 VW2 = VB2 + VB3 VW4 = VB4 + VB5 VW1 = VB1 + VB2. If you use VW0 and VW1, there's overlapping since both use VB1.

I tried something similar but included NAI. Can you check and tell me what's incorrect?

You don't need NAIs; use Parameter-VM-Mapping for this.

I tried, but I'm struggling with it—sorry for all the trouble! I'll send some screenshots since I can't attach more than one image.

Sorry, I'm unable to help with that. I don't know your HMI or its capabilities, and the screenshots don't help me much. Everything looks good from the [product_name] perspective.

For future reference: If you have multiple screenshots or files, compress them into a ZIP and attach that.

I've tried many options, but nothing works. It's disappointing, but I'll have to use a different approach. Thank you for your help!

From the video, the day changed, indicated by the Latching Relay SF011 being set. You set 5 for switch-on and 15 for switch-off. The output activates when the count is 5 and deactivates at 15. The hour timer has only run for three minutes, so it hasn't sent an hour pulse to the counter yet. That's why the counter reads zero. Can you see now why the output hasn’t switched on yet?

Yeah, that was my mistake! I'll change on-time to 00 and see what happens.

It's working now, sorry for the confusion!

The analog input on [product_name] typically interprets a 0-20 mA current signal (or 0-10V voltage) and translates it to 1000 units. For a 4-20 mA sensor, 4 mA serves as the zero point, leaving 800 usable units from 200 to 1000. Therefore, both amplification (gain) and zero-point adjustment (offset) are required. If you amplify the 1000 units with a gain of 1.25, this becomes 1250 units. Applying an offset of -250 shifts the measurement range from -250 to 1000.

Thank you, your explanation is accurate and very helpful. If we want to convert a 4-20mA signal to display 0-1000 units on [product_name], we should set the gain to 1.25 and the offset to -250. However, I would like to know if there is a formula for calculating these values myself for 4-20mA sensors. One formula could be: gain = (max sensor value - min sensor value) / (max normalized value – min normalized value). For example: gain = (20 - 4) / (1000 - 200) = 0.02. Offset = [(min sensor value x max normalized value) – (max sensor value x min normalized value)] / (max normalized value – min normalized value), so offset = [(4 x 1000) - (20 x 200)] / (1000 - 200). Best regards, [user_name]

When setting up a 4-20 mA sensor in the analog amplifier, manual calculations are unnecessary as the [product_name] software computes these automatically. You simply select the 4-20 mA sensor type, input minimum and maximum limit values for the measured range, and specify decimal places. The software then determines the gain and offset for you. For example, with a 4-20 mA sensor ranging from -30 bar to 90 bar and one decimal place: Type: 4-20 mA, Minimum: -300, Maximum: 900. The software calculates a gain of 1.5 and an offset of -600.

Thank you for your reply. I am aware that [product_name] calculates gain and offset automatically and that it's sufficient to input only the minimum and maximum values. Based on your example—gain = 1.5 and offset = -600—I'd like to understand how to manually calculate these for a 4-20mA sensor. Hello experts. I have a question about connecting a three-wire pressure transducer (atlas copco [article_no]) with a 0.5-4.5V range to the [product_name] analog input (0-10V). The transducer has Signal, GND, and V+ wires. I've tried several wiring methods, but the analog value never increases along with the pressure shown on the manometer.

You haven't specified the sensor's voltage supply value. If your supply is 24 VDC, you can use the [product_name]. Otherwise, you should connect the GND from the sensor supply to the GND (0V) of the [product_name] so both reference potentials are the same.

Thank you for your interest in my question. The sensor requires a 5VDC supply, so I believe I need an external power source. What is the best way to connect the sensor after that?

You will need an external power supply for the sensor. A simple voltage stabilizer IC (Type 7805, approx. 1 Euro) should work. Connect 5V+ from the supply to the sensor's V+, the sensor's signal output to the [product_name] analog input, and 5V- (GND) to the sensor's GND. Make sure to connect 5V GND to the minus (M) terminal of the [product_name] power. Note, you must have a DC version if you want to use analog input on the basic module. Since the input works from 0-10V and the sensor outputs 0.5-4.5V, the measurement resolution will be less than half the normal—typically, the resolution for 10V is 1000, so for 4V, it's about 400. Good luck.

Thank you very much. Could you please help me improve the program from this thread: [url] so I can use it with my 0.5-4.5V sensor? I'm new to [product_name] programming and find it difficult.

What is the sensor's pressure range and which [product_name] module are you using?

The sensor range is 0-10 bar and the [product_name] I have is [article_no].

You need to perform some calculations. With a sensor output of 0.5V-4.5V (4V span) and the [product_name] working in the 0-10V range, consider: 0.5V to 4.5V equals 4V for 0-10 bar. If the input span were 10V, it would cover 25 bar (10/4 x 10). Since the sensor starts at 0.5V, not 0V, the offset is 1.25 bar (0.5V in a 25 bar range). So, sensor offset = -1.25 bar; end range = 23.75 bar. Set your analog amplifier block accordingly.

Thank you for your help.

Hello, Could someone explain why the second counter isn't exactly 10 times the value of the first counter? The first counter adds pulses every second, while the second counter adds pulses every 1/10 of a second. Where might I be making a mistake?

You are testing only in simulation mode, not on the actual [product_name]. Simulation doesn't always match real-life behavior. Also, check if the Asynchronous Pulse Generator starts with a high output; if so, after the first cycle, both counters will be at 1. One second later, the 1s counter will show 2 and the 1/10s counter will show 11. Two seconds later, you'll have 3 and 21. Three seconds later, 4 and 31. And so forth...

Thanks [user_name], your answer was very helpful. Now I'm facing the opposite issue: the simulation works fine, but the actual device doesn't. In reality, the 1/10s counter quickly jumps to 32767 in a short time. I’ve attached my program. Pressing I3 starts both counters; the 1s counter tracks liters and isn't reset, while the 1/10s counter tracks the 5-second cycle and is reset at the start of each cycle. I appreciate any guidance.

As mentioned before: simulation is not the same as real operation with the [product_name]. When the asynchronous pulse generator switches to a high signal, the output remains high for 0.01s—during which the program cycles multiple times, causing the count to repeat. Instead, the pulse should only be counted once per cycle. You can fix this by adding a positive edge between the asynchronous pulse generator output and the OR block.

Thanks [user_name], using a positive edge resolved the issue with excessive counting.

I aim to keep T1 as low as possible, but not under 55°C to avoid bacteria risks in the domestic hot water. The boiler temperature ranges between 70°C and 95°C, so a mixing valve is needed. When it's colder outside (T2, measured with a PT100 outside sensor), more heat is needed indoors, so T1 is increased to ensure enough energy and prevent too low return temperatures to the boiler. My calculations suggest that with outside temperatures above 10°C, 55°C water is enough, but at -10°C, you need 70°C for adequate heating. This is my first winter in the house, so these numbers are mostly estimates. Calculating energy needs in an old farmhouse is difficult—it's ideal to use a PLC so I can adjust values over time to optimize energy use (for example, if in the future 65°C suffices at -10°C, that's better). The interval solution would work, but if the outdoor temperature sits on a step boundary, I might see fluctuations. Also, I think continuous adjustment would save more energy, so small outside temperature changes cause small, logical adjustments. Over the winter, I plan to make further refinements.

I've attached a proposed solution, including an Excel file and a [product_name] program. The Excel sheet helps calculate the GAIN and OFFSET parameters for use in the [product_name] program. Since a single analog amplifier allows max 12.5x gain, two amplifiers are used in series: one with gain 10, followed by one with gain 2.5. Hi, I'm running into the VM Mapping line limit, which says the number of lines must not exceed 64. Is there any solution for this with the [product_name] [article_no]? Thanks, [user_name].

[user_name], I don't have a direct answer for your question. Out of curiosity, why are there so many mapped links? Perhaps some of those parameters are the same and could be grouped together? If so, we could help distribute the VM values to various destinations. More details about your VM's purpose in the application might highlight other options.

The answer is both yes and no. If you use bits, you can create a BYTE with 8 bits or a WORD with 16 bits, letting you pack more data into a single line. Bit-to-byte or word conversion can be done with a shift register and additional programming. Another solution is multiplexing, though this also requires coding, but it's feasible with the [product_name]. In many cases, you don't need VM addresses for Inputs/Outputs and Markers since these addresses often exist in the Ethernet data already. Check the Help section of [product_name] for address details. Your need for numerous VM addresses depends on your programming and requirements. Why do you have such a high count of VM addresses?

Thank you for your replies. I have a lot of mappings because my [product_name] is connected to an HMI screen, with each setting mapped and an HMI tag assigned in [product_name] HMI software.

Yes, that's a substantial amount. Check the Help section of [product_name] software and look for VM Mapping. There, you'll see many standard addresses available in Ethernet connections, so manual VM address assignment isn't always necessary. For example, addresses V923.0 to V923.7 correspond to digital inputs, and analog marker 1 (e.g., AM1) equals VW952, so using an analog marker for certain signals might help. If you display the value of AM1 on your HMI, you just need to create a tag with address V952 (a WORD) in the HMI software. In [product_name], connect AM1 to the signal, and avoid extra VM mapping. This should free up VM line space for other signals.

From a usability perspective, there are likely too many parameters at play. Consider these steps: 1) Separate parameters used regularly from those that are only machine-specific or installation-related. 2) Identify which parameters share values. Actions: 1) Place machine parameters, adjusted infrequently, on [product_name] user messages, so technicians can modify them through the built-in screen, and regular users don't need access. 2) PLC code can link one VM to multiple parameters. 3) Use demultiplexing—one VM selects the block parameter to change, another VM adjusts it (using an analog block with memory). The HMI then manipulates the selection VM depending on which parameter is being set.

Thanks for your help. Could you clarify steps 2 and 3 with some basics? I'm sure I can combine some settings in the program. I'll try implementing this and share results soon.

I won't be able to design an approach for suggestion #3 at the moment, sorry. For step #2, you can check the attached project—it's untested, but I've used similar logic before and it should work. Looking forward to your feedback. [user_name]

Hello everyone, I have two high-speed input signals from the same engine shaft and need to measure engine direction (left or right). If pulse from input 5 comes before input 6, the engine is turning left; if input 6 comes first, it's turning right. How can I translate this into a 0 or 1 direction status in programming? I've tried various methods, including relay latching, but haven't found a solution. The pulses follow each other closely. Thank you!

The [product_name] isn't well suited for tasks like this. Its high-speed inputs can handle signals up to 5 kHz if they go directly to a counter or threshold switch, but direct logic evaluation in the program is cycle-dependent. Because of this, it's not guaranteed that your program will reliably detect which pulse arrived first.

Hello, thanks for the response. My signal frequency peaks at 40 Hz, so it's relatively low. Could I implement something with a timer?

At 40 Hz, this should be feasible. Are the signals overlapping? Are you using an encoder? Please provide more details.

Hi, in this setup, the engine runs between 1 and around 40-50 Hz. There are two sensors positioned 90 degrees apart on the shaft; the engine can rotate in both directions. Counting both signals works fine, but I need to know the direction. If i5 pulses before i6, the shaft rotates clockwise; if i6 pulses before i5, it's counterclockwise. The signals don't overlap. The intended logic is: clockwise rotation = output 0, counterclockwise = output 1. This will control counting direction. Is this sufficient detail? Thanks again!

When you mention 40-50Hz, do you mean engine speed or the frequency provided by a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)? Standard asynchronous motors usually reach about 1500 RPM at 50Hz, which is quite fast. If your sensors' signals don't overlap, determining which comes first is even harder; keeping track of time delays between signals is critical. You’d need to measure the interval between i5 and i6, and vice versa, then compare these times to infer direction. This is complex even for larger PLCs. You might consider monitoring motor control commands (forward/reverse contactors with auxiliary contacts), or if using a VFD, connect its analog output to an analog input for feedback instead. These are just examples.

Hi, I’ve shared a small program for [product_name] that works for frequencies not exceeding 5 kHz. For fast inputs (I4 and I5 on [product_name model]), you can detect which signal arrived first and use it for direction. I've used this method with small encoders providing two signals at low frequency. If you want an approach using [product_name], this could work.

text:
Apologies if this is a basic question, but I haven't managed to find a solution in the manual or on the forum. I want to set a default state for the network input after a power interruption or update. Currently, the state always defaults to zero when the program first runs. I thought assigning a value to the Variable Virtual Memory connected with the network input at startup would work, but I haven't figured out how to do this. Thanks!

When the [product_name] device is powered on or restarted, all VM memory values reset to 0 because the VM memory isn't retained.

That's the default behavior. What I'm aiming for is to have the value set to 1 upon startup. There's a startup signal called M8. Is it possible to use this somehow? The manual notes: "The M8 flag is set during the first cycle after startup and can be used in your logic diagrams for initialization."

Unfortunately, that's not doable. You can't assign specific states (0 or 1) to network inputs directly in the [product_name] logic diagram.

It's a bit more complicated, but I've encountered a similar issue before (network input state retrieval is delayed after device startup). A simpler workaround is to read the network input using a delay block—for example, only accept the input's state change if it remains True for two seconds. For analog inputs and variable memory, one method involves using an analog multiplexer: feed the network analog input through an amplifier, and route its output to one multiplexer input. Assign a default value through another amplifier offset to the multiplexer’s second input. Link the multiplexer output to the network output at the VM address (like VW10). A better method is to use Parameter VM Mapping, assigning the multiplexer output to the address directly. You now have a choice between input or default value based on how the multiplexer is switched (using M8 flag with a delay trigger after startup). After a few seconds, switch the multiplexer back to the network input once the connection is restored. To further improve, you can retain the previous analog input value using a functional block with retention, so the last value is stored and restored on power-up.

Thanks for the input so far! I'm working with digital inputs and outputs. I've found that simply connecting status 1 (high) to the network output sets its value to 1 at startup, but then it's stuck at 1. Using a latching relay triggered by the M8 initialization flag works as well, but once set, the network input stays at 1 even if an external signal tries to reset it—the relay overrides the change. My current solution is to use an additional network input to reset the relay, giving me control over the original input, but this means splitting states between two network inputs. Is there a way to use network outputs to set three states: 1, 0, or no value (unlocked)? I'm new to this, so it's a learning process.

Network inputs are digital, which means they can only have two states: 0 or 1.

I may have worded my question poorly. Since network input states are limited to 0 and 1, is it possible to have multiple sources set the network input, such that an external network command can override the initial value of 1 and change it to 0? For example: in diagrams it looks like the network input behaves like an AND gate (if any source sends 1, the result is 1). Externally, using a protocol command, it seems more like a latch—the input stays at 1 until you explicitly send 0. Is it correct that similar latch logic can't easily be achieved with diagrams in [product_name] programming—meaning, send 1 internally until overridden by an external command?

No, you shouldn't connect multiple outputs to a single input—it's not the proper approach. Instead, use an OR gate. Since the device version isn't specified, I can't give a detailed diagram, but here's an idea: Connect network input to one side of the OR gate; link an off-delay block triggered by the M8 flag to the other side of the OR gate; wire the off-delay reset to the network input. Set the off-delay block for a few seconds (enough time for network synchronization). If the network input goes high before the timer runs out, it resets and won't interfere further. This lets you manage just one network input (though using an RS trigger with two network inputs is also an option).

Here's another method you could try...

I've set it up with the initialization flag and latching relay plus delay, combined with network output, and it's working as needed. Thanks for all the help! Your suggestions really clarified things and solved my issue.

Hello, I'm building a test unit for 0 to 50 Bar measurements, aiming for 0.05 Bar increments. The only pressure sensor available to me is 0 to 60 Bar (4-20mA), which I plan to connect using a 500 Ohm resistor to produce a 2-10V input. Could someone advise on how to set the gain and offset appropriately? It's important for me to maintain the 0.05 Bar increments. Thanks for your help.

It's best to use an analog amplifier for processing analog signals. Connect the analog input to the amplifier first, where you can set the sensor’s minimum and maximum values; offset and gain are adjusted automatically. You can then use the amplifier’s output for further analog processing. Quick calculation: for a 2-10 Volt input representing 0-60 Bar, you'll need to map that range to 0-10 Volt. 10-2=8 Volts, so 60/8*10=75 (range), and 60-75=-15. Settings should be: Max Value 60 (or 600 for greater accuracy), Min Value -15 (or -150 for greater accuracy).

Thank you—I've implemented your suggestion and it works. I applied a threshold to restrict measurement to 50 Bar. Is there a way to achieve a resolution of 0.05 Bar, with output values like 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, etc.? Or would it be more effective to use a 0-50 Bar (0-10V) sensor directly?

The resolution is determined by the capabilities of the [product_name] device. Changing the sensor won't address the resolution limitations. In [product_name], resolution is 10 bits (1024 steps), so 60/1024 = 0.06 Bar per step. Alternatively, if you use a sensor with a narrower range, such as 40-60 Bar, you would get a resolution of 20/1024 = 0.02 Bar per step.

Thank you again. I think sourcing a 0-50 Bar sensor will be necessary since I need to test the full range, and the 0.05 Bar resolution allows for clear and precise setpoints, such as 2.00 Bar. Furthermore, using a 0-10V sensor means I can connect it directly without extra components like a 500 Ohm resistor. Unless there's another approach I should consider?

Since [product_name] uses integer calculations, all computations must be scaled appropriately (factor of 100), and you should configure two decimal places in block properties for display. I am working on setting up an IO field in a basic HMI device to input an analog setpoint value for a [product_name] V[version_no] project. After creating the IO field and configuring the HMI tags, the value entered in the IO field updates the analog input in the [product_name] project as expected. However, I want to have a predefined start value loaded automatically when both the PLC and HMI power on, instead of the value defaulting to zero. I set a 'Start Value' for the relevant tag in the engineering software, but it does not behave as intended—when the system powers on, the IO field and the PLC analog input both show '0'. Interestingly, if the HMI is disconnected from the PLC (e.g., the LAN cable is removed) during power-up, the IO field on the HMI displays the correct predefined value set in the 'Start Value' field. This suggests that with the HMI and PLC connected, the 'Start Value' does not load properly for either the IO field or the PLC analog input. I have attached relevant images and screenshots. This issue is similar to what you encountered with digital signals in your other topic. The HMI device itself cannot save data; any values from an input/output field need to be stored by the PLC. Therefore, values from the HMI should not be directly processed in the PLC through analog network input. Instead, these values should be written into a parameter of an analog block (such as a mathematical instruction) using parameter VM mapping. If you store a value directly in a parameter using parameter VM mapping, the value is saved in the flash memory and remains intact even after a power cycle.

About the register 406000: The following is general Modbus information, applicable to all Modbus implementations and not tied to any specific company or device. The leading digit '4' (e.g., 406000) designates a Holding Register, not an Input Register (Input Registers start with '3'). According to the Modbus specification, Input Registers are read-only, while Holding Registers are always readable and may be writable, depending on device firmware. Device documentation will state if the register is read-only or read-write. To read Holding Registers, use Modbus Function Code 03. To write to a single Holding Register, use Function Code 06. To write to multiple consecutive Holding Registers, use Function Code 16 (decimal) or 10 (hexadecimal). Assuming register 406000 is set up as read/write, this should be possible if permitted by the device.

Hello [user_name], This issue is more about contact load than the relay cycle time. Incorrect load on the contacts can cause relay failures.

Hi, It seems the problem relates to the type of load being switched. The description suggests the relay contacts are overheating and sticking together. Both valves and lamps present non-ohmic loads, which can affect relay lifespan. Valves might offer protection options from the vendor, but lamps are more difficult because they can create a substantial inrush current—sometimes thousands of times higher than normal—when switching on. To address this, an 'inrush current limiter' should be used in such scenarios; otherwise, the relays may fail shortly after installation. Coupling relays might only transfer the issue elsewhere in the circuit. Hope this information helps.

It's interesting to see relay failures becoming more frequent, especially as more people switch from traditional incandescent and fluorescent bulbs to LED fixtures. The failing relays are often stuck on. Notably, when LEDs replace higher-wattage fixtures and have been switched many times, relays eventually get stuck on. This has been reported in various applications, such as aquatic tank lighting, where users transitioning from fluorescent tubes to LEDs started facing relay issues. The root cause tends to be cheaper LED lights and their electronics, which create large capacitive loads. When relays switch these, they can experience significant current spikes, leading to welded contacts over time. There are several solutions: switch back to incandescent or fluorescent lighting, use a relay with a higher surge rating, or install surge suppressors and snubber networks across the contacts. Some snubber networks allow enough current to light or flicker the LEDs, so they must be carefully designed. Sometimes combining an incandescent with LEDs resolves this. Quality LED fixtures with built-in surge protection are less likely to cause problems. I personally used a small capacitor across my first LED fixture to solve unintended lighting due to snubber current in my hallway when transitioning to LEDs.

Hi, [company_name] offers an inrush current limiter for this purpose. You need one limiter for each relay contact you wish to protect. Hope this provides a solution.

Second, for the setpoints: there are three setpoints, VM1, VM2, and VM3. However, adjusting setpoint 2 affects setpoint 1, and changing setpoint 3 affects both 2 and 1, despite there being no programmed link between them. Thanks in advance to anyone who can assist.

Hello [user_name], welcome to the forum. It would help to review your [product_name] web editor project and control program to see what might be causing the issue. Based on your description, it sounds like the web editor doesn't show decimal places for temperature readings, which is a known limitation. [company_name] is aware of this problem but hasn't released a fix yet. Regarding your setpoints: if changing one setpoint affects others, it's likely because the addresses you're using are overlapping. The addressing works at the byte level, and an analog value uses two bytes. For example, if your addresses are VW0, VW1, and VW2, these overlap byte-wise: VW0 uses VB0 and VB1, VW1 uses VB1 and VB2, and VW2 uses VB2 and VB3. This means VB1 is part of both VW0 and VW1, and VB2 is part of both VW1 and VW2, causing the interference you observe. It's best to address words (VW) in steps of two, such as VW0, VW2, VW4, etc.

Hello everyone! I'm new to both this forum and to [product_name]. As a student, I'm working on a project to irrigate 4 types of crops. How are you measuring the running time for each pump? Are you using the operating hours counter block from [product_name] to track this?

Yes, I'm tracking each pump using the hours counter block from [product_name].

That's where the challenge lies. The hours counter provides a value in DInt (32-bit), but the compare function in [product_name] processes only Int (16-bit) values. You can work around this by using the VM area, but it's a complex solution. I can share an example, although it might take some time to prepare.

I initially attached an example, but I removed it since the solution wasn't functioning correctly.

You put a lot of effort into this, and I wouldn't have managed it on my own. Thanks for your support!

One more question: what's the difference between 'low word hours counter' and 'high word hours counter'? I need outputs like 'q1', 'q2', 'q3' to indicate which motor (1, 2, or 3) has run for less time than the other two, and I need to adjust the logic.

As mentioned earlier, the operating hours counter outputs a 32-bit value, but [product_name] lets users work only with 16-bit values. To handle this, you need to split the 32-bit (DWord) value into two 16-bit words. For example, let's say you have two counters whose values are stored in the VM area as double word (32-bit) at VD0 and VD4. VD0 contains VW0 (high 16 bits) and VW2 (low 16 bits); VD4 contains VW4 and VW6 similarly. First, compare VW0 and VW4 (the high words) — if VW0 is greater than VW4, then the first meter has a higher value than the second, and you don't need to check the low words. If VW0 and VW4 are equal, then compare the low words (VW2 and VW6) to determine which has run longer.

That explanation makes sense now, thank you!

Follow the connection table setup. VM address 1 corresponds to VD1 (double word in the VM area starting at address 1): VD1 = VW1, and VW3 = VB1 + VB2 + VB3 + VB4. So, two HR words (starting at address 1) go to [product_name] VW1 (address 1) for two words.

I tried as shown in the attached screenshot, using both odd and even HR addresses, but still get zeros. Here's what Modbus Poll reads.

Static connections use fixed port addresses: Connection 1 = 502, Connection 2 = 503, Connection 3 = 504, Connection 4 = 505, Connection 5 = 506, Connection 6 = 507, Connection 7 = 508, Connection 8 = 509.

I tried your code with unit number 27 and tested addresses 152, 153, and 154, but clicking the glasses icon still shows zero. Modbus Poll reports a value of 131 (32-bit signed big-endian), but [product_name] responds with zero for those addresses.

I've investigated further but still no luck. Using the NAI method to read from Modbus only supports integer values, not floating point. The Modbus connection table also seems limited to integer options. Which variable should store the Modbus float for conversion with the F/I block?

It seems you misunderstand my instructions. A holding register (HR) has two words (4 bytes). A word in the VM area of [product_name] is 2 bytes. For one HR with 2 words (4 bytes), write them into the VM area sequentially starting from a given address. Example: HR1 (2 words) -> VW1 (start address, uses 2 words). So HR1 goes into VW1+VW2+VW3, and the next available address is VW4, VW5.

It appears the Modbus connection setup is incorrect. For VM mapping, [product_name] is used as server and the Modbus device as client; for NAI mapping, [product_name] is client and Modbus device is server. Your application needs [product_name] to be the client reading from the Modbus server. Try the attached program, which is in diagram mode (easier for single [product_name] setups). Use only locally mapped variables instead of green NAIs. In menu: tools -> ethernet connections -> Connection1 (Modbus Client), the VM mapping is inside. A float requires 2 registers (4 bytes); for example, map to VM0 (uses VB0-VB3, VW0 and VW2). For double, 4 registers (8 bytes)—increase mapped registers if needed. To read several registers in sequence, simply alter the read/write word count. For example, 6 registers (for 3 floats starting at HR500) mapped to VW0 correspond to VM0, VM4, VM8. Adjust the HR and ID (27?) as needed and the correct value should appear in the display.

Thank you for your help. Sorry for repeated questions, but the help system isn't very clear. An online tutorial would be helpful for these issues.

The main challenge is locating all relevant information. Details of the controller are in the online help or instruction manual for [product_name]. Start by understanding variable memory—this is a byte area from VB0 to VB850. Prefer even numbering (VW0, VW2, VW4) for words as each takes two bytes (VW0=VB0+VB1). For double words, use quad numbering (VD0, VD4, VD8), each is four bytes (VD0 uses VW0+VW2 or VB0+VB1+VB2+VB3). Use the memory as needed but avoid overlapping areas. Learn about Modbus registers via search engines and the Modbus device manual's value table. Many Modbus devices begin at register 0 while [product_name] starts at 1, so often there's a +1 offset. Additional notes: HR (holding registers) for read/write of stored/calculated values, IR (input register) for analog input reads, Coil for read/write bits (status or commands), DI for digital input bits, etc. This is a broad topic—there's always more to learn.

The frequency converter is not a [company_name] product. For the connection between the automation module and frequency converter, a specialized RS485 to Ethernet converter will be used, with device number, data port, IP address, and baud rate configured. An unmanaged switch was set up to organize the local network. The automation module uses the IP address 192.168.11.101, and the converter (along with the modbus device) uses 192.168.11.102. This connection method worked well for reading data from a temperature and humidity sensor via Modbus (temperature and humidity transmitter). However, I could only read data from the Modbus device; writing data was unsuccessful, even though it should be possible. Please see the attached network analog input configuration. Given this, my questions are: - How do I properly send requests and receive responses from the Modbus device using function codes like: - 0x03 to read multiple registers - 0x06 to write to a single register - What functions or constants are needed to implement this? - Should I use "Modbus client connection configuration"? - How do I set up "Data transfer" if needed? Practical example: I need to set the rotation speed (e.g., 32 Hz, decimal 320, hex 140), specify device address (unit ID), function code (0x06), and register address (for example, 0x2001 for rotation speed in my frequency converter; this is two bytes: first 0x20, second 0x01). Is that the correct Modbus address format? Register value for the desired speed must be split into two bytes: 0x01 and 0x40. What is the right approach for this? Concerning CRC: what is it and how is it used in this communication? What is CRC? Please refer to the relevant wikipedia article for more information.

Thank you for the feedback. I have attached the compressed program file. This solution addresses a control system with limited I/O. Input I1 manages the mixer motor via Q1; another motor drives a carriage to a limit switch at I2. Q2 and Q3 provide three speed signals for the controller running Q1. A separate control system activates the mixer motor at I1, and after a short delay, the carriage reaches the upper limit—this triggers I2 and stops the drive motor. After this, another system starts a 15-second delay, then moves the carriage away from the top limit for a set distance. Three seconds later, B001 completes, triggering B002 and B006; Q2 and Q3 change state, switching Q1 to the second speed. After five seconds, B002 times out and turns off Q2, setting the third Q1 speed. During the next five seconds, while B006 runs, another controller deactivates I1 and Q1 gradually stops. Keep in mind that analog outputs are always active power sources and remain connected to their terminals, even if set to 0V. These outputs continually try to maintain the specified voltage or current. Picture two batteries connected in parallel with a resistor and a voltmeter. If the resistor becomes zero ohms, the batteries would oppose each other, causing heat and potential damage as the resulting voltage wouldn't be simply 5V or 1V. Applying this scenario to the [product_name] device could result in damage to its electronics.

You can take outputs from blocks B001 and B002, link them using an OR logic gate, and feed the result to a single output (e.g., Q2 on [product_name]).

To repeat from earlier: Do digital outputs disconnect from source voltage when turned off, or do they remain connected and simply output zero?

Transistor (PNP) outputs stay connected, but are more robust. Connecting an external source (like a switch) to the output isn't ideal, but can work if you include a diode for extra protection. Relay outputs do disconnect. Be cautious when using mixed voltage types.

When using the [product_name] [article_no], there are three main ways to log data: • You can use a custom DataLog without an SD card, but you’re limited to 512 bytes of logged data. Once the limit is reached, the oldest entry is removed to make room for new ones (FIFO method). • With a DataLog on an SD card, you can create up to 50 log files, each containing 20,000 entries. After reaching the file limit, a new log file is started. • With the [product_name] Access Tool, data is logged directly to a PC using Excel at a fixed interval of one second, which cannot be changed. If these approaches don’t meet your needs, you may need to find third-party apps or software that offer more customizable options or consider programming your own solution.

The encoder is an ES5-10CN8942 from Delta, with solid shaft, open collector output, and 1000 PPR, operating at 7-24V DC. I've previously connected an encoder to a [product_name] ([version_no]), which worked perfectly thanks to help from this community. After reviewing various forums and the [product_name] software help, I learned that inputs I3-I6 support high-speed counting (up to 5kHz) if wired directly to the counter block. I set up a basic test where I3 is linked to a counter with a trigger limit of 1000 and powered the encoder with 24V DC. When monitoring the system, no counts were registered regardless of encoder rotation. Offline simulation worked, indicating correct code, but hardware wasn't responding. Could something be wrong with my wiring? Any advice or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Online simulation with [product_name] software isn't supported. You can monitor the running program on the actual [product_name] device if your computer's code matches what's on the device. Note that updates are very slow when viewing inputs in real time—if you turn the encoder too quickly, you won't see accurate feedback instantly, but ultimately, the displayed counts will update on your PC (albeit slightly delayed). PC simulation mode is also slower than the real device. Regarding wiring: with open collector output, you can't connect the encoder directly to the [product_name]. The input must use an open emitter output from your encoder. Try using a pull-up resistor (around 1kOhm) between the + and the digital input—the encoder will then be able to sink the signal properly.

If your encoder’s supply voltage is different from your [product_name]'s voltage, make sure to connect the 0V (M) lines together. If they share the same supply voltage, this step is straightforward.

Exactly—if the power supply isn’t the same for both devices, the encoder won’t operate correctly with your [product_name]. I added a 10 kOhm pull-up resistor and that solved the issue perfectly! Thanks!

Can you clarify, especially what you meant by 'external course'?

Hi [user_name], you didn’t mention which [product_name] hardware was used during the online test. For high-speed counting, you need a transistor-type (24V) module—not the relay version. Ensure the input is wired directly to the counter pin for achieving 5kHz speeds. The input threshold voltage on the [product_name] differs from that of the [version_no]. Use a voltmeter to check the actual voltage from the encoder. While a 10kOhm pull-up resistor is common, something closer to 1.2kOhm (0.5W) is usually expected. Are you only using one encoder phase? Confirm with a voltmeter that the voltages react as required. Also, sharing your program segment and a wiring sketch could help double-check everything.

Why is that? The data specs for the digital inputs are consistent regardless of whether you use the transistor or relay variant.

Glad this was brought up. Recently, I checked the [product_name] manual for the OBA8: the appendix outlines input behavior and specifications for different variants. Any thoughts?

The 24V DC-only modules (OBA8) come as 24CE and 24CEo (transistor output, 24VDC) and 12/24RCE plus 12/24RCEo (relay output, 12/24VDC). For these, the digital input specs—the speed for normal (4Hz) and fast count input (5kHz)—are identical. However, variants like 24RCE and 24RCEo (relay output, 24VAC/DC) do not support fast counting, as they can operate on AC as well.

That's right, it's about the pure DC variant—not the relay one! Thanks for clarifying. Our factory purchased the 24RCE model, which was not ideal for our needs. We focused on the relay detail, but ultimately had to replace it.

Only [product_name] modules with a pure DC supply (24VDC and 12/24VDC) offer analog and fast counter inputs. The AC/DC and 230V models lack these features.

Just to confirm, I’m using a single phase as you suggested, [user_name]. Previous posts from you and other forums mentioned that quadrature phase isn’t possible with [product_name]. I tested two NPN encoders on I3 (5kHz) and both functioned well—one from Delta (1000PPR), another from Omron (500PPR). My setup uses a DC-only module: '12/24 RC', which supports 8 inputs and 4 outputs. I’m still unsure how to precisely calculate the ideal pull-up resistor value, so additional guidance would be appreciated. Regarding the 'External of course' phrase, I meant that both encoder and [product_name] use the exact same 24VDC supply, and their power sources are connected via the same L+ and M wires. Sorry for any confusion earlier.

To clarify, fast counting works very well on both the [version_no] and my DC-only [product_name] module. With a 5kHz max speed and a slow, 24V geared motor, that’s more than sufficient even at hand-operated speeds. For example, at 5kHz you could register up to 5000 PPR per second; with three encoder rotations per second, you’d see up to 3000 pulses—well within capability. I also connected the relay to the [product_name] display module and observed that core relay performance is much faster than the display, which is impressive for a smart relay.

Could you clarify if your issue is now resolved and what changed? Regarding pull-up resistors: the highest current flows when the encoder's open collector transistor pulls I3 low. Ensure the transistor's amp rating isn't exceeded, and calculate resistor power consumption using P = (V^2) / R. When the transistor is OFF, the pull-up supplies voltage to I3. Keep in mind I3's internal resistance—resistor and input impedance are in series, so if the voltage drop across the pull-up is too great, I3 will get insufficient voltage. Use Ohm's law (V = I x R) for this calculation. Measure I3’s voltage directly while rotating the encoder by hand. Checking the encoder’s specification sheet may give further clues. Helpful?

Yes, that's the exact circuit I referenced. The problem was resolved after adding the pull-up resistor. Thanks for your explanation about resistor calculations—I understand now why a value near 1.2kOhm was suggested. I calculated a current around 0.5A at I3. Since I only had a 1.5kOhm resistor on hand, I used that, and compared results against a 10kOhm resistor—the module read counts correctly in both cases, showing no visible difference. It seems the problem is solved, and resistors between 1.5kOhm and 10kOhm performed equally well in my setup.

Keep in mind: When you use pull-up resistors, the [product_name] input will be inverted—sensor output high means logic input low on your device.

Here’s an example from a specification sheet: if the voltage on the input pin for ON (transistor OFF) is less than 8.5V, problems begin. If the signal never exceeds 5V, the input will always appear OFF. All microcontroller-based devices have an ON/OFF voltage specification—do some measurements and math with your selected resistor values to ensure proper operation.

Internal markers (flags) are used to complete one relay coil line and then use the result as a normally closed contact on another line. These flags operate internally. To use internal markers in ladder logic, add a coil and then select 'IM' from the dropdown or type it at the top of the list. There are no restrictions on the number of internal markers, but you need to keep track of which numbers you are using. The VM area is a dedicated memory space used for data exchange between the [product_name] and external devices. Setting up VM mapping offline allows you to configure how data from the [product_name] will be transferred to a partner device. Once online, the mapped VM area will send or receive data according to the predefined addresses between the [product_name] and the external device.

Within the VM area, fixed addresses are designated for various types of I/O, including: - digital inputs - digital outputs - analog inputs - analog outputs - digital network inputs - digital network outputs - analog network inputs - analog network outputs - digital flags - analog flags

Extensive information about fixed and variable addresses can be found in the help section of [product_name] software. Look up 'VM Mapping'. Be aware that some addresses in [article_no] differ from those in [article_no].

For VM mapping specific to [article_no], refer to the attached [document].

How is VM mapping structured for general access? For example, does VB1 overlap VW1 (or perhaps VW0), or are byte-addressable and word-addressable memory areas stored in different tables? Is it: | VB0|VB1| (VW0) Or: |VB0| --- | (VW0) |VB1| --- | (VW1) Or do you have separate memory regions: |VW0| ... |VWn| ... |VB0|...|VBn|

V0.0 - V0.7 corresponds to VB0 V1.0 - V1.7 corresponds to VB1 V0.0 - V1.7 equals VB0 plus VB1, representing VW0 V0.0 - V3.7 includes VB0, VB1, VB2, VB3, resulting in VW0 plus VW2 or VD0. Addressing is organized by bytes. In case of words (VW) or double words (VD), the address (e.g., VD4) starts from the first byte (for VD4, it's VB4). The address for a V bit (Vx.y) combines the byte address (x) and the bit address (y). For example, V0.4 is bit 4 within byte 0.

Good morning everyone, I'm looking to create an automatic position control solution for a shutter in my machine. The goal is to open and close it in five steps, each step activated by a corresponding switch. I want to use a stepper motor and a rotary encoder for position feedback; however, I'm struggling with the programming aspect. Any guidance or examples would be much appreciated. Thank you!

Hello, Could you share more details? Specifically: 1) Does your stepper motor have an integrated controller that can simply receive up/down signals? If not, you might consider using a regular motor with gears. 2) How will you select the desired position—via a rotary switch or time-based control? Describe your stepping cycle. 3) Using a fast counter input to register encoder pulses can help track position, counting up or down as needed. Be sure to include a counter reset (for example, activate a full closed limit switch and press a reset to set the counter to zero). Please provide this information so I can assist further.

Hello, Generally, combining stepper motors directly with [product_name] is not feasible. Stepper motors need a minimum start/stop frequency, which [product_name] can't supply. The maximum output frequency is determined by the scan time—typically 0.1ms per function block, so for 200 function blocks, the scan time is about 20ms (resulting in roughly 50Hz frequency for transistor outputs). Relay outputs are much slower, maxing at 0.5Hz. Instead, consider using an external stepper drive that can be programmed for your five target positions and speed settings, and trigger these via digital input signals. Some manufacturers offer such stepper drives. Hope this provides clarity.

Good morning, my [product_name] device is connected to two digital sensors. I want to track how long each sensor was ON during the last 24 hours. For example, if I check at 16:16, it should show the ON duration for each sensor from 16:16 the previous day up to 16:16 today. Is this possible?

No, that's not currently possible using built-in functions.

Would a data log solution work for you? This would require processing the information externally on a PC to obtain the result you want.

It's challenging to calculate total ON time when the input signal frequently changes.

Do you plan to check the sensor times every day at the same specific time?

No, I plan to check at various times and cannot connect the device to a PC. My idea is to press a button on the [product_name] operator panel and get the sensor ON duration for the last 24 hours.

You cannot access previous states within the [product_name] program. What you can do is start a time counter for the appropriate input. Then, when you send a trigger, say at 16:00, the total ON duration is stored and the counter reset. The next day, at a new time, you repeat the process. This records the duration between each trigger, but it's not a rolling 24-hour window.

Alternatively, you can use a pulse from a weekly timer to trigger at the same time each day. How precise does the timing need to be? Do you need seconds, or just hours and minutes?

Accurate answers depend on how precisely the problem is described. For your second question, you need a counter that tracks pulses from a weekly timer. Once two pulses are counted, the operating hours counter should be evaluated and then both counters (operating hours and pulse counter) reset.

Note: all block parameters using this scaled value need to be multiplied by 10 (values appear as xxxn). This is [company_name]'s official method for PT100 scaling but it's not fully accurate. For more exact scaling, use two amplifiers in sequence with these settings: 1) gain = 10, offset = 0; 2) gain = 2.5, offset = -5000. Use two decimal digits in your textboxes. Remember to multiply block parameters by 100 now. Your format will be xxx,nn °C on text displays and xxxnn in block values. This way, you achieve 0.25°C resolution accurately. I'm not entirely sure what you want to achieve. With the threshold set to switch ON at -120 and OFF at -119, the trigger acts exactly as configured. With the ON = -121 and OFF = -120 parameterization, the threshold trigger operates within just one unit. If the real [product_name] amplifies the signal and skips over this narrow range, it may miss the value (-121). The analog-to-digital converter requires time to process the analog signal.

If the value fluctuates, you need a hysteresis—like ON at -120 and OFF at -130. The difference is the hysteresis: ON => OFF. Here's an example setup: A 1.5 kOhm resistor in series with a PT100 sensor to a 10V input, powered by 24V. PT100 resistance at 0°C = 100Ω, at 100°C ≈ 138Ω. 1500Ω to 100Ω gives 22.50V and 1.50V at 0°C, while 1500Ω to 138Ω gives 22.08V and 1.92V at 100°C. The voltage difference ΔU = 0.42 V over a temperature difference of Δϑ = 100°C. The resolution is about 0.01V = 2.38°C, roughly 2.5°C per step, which is poor. The margin of error is also large for the input range.

Suppose the range is 0 - 80°C. If I input 2V and get a value of 202, can I subtract 202 from the analog input to set the zero point? Is it possible to perform such a mathematical adjustment on the analog input?

Here is the screenshot.

Regarding the basics: The A/D converter for an analog input translates 0-10V or 0/4-20mA signals into approximately 1,000 units. If you use a 2-10V (or 4-20mA) input, you only get 800 units, since 200 units for 0-2V (or 0-4mA) are not used. To adjust for this, you need to set the analog amplifier so that a 0-10V (or 4-20mA) signal covers the range, and shift the starting point (OFFSET). For example, 80°C over 800 units results in 0.1°C per unit. At 0.1°C for 1,000 units, you get 100°C. With a measuring range of 80°C, there is an offset of 20°C (200 units). This means the adjusted measurement range stretches from -20°C to 80°C.

I hope this explanation clarifies things. Thank you for your feedback and rating.
