text: Hello everyone, The [product_name] [article_no] introduces several new function blocks. I’d like to share a practical evaluation of the “average” block here: The “average” block calculates a periodic average over a number of past values. While this is technically feasible, using all analog inputs within reasonable circuit complexity only allows up to n = 32 values (with an entry value range from 0 to 1000). Despite these limitations, the block is impressive – according to the manual, n can be up to 32767 (depending on sampling time), and each entry value can cover the full analog range from -32768 to 32767. A drawback is that the minimal total sampling time (St) is just 1 second, meaning measurements are spaced by St/SN. Using this block for analog input signals requires paying attention to these constraints, as low scanning rates may lead to undetected measurement errors or inaccurate block results. For previous versions like [product_name] [article_no], there was a way to filter analog display values in text messages, though this also risked low scanning frequencies. Similar filter blocks can help make displayed values appear more stable, but this isn’t ideal when those values are needed for further calculations. It’s clear that changes in analog input updates controlled by [product_name] hardware could lower the scanning rate, but this can’t be adjusted further within the system. In general, reducing scan or update frequency should be avoided to ensure digitized analog signals are as accurate as possible. Unfortunately, block parameters cannot be defined by reference. Block behavior when activating the “EN” and “R” input pins: - If entry “R” is enabled, the block skips the current sampling time and ignores the output. - If “EN” is set to “0” briefly, sampling is paused (but not reset). This means you cannot restart sampling without clearing the output, which hinders potential mid-cycle adjustments or alignments. Additionally, circuit designs reusing the block’s output must account for the output being forced to zero during St instead of retaining the previous measured value. Summary: As an alternative (to previously published circuits), the “average” block (available only on [product_name] [article_no]) can filter analog inputs, provided these parameter requirements are met: - St / SN = 0.300 s (Basic module analog inputs) - St / SN = 0.050 s (Expansion module analog inputs) Best regards, [user_name]

Correct—if you have small relay coils operating at the same voltage as your [product_name], typically 24VDC, it's possible. Beam me up Scottie! Preferably through GSM remote service to my [product_name]. PSTN/Fixed Line Remote Service ========================= A similar method was demonstrated for [product_name] back in October 2003 for [article_no] (refer to attached zip file). The documentation outlines some insights on communication—like how crossover Tx & Rx means modem DCE to [product_name] DTE, and how modem AT command settings are relevant. This process was later replaced with the Modem Cable and Wizard in [product_name] V6, but essentially, the fundamental checks remain—review COM port settings and validate the modem cable with a multimeter. GSM-Based Remote Service ===================== This has been an ongoing topic. Here are some details I've gathered, hoping others might contribute more experiences or information. I've investigated this for several years and identified three main challenges: 1) 11-bit GSM modem support Although this is typically cited as the primary issue, other factors may also contribute. Most GSM modems support only 10-bit character framing such as 8N1 or 7E1 (with configurations for start bit, data bits, parity, and stop bit). Some modems can be configured with AT commands to change this setup, and a few even allow 11-bit communication on the RS232 side (PC & [product_name] interface) while maintaining 10-bit communication over GSM. Many modem manufacturers use a 'wireless module' or 'cellular engine' from companies like: - [company_name] (now Centerion) - Wavecom/Sierra Wireless - Sagem - Motorola - Telit - Sony Ericsson Check whether these support 11-bit protocol and how to configure their AT commands accordingly. [product_name] typically requires 8E1 industrial framing (start bit, 8 data bits, EVEN parity, and stop bit), offering basic error detection and correction. Some industrial modems are capable of 11-bit framing (see attached file), though I haven’t personally tested or verified their internal modules. 2) Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Communication Synchronous communication uses extra handshaking lines for the devices to synchronize clocks and coordinate data transmission statuses. Asynchronous methods do not synchronize transfer rates, requiring one side to interpret the flow and timing of bits without explicit coordination. More details can be found in the attached document and further explained through external sources like Wikipedia. Adapter wiring suggests asynchronous communication, though specific AT modem settings may introduce some confusion. See attached documentation for more details. 3) Transparent vs. Non-Transparent Data Transfer Excerpts from a cellular provider (included in the documentation) help explain this further. The Radio Link Protocol (RLP) used in non-transparent mode introduces network-based error correction, which could impact communication reliability with [product_name]. Non-transparent communication employs RLP for enhanced error correction and data integrity, utilizing acknowledgement signals and buffering to ensure an uninterrupted transmission. Transparent data, on the other hand, means no additional GSM-side error correction. Not all cellphones and modems support non-transparent (RLP-based) transmission. Faxing standards (Group 3) use transparent protocols. That’s all for now—please share any further clarifications or experiences.

Hello, sorry for my basic question, but could someone clarify what exactly an open connector is and in which situations I should use it? Thanks in advance.

Did you check the help section for the block? Everything is explained there. Some blocks require the output to be connected even if you don't actually use the output. That's when open connectors are needed. If the output isn't connected, you won't be able to upload the software to the device. For example, with the message block, leaving the output unconnected causes an error when uploading. Connecting the output to an open connector resolves the issue and lets everything work.

Hi [user_name], thanks for your feedback. Let me explain the reason open connectors are required! [product_name] function blocks operate on a platform similar to Java, where each block has multiple inputs and always exactly one output, even if it’s just a message text. Successful execution of a function block requires that all inputs and outputs are defined or terminated. The open connector is used to terminate an output that doesn't need to be connected elsewhere. Outputs, digital markers, and analog flags can also serve as terminators but are best not used, as it wastes valuable programming resources. In simulation mode on a PC, terminations are less critical because the thread environment handles everything. However, on the microcontroller inside the [product_name], missing terminations will prevent download or compilation because the thread environment expects definitions for all outputs. If you run out of open connectors, you can use OR gates in a cascade to have one open connector serve multiple terminations. For analog signals, you can use an analog threshold trigger as a placeholder, with its output tied to an open connector. While it may seem inefficient, this method works. I heard at a recent trade fair that the next [product_name] will offer more open connectors, making things simpler. Happy programming!

Hello, I'm experiencing an issue with the analog threshold trigger during temperature regulation. When I set a shutdown temperature, such as 28°C, the relay doesn't switch off immediately as the temperature nears 28°C. Instead, it starts clicking as if the temperature is fluctuating. This only happens when the temperature slowly rises or falls. If the temperature changes rapidly, there's no problem. I'm using a generic RTD 0-10V converter, with the analog input and measurement range set to -50°C to 100°C, and the analog amplifier configured similarly. When I test with a different converter, the issue doesn't occur and everything works as expected. Is there a way to fix this without having to replace all four converters? I appreciate any responses.

Have you considered setting a hysteresis between the ON and OFF values for the threshold trigger? Please provide your settings so we can take a look.

Hello, thank you for your fast response. I've attached the program and an image showing my setup. The idea is for the electric heating element to warm the water and turn off automatically once the water reaches the target temperature.

If I understand correctly, you want the output Q1 to be ON when the temperature is below 25°C, and OFF when it's above 25°C, right? Here's what I suggest: Set your analog amplifier with Gain: 1.5, Offset: -500, and Decimal places: 1. This gives you a temperature range of -50.0°C to 100.0°C, making temperature control easier. For the threshold trigger, set ON at 250, OFF at 240, with Decimal places: 1. Add a NOT block between the threshold trigger and output Q1. This setup provides a hysteresis of 1.0°C. If the temperature drops below 24.0°C, Q1 switches ON. When it rises above 25.0°C, Q1 switches OFF. If it falls below 24.0°C again, Q1 will turn back ON.

That's exactly what I needed. Now everything works as intended. Thank you for helping to resolve the issue quickly.

I'm attempting to connect [product_name] software with a [product_name] PLC ([article_no]), which is linked to my router. While it connects properly within my LAN, I can't establish a remote connection. I've set up port forwarding (port 10001) to the PLC's IP (192.168.1.90). Although my router gets its IP via DHCP, my PC always uses the same address and I've verified it's accurate. Despite correct settings, each remote attempt produces a 'Cannot access the IP address xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx' error (referring to my router’s public IP). Pinging works when I disable the router's firewall, but even then, the [product_name] software can't connect. Are there alternative steps to try, or does this require a fixed IP address for external access? Thanks for any advice.

After extensive troubleshooting, I found a partial solution. The [product_name] PLC is set with a fixed IP (192.168.1.90), and my PC uses 192.168.1.99. Instead of forwarding port 10001 to the PLC, I forwarded it to my PC, then used rinetd (also available for Windows, see [url]) to reroute from PC to PLC on port 10001. Now, data passes through my router and PC before reaching the PLC, which works. However, I’m unsure why direct router-to-PLC forwarding fails while passing traffic through the PC works. Any insights would be appreciated.

I discovered a simple solution: the gateway address in the PLC was incorrect—it should be set to the router’s IP. After correcting this, everything worked, including remote access via the mobile app.

Hello [user_name], I found this discussion through Google and I'm experiencing the same issue. I can connect to my [product_name] PLC locally (using 192.168.1.121), but can't reach it from the internet. My PLC is connected to a router (LAN IP 192.168.1.1, used as gateway), and I've forwarded port 10001 to the PLC's IP. External access still doesn't work. Could you clarify your settings for both the PLC and the [product_name] software? Do you use internal/external IPs or specify a port in the configuration? Thanks in advance, [user_name].

Hi [user_name], Here are the details: For the [product_name] PLC, set its IP to something below 192.168.1.100 (e.g. 192.168.1.90) to avoid DHCP conflicts, and confirm no other devices use this address. Netmask: 255.255.255.0. Gateway: 192.168.1.1. You can let [product_name] software auto-configure these settings. On the router, forward port 10001 to the PLC's IP. In [product_name] software, go to Tools > Ethernet connections, enter the internal PLC IP, netmask, and gateway. Under peer-to-peer connections, add a new Ethernet connection and configure local (server) TSAP as 02.00, enable server connection, accept all requests, and remote (client) TSAP as 01.00. Don't enable 'keep alive'. Save and upload the program—this overwrites the PLC’s IP settings. For remote internet connections, go to Tools > transfer > Configure Network address, add your router's external IP (find it at whatismyip.com), with the netmask set, but leave the gateway blank. This should enable remote access. Hope this helps!

Hello [user_name], The 0–10 V DC analog inputs on [product_name] or its AM2 expansion module cannot connect directly to a load cell. The device samples and digitizes input signals, providing 10-bit resolution (0–1000 value). Only voltage changes greater than 0.01 V (10 mV) are detected, so very small load cell signals won't be recognized due to insufficient resolution. Load cells typically use a Wheatstone Bridge configuration and require stable temperature for accurate measurement, along with signal amplification. [product_name] does not have a built-in load cell module for this. You may need an external load cell module that balances the bridge and outputs an amplified signal (e.g., 0–10 V, 0–20 mA, or 4–20 mA) proportional to weight. You cannot write to a physical digital input; you are only able to read the state of a physical digital input.

To change the state of Q1, you can: 1. Remove the connection between I1 and Q1. This allows you to control Q1 directly with C#. It's also possible to directly write to M1-M64, provided the left side of the flag is open. 2. Add an OR block between I1 and Q1, and add a network input NI1 to the OR block. This gives you the ability to change the status of Q1 through either I1 or NI1. For NI1, you can use a local VM address (e.g., V0.0, which is the first bit of the DB block). Usable addresses for bits include V0.0-V0.7, V1.0-V1.7 up to V850.0-V850.7. You can also use bytes (VBx), words (VWx), or double words (VDx) for statuses, counters, or integer values, but be sure not to overlap addresses (if using V0.0, avoid using VB0, VW0, or VD0 at the same time). Which client are you using for your C# program? Regards, [user_name]

You need to link the slider value into the program using a free marker or analog network input, and alternate between manual and random using a muxer. The OR logic won’t function as expected; activating one switch blocks the other. It's easier to switch modes with a button and use a pulse relay, where the relay state is shown in the web editor via network output or marker. I’ve integrated these changes into my previous example. Hope this helps. Best regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

I’ve tried several methods but couldn't make the proper connections.

Look at the two instructions marked by blue arrows in the image. To read help on the instruction: hover over for the tooltip, then select the '?' symbol marked by the red arrow. Reviewing each instruction helps beginners understand which program blocks are available.

Thank you for your support. I’ve found the '?' and right-click help tools valuable. I’m trying to use a math formula block before block 001 to set '3' as the base instead of zero, but my attempts aren't working—I end up with values like 32767 by only adding an offset of 1. If I want random analog values between, say, 3 and 6, I should set the random generator block 001 to 0–3 seconds, then add 3. This total is referenced in VM54—is this correct? I'm unsure how to establish these parameter relationships. Your advice is appreciated.

Hello [user_name], The random generator’s time values generate corresponding numerical values. Ten seconds translates to a max value of 1000. To obtain values from 300 to 1000, subtract min from max and add the minimum (offset). In the program, set the random generator to seven seconds (=700 = 1000 max minus 300 min) and add 300 in an arithmetic block (B011). Manual input is also capped at the minimum. If the maximum should be limited to 1000, adjust the math after the slider. Or, if you only want to restrict the random value (not the slider), move B011 as needed. Best regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

Hello [user_name], I've noticed in your example, when running a simulation or deploying on the controller, the value of B005 Random generator is retained and immediately written to AM1 when restarted. It doesn't reset to zero as expected. How can I ensure everything starts from zero?

B005 only sets the interval for the next random value, ensuring a new value for each interval. Thus, the total time of TH+TL of B005 should never be less than TH of B001. The actual randomization occurs in B001. When the controller starts, AQ1 outputs zero. B001 then provides a new random value, so it won’t reset to zero when toggling between slider and random. To implement an on/off function, replace B003’s permanent activation with an input. Best regards, [user_name]

To cover a distance of 4 km, a radio link is needed, but keep in mind that the farther the distance, the lower the bandwidth with typical frequencies. For example, a 2.4 GHz connection typically reaches only 300m, while 869 MHz can reach 3,000m but may not have enough bandwidth for [product_name] or software like [product_name] Soft Comfort. Modbus connections might be an option. Depending on terrain, repeaters may be required, and line-of-sight and weather play a big role. Specialists from Schildknecht have experience assisting with radio link selection. For tank sensors, consider what the tank is made of, the type of liquid, and the maximum fill height. For tanks that don't freeze, tachometers or pressure sensors are suitable; ultrasonic or radar sensors often struggle with condensation. Monitoring tanks that freeze is difficult – pressure sensors may get damaged by ice. From my experience, I often use sensors from brands like Peppler & Fuchs, E&H, IFM, or [company_name]. Kind regards, [user_name]

If mobile service is available at your location, you could use a mobile communication module or interface module for [product_name]. The same hardware can also send SMS notifications. Alternatively, certain modules allow data to be forwarded to AWS cloud dashboards, eliminating the need for a public IP. SMS notifications for power status are also supported. If mobile coverage isn’t available, some Wi-Fi routers permit longer distance connections, though in Europe the range is limited to about 300 meters and in the USA sometimes extends miles. Radio modems have also been used for such distances, but you must comply with local regulations regarding radio transmissions. Power line modems, which use the electrical network, could be another solution, though their effective range may not reach 3,000 meters. Good luck.

How many WORDs are used for the floating point number? One for 'float' or two for 'double'? Float means two WORDs, double means four WORDs. [IMAGE]

You might receive a value, but not every bit pattern is a valid float. For Float, you need at least 2 words (4 bytes); for Double, 4 words (8 bytes). In the Data Table, select VD0 and view it in hexadecimal, also add VD4 and VD8, and for more words, adjust incoming parameters. You can check the pattern or hexadecimal value for floats at [url]. Hi, I've attached a sample Data Log created without an SD card. Logging started at 6:33:00, but the oldest entry available is from 6:38:28. This indicates that older entries are erased as new data is recorded. A new Data Log isn't created until the current log is uploaded from the device. Uploading can only be done through [product_name] software. No, that's not quite right. Data logging started at 6:33:00, and I uploaded the Data Log at 06:41:18 to my PC. However, only the entry from 06:38:28 onwards was available—that means entries from 06:33:00 to 06:38:27 were overwritten. If I had uploaded the Data Log even later (at 06:51:18), then only entries from 06:48:28 onwards would have remained. This illustrates how FIFO memory works: the oldest data is removed first as new data is added.

For digital values, it is best to use pulse signals (similar to button presses, not switches) and latch or pulse relays in [product_name]. For analog values, I have attached some examples. This program.

Ha, ha, ha... that's a good joke. You've misunderstood something. In VM byte 0 (VB0), which you use for the weekday parameterization of the weekly timer, bits V0.0 to V0.7 correspond (V0.0 - V0.7). The weekly timer parameters are persistent and must be; otherwise, the device would lose its settings after a power loss. When you read bits V0.0 and V0.1 via network input in your [product_name] program, they show a high signal if Sunday and Monday were activated, but this is because of parameter retention, not because VM memory is persistent.

Answering three questions points toward the solution: 1) How many local inputs and outputs can the [product_name] base module address? The last two expansion modules blink because the base module supports a maximum of 24 digital inputs and 20 digital outputs. The maximum configuration is the base unit and two expansion modules, for example: 8 inputs (base unit) + 8 inputs + 8 inputs (expansion modules) = 24 inputs. To use more inputs or outputs, you would need an additional base module. Further details about system limits are available in the manual, which can be downloaded from: [url]

You can't use four [product_name] modules on a single [product_name] base unit since it's limited to 24 inputs and 20 outputs. Let me highlight some fundamental points about the current [product_name]: It can handle a max of 24 digital inputs, 20 digital outputs, 8 analog inputs, and 8 analog outputs, achievable only with expansion modules. The basic unit offers 4 analog inputs (0-10V), and if all are used, only 4 digital inputs remain. Expansion modules can add channels as needed, though analog outputs require specific expansion modules. Data logging is possible—up to 20,000 log entries per CSV, with auto file creation, and a cap of 50 files per memory card. Note that deleting files needs removal of the card to a PC, as the software can’t do it directly. SMS capability requires an additional communication module, which can only work with one PLC. Calculating the required expansion modules is a complex task specific to your needs—an overall cost calculation is necessary. Whether this system matches your requirements is up to you to judge.

You’ll encounter limitations with the [product_name] when calculating analog values. The analog inputs feature 10-bit resolution, and values are limited to 15 bits plus sign (-32768 to +32767). Basic arithmetic is supported, but if your sensors operate nonlinearly, special methods are required. When creating custom web pages, presenting decimal values is challenging since this product handles integers only, and workarounds can be complex and inefficient. Depending on your demands, you might want to consider using a [version_no] controller for more advanced processing, or stick with your custom solutions like Arduino if you’re comfortable with C++. Regards, [user_name]

I was unclear whether multiple controllers could be networked together to expand the system’s input and output capacity. Appreciate your reply.

If you intend to control all aquariums, the [product_name] is adequate, and a PC running 24/7 can collect and monitor data via common industrial protocols. Crop your sensors for compatibility in terms of scaling and tolerance with analog inputs. [version_no] controllers cost more but offer better accuracy and floating-point values, supporting complex formulas for nonlinear sensors. Connection to a PC is done over industrial protocols. Review controller specifications for expansion possibilities to accommodate your requirements. If a PC isn’t planned, examine controller or display storage limitations for historical data. For deeper insight into [version_no], consider further resources. Example: Storing 100 integer values per minute requires significant memory over hourly, daily, or weekly periods, especially with floating point data. Regards, [user_name]

The situation is more complex given your nearly hundred inputs of varying types and numerous outputs, including some requiring motor controls. For a project of this magnitude, larger PLCs are advisable; the specific choice depends on your solution strategy. If rooms are nearby, a centralized system using one or two PLCs with expansion modules may suffice, and remote terminal blocks can link panels throughout different areas. Depending on the sensor's output, you might use a pull-up resistor (e.g., 4.7kOhm to 24VDC) so it can operate with [product_name]. PNP sensors are preferred as they need no extra components. Yes, that setup is fine. When the sensor is not triggered, its output is open and the 2.2k resistor pulls input I1 to 24VDC, making I1 HIGH. When the sensor is triggered, the output closes and input I1 goes to 0V (M), making I1 LOW.

You have flexibility in resistor values and can calculate for the following: 1) Low level = NO contact closed; resistor should not exceed the maximum sensor output current (U/I=R, so 24V/0.3A=80 Ohm). 2) High level = NO contact open; the external resistor is in series with the controller's input resistor (~70kOhm), and sufficient voltage is needed for input HIGH. Values between 1kOhm and 10kOhm provide a good margin for both, so nothing will be damaged. Check operation instructions for required low and high levels of the inputs. With a 10kOhm resistor in series with ~70kOhm input, you get about 21V at the input. Regards, [user_name]

Also, consider adding a 'health' bit sourced from the remote panel connection. My intuition points to the remote link as the problem. Placing counters at each critical junction (such as signal inputs to blocks like B021 and B24) and enabling RETENTIVE mode will help narrow down trouble spots. Please update us with your progress. [user_name], I added the M8 flag and additional checks as you advised. After some investigation, I discovered the issue wasn't tied to main power outages tracked by the flags. Hello, I'm using a [product_name] with a communication module in a remote setup and want to receive notifications (SMS/email) if something goes wrong, and monitor the system remotely. I'm considering the [product_name] communication module for this purpose. One critical feature is notifying about power outages, so I'm searching for a 24V power supply with backup (such as supercapacitor or a small battery) that could keep the module running long enough to send an SMS. My plan is to connect a relay's normally open contact (powered by 230V) to a digital input, so when mains power drops the relay opens, input goes low, and an SMS is sent. I assume only a few seconds of backup are needed, but if anyone has experience on how quickly such a solution can trigger notification, please share. As an alternative, I looked at the Advantech ICR 3211B, which features a built-in supercapacitor and can support last-gasp SMS notifications (see [url]). I feel it offers several advantages for a similar price, such as allowing OpenVPN client configuration (making a public IP unnecessary), and deploying custom applications (like Node-red, MQTT, etc). Integrating it with [product_name] would require more work compared to the native module, but switching to a newer [product_name] version with cloud connectivity could make the module sufficient for my needs (mainly SMS and internet, no need for VPN). Any advice is appreciated, thank you!

Hi, Your idea for powering the communication module during power outage to send SMS notifications is feasible. For backup power, options range from batteries and capacitors to a UPS—anything that supplies enough power for the module to complete SMS transmission. Regarding the Advantech device: it should work well with an AWS solution. With NodeRed, you should be able to set up communication with your [product_name] using either S7 or Modbus TCP protocols. If you're familiar with AWS programming, you could also use a generic LTE router with a LAN interface. Notification from AWS upon a [product_name] power failure shouldn't be a problem, because any configured data sent by [product_name] to AWS contains a timestamp. Just monitor this timestamp, and if it doesn't update as expected, it means connectivity is lost. Then trigger SMS or email alerts from AWS as needed. Hope this helps.

Thank you for your response [user_name], We've chosen to use the [product_name] communication module mainly because it's compact and fits easily into the existing cabinet, while the Advantech module was a bit too deep and the placement of its Ethernet ports was problematic. I looked into supercapacitor-based UPS options and found several (see [url], [url], [url]). They're all similarly priced, but feel excessive for our needs. The module requires at most 125mA at 24V and 250mA at 12V; simulations show a 47000uF capacitor could power it for around 3–5 seconds before dropping below 11V. I made a simple charging circuit using two transistors to limit charging current, but our 24V power supply already features current limiting based on its datasheet. Its internal capacitors might provide enough power for a few hundred milliseconds, but given the module's slow startup/shutdown, that's likely insufficient for sending notifications. No field testing yet. All parts for my hardware workaround cost about €20, mostly for the supercap. If it works reliably, I may share the schematics here. I like your idea of monitoring timestamps in Amazon cloud and notifying accordingly, but I prefer to keep things local. Still, I'll explore it alongside my hardware solution. Cheers!

Another concern with the communication module is a vague warning in the manual that left a poor impression after I'd already decided to use it. Does anyone have details about these rare cases mentioned? The manual lacks specifics. I expected industrial-grade reliability for a device in this price range, not behavior akin to a DIY Raspberry Pi setup. Currently, the only way to put the device in safe status is by holding the SET button with a tool for over 5 but less than 10 seconds, or via the web interface—only if someone is present. If this is a real reliability issue, why can't it be set via one of the inputs when mains fails and backup power is available? That would allow an SMS to be sent and the device to enter safe status before losing power. As things stand, this feature is impractical unless preconfigured. Sorry if this reads as a rant—I expected more from [company_name].

Hi, One more thing to mention: The duration you need to power the communication module with emergency backup depends on its configuration. For example, if you set the watchdog time between the module and [product_name] to 10 seconds, you'll need to supply power for at least 10 seconds plus the time needed to send the SMS. Also, ensure the emergency power solution works reliably. The module might draw significantly more current when sending—not unlike earlier GPRS modems—so keep that in mind. Regarding the warning in the manual, I haven't personally come across it. It's probably best to file a support request to [company_name] for detailed clarification. Hope this helps and good luck.

I've set the process image update interval to 10 seconds, but can't find a proper watchdog function in the manual. It seems the module might trigger a diagnostic event on lost communication, but I can't find a way to use it for custom messaging. My plan: a simple relay with a 230V coil driven by mains, and a normally open contact connected to 24V and module input I1. When the mains fails, the relay opens, input I1 goes low, and triggers SMS. I'll definitely verify that my hardware solution lets SMSes go out before installing. The components have arrived, and I plan to test this in the next week.

I stumbled across this old thread and was curious how you resolved the issue. I'm now starting a new project with the new communication interface module from [company_name]. I would have used the older module, but [company_name] never released a North American model. Previously I used an Insys Imon U-300, but since that's 3G only, it won't work after the 3G shutdown. I addressed the power backup by using batteries, though this might be more than you need or take up too much cabinet space. It's inexpensive though. My setup: batteries and charger/power supply at the cabinet bottom; incoming power monitoring relay below.

Hi [user_name]! Glad you found this thread! I never posted an update after solving my issue, so here goes: Batteries weren't an option for me because space was limited in the cabinet (it couldn't even fit the Advantech module, which had more features and built-in backup). I discovered that the existing device's power supply had robust current limiting and handled unlimited capacitive loads per datasheet ([url]). This let me build a supercap circuit with just a diode (I used two 1N4001s in parallel for 2A charging, though that was likely excessive) and a 47mF/40V capacitor. I used a relay with 230V AC coil on mains to signal the module input when power failed. This power supply's own capacitance held output for about a second after loss of mains, enough for one SMS (usually), but I needed to notify at least four numbers. Adding the 47mF capacitor extended backup to ~5s (I'll share a photo next post). That was sufficient for 4–5 SMS, though not emails, which fit my requirements.

Here's an oscilloscope screenshot of the backup supply circuit mentioned earlier: Blue channel = relay to module input I1 Red channel = PCB to module power L+

On the 'sudden disconnection of the power supply' warning I mentioned earlier, I raised an official support ticket with [company_name] in Sweden. They forwarded my query to Germany, and I eventually received a follow-up reply. The Swedish product manager for [product_name] also got in touch and provided a much more detailed answer, assuring me of the reliability of the communication module (and its sibling, which apparently shares the same hardware). They mentioned that in numerous deployments, power cycling wasn't problematic. According to them, the manual could have been clearer or reworded. I haven't checked the latest documentation, so I'm unsure about any updates. After these clarifications, I proceeded with the module, and it's worked without issues since last June.

Thanks for your reply and details. This info could be useful for future projects. For the project I referenced, the client required operation during power failure. The battery backup provides about 2–4 days of runtime, depending on transmission volume. In the new communication module from [company_name], a supercapacitor is included, granting about 30 seconds of run time. It can automatically send SMS notifications on power on and power off. I'm still learning the system; so far, only power on/off SMS works. It won't send emails.

Thanks! Appreciate you sharing. If days of autonomy are needed, then batteries make sense. What exactly is a [company_name] CMI? I'm unfamiliar with that. Edit: Realized you meant the CIM after reading your other posts. It looks interesting, with a supercap and more built-in LAN ports. However, lack of email support and different configuration compared to the previous communication module might be limiting for some requirements. No email notifications is a dealbreaker for my current application.

Yes, it's the [company_name] CIM (not CMI), thanks for the correction. I'm disappointed; the CIM lacks both email capability and onboard I/Os compared to the previous communication module, and it doesn't match the functionality of the Imon U-310 (despite being more expensive once fully equipped). The U-310 could directly manage I/Os and flags by number without address configuration, and could combine inputs with timers/counters to trigger SMS or email. I haven't checked the 2040's current price but believe CIM is even pricier when adding the needed cellular module and antenna accessories. If [company_name] wanted to rush the CIM to market without email support, they should've at least allowed SMS-to-email bypass, which many cellular networks use. Entering an email address instead of a phone number should route SMS to the intended email, but CIM restricts recipient field to numbers only. While I'm not fully satisfied with the CIM, I'm glad at least there's an option for North America. Years ago, it was promised the older module would be released here, but it still hasn't happened.

Hello everyone, To compare constant values (less than 19999) with an analog value efficiently, you can use a block like an "analog threshold trigger". Below are general techniques for testing an analog value Ax against a constant n (which can be zero): A) To test if Ax equals n: Configure the block parameters as GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = n, Threshold OFF = n + 1. For example, if n = 0: ON = 0; OFF = 1. Q output is ON when Ax = 0. B) To check if Ax is greater than n: Set GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = OFF = n. If n = 0: ON = 0; OFF = 0. Q output is ON when Ax > 0. This works as a positive number test. C) To check if Ax is less than n: Set GAIN = -1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = OFF = -n. For n = 0: GAIN = -1.0; ON = 0; OFF = 0. Q output is ON when Ax < 0. This tests for negative values. D) For Ax >= n: Use GAIN = 1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = n, Threshold OFF = n - 1. For n = 2: ON = 2; OFF = 3. Q output is ON when Ax >= 2. E) For Ax <= n: Set GAIN = -1.0, OFFSET = 0; Threshold ON = -n; Threshold OFF = -n - 1. For n = 2: GAIN = -1.0; ON = -2; OFF = -3. Q output is ON when Ax <= 2. With this block, you can also check if an analog value falls inside a range (ON = k1 - 1, OFF = k2, within limits -20000 to 20000). For values or ranges outside this domain, use a "comparator" block in analog mode for direct comparison between two analog values. Guidance for comparing two analog values is available at [url]. Additionally, there is an extended circuit for broader use along with parameter explanations. Please refer to the example circuit "[document]" attached. Best regards, [user_name]

Any suggestions or ideas would be appreciated. I'm struggling to understand why my analog input amplifier blocks, with a -10VDC input on my [product_name] device ([version_no] running the latest firmware and using [version_no] [product_name]), are giving mismatched output values in VRW1 and VRW2. For example, when both the input and amplifier block output show 1000 (full scale), I expect the VRWs to also read 1000, but they read 771 and 768 instead. When the input is zero, the output is also close to zero as expected. It seems like some scaling is happening, but I can't identify why. The same logic on AI3 and AI4 works correctly—1000 in, 1000 out; zero in, zero out. Why are the VR stored words apparently getting scaled or changed? Any ideas? Thanks, [user_name] in New Zealand

Your issue is due to an overlap in VRW address allocation. The memory addressing is byte-based rather than word-based and starts at address 0. When using words (2 bytes each), you need a gap of 2 between addresses—for example, VRW0, VRW2, VRW4, and so on. Incorrect allocation causes data overlap, while correct allocation avoids this issue.

Thank you very much for your help.

This caused certain analog values stored in VRWs to be scaled incorrectly, affecting confidence in data reliability. Another user clarified that correct VRW usage requires word-aligned addressing to prevent overlaps.
user_expectations: The user expects the amplifier block output to be accurately reflected in the corresponding VRW memory location, without any unintended scaling or changes. Consistent and reliable analog data storage across all channels and memory addresses is anticipated.

You should use an analog amplifier with a gain of 0.1 and configure it to show one decimal place. See the attached file for reference.

text:
Hello everyone. I want to load a program from an SD card every time the controller boots. If the SD card is missing during boot, the program shouldn't run. At the same time, the SD card should be copy protected. Is this possible? Thank you.

No, that's not possible. When the controller restarts, it checks for an SD card with a program. If a valid program is found, it checks whether it's different from the one in flash memory. If so, it loads the program from the SD card to flash memory. But once the program is loaded into flash, the SD card can be removed—the device no longer requires it. There is no setting that forces the controller to only operate when the SD card is present.

Hi, You can try the following steps, but ensure you have a backup of the [product_name] Soft Comfort program: - Download the program to the controller. - In the controller's settings, go to the SD card menu and activate copy protection. - Copy the program from the controller to the SD card. - Copy the program back from the SD card to the controller. After removing the SD card, the controller should display 'No program.' Even with the card removed and power cycled, the controller will show 'No program' and won't execute anything. This solution mostly addresses your requirements, but the SD card needs to remain inserted at all times. You could also set a program password. That way, if the SD card is removed and connected to a PC, the program can still be accessed if the password is known. Hope this helps.

Hello [user_name], I followed the instructions, but after removing the SD card and restarting the controller, the program was still available on the device.

Everything works perfectly now. To transfer NQ1 (0.0), NQ2 (1.0), NQ3 (2.0), and NQ4 (3.0) from client to server, it's configured as VB0 (4 Bytes) to VB0 (4 Bytes). No. First, the NI and NQ addresses don't directly align with the V-bit addresses. You can pick a V address for NI1 such as V0.0, V3.7, V800.1, or others via block properties. Second, transferring a V-Byte like VB0 includes the V-Bits V0.0 through V0.7. If you move 4 V-Bytes starting at VB0, then you transfer VB0 to VB3, covering V-Bits V0.0 up to V3.7.

Let me clarify with an example for easier understanding...

Client assignment: NQ1 = V0.0, NQ2 = V0.1, NQ3 = V0.2, NQ4 = V0.3; Server assignment: NI1 = V0.0, NI2 = V0.1, NI3 = V0.2, NI4 = V0.3. Thus, Client VB0 (1 Byte) transfers to Server VB0 (1 Byte). This setup allows 1 Byte to represent up to 8 inputs or outputs—does that sound right?

Yes, 1 Byte equals 8 Bits. The assignment can be customized as needed. For instance: Client assignments could be NQ1 = V0.0, NQ2 = V0.1, NQ3 = V0.2, NQ4 = V0.3, while Server uses NI1 = V0.2, NI2 = V0.1, NI3 = V0.3, NI4 = V0.0. Other arrangements like Client NQ1 = V0.3, NQ2 = V0.0, etc., mapping to corresponding Server addresses, are also possible.

In your example, does it mean Client NQ1 = V0.0 sends data to Server NI4 = V0.0 instead of NI1 = V0.2, since the bits don't match?

If data is generated faster than it can be written, data loss may occur. To prevent this, ensure the enable signal for the data log block is triggered no more frequently than every 500 ms. Without a micro SD card, only 512 bytes can be stored, and excess data is lost. All parameterized values are logged, regardless of whether changes have been made.

For example, the bit that tracks the pool cover position set by the communication module sometimes resets to 0 after a new program is uploaded, even though the value remains 1 on KNX. Is there a better approach for managing the two data points—pool cover position and user input (open/close)—to reliably produce the output signal as in my diagram?

Hello, I'm fairly sure KNX works by sending telegrams based on its configuration. For instance, a KNX button only sends a telegram when pressed. If you download a new program to [product_name], KNX does not transmit a telegram, and previous telegram statuses are reset. Try power cycling [product_name] and the communication module—this could trigger a refresh of the latest KNX telegrams.

Thanks for the clarification and reference image. Does this mean that when [product_name] stops and starts, the flags and VM memory are retained, but when uploading a new diagram and restarting, all flags and VM are reset?

Yes, that's correct.

This makes sense now. I checked the configuration in the communication module and ETS/KNX, and by default the channels aren't set with the ETS update flag. Once I enabled the update flag, when a new diagram is uploaded and [product_name] stops and starts, the communication module sends a read request to the KNX group, and the pool cover sensor responds. With the update flag active, the module writes the received value back to [product_name], keeping it updated.

So, has your issue now been resolved?

This brings up another challenge: Is there any way to store or retain data solely within [product_name]? For instance, the user input (open/close) is saved in variable memory in the diagram. If it is set to OPEN and the pool cover sensor confirms OPEN, but [product_name] is reset for a new program upload, the logic assumes the user input defaults to CLOSED. Since KNX/ETS can't respond as the pool sensor does (it's just a telegram group meant for sending data to [product_name]), this doesn't solve the issue.

After transferring a new program to [product_name], the system performs an absolute cold start, meaning no state is retained. Even latching relays with retentivity set lose their state; they revert to zero after a program transfer and a restart of [product_name].

The documentation indicates that expansion modules must receive power before—or exactly at the same time as—the [product_name] base unit (CPU). Since the [product_name] takes several seconds to boot, both can get power at once, and when the CPU checks for modules, they're already powered. If power is supplied to expansion modules only after the CPU has finished booting up, the communication LEDs will remain red, signaling no connection from the left side. This happens because the CPU didn't detect any expansion modules at startup, so it's not communicating actively. However, after some testing, I found that if the full rack/configuration has been successfully powered on once, it's possible to remove power from expansion modules while the CPU keeps running, and reapply power later—communication resumes to all modules. I tried this setup with a CPU and several expansion modules, all at 24 VDC. This allows the CPU to establish bus communication, and expansion modules reconnect when powered up again. However, please note: 1) This may not work with communication modules (KNX/EIB or AS-i). 2) My tests are only with 24 VDC modules/CPUs—not 230V AC. 3) Unexpected behavior may occur in your running program—the CPU might read changed input states due to switching. 4) Warranty may be affected by repeatedly switching modules like this. 5) [company_name] likely doesn't recommend or approve this method! 6) Do not attempt in explosive environments—there's a risk of sparks when modules power up again. Keep in mind, expansion modules draw their highest current when all relays are activated, or when analog outputs are fully engaged. Good luck with your project!

Hi, this function block amplifies an analog value and outputs it as an analog signal. If you select the block and press F1, a help window will appear with a description of the block and details on how to configure its parameters. Hope this clarifies things. Regards,

[product_name] analog inputs accept standard signals such as 0-10V or 0-20mA. These inputs may come from sensors with different ranges and units, so scaling is required to reflect the actual range of physical signals. Hello, I'm trying to activate a relay on a connected Modbus 30-channel relay module. According to the manual, I need to send the following Modbus TCP command to switch Relay 1 on: 00 00 00 00 00 06 01 05 00 00 FF 00. I want this command sent when DI1 input becomes active. [product_name] only supports signed integers for analog functions. To send the 'on' command for relay 1 on the Waveshare module, transmit the integer value -256. For the 'off' command, use the value 0. Please refer to the attached document.

Thanks for your guidance, but it's not functioning as expected. Why should -256 be sent? Are the Modbus settings configured correctly? I also tried different starting addresses like 1 and 2. Any suggestions?

Keep in mind that [product_name] uses 1-based Modbus addressing, while the Waveshare module uses 0-based addressing. The first address for Waveshare is 0, so accessing HR0 from [product_name] requires HR1 in the connection table. The 'on' command is FF00 (hex), which is equal to 65280 in decimal, and 65280 unsigned represents -256 in signed format.

That explanation makes sense. Should my program work now, or is there another possible mistake?

There might be an overlap in VM memory due to double allocation of VW0.

Based on the byte count, you're referencing a MODBUS TCP frame. The breakdown is as follows: 00 00 (Transaction Identifier, 2 bytes); 00 00 (Protocol Identifier, 2 bytes); 00 06 (Length Field, 2 bytes); 01 (Unit Identifier, 1 byte); 05 (Function Code - 'Write Single Coil', 1 byte); 00 00 (Coil Address, 2 bytes); FF 00 (Coil Value, 2 bytes - turns the coil on). For more details, consult the protocol documentation.

If you use Modbus with [product_name], you don't need to know detailed protocol structures. @[user_name], could you upload your program as a zip file?

@[user_name], I conducted a test with a [product_name] and a Modbus server simulator. Check the attached screen recording.

Here is my program. I suspect something is wrong with the VW addresses. Please see my next post.

It looks promising. Could you send the program? I suspect an issue with the VW addresses. I added a second input, but writing to VW2 also modifies VW1 from 0 to 256. Is it correct to have 2-word lengths in the Modbus table, and should the ID be set to 1?

The Modbus connection table contains these entries: VW0 - 2 Words - HR1 - 2 Words; VW2 - 2 Words - HR3 - 2 Words. The first entry writes VW0 and VW2 to HR1 and HR2, while the second entry writes VW2 and VW4 to HR3 and HR4. Holding Registers and VW variables are both words (16 bits), but HR addressing is word-based while VW is byte-based. For example: HR1, HR2, HR3, HR4... VW0, VW2, VW4, VW6... So the increment for VW addresses should be 2 instead of 1, as in the case for HR.

I made the changes, but it still isn't working. I set the sending interval to 2 seconds. The relay's RXD and TXD indicators light up every 2 seconds, indicating that communication is happening. Is there another way to transmit FF00 instead of -256?

Sounds great ...

I have another question. I want to connect 9 Modbus relay modules, but there are only 8 connectors available. Is there any way to add one more? When I try to configure [product_name] as master, I can't add more entries in the connection table. Any ideas?

No. [product_name] supports up to 16 connections, but only 8 as clients. However, you can route the relay-on commands for the ninth device through one of the first eight.

Hello, I'm having difficulty publishing the processed (amplified) data from my analog sensor setup. My signal flow is: "AI1" -> "Analog Threshold Trigger" -> "Q1". So far, I've only managed to publish data from "AI1" and "Q1". Can anyone advise how to publish the amplified value that appears in the Message Text as "Ax, Amplified"? Thanks!

Hi, 1. Use VM-Mapping via the Tools/VM-mapping menu for your "Analog Threshold Trigger". If you haven't changed the VM address, then you'll find the amplified data in VW0 of the [product_name] VM-Memory. You can verify this in the data table during simulation or online mode. 2. In your cloud data table, set VW0 to be forwarded via MQTT. Hope that helps!

Thank you for explaining this method. I set up the VM-Memory, and now this information is being published. Is my approach correct?

Hi, Your setup isn't correct. The memory within [product_name] is organized by bytes. Your configuration is: VW1 consists of VB1 & VB2, and VW2 consists of VB2 & VB3, which causes overlapping of memory addresses. The [product_name] memory space ranges from address VB0 to VB850. So for VM-Mapping, use VW0, VW2, and VW4, and match these addresses in your cloud data configuration table. Also, you can't write to your current data configuration. You can spot this by looking at the marking in the VM-mapping table. If you want write access, the 'Parameter' column marking should show a paper and pen symbol, not a circle. Please refer to the screenshot. A description of [product_name] memory can be found in the LSC help under "VM". Hope that clarifies things!

Thanks for the explanation. Now it's working perfectly.

Hi! You can physically attach a large number of expansion modules and create a very extended [product_name] configuration; however, the software only supports: - 24 digital inputs (channels, not modules) - 16 digital outputs - 8 analog inputs - 2 analog outputs If you connect the maximum permitted digital I/O modules (for example, 4 digital modules with 8 channels each or 2 with 16 channels, subject to supply voltage), the last 4 digital outputs cannot be controlled via software. This is due to limitations in the expansion bus communication and synchronisation, and changing it would cause older modules to lose compatibility. If you use on-board digital inputs as analog inputs (0..10V) on modules like [product_name] base modules, you can only add a limited number of expansion analog input modules (up to 3 if using 2 on-board analog, up to 2 if using all 4 on-board analog). These can be configured in the software settings. When using on-board digital inputs as analog, you can't use the same input numbers for digital handling in your program, reducing usable digital inputs. If additional modules such as communication or network modules are added, physical digital and analog inputs/outputs need to be available for mapping. As for the label question, the display tells you that certain digital inputs (such as I1, I2, I7, I8) can be used as analog inputs (AI1–AI4) depending on module version. The numbering is designed to maintain compatibility with older designs and programs. Hope this helps clarify things and supports any diagrams or reference material you’ve seen. Cheers, [user_name]

Hello, I have a question regarding analog inputs. As known, input I7 in [product_name] [article_no] can be used as an analog input (0-10V). What happens if more than 10V is supplied to that input? For example, if 24V is connected to I7, does [product_name] treat it as if 10V was supplied, or does it behave differently, mapping 0-24V to the internal value range 0-1000? I want to confirm that anything above 10V is interpreted as 10V, with the internal value capped at 0-1000. Also, can I use I7 and AI1 simultaneously in one program? How does [product_name] handle this scenario?

When using I7 as an analog input (0-10V), the maximum value is 10V, equating to an internal value of 1000. If you connect 24V DC, it's necessary to use resistors so that only 10V reaches the input, with any excess voltage dropped across the resistor. Voltages up to 12V DC are generally not problematic (12VDC would still correspond to a 1000 internal value).

Input terminals can function as either analog or digital, depending on your programming. If AI1 (I7) is set in the analog comparator and 24V DC is connected, the value becomes 1000. Both can be used at the same time—see attached example program. If the analog value passes the digital '1' threshold, the digital path activates; below 10V, the analog path works as expected up to 1000. The voltage level for digital '1' activation varies, but the manual provides a reference value. For [product_name] [version_no] units, digital '1' is typically recognized around ~6V DC. Please refer to the documentation for precise details.

Greetings [user_name], [user_name], and [user_name]! The explanations above are correct. It’s possible to use both analog and digital inputs simultaneously in a program, but it's important to be cautious about their interaction. On a [product_name] [version_no], digital inputs are defined as: signal '0' for voltages below 5V, and signal '1' for voltages above 12V (since it's designed for 24V DC digital inputs). Therefore, an analog signal between 0-24V DC will be mapped internally between 0-1000 while the input remains within the 0-10V (possibly up to 12VDC) range. Around 12V DC, the digital input I7 switches to 'high', but this threshold is not exact—you may need to experiment. Note that analog-capable inputs (I1, I2, I7, and I8) have lower current sensitivity and higher impedance (72 kOhm) compared to other digital inputs. On [product_name] [version_no], digital '1' is recognized above 8.5V DC due to expected digital input ranges of 12-24V DC. The analog signal will be processed within 0-10V, corresponding to 0-1000 internally, and remains fixed at 1000 for signals above 10V DC. The digital input switches at about 12V DC on one model or 8.5V DC on another. This dual-use acts as an analog threshold trigger, with threshold values set at 999 or 849 based on your selected sensor type; see the documentation for details. If you connect an analog signal around 5.7V DC (internal value 571) and then change the input to 12V DC or 24V DC using a switch, the digital input will activate, and the analog value will jump to 1000, which may affect your program logic. Use caution!

A simple approach is to activate a timer (for example, an on-delay timer) using the output of the threshold trigger. Set the timer to measure in 1/100 second intervals, with a maximum delay of 99 seconds, and display the timer's current value on the screen. As long as the output signal stays on for less than 99 seconds, the timer will show the elapsed time while the output is active.

There is a challenge here: [product_name] does not have a built-in stopwatch feature. You can start and stop a timer (like an on-delay) with a threshold, but stopping the timer resets its value to zero, so you only see time while it’s running. What you likely need is a custom stopwatch. There was a solution shared on the German forum (thanks to [user_name]). Please check the attached [document]. You just need to adjust the minimum and maximum values for the analog threshold triggers B016 and B018, and consider when to reset the timer (input I3)—perhaps when pressure drops below 1.5 bar. To use the stopwatch without an analog value, I kept inputs I1 and I2.

I am using [article_no] controller and configured channel 17 as my first analog input (4-20mA). My temperature sensor setup includes a PT100 RTD sensor with a 4-20mA converter, where 4mA represents 0°C and 20mA corresponds to 150°C. The connection between the sensor and controller is correct, and once powered, the sensor always displays 150°C. When checking resistance on the RTD sensor, I read around 109-110 ohms. My question: does the controller with [article_no] only support 0-10VDC analog inputs, or does it also handle 4-20mA? Please share any relevant information.

To clarify: the analog inputs on these base modules accept only 0-10V signals. If you need to process a current signal like 0/4 to 20mA, you should use a 500 ohm resistor to convert it into a voltage signal of 0/2 to 10V.

Thank you for your explanation. The sensor already includes a built-in PT100 RTD to 4-20mA converter.

Could you specify your next question? As previously mentioned, you can achieve a voltage signal by incorporating a 500 ohm resistor with the current signal.

My question is whether the analog input can accept a direct 4-20mA signal.

Did you have difficulty understanding the previous responses? The analog inputs are not compatible with direct 0/4 to 20mA signals.

[article_no] only supports 0-10V for analog inputs (up to four analog channels). If you want to use 0-20mA, 4-20mA, or PT100 signals, you will need additional expansion modules. [url] There are also third-party converters (4-20mA to 0-10V) available.

As mentioned before, using a 500 ohm resistor as a converter works as well.

[url] Here is a practical example: If a 0-10Vdc input is used to measure a 4-20mA signal, Ohm's law applies: R=V/I, where V is voltage and I is current. For 10V and 20mA, the required resistance is 500 ohms. With 20mA through a 500 ohm resistor, there is a 10V drop; with 4mA, it drops 2V. So, a 4-20mA signal across a 500 ohm resistor yields 2-10V. The resistor's tolerance should be 1% or less, preferably 0.1%, to maintain accuracy. Any variation can affect measurement precision. After installing the resistor, check actual readings and adjust your software as necessary. For instance, a 500 ohm resistor might measure 497.5 ohms, resulting in a voltage range of about 1.99 to 9.95V instead of 2 to 10V. Connect the resistor across the voltage input terminals of your data acquisition device, and then connect your 4-20mA signal across the same terminals. As current flows, voltage is created and measured by the system. Ensure you properly ground the power supply if required.

The [product_name] displays "NETWORK ERROR" and "EM BUS ERROR", although no expansion module is present and communication with the [product_name] is operational. Additionally, digital inputs measured with a multimeter read as "1", but the [product_name] itself shows them as "0". I am unable to access the [product_name] program, possibly due to protection. I tried diagnosing the issue using the demo version of [product_name] [product_name] [version_no]; see attached images. Inputs I1 to I6 measure as "1" with a multimeter, but the I/O status shown in the demo software indicates they are "0". This behavior started after the system was disconnected from power for several days (3–4). Does anyone know the root cause?

With the demo version of [product_name] [product_name] you cannot transfer or retrieve programs to or from a [product_name]. You can only create and simulate programs, but online monitoring isn't supported.

Understood. However, the issue persists. The system was functional before the power disconnection. After restoring power, it fails and shows "Network Error" and "EM BUS ERROR".

Could you provide images of the error messages? Have you tried pressing the OK button?

Yes, I've cleared the errors, stopped and restarted the program, but the "NETWORK ERROR" and "EM BUS ERROR" remain. I've attached an image for reference.

Here's another image.

I recommend submitting a Support Request.

Hello. How can I change the state of the softkey through the website? I attempted to add the softkey block to the variable memory configuration table, but was unsuccessful.

Softkeys are not functional within the web editor; they only work on the display or through the operator panel. In the web editor, use a digital value and configure a digital network input in the program. To monitor the softkey status, show the condition of M2 in the web interface.

Does anyone know how to achieve the following function: I have pulse timers setting an M2 flag for time triggering, and I've included a programmable switch to enable or disable this function from the panel level. I've also shared an option from the website.

It's not possible to operate or display a softkey using the extended web server. Softkeys can only be accessed via the display, operator panel, or the device’s simple web server. In the extended web server, treat softkeys as digital values, assign them to a bit in V-memory, and reference this in the program as a digital network input.

That’s how I would address it using the extended web server.

The network input probably doesn't retain its state after a power cycle, right? I would like the parameter to be persistent. I considered using the pulse relay but it's not accessible from the panel. Ideally, I want a binary parameter editable from both the panel and website, with state stored after restart.

By panel, do you mean the device's display?

Yes, either the device display or operator panel.

Here is one possible solution: Use a softkey as a momentary button. Send a V-bit from the web server, which operates as a switch, not a button. In the program, convert the switch function to a push button by matching the digital network output address to the input. Link both outputs (softkey and network input) to an OR block, then connect the OR block's output to a pulse relay's trigger.

There’s still an issue: users at the panel may not know whether the function is enabled or disabled, or whether status is on or off. On the website, you can show the network output connected to the pulse relay to get on/off status.

To show pulse relay status, use the ON-OFF function in a message text displayed on the device.

I can display the pulse relay status (auto/manual mode) in the message text, and place the softkey next to it to switch modes.

From the programming shown earlier, I don't interpret the softkey as a manual/automatic switch but rather as a release function.

The function is implemented as discussed. Simulation works correctly. I’ll do a check on the actual device tomorrow.

It looks good.

Overall, it works. However, changing the parameter from the display can be confusing for users. Beside the text "Change" there's always an off button, and only the mode (auto/manual) is shown to the left. We'll need to clarify this in the user manual.

As I stated previously, to my understanding, the function is a release, not a manual/auto switchover. Has your problem been resolved?

Yes. Thanks for the assistance.

Hi, is there a better solution available now? My setup is similar: I control two rollup motors, automatically (temperature/wind) or manually. I use a software switch to select auto mode. When it’s off, motors are manual; when auto is on, motors respond to sensors. While I can toggle the switch directly on the device, I can't find a clean solution for the web interface. Requirements: changes on either device or web should be reflected on the other, and settings should be preserved across both.

Hello [user_name], welcome to the forum. This can’t be done with a softkey, since the web server only displays its status—it can’t change it. You'll have to find another method.

Hi [user_name], thanks for the welcome and the quick answer. It's unfortunate that there’s no straightforward solution; that would have been very useful. I’ll try to come up with a workaround. Thanks,

One workaround might be possible, but it comes with a drawback: the device setting can be misleading for users. For example: Automatic mode: [ ] Off [x] On. But as far as I understand, there's no solution for this issue. In the display message, I've added the soft switch state (editable) and the XOR state that shows "Manual" (off) or "Auto" (on). I'll upload additional posts with configuration screenshots.

When the software switch (B002) is set to "on," the mode switches to "Auto" as expected.

With B001 still on, if we set V0.0 to 1 (as the only way to get "button presses" from the web), the mode goes to "Manual." But B002 remains "on", which may confuse users with the interface.

If B001 is set to "off," the mode returns to "Auto"—still confusing. Any suggestions for improvement are welcomed. I think the main issue is the soft switch state (B002) can't be changed programmatically. Is there a way around this?

That’s exactly the problem with the softkey. Here's another suggestion: Treat the softkey and the web server bit both as buttons, not switches. Connect both to an OR block, then send the output to the trigger input of a pulse relay.

Good suggestion! I've implemented as recommended, and it seems workable for now. For the softkey used for switching states, it always shows "Off" on the display. Is there a way to change that to "Switch mode" or similar? Thanks for your help!

No, that's not possible. The status texts "ON" and "OFF" are fixed and can't be changed. You'll always see "OFF" since it only shows "ON" for a single cycle.

If you want to upload multiple images or files, combine them in a ZIP archive and attach it.

Hello, that's exactly the solution I was looking for—a device program for two rollup motors with wind and temperature sensors. Could you please share your program?

Reading from the module and the Basis Module also functions as expected. The issue comes when attempting to write to the Basis Module. According to the [document], only the first 128 bytes of the Basis Module's variable memory are accessible for reading and writing. The default VM addresses for flags and outputs are above 800, so they're outside the accessible range. My question: How can I change the default VM addresses to enable writing to the Basis Module? I've already used Tools > Parameter VM Mapping, but it only allows setting VM addresses for amplifiers, thresholders, and counters. Flags and I/O seem to have pre-assigned addresses (referenced in Help > Contents > Parameter VM Mapping). Thanks for your assistance.

Hello, When using a network input, you can specify a V address. Best regards, [user_name]

Thanks for your reply. I've now created a network input at VM0,0 and a network output at VM1,0. When texting, I write "[product_name]=VM1.0,1,BYTE". However, the response is "[product_name]=VM1.0,1,BYTE: No Success". The same happens with VM0,0. It appears that reading or writing to the VM from [product_name] isn't working. Could it be that network I/O marked as "local" cannot be accessed by [product_name]? Is it necessary for the VM to be configured in the Parameter VM Mapping? Thanks again for your help.

Which firmware version does your [product_name] module use?

Hello, You've configured a network input at VM0,0, so you can write to VB0 (a byte, meaning 8 booleans like VM0.0 to VM0.7). You've configured a network output at VM1,0, so you can read VB1 (also 8 booleans from VM1.0 to VM1.7). You might want to try this method. Best regards, [user_name]

The correct syntax for sending via BYTE datatype is: - Password;[product_name]=VM0,1,BYTE for 1-signal - Password;[product_name]=VM0,0,BYTE for 0-signal This example sets the VM bit V0.0 high or low.

Thank you for your response. I'm getting the same result: When I write "[product_name]=VM1,1,BYTE", I receive "[product_name]=VM1,1,BYTE: No Success". Firmware version for [product_name] is V2.1.5. Firmware for [product_name] with article number [article_no] is 1.82.01.

I'm sending "123;[product_name]=VM15,1,BYTE" and the answer is "[product_name]=VM15,1BYTE: No Success". Regarding data types and range of values for reading/writing: To set specific bits, use the appropriate data types. Hello, I'm new to PI controllers and I'm having trouble understanding something. I set up a small test to learn how a PI controller works, with the setpoint at 200 and the direction set to upwards (+). I expected that if the process value goes above 200, my analog output would increase, and if the value drops below 200, the output would decrease. However, I'm seeing the opposite behavior. Can someone clarify this for me?

The PI controller in [product_name] only operates in one direction at a time, so you need to select the appropriate control direction. For upward control direction (Dir = +): If the process value drops below the setpoint, the controller reacts and tries to bring the process value back up to the setpoint. If the process value goes above the setpoint, the controller does not respond. For downward control direction (Dir = -): If the process value exceeds the setpoint, the controller adjusts and tries to bring the process value back down to the setpoint. If the process value is less than the setpoint, the controller does not respond.

Thanks for the explanation, I got the directions mixed up. However, I'm still unclear about your statement regarding the controller not working when the process value exceeds the setpoint for positive direction or falls below for negative direction. Based on my tests and what the internal help says, in the negative direction, if the process value goes below the setpoint, the analog output decreases, and if it goes above, the analog output increases.

The PI controller's output never goes below zero—it ranges from 0 to 1000. For upward control: If the process value is less than the setpoint, the controller gives an output between 0 and 1000. If the process value goes above the setpoint, the output drops to 0. For downward control: If the process value exceeds the setpoint, the output is between 0 and 1000. If the process value is below the setpoint, the output drops to 0. Does this clarify the behavior?

I understand your point. For example, with negative direction, the output ranges only from 0 to 1000. If the process value rises above the setpoint, the output increases. If the process value matches the setpoint again, the output stays at its last value. However, when the process value falls below the setpoint, the output doesn't instantly go to zero; it gradually decreases, and if the process value returns to the setpoint before reaching zero, the output stabilizes at that last value, as far as I know.

Sorry if my previous message didn’t cover all possible output scenarios for every process value. My main intention was to explain the overall principle.

Thanks for the clarification, I was a bit confused.

Hello, if you connect different phases to one input group, [product_name] will briefly operate (milliseconds) before being damaged. It's strongly advised not to connect different phases to the same input group!

Hello all, I appreciate your input—it's been very helpful. Thank you [company_name].

Hello everyone! Not sure if you've found a solution, but here are my suggestions: 1) [product_name] is the only logic module available that can handle inputs from different phases. 2) However, inputs from different phases must be routed to separate input groups. 3) Input group 1 (I1 to I4) should be on the same phase as the supply (L N) on a [product_name] 230RC. 4) One input from the supply phase can be connected to any input in I1..I4. 5) Inputs from another phase should be connected to the next input group (I5..I8). 6) You'll see a gap between group 1 and group 2 on the [product_name] 230RC, which provides potential isolation between the phases (380V). 7) Inputs from a third phase should be connected to an input on an expansion module for proper 380V isolation, with the DM8 230R acting as the third input group. While this configuration may seem inefficient, it's necessary to protect the device and ensure isolation between phases. Hope this helps!

Hello, I have an old program that used internal analog inputs ANAIN1 and 2. Now after adding an [product_name] analog expansion module to my system, the previously available analog inputs are no longer visible, and the first channel for the new module is ANA1. Can anyone explain what might have happened? Regards

It's best if you share more details, like screenshots, so someone can assist you better. Are you saying your previous analog outputs disappeared after adding the module? Did you create a new program in [product_name]? If so, maybe you set the hardware configuration incorrectly, perhaps with zero analog I/O. Please check your I/O settings if you've modified the software.

The addressing of analog inputs for the expansion module depends on several factors. In the configuration file settings, under offline I/O options, you control how many analog inputs are enabled on the base module. By default, two analog inputs are available, addressed as AI1 (I7) and AI2 (I8). The first analog expansion module uses: Channel 1 = AI3 Channel 2 = AI4 If the base module has no analog inputs activated, the expansion takes addresses AI1 and AI2. With two analog inputs enabled on the base, the module starts at AI3 and AI4. If four analog inputs are enabled, the expansion's inputs begin at AI5 and AI6.

[product_name] 24RCE does not include onboard analog inputs. Thus, the addresses for the first analog expansion module will be AI1 and AI2.

Hello [user_name], You are correct, something seems amiss in the old program. I removed the expansion module, but the integrated analog inputs AI1 and AI2 still do not function. I have set the onboard analog input settings to enable 4 AIs—should I do anything else to activate them?

What module type should I use if I need four relays and 24V voltage support? Regards

Simply removing the module may not be enough. First, confirm which version of [product_name] you have and how many analog inputs can be configured. You should also download the configuration to the controller. Start by uploading your project from the controller to your PC and inspecting the current configuration. It’s possible you made a download by accident. Also, consider sharing some screenshots for clarity.

A new ([article_no]) analog expansion module will NOT work with older ([article_no] and earlier) controllers. What is the full type number of your base and expansion modules? You can typically find the type number of your base device below the cursor keys. Depending on the base module, the analog inputs on the expansion module could be AI1 and 2, AI3 and 4, or AI5 and 6. The expansion module requires its own 24VDC power supply. Is the LED indicator on the expansion module green or red? If your base unit displays a standard clock, (if not, press the down cursor several times), then use the left or right cursor keys to view the real input value of the analog inputs. This will show which analog input changes when you connect something to the expansion module, helping you identify the input number.

Could you provide more details, such as the part numbers for your base and expansion modules? Please update this thread if you've achieved your intended result.

The main issue appears to be that the 24RCE model operates on 24V AC/DC. This version does not have analog inputs, so you cannot use them in your program. For analog inputs, you need either the 12-24V DC version (12/24RCE with relay output) or the 24V DC version with transistor output (24CE). Selecting the correct product is easy to overlook—I made this mistake myself once.

You can use analog inputs with the 24RCE by adding an analog expansion module. Note that the analog range for [product_name] is 0-10V DC. At this point, some recommend connecting another [product_name] in series, such as a 12/24RCEO. I'm curious: by connecting another [product_name], are you upgrading the capabilities, or merely extending them? To clarify, certain models have AI capabilities—the program does not recognize this automatically, so manual editing is necessary. In properties, AI settings determine whether you have matching analog inputs (as explained by others), allowing either high/low or 0-10V analog processing. AI functionality typically comes in input pairs; you choose according to your needs. Adding an extension card can complicate things. If you have a card like one for PT1000 sensors and no analog inputs except for PT1000, then set AI to "Enable 0 AIs" in configuration.

I connect a 0-2 V source to the analog input and use an analog amplifier after the input, set for 1-10V sensor, gain of 10, and offset of 0.
