Hello, The analog input shows values from 0 to 1000, which corresponds to a voltage range of 0 to 10V. This means the smallest step you can measure is 10V divided by 1000 digits, which equals 0.01V per digit. No matter how you scale or multiply, the lowest voltage change the system detects on an analog input is 0.01V. Hope this answers your question.

Hello [user_name], Unfortunately, the system can only measure down to 0.01V, and you require 0.001V resolution, so it's not possible to achieve the accuracy you need. If you use a highly accurate amplifier before the input to convert your 1-2V signal into a 0-10V signal, you may get closer. However, the amplifier must be very linear, and the system input itself typically does not perform better than about 0.02V ± 1 bit, and may vary more (there might be documentation about this, but I can't locate it right now). Therefore, achieving a true 0.001V reading is not possible with this setup. I have used a Weidmuller module for a similar task on the system, but the required accuracy was lower than yours.

Welcome to the forum. If the voltage at a digital input is less than 5 VDC, it's detected as a low (0) signal. For voltages above 12 VDC, it's considered a high (1) signal. The highest permissible voltage at an input is 28.8 VDC. The [product_name] base module only evaluates voltage at its inputs—not current. Additionally, on base modules powered by 12 VDC or 24 VDC, four inputs can function as analog inputs (within 0-10 VDC range).

All inputs can handle a maximum of 28.8 VDC between the supply voltage minus (M) and plus terminals, with M set at 0 VDC.

Avoid using input voltages between 5 and 12 VDC. In this range, the input may unpredictably be detected as either a 0 or a 1, so it's not reliable.

Are you certain the sensor is actually a PT type? Try measuring both the temperature and the resistance at the sensor. Comparing the resistance value at the measured temperature against a PT100 table will confirm whether the sensor is truly a PT100.

A PT100 sensor functions as a resistor that changes value based on temperature. The PT sensor you are considering should operate in the -50°C to 400°C range. Note that a sensor labeled 'K' refers to a thermocouple, not a PT sensor, and can't be used directly. For thermocouples, you would require an external transmitter and appropriate compensation wiring.

Thank you for the example, it works well. How did you determine the mapping for virtual words and double words? For instance, Counter 1 is mapped to VD10, VD14, VD18 & VD22. How was this decided? Was there a [document] from [company_name]? Similarly for timers, T002 is mapped to VW26, VW28 & VW30, and T003 to VW32, VW34 & VW36.

The mapping in the VM area is structured by bytes. Bit: Vx.y, where x is the byte number and y is the bit number in the byte. For example, V9.4 is byte 9, bit 4. A byte consists of 8 bits; VB0 covers V0.0 to V0.7. A word is 2 consecutive bytes; VW0 covers VB0 and VB1. A DWord is 2 consecutive words; VD0 covers VW0 and VW2 (VB0 to VB3). The VM area contains 851 bytes, from VB0 to VB850.

Is the assignment sequence 'top down' or 'first in, first out'? Does C0001 start at VD10 because that's the first item read by the controller in the ladder code? If T002 was T001 (and C0001 was C0002), would it start at V10?

No, the addresses can be freely assigned. Just make sure not to duplicate or overlap assignments. For example, if you use bit signals V0.0 - V0.3, do not use VB0, VW0, or VD0 to avoid conflicts.

Hello everyone, Is it possible to connect a [company_name] QAA32 to the analog input of a [product_name] [article_no]? I've attached the datasheet for reference. Thank you.

Hi [user_name], The [product_name] does not natively support NTC sensors, as it lacks resistance measuring analog inputs. The PT100 module measures resistance of a Pt100 temperature sensor, but it uses a bridge circuit to internally calculate the temperature value. You might be able to set up a circuit using an NTC sensor and stable resistors to create a voltage divider, then connect to either an onboard input of a [product_name] 24, 24o, 12/24RC, 12/24RCo, or use an AM2 expansion with analog inputs to get a 0–10 V or 0/4–20 mA signal into the [product_name]. You can then use analog amplifier blocks to scale your values. Direct function curve conversion as described in the datasheet is nearly impossible, so a linear approximation will be necessary with tolerances for increased error. Hope this helps!

Thanks [user_name]!

Hi [user_name], I've developed a simple and inexpensive NTC-to-pulse converter that lets you read temperatures using standard digital inputs on the [product_name]. You can build this module yourself, or purchase an NTC temperature component for about 0.5 EUR. With a digital input counter using a threshold trigger and a gate time of 30 seconds, example readings include: 0°C = 6 pulses, 30°C = 20 pulses, 85°C = 65 pulses, 100°C = 74 pulses, etc. Note, the pulse count is limited as the [product_name] can only detect up to 4Hz frequency at regular digital inputs. I originally designed this converter for monitoring generator temperatures in wind turbines, where analog signals can't be sent reliably over long cables. I've also used it to control water heaters, batteries, and chargers—each digital input can handle a separate temperature sensor. For more details, see [url]. Best regards, [user_name]

I'm trying to adjust the 'connection time' for a weekly timer through a webserver created with [product_name], but it's not working. Adjustments for other timers are straightforward, but the weekly timer is problematic. When I try to set the 'connection time', it appears as a 4-digit hexadecimal value. The switching times for the weekly timer are encoded in BCD format. If you transfer the switch-on time as a word to memory, hours are stored in the left byte and minutes in the right byte. For instance, if the switch-on time is at address VW0, the bits V0.4 to V0.7 represent tens of hours, V0.0 to V0.3 represent ones of hours, V1.4 to V1.7 are tens of minutes, and V1.0 to V1.3 are ones of minutes. Therefore, you need to use the hexadecimal format in [product_name]. Create two separate input/output fields for each byte: one for hours and another for minutes. Hi, Generally, I am aware of three situations where the USB programming cable may not work: 1. Incorrect cable installation (connecting the cable to the PC before installing the driver). Please refer to the [company_name] FAQ to resolve this. 2. Incompatible or outdated driver for the USB cable. Make sure you use the latest version from the [company_name] website. See: [url] 3. The USB driver may assign a high virtual COM port number, or active Bluetooth devices may conflict. Check in the system control panel under device manager, Ports (COM and LPT), and locate the relevant USB-to-UART Bridge. If Bluetooth devices are enabled, up to 10 COM ports may already be assigned. Installing the USB cable after these devices can result in the software scanning all available COM ports, potentially taking a long time or failing to find the correct port. To resolve this: 1. Uninstall the driver for the USB cable. Optionally, remove Bluetooth devices if unnecessary, then reinstall the USB driver. 2. If Bluetooth devices are still needed, try to assign a COM port below the Bluetooth range: Go to device manager and select the correct USB-to-UART Bridge, then open properties, tap the settings, and under advanced, change to a free port number (typically 4 and above, as lower ones may be reserved). After this, open the programming software, go to Tools > Options > Interface and let it search for the correct COM port. These steps should assist. Please note, information about the USB cable's COM port is only available when it's connected to the PC. Hope this helps.

Hello everyone, I'm new to this forum and looking for advice. I have a [product_name] base module ([article_no]) and want to display a fluid level measured by a variable resistance probe (range: 33 ohm to 240 ohm). I also have the [product_name] RTD module for temperature readings and the standard analog module for voltage/current measurements. High precision isn't essential. Which connection method would you recommend? If I use the PLC's 24VDC, I'd need to add a 350 ohm series resistor, resulting in a voltage reading between 2V and 10V and a maximum current of 62mA, consuming about 1.5W continuously. Is this current too much for the PLC? Alternatively, powering the probe with 5VDC and a 220 ohm series resistor would bring consumption down to 0.1W, or even lower if using a 1.2V battery and a 27 ohm resistor (0.025W). Any suggestions? Thank you.

Welcome to the forum. The best approach is to use a probe with a standard 0-10V or 0/4-20mA output. Other methods with your current probe are more of a workaround and less reliable.

You can generally use your proposed method, but the current going to the PLC may not be as you calculated. Most of the current will pass through the external resistors; the analog input of the base module has a high impedance (~70kOhm). With 24V maximum, current would be roughly 0.34mA. Regarding the resistors: the 350 ohm is on +24V, the 33-240 ohm is on 0V, and the junction between them goes to the analog input (ignore the 70kOhm impedance for calculations). Maximum current is 24/(350+33)=62.7mA, minimum is 24/(350+240)=40.7mA. For power calculations: P=I²xR. 0.0627²x33=0.13W, 0.0407²x240=0.4W. For Umax=10V, you need 0.4W. Check your variable resistor specs for suitability. Also confirm power ratings for the fixed resistor. Remember, resistor values can vary with temperature. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you for your input, [user_name]. I'm glad our calculations match. The power you calculated is what dissipates in the probe itself. If you also include the 350 ohm series resistor, the total power is roughly 1.5W. How would you suggest connecting this setup to the [product_name]? Also, what are your thoughts on using a 5VDC supply (instead of the PLC's 24V), or even a 1.2V battery, and linking everything to the 4-20mA analog input? Best regards and stay safe.

As previously described, connect the resistors in series from +24V to 0V: first the 350 ohm, then the 33-240 ohm as a voltage divider, with the junction wired to the analog input (for example I7(AI1)). Reducing voltage does decrease power consumption, but may impact resolution. If probe resistor temperature is an issue, increasing the 350 ohm resistor can help, though it will reduce full measurement resolution. Is the relationship between resistance and fluid level linear or not? Nonlinearity could complicate measurements, and using a spreadsheet to visualize this may help. The [product_name] system only supports basic arithmetic; complex approximations require polynomial functions. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you, [user_name]. I understand the wiring and the trade-off between reduced power and resolution loss by increasing the resistance. I'll consider this topic resolved. Regards to you.

It's recommended to use a dedicated measurement interface and probe designed for liquid level detection. 1. Using DC current may lead to electrical corrosion of the probe. 2. Make sure to install input protection for the PLC to prevent damage from voltage spikes.

Hello everyone, I am attempting to read the date and time from [product_name] using Modbus. According to the [product_name] manual, these are located at VB985...VB990, but I am unable to convert these addresses for Modbus FC3 or FC4 functions. Can someone provide an example? Thank you in advance.

Who is acting as the client and who is the server in your setup? Which [product_name] version are you using?

Hello [user_name], thank you for your assistance. [product_name] FS4 is configured as the server, and the test client is Modbus Tester from Schneider Electric or the PowerHud Modbus tester tool. I've also tried making requests with other PC libraries and tools, but none have worked.

This can be accomplished, but there are limitations. You can access this VM memory area remotely through Modbus, although only by word rather than byte. For this, the holding register function FC3 must be used. You need to read HR492 to HR495. HR492 = VW984 = VB984 + VB985. VB985 contains the year. HR493 = VW986 = VB986 + VB987. VB986 is the month, VB987 is the day. HR494 = VW988 = VB988 + VB989. VB988 stores the hours, VB989 the minutes. HR495 = VW990 = VB990 + VB991. VB990 represents the seconds.

Thank you very much, this solution works perfectly.

Hello [user_name], you are using an incorrect keyword for changing the digital output on the CMR itself. The [product_name]=xxxx command is intended for updating the values stored in the BM variables memory, not for directly controlling CMR outputs. To switch the digital outputs on the CMR, use the following structure and keyword: <password>; OUTPUT=O<1/2>,<1/0>, or <password>; OUTPUT=<signal name>,<1/0>, or <password>; OUTPUT=<signal name>,<constant name>. In your case, the message should be: <password>;OUTPUT=Q1,1. Please make sure not to include spaces in the SMS command. You can refer to the manual on page 184 from the January 2021 English version.

Thank you for your help! I am able to activate the outputs on the CMR, but my goal is to activate the outputs of the BM module via SMS, if that's allowed.

Hello, apologies for the earlier confusion. It's not possible to directly write digital outputs of the BM module. The CMR can only interact with BM by accessing its variables memory. You can read BM variables like DQ and DI, but only to trigger actions at the CMR. To achieve your goal, you need to link your target DQ on the BM module with a network output/input (though I'm not completely certain, it likely needs to be a network output) and assign it to a variable memory signal in the CMR. You can then write that signal at the CMR using your previously mentioned syntax. Hope this clarifies things for you. Best regards.

I am working with a 2-wire PT100 sensor, connecting it to a [product_name] [article_no] model that runs on 12/24V. What is the correct way to wire it to the controller? The AM 2 PT100 module allows direct connection, but when I connect the PT100 directly to the [product_name] at L+ and I7 or I8—and configure the program sensor to PT100—A1/A2 displays 1000. The closest I have come to a successful setup uses a resistor network as a voltage divider: a 560 ohm resistor from M to I7 and the PT100 from I7 to L+. With this, I read 177 at room temperature. My aim is to operate a solar water heater pump. I found and downloaded a program in another thread, so I’m set on the programming side.

Hello [user_name], a caution for your setup! 1) The PT100 sensor is a resistor with a value of 100 ohms at about 0°C, and its resistance changes in a fairly linear way over the temperature range -50...+200°C (exact values can be found online). 2) The AM2 PT100 module from [company_name] uses a bridge circuit with the PT100 as one leg, so resistance changes have a significant impact on the measured value. 3) This is why PT100 modules allow both 2-wire (less precise) and 3-wire (more precise) connections—the 3-wire option makes it possible to compensate for resistance in the wiring by passing known currents and measuring wire resistance, which then gets subtracted. It's been a long time since I last described this process, so my explanation might be a bit fuzzy. 4) If you connect the PT100 sensor as you described, directly to a 0..10 V analog input on a [product_name] [article_no], together with a resistor voltage divider, you need to be careful when choosing the resistor values, their tolerance (temperature stability), and their power rating (in Watts). 5) Standard 1/2 or 1/4 W carbon resistors typically have a tolerance of 5-10%, meaning their value can shift by 5-10% due to temperature changes. So a 560 ohm resistor might vary by up to ±56 ohms, which could mask the PT100's resistance change that represents the process temperature. Actually, it's a pulldown resistor you should be using. Based on the instructions, 24 VDC connects to terminal S0+. S0- goes to the [product_name] input, which is wired internally to M, so you can't use a series resistor as described. Instead, connect a 2.2 kOhm resistor in parallel to the [product_name] input.

Apologies, I used the wrong terminology earlier. I followed your diagram but still didn't receive any pulses, which is why I wanted to calculate the resistance.

If you wire it as I described, the input resistance for the [product_name] doesn't matter. With a 24 VDC supply for the S0 output, the calculation is: 24 VDC / 0.01 A = 2400 Ohm. If you're not getting pulses from the [product_name], the issue lies elsewhere.

Your [product_name] device is in the 192.168.2.x subnet with a gateway of 192.168.2.1, while your WLAN adapter is in 192.168.1.x with a gateway of 192.1.1.x. These network segments aren't compatible. This setup works only if all devices are configured within the same subnet. Your PC currently has three network subnets configured—you need to choose just one subnet for all devices. For instance: - PC network card: 192.168.0.x - WLAN adapter: 192.168.0.y - [product_name] controller: 192.168.0.z

Check your Wi-Fi network’s subnet—the first three segments of its IP address—and use those for your controller settings. All devices must have IP addresses that share the same subnet, with the final segment unique for each device. You can find these values in your mobile phone’s Wi-Fi settings. Example IPs might be 192.168.0.nnn, 192.168.1.nnn, 192.168.178.nnn, or 10.0.0.nnn. PCs, Wi-Fi devices, and network components can only detect each other if they're in the same subnet. Refer to your Wi-Fi router’s DHCP configuration for the current subnet range. Typically, DHCP starts at a specific address (such as 101) and covers a set number of clients (around 50 is common for home use). Assign a static IP to your [product_name] controller within the same subnet but outside the DHCP range (e.g., 080, 081, etc.), to avoid future conflicts. The values do get transferred from one UDF to another.

I could have clarified better—while the values are being transferred, they aren’t being picked up by the up counter. The timer does receive its value, but the up counter doesn’t read its value.

In my current version, there are two settings to choose from. If you simulate, swapping between program 1 and 2 clearly changes the activation time for the 551 UDF outputs—from 120 seconds in program 1 to 5 seconds in program 2. However, for both programs, the counter doesn’t increment to the target value, and instead stops after one cycle. The UDF should count how many times it toggles the outputs, but it only toggles once. This inconsistency contrasts with previous tests where hardcoding the values in the 551 UDF worked flawlessly.

You initially questioned if values would transfer to subsequent UDFs. They do. You didn’t mention that the next UDF (551) isn’t functioning as expected. I can’t quickly test your UDF logic without knowing your design intent. The UDFs lack documentation.

Since the problem wasn’t clear to me, my initial statement was incorrect—sorry about that. The program is still being developed and lacks detailed comments in the UDFs and blocks. Here’s a brief overview of how the right-side UDFs work: The 551 UDF receives start and stop values from the left, has three timers and two counters. The first timer activates the ON cycle output, the second activates the OFF cycle output. When both timers finish the required count—stored in ON and OFF counter blocks—a pause timer runs once. Afterwards, the Cycle Finished output is activated and the UDF is done. To manage timer and counter values externally, I used an analog MUX block based on input state and split time and counter values into two UDFs, due to parameter restrictions. These UDFs reliably pass their values to the main UDF, but this is where issues arise: although the timer correctly receives its value, the up counter within the receiving UDF does not. I’ve tried every adjustment, but the 551 UDF never receives its ON/OFF count value.

No need to apologize, you didn’t trouble me. To clarify: Did you first create the UDF circuit as a regular program, test it, and then copy the relevant blocks into the UDF? If yes, this could be the problem. I’ve encountered similar issues where UDFs don’t function properly after blocks are copied. In my experience, rebuilding the UDF from scratch, following the template rather than copying, resolved it.

Thanks for your suggestion. I’ll try rebuilding the UDF without copying and update you on the outcome.

Looking forward to hearing your results.

After extensive testing, I discovered that a counter within a UDF does not accept values from outside, so it never increments. This seems to be a bug in the [product_name] Soft Comfort software suite. It complicates my project more than anticipated. To explain: when I place a counter both inside and outside a UDF, the external counter works correctly, but the internal one does not.

I created a small example with two UDFs and a program. The attached screen recording shows that the counter in the Counter UDF counts down properly. I think your issue may be setting up down counters (using the LOW block on the Counter Input DIR) but not defining a start value—so it defaults to zero. A counter can’t decrement from zero.

I am getting closer to a solution and noticed the same issue in your example. If I use a clean program and assign the values directly to the counter, it works: the output only turns on when the threshold is reached. But when the counter gets values from another source, the output is HIGH immediately, without waiting for the threshold. I made a sample program—see the counter’s output: it’s ON the entire time when values are sent in, but behaves correctly when hardcoded. Problem identified, but no solution yet.

Second test: same UDFs, but now set to count up. The counter and its output work as they should.

That solved the issue. Didn’t expect that to be the cause. Now the project runs smoothly :) Thanks for everyone’s help.

I did further tests. The counter activates if only the ON parameter is set as a reference. If the OFF parameter is also referenced, it functions as expected. However, if the OFF parameter is less than ON, the OFF value must be at least 1, not zero.

Digital flags store the logical state at their input and pass this value to the output in the following cycle. Flags can be used for remote control, and their state can be set to 0 or 1 remotely when not connected to logic inputs. Remote control is also possible via the internal web server. VM mapping serves a different function and is not related to flags.

Please check the attached file for more details.

With a 4-20 mA signal, only 800 out of the 1000 A/D converter units are usable. The temperature range covers 90°C, so you have: 800 * X = 90, meaning X = 0.1125. To span the 90°C range, multiply the 800 units by 0.1125. However, the analog amplifier only accepts values with up to 2 decimal places, so you could only use 0.11 or 0.12, which would distort the result. Therefore, the scaling is done in two stages: first, multiply by 1.25 to convert 800 units to 1000; then multiply by 0.09 so 1000 units become 90. 1.25 * 0.09 = 0.1125. For a decimal place, set the second amplifier’s gain to 0.9, Min to -300, Max to 600, and OFFSET to -300.

The issue is caused by the limited 10-bit resolution of the analog inputs in [product_name]. The A/D converter turns any input (whether voltage, current, or PT100/1000) into 0–1000 units. The [product_name] expansion sets a temperature range from -50 to 200 °C, so the resolution becomes 0.25°C per unit (250/1000 = 0.25). As [product_name]'s system uses integer values only (not float or real values), decimal places aren't truly processed—it's just for display formatting. Selecting 0.1 resolution for PT100/PT1000 only alters how many decimal places are shown in the message text, not the actual measurable resolution. For resolution 1 with no decimal place selected, the text will show values from -50 to 200 °C, updating by 4 units per 1°C, and the system rounds the value. For 0.1 resolution with one decimal displayed, the text shows -50.0 to 200.0 °C, updating by 1 unit per 0.25°C, but again rounding occurs. Examples: At 0.1 resolution, readings go like 0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, showing jumps of 0.2°C or 0.3°C when the unit changes.

It's helpful to use the simulation feature to better understand how this operates.

A suggestion: The "Average value" block in [product_name] may make the displayed temperature appear smoother, though it doesn't improve measurement precision.

Hello, I am setting up a system to monitor AC current of a 3-phase motor using a current transducer (LEM AT5B). The transducer provides a 0-5V signal output for 0-5A current, which will connect to the [product_name] controller. Since the transducer is self-powered, it doesn’t require an external supply and simply has a ring for the wire and a 0-5V output terminal. My concern is that, due to being self-powered, the output voltage may be too weak unless the analog input of the PLC has a very high impedance; otherwise, the signal might be suppressed. Am I correct in my assumption? The transducer manufacturer specifies a load resistance RL ≥ 1 MΩ, which is quite high.

The analog inputs (0-10V) of the [product_name] controller have input impedance in the range of 72 kΩ to 80 kΩ.

Keep in mind that the sample rate of the analog input isn’t very high. If the sensor is just a core and coil, you might not get reliable readings as-is. For better results, the signal should be rectified and smoothed to DC before connecting it to the analog input of the [product_name] controller. Best, [user_name]

Consider using an AT5B420L model with a 4-20mA output. You can connect it to a [product_name] base module as follows: connect DC24V to one + terminal, the - terminal to a 500 Ohm resistor, which goes to ground. The voltage across the resistor will be between 2 and 10V depending on the current (0-5A). Alternatively, you could use an analog amplifier with a high impedance input, but getting a new sensor may be more cost-effective. Regards, [user_name]

That’s what I was thinking as well—if the DC output is pulsating, measurement accuracy would suffer. I hope these transducers have built-in circuitry to make the output usable for basic PLCs, given their price.

[user_name], how do you decide which connection method to use for the 4-20mA output, since there seem to be two ways?

The final wiring diagram is the correct version for the AT5B420L. The sensor requires a load resistor up to 600 Ohm, so 500 Ohm works. Supply voltage should be 20..30V DC, thus DC24V is suitable. I’d recommend this connection for analog inputs on the base module. If you use an AM2 expansion module, the required resistor is already built-in, so you can use the current output directly. Make sure your base module actually includes analog inputs—there are extra labels on the case if they’re present. For scaling, use an analog amplifier, pick a 4-20mA sensor type, and configure the left side for area definition (e.g. 0..5000 with three decimal places for 0.000 to 5.000A, or no decimal places for 0..5000mA). Regards, [user_name]

Additional info: Under normal operation the voltage across the resistor shouldn’t exceed 10V, so the power loss will be P = U²/R = 0.2W. In worst case, at 24V, it’s about 1.15W. I often use a 499 Ohm resistor rated for 0.6W with 4-20mA sensors, and haven’t had issues over 20 years. Select your resistor based on your risk assessment. Regards, [user_name]

Reviewing the data again, it shows you're getting a DC-RMS signal. The step response time (90% Ipn) is 300ms. So, it’s likely to work with the analog input of the [product_name] controller.

Thank you, this was helpful. I have further details to add: 1) I am reading from a public IP, not a local network. 2) I tested with QModMaster and received correct values, such as 6000 from register 40085, indicating a frequency of 60Hz. 3) The Fronius register map shows values as int16. 4) After using a float/int converter, I received -32768 as the line-to-line voltage from register 40078, and 32767 as the real power from register 40087. I am not sure what the issue is.

It looks like you have overlapping in your VM addresses. Could you share the Modbus register table for the inverter?

I suspect the problem is with the format. I'm attempting to read as uint16, but I'm unsure how to configure this in [product_name].

Your main issue is with overlapping addresses in VM memory. The addressing is based on bytes, not words—a word consists of two bytes. The address of the word is determined by the left byte. For example: VW0 = VB0 + VB1, VW1 = VB1 + VB2, VW2 = VB2 + VB3. As you can see, VW0 and VW1 both use VB1, VW1 and VW2 both use VB2. To avoid overlap, set the addresses of VWs at intervals of two bytes, like VW0, VW2, VW4, etc. The standard analog network input (NAI) is designed for INT16 values (range -32,768 to 32,767), not for UINT16 (range 0 to 65,535). If the value exceeds 32,767, [product_name] interprets it as a negative number.

You’re considering hardware changes so you can manually energize the output relay using an external switch (let me know if I misunderstood). In my opinion, this isn't an ideal solution. Instead, I suggest using a switch with two contacts: one normally open and one normally closed, controlled manually or perhaps with a relay that governs the power to the [product_name]. I've attached a drawing showing this setup. The normally closed contact connects the [product_name]'s output to the controlled device, while the normally open contact connects the power source to the device. The switch toggles between "always powered on" and "power controlled by [product_name]". You can also automate this using a relay that follows the [product_name]'s power status, switching the device to always ON when the [product_name] turns off. Hope this helps. Regards, [user_name]

Dear [user_name], No worries, I don't plan on modifying the hardware of my [product_name]. Your proposed solution is similar to what I had in mind, but my concern is that there will be a brief loss of voltage during switching. Ideally, I want uninterrupted voltage on the output, except when the [product_name] deliberately turns it off. My idea was to place a relay or contact between the phase and the Q1 output (as shown in my drawing), allowing me to turn the switch ON before stopping the [product_name]. I'm confident this works while running and Q1 is on, but I'm unsure what happens if the [product_name] tries to turn off the output while there's still voltage present. Will the relay in Q1 withstand this? Thanks for your helpful response. I look forward to hearing from you or others soon. Best regards, [user_name]

Dear [user_name], I understand your concern. Could you clarify if your [product_name] uses relay or transistor outputs? Also, what is the code or firmware in use? The solution depends on these details. Regards, [user_name]

I'm unsure if you're asking about the programmed code or the device's firmware version, but I assume it's the firmware. If so, I’ll need to provide that information later. You're very active in this forum and I really appreciate your help. Best regards, [user_name]

Dear [user_name], I believe your approach is acceptable. Just ensure that when both paths (via contact and output relay) are supplying power, the resistance drops, leading to higher current through the device. Please check that this current won't exceed safe levels. Regards, [user_name]

I'm new to this forum and have searched here and online but couldn't find a solution to my issue. I have several [article_no] modules and a serial cable, running [product_name] version [version_no]. When I try to connect to the module, I get a message saying "unable to connect to IP address COM1," which seems to be a common error, yet there's no clear fix available. I've tried on two different computers—one with Windows 10 64-bit and another with Windows 7 32-bit—and the result is always the same. The serial port is definitely COM1; there are no other options. From what I understand, you don't need to configure the module to start communication; it should begin once the physical connection via the COM port is established. Is that correct? I'm trying to determine if the problem is related to the connection, the module, or the computer itself. Could it be that the computer isn't allowing [product_name] to access COM1, regardless of whether the module is connected? Or does this message mean that no module is responding to a request sent through the COM port? Any advice or suggestions would be appreciated.

Are you sure your message is about connecting to an IP address? That typically refers to an Ethernet connection. First, make sure to select the [product_name] cable option, then choose the correct COM port for your cable. You can identify the correct COM port using your PC's hardware manager, especially if you're using a USB cable. Regards, [user_name]

This error occurs when trying to reach a [product_name] device via the "[product_name] Cable" option and the selected interface—in this case, COM1—but the device can't be accessed (see attachment). I use a PC with Windows 7, [product_name] V[version_no], and an original serial cable from [company_name]. My PC doesn't have a native serial COM port, so I use a USB-to-RS232 converter with an FTDI chipset. When I plug the converter into a USB port, the PC creates a virtual COM port. Using this virtual COM port, I can successfully connect to my [article_no] module without issues.

Hello, It looks like the converter might be the source of the problem. Try these steps: + Open your system's control panel and go to Device Manager, then expand the COM & LPT section. + Connect your converter to the PC and observe which entry is added. + The correct COM port for your converter will be listed there. After that, start [product_name], try to connect, select the USB cable option, and choose the correct COM port as identified above. Hope this helps.

From my experience, [user_name] is correct. The FTDI chip in a converter often causes issues because Windows updates the driver to the official one, and if you use a USB-to-RS232 converter with a non-original or counterfeit FTDI chip, the updated driver blocks these fake chips. You can search online, such as on Google, for solutions to roll back the driver for non-original FTDI chips. I had a [article_no] device that was reportedly damaged by lightning. There is an unmarked component connected across the power terminals on the rear of the PCB which seems to be shorted—can anyone identify what it is and its value? I don't have a spare one to use for reference. It resembles a capacitor but could also be a MOV or some type of fuse. I can share a picture if needed.

Please upload a clear, focused picture. I'm not familiar with the type of input protection that [product_name] uses, since I haven't disassembled one yet.

After removing the component, the controller powers up without issues. It was a small, unmarked surface-mount part, roughly 1mm square. Once I took it out, it got lost—probably somewhere in the carpet under my desk.

The part is likely a crowbar diode, positioned in parallel across the input to protect against over- or reverse-voltage by shorting. Using the [product_name] without it is possible, but adding a new one will restore the protection.

For all versions rated at 230 Volts, I always add an extra 275MOV directly onto the terminals. In the event of overvoltage, it activates first and blows the fuse. This method works well when the power supply isn't stable, such as when using heavily loaded or misused generators. It's easy to explain to the customer: just reset the fuse; if that doesn't work, replace the 275MOV. These have consistently protected my [product_name] devices. Previously, I saw many burned power supplies from [product_name]. In my home, I use 12 programmable controllers and live in an area prone to lightning strikes. One of my controllers starts the generator during outages (which happen multiple times a year), and thanks to my protection setup, I haven't lost a controller—even after several strikes, although a generator was lost due to a nearby strike.
